This is a law God has placed in every created life: whatever has life will multiply. Cells divide, seeds scatter, dandelion down rides the wind for kilometres. When a life stops multiplying, there are usually only two reasons: either it isn’t mature yet, or it is already sick.

Spiritual life is the same. A church that doesn’t bear children, a believer who never brings anyone along — this isn’t some heinous crime; it is that they haven’t yet grown up, or something somewhere is sick.

Before his ascension the Lord Jesus handed this commission to the church afresh: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

The Greek word for “witness” is martys (μάρτυς), which later became the English “martyr”. Why? Because the believers of the early church discovered that a true witness is not a matter of a few fine words but of proving it with your whole life. The weight of a witness has never lain in eloquence but in the cost.

Multiplying Life Is Not Giving but Making People Long

Here the lesson makes a very important correction, worth chewing over slowly.

What is multiplying life? It is not “I give life to others” — in fact, I have no life to give anyone; life is only in the Son of God.

Rather, it is “I live out life, and make people long for Jesus.”

This distinction is crucial. The first is called selling; the second is called witnessing. The first makes people weary; the second makes people hungry and thirsty.

When people see Jesus in you, they will long to receive this life.

The Lord Jesus said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) Notice, light doesn’t need to shout, “I am light!” Light only needs to shine, and the darkness naturally retreats.

He also said: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:35) Know — not hear it, but recognise it. It is something seen.

Church history has a beautiful example. Acts 11:26 records: “The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.” The name “Christian” means, in the original, “those who belong to Christ, Christ’s followers”, and was very likely first given to them as a nickname by the Gentiles of Antioch. In other words, the name was not self-chosen by the disciples; outsiders saw it in them. They lived so much like Christ that a whole city had to invent a new word to describe them.

Brothers and sisters, what we need today is not Christians who talk better, but Christians who are more like Christ.

Be Imitators of Me, Even as I Also Am of Christ

Paul said something extremely bold: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1)

Some people find this saying proud. In fact it is exactly the opposite. Paul dared to say “imitate me” because he immediately added “even as I also am of Christ” — he is not the goal but a signpost. He is not asking people to look at him, but to follow his line of sight and see Christ.

This is the heart of spiritual parents. True spiritual elders don’t say, “You must listen to me,” but, “Follow me — I am walking towards Christ.”

The psychologist Albert Bandura, in his social learning theory, showed that people learn mainly not through lectures but through observation and imitation. In his famous 1961 “Bobo doll” experiment he found that children who had watched an adult attack an inflatable doll were markedly more likely than the control group to behave aggressively when later left with the doll themselves. This research laid the foundation of “observational learning”, and it reminds us of something sobering: for children, newcomers and seekers, seeing how we act is far more powerful than hearing what we say.

Our families don’t grow up listening to our sermons; they grow up watching how we live.

Paul handed this chain of life on to Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

Count them: there are four generations in this verse — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. The gospel is not a one-generation affair; it is a matter of four generations, forty generations. This is the life of a disciple; this is how life carries on.

Applying the 321 Vision: The 235 Relationships

Kingdom 321 speaks of the 235 relationships, which are the most concrete pathway for multiplying life.

The “2” is a spiritual companion: find a brother or sister who is also pursuing selflessness, and support one another, remind one another and pray for one another. Ecclesiastes says that two are better than one.

The “3” is spiritual parents and spiritual children: you need spiritual parents, and you need to begin having spiritual children — like Paul with Timothy, like Barnabas with Saul.

The “5” is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers” (Ephesians 4:11). God never wants lone rangers; he wants teams.

And the last of the eight stages of changing our mindset is precisely “Multiplication”. If a mindset stops with you, it isn’t finished yet; it must keep being passed on through you.

This is exactly 321’s Goal: establish God’s system. A system is not an organisation but a network of life; it is held up not by institutions but by people, one by one, who live out Christ and are connected together.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set the four key points of this lesson within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations correspond exactly to this lesson’s three needs. Jesus is my role model — this is the benchmark for living out life: Matthew 5:48 says to be perfect as the Father is perfect, and 1 Corinthians 11:1 says to imitate Christ. The Bible is my standard — this is the food for cultivating life: Peter says to long for the pure milk of the Word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — this is the power for growing life: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. What does it mean to live out life? Living out life is letting Jesus truly reign as King in the person that I am — reigning over my time, money, emotions, tongue, family and workplace. What does it mean to multiply life? Multiplying life is letting Jesus receive more glory. The Lord said: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.” (John 15:8)

The Goal: establish God’s system. One person living out Christ is a witness; a group of people living out Christ is a system; a generation living out Christ is revival.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The obstacle to all four key points of this lesson is, in the end, one and the same: “self”. The self-centred life treats salvation as part of its own collection; selflessness lives out salvation as a display of Christ.

Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Paul says: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:5–7) “Emptied himself” is selflessness; the Lord himself is the role model of selflessness.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The four key points of this lesson walk exactly this path: receiving life and living out Christ is life; bearing fruit in the 920 practice is relationships; multiplying life and building the 235 is ministry. The order cannot be reversed; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The first thing this lesson sets out to change is one mindset — salvation is not the finish line but the starting point. If that one mindset changes, your life will change, your daily routine will change, your family relationships will change, and in the end your service will change too.

The shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. From man’s perspective, believing in the Lord is for peace and smooth sailing; from God’s perspective, believing in the Lord is for growing into the stature of Christ. From a temporary perspective, whether or not I read the Bible today makes little difference; from an eternal perspective, each day’s cultivation is sculpting the self that will one day see the Lord face to face.

The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First let the Holy Spirit guide (Spirit), then let the Bible open your eyes (Understanding), then life is shaped (Life), and only then do you enter service (Service), with the glory going to God in the end (God). Many people skip the first three steps and go straight to “Service”, and end up serving themselves dry. This lesson reminds us to return to the order.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take each one deeper, one by one.

Practice 1: Examine your life — am I “receiving life”, or “living life”?

The lesson says: ask yourself every day, did I live out Jesus today?

Information: First know the truth. Today’s lesson is the information — receiving life is only the beginning; living out life is the purpose. Copy Matthew 5:48 onto a small card.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn this information into personal light for you. Pray: “Lord, show me which part of my life I have received but not lived out.”

Conviction: Not just knowing, but truly yielding in your heart. Admit before God: in the past I treated salvation as an insurance policy, not as life.

Implementation: From today, spend three minutes each night before sleep asking three questions. In what did I live out Jesus today? In what did I live out myself today? In what will I entrust myself to him afresh tomorrow?

Evaluation: Every Saturday evening, leaf through the record of the past seven days and see what keeps recurring.

Correction: For the weakness that keeps recurring, ask the Lord for a verse to be your standard for the coming week.

Repetition: Don’t give up because you forgot on day three. Lally’s research tells us that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a habit to become automatic. If you forget, start again — don’t condemn yourself all over again.

Multiplication: After a month, teach this practice to another brother or sister.

Practice 2: Deliberately cultivate habits of life

The lesson says: establish a steady life of prayer, Bible reading and obedience to the Holy Spirit, so that your life is fed.

Information: Spiritual life doesn’t grow naturally; it only grows deliberately. 1 Timothy 4:7 says “Exercise yourself toward godliness” — and that is the word for an athlete’s sweat.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you which root in your life is most short of water. Is it prayer? Bible reading? Or obedience?

Conviction: Admit a fact — in the past it wasn’t that I had no time; it was that I hadn’t put it in my schedule.

Implementation: Set three small, concrete things you can sustain. First, a fixed time — for example, twenty minutes every morning. Second, fixed content — for example, reading one book of the Bible, a chapter at a time, copying out one verse. Third, a fixed response — after reading, write one sentence: “Today, the one thing I will do in obedience to this verse.”

Evaluation: Each week, check how many days you managed — just record it, don’t judge it.

Correction: If you only managed two days in a week, don’t raise the target — lower the threshold. Better ten minutes for seven days than a resolution of an hour kept for zero days.

Repetition: Let it become like brushing your teeth — something that needs no willpower.

Multiplication: Find a companion and report to each other once a week. That is the “2” in 235.

Practice 3: Become a witness — let people see Jesus in me

The lesson says: in the family, the church and the workplace, live out love, humility and obedience, and become a role model for others.

Information: Witness is not selling; it is living out. People are not argued into the kingdom of heaven; they are drawn into it.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to let you see that the hardest person to love near you is the very best practice ground God has given you.

Conviction: Honestly face the question — if they watched my life, would they want to know my Lord?

Implementation: This week, do one thing out of love in your family, one thing out of humility at church, and one thing out of obedience at work. And none of them needs explaining.

Evaluation: At the weekend ask yourself: how many of those three things did I do? As I did them, was my heart willing, or reluctant?

Correction: If it was reluctant, don’t stop doing them; go back to the Lord and ask him to renew your motives as well.

Repetition: Keep it going through the 920 practice. Every person you have a relationship with is your “2”; before them, live out selflessness.

Multiplication: When someone asks you, “How come you’re different from before?” — that is the door opening. At that moment, introduce Jesus to them.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, at the end the lesson gives us a short but powerful gentle reminder: life is not something to possess; it is something to live out.

Receiving life is grace; living out life is response.

Grace comes first; response follows. God never wants us to trade our response for his grace, but neither is he ever content for his grace to stop halfway in us.

When you begin to live out Jesus, your life will never be the same; when many people live out Jesus, revival truly comes.

Revival has never been a special meeting; revival is a group of people beginning to be truly like Jesus. The revival in Antioch began with a group of people who lived like Christ. Today’s revival must begin with you and me too.

So let us make this declaration of faith together: Lord, I don’t only want to receive your life; even more, I want to live out your life. Make me more like you day by day, and let people see you in me, so that I become a witness to life and a blessing.

Let us not only receive life, but live out life, and let life be multiplied.

Let Jesus reign as King within us; let Jesus receive all the glory through us.

That seed which slept for two thousand years sprouted within eight weeks once it went into the soil. Brothers and sisters, the life within you has never lacked power; it lacks only one decision: today, I will place myself in God’s hands.

keyVerses: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)
practices: Deliberately cultivate habits of life
Become a witness — let people see Jesus in me
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
Thank you for giving us your own life — a grace we can never repay.

Lord, forgive us. We have often treated salvation as a collector’s item, put away in a drawer, without letting it be lived out in us. We have life, yet we have not lived out life; we have your name, yet not your likeness.
Lord, we ask you to work in us yourself today. Deal with the “self” within us, so that we can truly say: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Give us a longing heart, to place ourselves every day before your word and your Spirit — to be fed by you, cultivated by you, pruned by you.
And make our lives a blessing to others, so that our families, colleagues and friends see you in us, and so long for you, seek you and receive you.
Lord, we place ourselves in your hands. Reign as King within us; may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48) The original word for “perfect”, teleios, means “having reached the purpose for which one was made; mature”. Think honestly: which area of your life have you “already received, but not yet lived out”? With what specific small thing will you begin to let it be hatched?

Question 2: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1) If someone were watching your life right now, which side of Christ would they be most likely to see in you? And which side of you would be most likely to make them stumble? Name one person you are willing to begin walking alongside with your life, and pray for them.
l115.title: Living Out the Life of Jesus
l115.subtitle: 321 Morning Devotion · Lesson 115 · Subtitle: The Purpose of Receiving Life
l115.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: No One Grows Up “Naturally”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to lesson 116 of 321 Morning Devotion. Our title is “Nurturing Life”, and our subtitle is “The growth of life lies in nurturing life”.

Let me first ask you to picture something. In a hospital nursery there is a row of little cots, and in them lie babies only a few days old. They can do nothing at all. They cannot walk, they cannot talk, they cannot feed themselves. Yet thirty years later, one of them has become a doctor, another a teacher, another a mother, another a preacher.

What happened in between?

Not one baby grew up by “waking up one morning”. In between there were more than ten thousand days: a mother getting up in the middle of the night to feed, a father’s hand steadying the baby walker, one meal after another, one word after another, one fall after another and one lifting-up after another. We often say, “Children just grow up naturally.” In fact, no child in the world grows up naturally. Behind every child who has grown up stands someone who nurtured them, year in and year out.

The twentieth century left us a heartbreaking testimony. After the political upheaval in Romania in 1989, the world saw the state of its orphanages: thousands of babies had beds, blankets and food, but no one held them, no one talked to them, no one answered their cries. Later, the Bucharest Early Intervention Project (from 2000), led by the American researchers Charles Nelson, Charles Zeanah and Nathan Fox, followed these children over many years. They found that children who were merely “kept alive” lagged markedly behind in language, cognition and emotional development, while those placed in foster families, with someone caring for them one to one, improved markedly — and the earlier they were placed, the greater the improvement.

Brothers and sisters, this study states a piercing truth: merely being alive is not the same as growing up. Having food is not the same as being nurtured.

The lesson’s introduction puts it very clearly. Many people long to receive life, and long to live life out, yet they overlook the most crucial process in between — nurturing life.

Without nurture, there is no growth; without growth, there is no living it out.

This is a spiritual law, exactly like the law of nature. A baby who is not fed cannot grow; a sapling that is not tended cannot bear fruit. In the same way, spiritual life also needs to be nurtured.

In church we often hear two kinds of sighing. The first sigh goes: “I’ve believed in the Lord for so many years — why am I still the same old me?” The second goes: “I really want to live out the likeness of Jesus, but I just can’t.” Brothers and sisters, the answer to both sighs usually lies not in “trying harder”, but in “being nurtured”.

In today’s lesson we will look at four things together: first, the key to growth in life is not demands but nurture; second, the environment of life is the spiritual family; third, the food of life is doing God’s will; fourth, nurturing life has five steps — See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do.

May the Holy Spirit, this morning, plant that one word, “nurture”, deep in our hearts.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Pictures
sections.html: The three theme passages of this lesson come from three different books, yet together they make one complete picture: the food of life, the appetite of life, and the environment of life.

sections.heading: 1. The Background to John 4:34
sections.html:
The author of John’s Gospel is John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. Church tradition agrees that this Gospel was written around AD 80 to 90, generally thought to be in Ephesus, for believers scattered in many places, both Jews and Gentiles. John himself states his purpose in writing: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31). “Life” is the theme of the whole of John’s Gospel; the word appears more than thirty times in the book.

Chapter 4 records the Lord Jesus going from Judea to Galilee, and tells us: “He needed to pass through Samaria.” By the custom of the Jews of the day, they would rather take the long way round, east of the Jordan, than set foot in Samaritan territory, for there had been centuries of bitterness between the two peoples. Yet the Lord Jesus “needed” to pass through — and that need was not a need of geography; it was the need of the Father’s will.

The Lord Jesus, weary from the journey, sat down by Jacob’s well outside the town of Sychar. It was about noon. The disciples had gone into the town to buy food. Just then a Samaritan woman came to draw water. The Lord Jesus talked with her, from a bucket of water to living water, from five husbands to true worship, and at last revealed to her that he himself was the Christ. The woman left her water jar and ran back into the town to tell everyone.

The disciples came back with the food they had just bought and urged the Lord Jesus to eat. But he said, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.” The disciples asked one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?” Then the Lord Jesus spoke these stirring words: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34).

Brothers and sisters, notice the contrast. In the disciples’ hands was bread; on the Lord Jesus’ lips was the will of God. The disciples cared about “what to eat”; the Lord Jesus cared about “what to accomplish”. The renewal of that Samaritan woman’s life, a moment before, was to the Lord Jesus a satisfying feast.

In the original, “food” is brōma, real food that goes into the mouth and sustains life — not a snack, not a nibble. “To do” is poieō, meaning “to do, to carry out, to complete”. The Lord Jesus was not saying that the will of God was his topic, or his ideal, or his slogan. He was saying that doing that will was itself the food that sustained his life.

sections.heading: 2. The Background to 1 Peter 2:2
sections.html:
The apostle Peter wrote 1 Peter around AD 62 to 64 from “Babylon” (generally taken as a code name for Rome) to the sojourners scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia. The shadow of Nero’s persecution was closing in, and those who received the letter were Christians living in a foreign land, pushed to the margins and slandered.

In such circumstances Peter did not first teach them how to protect themselves; he first taught them how to grow: “as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow” (1 Peter 2:2). “Long for” is epipotheō in the original, to crave intensely, to yearn earnestly to have; “newborn babies” is artigennēta brephē, infants just born, who can do nothing but look for milk.

There is a spiritual secret in this verse: babies do not grow by “effort”; they grow by “appetite”. Not one baby drinks milk because he has resolved to grow taller. He is simply hungry, simply longing — and so he grows.

sections.heading: 3. The Background to 1 Timothy 3:15
sections.html:
The apostle Paul wrote 1 Timothy around AD 62 to 64 to Timothy, his spiritual son. Timothy had been left in the church at Ephesus, facing the troubles stirred up by false teachers and problems of order in the church. Paul wrote to tell him how to behave in God’s house, and gave a definition of “God’s house”: “which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15).

“House” in the original is oikos, which means not a building but “a household”. “Church” in the original is ekklēsia, “a company of people called out and gathered together”. So Paul is not speaking of a building; he is speaking of a spiritual family with fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, and life flowing among them.

Brothers and sisters, put these three passages side by side and we see God’s complete design for nurturing life: the church is the environment of life, longing is the appetite of life, and doing God’s will is the food of life. Environment, appetite and food — when all three are in place, life will grow. This is the lesson today’s study wants to lead us into.

sections.heading: 1. The Key to Growth in Life: Not Demands, but Nurture
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us first face a place where many people get stuck.

Many people think that “living out life” depends on effort, and that “becoming like Jesus” depends on willpower. So they grit their teeth, draw up plans and make vows: I will not lose my temper; I will read the Bible every day; I will love that person I really don’t want to love.

And the result? The lesson is very honest: the harder they try, the more it hurts; the more they strive, the more they fail.

Why? There is only one reason — they have overlooked “nurturing life”.

The law of the seed: though he doesn’t know how

The Lord Jesus told a parable we often overlook: “God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how. For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear” (Mark 4:26–28).

Notice what this farmer did. He sowed, he slept, he rose, he waited. The one thing he did not do was “pull the shoots up taller”.

Where the Chinese Union Version says the earth brings forth grain “of itself, naturally”, the original word is automatē — the root of the English word “automatic” — meaning “by itself, from within”. The growth of life comes from the inside out; it is not pulled out from the outside.

Mencius, in the chapter Gongsun Chou I, records the story of a man from the state of Song. Thinking his rice shoots were growing too slowly, he pulled each one up a little higher, then went home and said with great satisfaction, “I’m worn out today — I’ve been helping the shoots grow!” His son ran out to the field to look, and every shoot had withered. This is the origin of the Chinese saying “pulling up shoots to help them grow”.

Brothers and sisters, have we done too little of this in our spiritual lives? We don’t nurture, yet we demand results; we don’t water, yet we demand fruit; we don’t let the roots go down, yet we demand that the branches reach out. The lesson says: if we only demand results without the process of nurture, life will wither. This is not a rebuke; it is simply the truth.

Trees without wind fall over

In the 1990s, in Arizona in the United States, there was the famous “Biosphere 2” experiment. Scientists built a huge, sealed glass ecosystem with soil, water, sunlight and all kinds of plants — conditions that looked almost perfect. But the researchers noticed something strange: the trees inside grew fast and tall, yet one after another they toppled over before they reached maturity.

Only later did they understand why — there was no wind inside. In nature, it is by being moved by the wind day after day, shaken by pressure, that trees grow tough “stress wood” where the strain falls, and drive their roots deeper. A tree without wind has height but no resilience.

Brothers and sisters, when God nurtures our lives there is sunlight, and there is wind; there is the supply of grace, and there is everyday training. We often want to grow “without wind”, but God knows that a tree without wind cannot stand.

Once nurture begins, everything changes

The lesson then gives a beautiful promise: when you begin to nurture life, growth becomes natural, change becomes easy, and living it out becomes joy.

This is not feel-good fluff; it is the promise of Scripture. Paul says: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). And again: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

So even the “willing” is God at work within us. Our responsibility is not to manufacture life but to nurture it; not to pull up the shoots but to water them; not to force ourselves to change but to let life grow.

The Lord Jesus put this secret most clearly of all: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch never bears fruit because the branch strains; it bears fruit because it is joined to the vine.

Applying the 321 vision: from relying on the brain and ourselves to relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision reminds us again and again: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain, and you are troubled; rely on the heart, and you are glad.

“Becoming better by my own effort” sounds very spiritual, but in fact it is just another face of the old self’s self-centred life. Self-centred people want to complete even their own sanctification themselves, and even want a share of the glory. The third of the Three Foundations says: the Holy Spirit is my guide. If the Holy Spirit is the guide, then I am not the guide; if the Holy Spirit is the one who makes things grow, then all I do is sow, water and wait.

Paul could not have said it more plainly: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

So the conclusion of the first key point is this: not forcing ourselves to change, but letting life grow. The focus is not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances, but on Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. The Environment of Life: The Spiritual Family
sections.html:
“but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.” (1 Timothy 3:15)

Brothers and sisters, the lesson says: life cannot grow on its own; it must have an environment.

Let us remember this. There is no life in the world that grows up in a vacuum. Fish need water, seeds need soil, babies need a family; spiritual life needs the church.

God’s house is not a meeting place; it is the delivery room and nursery of life

We often think of “church” as an address, a time slot, a meeting. But the word Paul uses is “house” (oikos). What is there in a home? In a home there are parents, brothers and sisters, a dinner table, lamplight, making up after a quarrel, someone getting up in the night to care for you.

When Paul pastored the church in Thessalonica, it was precisely the picture of a family he used: “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8).

Notice that Paul gave two things: the gospel, and his own life. True nurture has never been merely passing on information; it is handing over a life. Today many people receive a great deal of information yet are seldom truly accompanied by anyone, so their knowledge has grown while their life stays where it was.

Paul also says: “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). “Formed” in the original is morphoō, “to form, to shape”, as an unborn child is shaped little by little in the womb into human form. The heart of spiritual parents is a willingness to go through the pains of birth once again, until Christ is formed in someone.

Relationships are a need we were created with, not an optional extra

Since 1938, Harvard University has been conducting a study that is still going on today, the Harvard Study of Adult Development, following the health and happiness of several hundred participants over their whole lives. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has said publicly many times that the clearest finding of this study, which spans more than eighty years, is this: what makes people healthier and happier is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, this echoes exactly what the Bible said long ago: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

The coast redwoods of California are the tallest trees in the world, able to grow to nearly a hundred metres, yet their roots are not deep. How do they stay standing? Because the roots of one redwood interlace and intertwine with the roots of the redwoods beside it, joining into one great mat. When the wind comes, it is not one tree bearing the load; it is the whole forest bearing it.

The lesson is right: leave the spiritual family, and life stops growing. This is not a threat; it is a law of nature. That is why the writer of Hebrews earnestly urges: “Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching” (Hebrews 10:24–25).

Not only being shepherded, but also shepherding others

The lesson then says something extremely important: not only being shepherded, but also learning to shepherd others; in the process of feeding others, your own life will grow faster.

This is exactly what the risen Lord said to Peter on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias: “He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs’” (John 21:15). The Lord did not first ask Peter, “Have you repented?” The Lord asked, “Do you love me?” — and then entrusted the sheep to him. Shepherding others was not Peter’s reward once he had matured; it was the call he received at the very moment he was restored.

In educational psychology there is a phenomenon with an intriguing name, the “protégé effect”. Chase, Chin, Oppezzo and Schwartz of Stanford University (2009) found in their research that when students learn “in order to teach someone else”, they put in more effort and learn more deeply than when they learn “to pass their own exam”. It turns out that those who feed others are fed first themselves.

The Bible said it long ago: “The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself” (Proverbs 11:25).

Applying the 321 vision: 235 relationships and the 920 practice

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely the outworking of “235 relationships” in the 321 vision. Becoming a “2” with someone selfless — that is, a spiritual companion; establishing a “3” — that is, spiritual parents and spiritual children; and going on to become a “5” — that is, spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team, each working alongside the others.

The spiritual family is not an abstract term; it is concrete relationships. Do you have a “2”? Do you have spiritual parents? Do you have spiritual children? This is not a question for the advanced class; it is a basic question of growing in life.

And the “920” practice reminds us: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”. Before each “2”, as we practise living out a selfless (0) life, we will surely bear the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23).

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The spiritual family is the place where life and relationships are nurtured. Paul paints this picture most completely: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love” (Ephesians 4:15–16).

sections.heading: 3. The Food of Life: Doing God’s Will
sections.html:
“Jesus said to them, ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.’” (John 4:34)

Brothers and sisters, if someone asked us, “What is spiritual food?”, most of us would answer at once: reading the Bible, prayer, meeting together.

The lesson says: these are very important, but they are not yet complete.

Food as the Lord Jesus himself defined it

By Jacob’s well the disciples handed the Lord Jesus bread, but he said something they could not understand. He said that his food was to do the will of him who sent him and to accomplish his work.

The Lord Jesus did not say: my food is to study the will of God, to discuss the will of God, to pray about the will of God. What he said was “to do”.

Here is a fork in the road where we easily take the wrong turn. Reading the Bible, praying and meeting together are “putting the food on the table”; doing God’s will is “eating the food, digesting it and absorbing it”. However lavish the dishes on the table, if you don’t eat, you will still starve.

In medicine there is a condition called malabsorption. It’s not that the patient doesn’t eat — he may eat more than anyone — but his gut cannot absorb it, so the nutrients are lost, his weight drops and he grows weaker day by day. Brothers and sisters, spiritual malabsorption is not rare in the church. Some people hear a hundred sermons a year and fill notebook after notebook, yet their lives make no progress at all. It isn’t that the preaching is poor; it’s that nothing is absorbed.

The lesson uses a wonderfully vivid picture: if we only hear the word and do not do it, it is like eating without absorbing.

James says it even more directly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). “Deluding” in the original is paralogizomai, “to deceive yourself with false reasoning”. So the person who only hears and does not do is doing his sums wrong with himself: he thinks that having heard is the same as having received.

The Lord Jesus also says: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock” (Matthew 7:24). The wise man and the foolish man heard the same sermon; the only difference between them was one word: do.

Intention is not the same as action

Psychology has made an honest discovery about this. In a meta-analysis published in Psychological Bulletin, the British researchers Webb and Sheeran (2006) showed that even when experiments succeeded in raising people’s “intention” to act, the change in actual behaviour that followed was only moderate. Researchers call this gap the “intention–behaviour gap”.

In other words, between “I really want to” and “I go and do it” lies a gulf that is all too real.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer is generally credited with a famous saying in The Cost of Discipleship: “Only he who believes is obedient, and only he who is obedient believes.” Faith and obedience are not two things that can be separated; they are two sides of one and the same life.

Doing God’s work is not doing tasks; it is believing in Jesus

But here we must be very careful, so that we don’t hear “doing God’s will” as “doing twice as many tasks”. The lesson deliberately includes a second passage precisely to close off that misunderstanding.

“They said therefore to him, ‘What must we do, that we may work the works of God?’ Jesus answered them, ‘This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.’” (John 6:28–29)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the Lord Jesus’ answer. The crowd asked “what to do”; the Lord Jesus answered “whom to believe”. They wanted a job list; the Lord Jesus gave them a person.

The lesson puts it superbly: doing God’s work is not doing tasks; it is “believing in Jesus”. The more we trust in Jesus, the more our life is fed.

So “doing God’s will” is not yet another performance report, nor cramming our diary full of service. The heart of doing God’s will is this: in every matter, to trust Jesus, obey Jesus and let Jesus reign as King. I no longer ask, “What can I do for God?” I begin to ask, “What does God want to do in me?”

The Lord Jesus himself lived this way. He said: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19). If the Son of God on earth did nothing on his own, who are we to dare to rely on ourselves?

Applying the 321 vision: let Jesus be King, and our perspective changes

Brothers and sisters, of the Two Core Values of the 321 vision, the first is “let Jesus be King”.

“Let Jesus be King” is not a slogan; it is stepping aside for him every day and in everything. The old self, living the self-centred life, wants to decide everything, control everything and score every point for itself; the new self, selfless, lets Jesus reign as King in everything and lets the glory go to Jesus in everything.

When I let Jesus be King, my perspective shifts from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from what is of the world to what is of God. The same matter, seen from a changed perspective, tastes completely different. Caring for your family: from a human perspective it is a burden; from God’s perspective it is a trust. A job: from an earthly perspective it is a way to put food on the table; from a heavenly perspective it is a harvest field.

At the well near Sychar the Lord Jesus’ weariness did not change, and the heat of the day did not change; but one woman’s life was renewed, and that “food” satisfied him. Brothers and sisters, when will you discover that obeying God is actually more joyful than indulging yourself? That will be the moment your life is being fed with real food.

sections.heading: 4. Five Steps for Nurturing Life: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson distils the way to nurture life into five steps, very simple and yet very powerful: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. This is the core cycle of spiritual growth.

Only what is simple can be kept up; and only what is kept up lets life grow.

Step one: See — read God’s word, and let the truth come in through your eyes

“Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.” (Psalm 119:18)

“Seeing” is the entrance. When John bore witness to the message he preached, he said: “That which was from the beginning, that which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, that which we saw, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). Faith has never been speculation plucked out of thin air; it is a revelation with content, one that can be read and searched.

But brothers and sisters, we must be honest: what do our eyes look at every day? How much time do we spend looking at screens, and how much time looking at God’s word?

The American researchers Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011), in a study published in the journal Science, found that when people know information can be looked up on a computer at any time, their memory for the information itself gets worse, while they are more likely to remember “where to find it”. The researchers called this the “Google effect”.

Brothers and sisters, one of the greatest dangers to our spiritual life is that we know where to find God’s word, but we have not let God’s word dwell in us.

So the training for step one is very concrete: every day, open the Bible yourself, look with your own eyes, read it passage by passage — not just the highlights someone else has summarised for you.

Step two: Listen — hear God’s voice, and let the Holy Spirit speak to you

“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17)

“Seeing” is me reading God’s word; “listening” is God speaking to me. These are not the same thing.

The Lord Jesus said: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). Hearing the Lord’s voice is not the experience of a select few at special conferences; it is the instinct of every sheep.

Isaiah describes it very tenderly: “and when you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it’” (Isaiah 30:21).

When the boy Samuel first heard God calling, he did not yet recognise whose voice it was. He ran to Eli three times. Only when Eli taught him how to respond did he say, “Speak; for your servant hears” (1 Samuel 3:10). Brothers and sisters, hearing God’s voice can be learned, and we often need spiritual elders to teach us how to discern it.

The third of the Three Foundations says: the Holy Spirit is my guide. The way the Holy Spirit guides is seldom an earth-shaking clap of thunder; it is that still, small voice, that gentle prompting or unease in your heart. Rely on the heart and you will hear it; rely on the brain and you won’t.

Step three: Think — meditate on God’s word, and let the truth enter your heart

“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.” (Joshua 1:8)

“but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.” (Psalm 1:2–3)

The Hebrew word for “meditate” is hagah, a word also used for the low moaning of a dove and the low growl of a lion. To meditate is to murmur God’s word over and over in your heart, chewing it like a cow chewing the cud, again and again, until the nourishment truly enters the bloodstream.

The German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) was the first to study memory with rigorous methods, and he proposed the famous “forgetting curve”: newly learned material, if not reviewed, is largely lost within a very short time, while spaced, repeated review greatly slows forgetting. Later research (such as the meta-analysis by Cepeda and colleagues published in Psychological Bulletin in 2006) has confirmed again and again that spaced review is far more effective than cramming everything in at once.

Brothers and sisters, meditation is spiritual spaced review. A verse seen in the morning, recalled at midday and chewed over once more in the evening sinks from the head down into the heart.

Paul says: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). What we think about, we become. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Step four: Speak — declare and share, and let the truth come out of your mouth

“But having the same spirit of faith, according to that which is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke.’ We also believe, and therefore we also speak;” (2 Corinthians 4:13)

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21)

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? A passage you have read, you may forget; a passage you have spoken out even once, you will find hard to forget.

Cognitive psychology calls this the “generation effect”. The American researchers Slamecka and Graf (1978) found in their experiments that material people produce themselves is remembered more firmly than material they have passively read. Roediger and Karpicke (2006), in a study published in Psychological Science, also showed that repeatedly “retrieving it and saying it out” leads to longer-lasting memory than repeatedly “reading it again”.

So “speaking” is not a performance; it is drawing the truth up out of your heart and saying it aloud. Speaking to God is called prayer and declaration; speaking to people is called testimony and sharing.

Paul says: “that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). From beginning to end, our faith is meant to be “spoken out”.

The “declaration of faith” section in the lesson is the training for this step. When you open your mouth and say, “Lord, I am willing to nurture the life you have given me,” you are not persuading God; you are letting the truth pass through your mouth and settle into your heart.

Step five: Do — live it out in practice, and let the truth become life

“If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)

The lesson says: only “doing” is true feeding.

This echoes the third key point exactly — the Lord Jesus’ food was to “do” the will of him who sent him.

Lally and colleagues at University College London (Lally et al., 2010), in a study published in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit takes on average sixty-six days, with wide individual differences, ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. This study gives us two reminders: first, don’t imagine you can change yourself in three days; second, don’t imagine you can never change.

The American historian of ideas Will Durant is generally credited, in interpreting Aristotle, with a widely quoted line: “We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.”

Doing the word leads to the next “seeing”; the next seeing brings new listening, new thinking, new speaking, new doing. The lesson says: the more times these five steps go round, the faster life grows.

Brothers and sisters, these five steps are a miniature of the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset”: seeing and listening are “Information” and “Revelation”; thinking is “Conviction”; speaking is putting that conviction into words; doing is “Implementation”. And the cycle itself is “Evaluation, Correction, Repetition”, until “Multiplication” — the life nurtured in you goes on to nurture the life of others.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: Nurturing Life Means Being Built into God’s System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we put today’s four key points back into the framework of 321, we see a bigger picture.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The five steps for nurturing life are exactly how the Three Foundations touch down in daily life. Seeing and thinking let the Bible be my standard; listening lets the Holy Spirit be my guide; doing lets Jesus be my role model. Leave out any one foundation and nurture goes off course: seeing without listening turns into mere knowledge; listening without the Bible turns into illusion; thinking without doing turns into empty talk.

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

This is the very heart of the third key point of this lesson. Doing God’s will is letting Jesus be King; and when my life is nurtured, grows and bears fruit, the glory does not go to me but entirely to God who makes things grow. “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples” (John 15:8).

The Goal is: establish God’s system.

A nurtured life does not stop at itself. It is placed into the spiritual family, built up as a living stone, joined to others, and becomes part of God’s system. “You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5). Notice where Peter says this — immediately after “long for the pure milk”. First fed, then built: the order could not be clearer.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

Brothers and sisters, the obstacle behind the first key point of this lesson, put plainly, is the self-centred life.

Self-centred people want to control even their spiritual growth: I want to make myself better, I want to see my own progress, I want others to see how I’ve changed. So the harder they try, the more it hurts; the more they strive, the more they fail — because they are using their own strength to do what only God can do.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When it comes to nurturing life, “let God be God” means: I sow, I water, I wait, and the growing I leave to God.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan most loves us to do two things: one is to give up, the other is to rely on ourselves. Those who give up stop nurturing; those who rely on themselves wear themselves out until they wither. Both roads lead to the same end. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Brothers and sisters, what we are nurturing is not our own old life but the new life of Christ within us.

Fivefold change and the priority of relationships

321 says: change is fivefold — mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

In today’s lesson, the first thing that has to change is our “mindset”: growth does not come by demands but by nurture; food is not knowledge but doing; life cannot grow up alone but needs the spiritual family.

Once the mindset changes, life begins to change; once life changes, daily living follows — your mornings are different, the words of your mouth are different, the work of your hands is different. When daily living changes, relationships change; and when relationships change, ministry flows out naturally.

So 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

235 relationships and the 920 practice

A nurtured life must enter into relationships: becoming a “2” with someone selfless, spiritual companions who hold each other up; establishing a “3”, having spiritual parents and also becoming spiritual parents to others; and finally becoming a “5”, working alongside one another in a fivefold-ministry team as spiritual comrades.

And in everyday life, practise “920”: every person I am in relationship with is my “2”; before him or her I live out selflessness (0) and bear the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, this is where nurturing life is headed: not that I become impressive, but that Jesus reigns as King in me and through me nurtures the next life, until God’s system is established and what the Lord’s Prayer says comes to pass: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).

sections.heading: 6. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them deeper using the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: Establish a daily rhythm of “nurturing life”

Read the Bible, pray and meditate at a set time every day, so that your life is continually fed.

Information: first settle the time, the place and the reading plan. Which part of the day? Where? Which book? Write it down; don’t just keep it in your head.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes as you read, so that one verse leaps out and becomes God’s word to you for today. “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).

Conviction: copy that verse out and say to yourself: today this word is true for me.

Implementation: carry that verse into today’s schedule and act on it in one specific matter.

Evaluation: in the evening, take three minutes to look back. Where did this word help me today? Where did I forget it again?

Correction: not self-blame, but adjustment. If the time is too early to get up, move it half an hour later; if you’re reading too much to finish, cut it down to ten verses. Only a plan you can keep up is a good plan.

Repetition: forty days in a row. Remember the study by Lally and colleagues (Lally et al., 2010) — a new habit takes on average sixty-six days to become automatic. Don’t pronounce yourself a failure on day five.

Multiplication: find someone and invite them to do the morning devotion with you. Your rhythm will become their rhythm.

Practice two: Deliberately practise “doing the word”

Today, choose at least one thing God has moved you to do and carry it out; don’t stop at knowing.

Information: know how important “doing the word” is — “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

Revelation: notice the prompting in your heart today that is clearest — and that you least want to act on. Usually that one is the very thing God wants.

Conviction: admit that it is not your own idea but God’s reminder.

Implementation: shrink it until it is too small to fail — make a phone call, say a word of apology, send a message of greeting, give a hug, make an offering. Do it today; don’t leave it until tomorrow.

Evaluation: once you have done it, does your heart feel light or heavy? Has joy come?

Correction: if you did it grudgingly, ask yourself whether you did it for people or for the Lord.

Repetition: one thing a day, for a whole month, and you will see a different you.

Multiplication: share your experience of doing the word briefly with your spiritual companion. Your small step will become someone else’s first step.

Practice three: Enter into spiritual relationships

Connect with a spiritual companion and with spiritual parents, and at the same time begin caring for and shepherding others.

Information: be clear about one thing — “Two are better than one” (Ecclesiastes 4:9). Life cannot grow on its own.

Revelation: ask God to show you who is the “2” he has prepared for you, and who are the “lambs” you should shepherd.

Conviction: stop saying, “I’m fine as I am.” Being willing to let others see the real you is humility, not weakness.

Implementation: this week, take the initiative to arrange to pray with a spiritual companion; and at the same time take the initiative to care for a brother or sister who came to faith after you.

Evaluation: in my relationships, do I only want to be served, or am I also willing to serve?

Correction: if you find you are always the one talking, practise listening; if you are always the silent one, practise speaking up.

Repetition: make it fixed, a weekly rhythm, not something you do only when you feel like it.

Multiplication: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). What you have received, pass on; those who are fed must become those who feed others.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please take home this last reminder from the lesson:

Life does not grow up naturally; it grows up by being nurtured.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Let Jesus Grow Up in Me
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we are nearly at the end. The lesson’s closing words say:

The change of a life is not a miracle of a moment, but a nurture that continues.

One of the greatest temptations of our generation is wanting things “instant”. Instant weight loss, instant wealth, instant holiness. But God never does instant; God nurtures. He took four hundred years to nurture a nation, forty years to nurture one Moses, three and a half years to nurture twelve disciples. God has patience to spare, because what he wants is not a performance but a life.

When you begin to nurture life, you will discover: living out Jesus is no longer hard, and being a blessing becomes natural.

Why? Because a life that is truly growing will naturally live out Christ.

No apple tree has to grit its teeth to produce apples. As long as it is healthy and joined to its roots, the fruit comes. In the same way, a life that is fed, nurtured and joined to the Lord day by day does not need to force itself to love — love simply flows out; it does not need to push itself to forgive — forgiveness simply happens.

So this morning I want to extend three invitations to you, brothers and sisters.

First, come back to nurture. Stop only demanding results. Starting today, give your life a set time to be fed.

Second, come back to the spiritual family. Don’t walk alone. Find your “2”, be joined to God’s house, and begin to shepherd someone.

Third, come back to the real food. Every day, in one specific matter, let Jesus reign as King and do his will.

May we be not Christians who try harder, but Christians who are better fed; not busier workers, but branches more closely joined to the Lord. None of the growth belongs to us; all the glory goes to Jesus. For “God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

May Jesus reign as King in us, and may Jesus receive all the glory in our lives.

keyVerses: “Jesus said to them, ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.’” (John 4:34)
“as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow” (1 Peter 2:2)
“but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.” (1 Timothy 3:15)
declarations: Let us declare together:

Lord, I am willing to nurture the life you have given me — not stopping at receiving it, but being continually fed and renewed. Let me see, listen, think, speak and do your word every day, so that your life in me keeps on growing!
practices: Establish a daily rhythm of “nurturing life”
Enter into spiritual relationships
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You have given us life, and you yourself will nurture that life. Forgive us: so often we long to receive and long to live it out, yet refuse to walk the path of nurture; so often we use our own strength to demand that we become better, and the harder we try, the more it hurts; the more we strive, the more we fail.

Lord, today we want to come back before you. Open our eyes, that we may see the wonders of your word; open our ears, that we may hear your still, small voice; guard our hearts, that your word may be meditated on in our hearts day and night; cleanse our mouths, that the truth may be spoken from our lips; strengthen our hands and feet, that we may truly do it.
Place us in the spiritual family, and give us spiritual parents, spiritual companions and spiritual children. Let us not only be shepherded, but also learn to shepherd others.
Lord, may your will be our daily food. May our lives grow day by day in you, bearing the fruit of the Spirit, until Christ is formed in us.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear” (Mark 4:28). Looking back on your journey of faith, have you more often “demanded results” or “nurtured the process”? Give a specific example, and say how you plan to adjust.

“Jesus said to them, ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.’” (John 4:34) Of the five steps — See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do — which is your strongest? Which is your weakest? How will you practise your weakest step this week?
l116.title: Nurturing Life
l116.subtitle: Growth in Life Comes from Nurturing Life
l116.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Why Do We Know So Much, Yet Fail to Live It Out?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin by asking you to be still for thirty seconds and answer one question honestly.

How long have you believed in the Lord? Three years? Ten years? Thirty years? In all that time, how many chapters of the Bible have you read? How many sermons have you heard? How many revival meetings, special conferences and discipleship trainings have you attended? How many recorded sermons are saved on your phone? How many memory verses are copied into your notebook?

Then please answer a second question just as honestly: over these years, how much has your life really changed because of all this?

I once met a brother whose Bible had been thumbed so much that the pages were coming loose, and whose flyleaf was crammed with notes. He could recite whole chapters of Romans, rattle off the theme of every book of the Pentateuch, and explain the features of the seven churches of Revelation with complete fluency. But his wife said to me with red eyes, “Pastor, at church he’s the Bible expert, but at home he doesn’t have one gentle word for me.”

I also met a sister who had been to more than thirty special conferences, and every time she wept in repentance and raised her hand to make a commitment. Yet after more than thirty of them she was still bound by the same bitterness, still unwilling to forgive the person who had hurt her twenty years before. She asked me, “Why, after hearing so many sermons, is my life still the same?”

Brothers and sisters, this is not just the problem of these two people. It is the most common, and the most painful, problem in the church today:

Why do we know so much, yet fail to live it out? Why have we heard so many sermons, yet our lives have not grown?

We often think the problem is that “we haven’t received enough”. So we go and hear more sermons, read more books, attend more meetings, follow more speakers. We keep upping the dose, only to find our lives are like an engine idling — the accelerator pressed to the floor, yet the car stays where it is.

Today’s lesson tells us a truth that cuts deep yet sets us free: the problem is not that we “haven’t received”, but that — we have not gone through the complete process of “nurturing life”.

The growth of life follows a complete process that God has designed. This process has five links, and not one can be missing:

See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do.

Miss any one link and life gets stuck; go through all five and life flows. Today, let’s look together at this process of life that God has designed.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Pillar and Ground of the Truth
sections.html:
Our theme passage today comes from 1 Timothy 3:15.

The writer, the recipient, the time of writing

The author of 1 Timothy is the apostle Paul. The recipient is Timothy — Paul’s spiritual son, a young man whose mother Eunice and grandmother Lois both had sincere faith (2 Timothy 1:5). After his third missionary journey and his release from his first Roman imprisonment, Paul wrote this letter some time between AD 62 and 64. Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus to deal with problems in the church: “As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine” (1 Timothy 1:3).

Ephesus was then the capital of the Roman province of Asia, with a population of about 250,000, one of the most important ports and religious centres in the eastern Mediterranean. In the city stood the Temple of Artemis, counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world and four times the size of the Parthenon in Athens. This city lacked neither religion, nor knowledge, nor philosophical debate — and it was precisely in such a city, one that “knew a bit about everything”, that Paul wrote to tell Timothy: the church is not a lecture hall; the church is God’s household.

The picture of “pillar and ground”

Paul says: “which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15).

“Pillar” in Greek is στῦλος (stylos), a stone column that holds up a roof; “ground” in Greek is ἑδραίωμα (hedraiōma), meaning a firm base, a support. Both are building terms, and both are “load-bearing” elements.

Notice which way this picture runs: it is not the truth holding up the church, but the church holding up the truth. The truth itself will not fall, but if the truth has no people who live it out to carry it, the world cannot see it. The job of a pillar is not to store the roof away, but to lift it up and hold it high, so that everyone in the city can see it.

So truth is not something to be stored away; it is meant to become the foundation of life. It is not something to be put on display; it is meant to be lived out and lifted up.

And let us not forget the very next verse: “Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). The one the pillar holds up is Christ, “revealed in the flesh”. God did not merely write the truth down in a book and leave it at that; God lived the truth out as a person. This is the ultimate “doing” — the Word became flesh.

The context

What is the earlier part of 1 Timothy 3 about? It is about the qualifications of overseers and deacons. Read 3:1–13 and you will find something astonishing: Paul lists a dozen or more qualifications, and only one of them has to do with “whether he can speak” — “apt to teach”. All the rest test “can he live it out?”: without reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, not a drinker, not violent, gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous, one who rules his own house well.

In other words, when God chooses the pillars that carry the truth, he looks not at how much they know but at how much they live out. This is exactly the theme of today’s lesson.

We should also look at the other two theme passages. Matthew 5:48, “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect,” is the conclusion of the section of the Sermon on the Mount about loving your enemies — Jesus does not want us to “understand” being perfect but to “live out” being perfect. In Philippians 4:9, “The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things,” Paul lists all four — learning, receiving, hearing, seeing — and then closes with one phrase: do these things.

Brothers and sisters, this is today’s message. See, Listen, Think, Speak — all of them point towards the same exit: Do.

sections.heading: 3. The Key to a Changed Life: The Complete Spiritual Cycle
sections.html:
Scripture

“which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.” (1 Timothy 3:15)

“Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart, for I am called by your name, Yahweh, God of Armies.” (Jeremiah 15:16)

Life is changed not by “knowing” but by “being fed”

Brothers and sisters, think about this: how does a baby grow?

Not because he has studied nutrition, not because he has memorised the food pyramid, and not because he can name every vitamin. A baby grows for one reason only — he is fed, and he really swallows the milk, digests it and absorbs it.

Spiritual life is the same. Jeremiah puts it beautifully: “Your words were found, and I ate them” (Jeremiah 15:16). Notice that the verb he uses is not “read”, not “study”, but “eat”. When the Lord Jesus was tempted, he too quoted Deuteronomy: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth” (Matthew 4:4).

God’s word is food. Food set out on the table does not satisfy anyone; only food taken into the body satisfies.

Five links, three stages

See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do — these five actions actually form three stages:

The first stage is “taking in”: seeing and listening. This is bringing the food in.

The second stage is “digesting”: thinking and speaking. This is breaking the food down into nutrients the body can use.

The third stage is “absorbing”: doing. This is letting the nutrients truly enter the bloodstream and the bones and become part of you.

Let’s look at them one by one; for every link, the Bible has clear teaching.

“See” — John 5:19: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” Jesus’ own ministry began with “seeing”. Paul also says: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). What you look at, you become.

“Listen” — Luke 8:18: “Be careful therefore how you hear.” Notice the Lord did not say “be careful what you hear” but “be careful how you hear”. The Hebrew for “hear” is שָׁמַע (shāma‘), a word that carries both meanings, “to hear” and “to obey”. The Shema prayer, which Israelites recite every day, begins with this word: “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). In Hebrew thinking, hearing without obeying is not “hearing” at all.

“Think” — Joshua 1:8: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it.” The Hebrew for “meditate” is הָגָה (hāgâ), whose basic meaning is “to murmur in a low voice, to mutter over and over”; the same word is used for the low growl in a lion’s throat as it holds its prey (Isaiah 31:4). Meditation is not zoning out with an empty mind; it is clamping on to God’s word the way a lion clamps on to its prey, turning it over and over until you have chewed the flavour out of it.

“Speak” — Romans 10:10: “For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.” The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). Speaking squeezes out what is inside; only when you put a truth into words do you find out whether you have actually understood it.

“Do” — James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

Five links, one lifeline. Seeing and listening bring the truth in; thinking and speaking chew the truth up; doing sends the truth into the bloodstream.

Stop at the early links, and life becomes “malnourished”

There is a phenomenon in modern medicine that fits this remarkably well. The World Health Organization calls micronutrient deficiency “hidden hunger”. People suffering from it are not thin, nor are they hungry; they eat three meals a day and may even look well fed. But because their bodies lack key nutrients such as iron, iodine and vitamin A, their immunity is low, their development is delayed and their eyesight is damaged. Reports from the World Health Organization and UNICEF indicate that more than two billion people worldwide are affected by micronutrient deficiency.

Brothers and sisters, there is “hidden hunger” in the church too. Such believers never miss a meeting, never fall behind in giving, know the hymns and can recite the memory verses; they look “spiritually very well fed”. But because the truth has never gone the whole way into their lives, they fall down the moment trials come, turn bitter the moment someone offends them, and panic the moment they suffer loss. It isn’t that they haven’t eaten; it’s that they haven’t absorbed.

The writer of Hebrews diagnosed this disease long ago: “For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food” (Hebrews 5:12). Then he names the cause: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14). “Exercised” in Greek is γυμνάζω (gymnazō), meaning “gymnastic training”; the English word “gymnasium” comes from this very word. Spiritual maturity is not something you hear your way into; it is something you train your way into.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
In the 321 vision we speak of “fivefold change”: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Have you noticed? This fivefold change corresponds exactly to the complete cycle of See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. Seeing and listening bring in new information, thinking renews our mindset, speaking confirms the new mindset, doing truly turns our life around, and in the end there flows out new daily living, new relationships and new ministry.

Put the other way round: why does so many people’s spiritual life get stuck? Because they get only as far as the first level and stop. They collect a great pile of mindsets, yet their life doesn’t move an inch. That isn’t called change; that’s called hoarding.

321 also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you are troubled, rely on the heart and you are glad. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The destination of See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do is not one more folder in our heads, but a little more of the likeness of Christ in our hearts.

sections.heading: 4. A Picture of Spiritual Growth: How a Meal Is Eaten
sections.html:
Scripture

“The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.” (Philippians 4:9)

Buying the food, cooking it, eating it

Brothers and sisters, let me use a picture everyone understands to make these five links clear.

Seeing and listening are “buying the food”. You walk into the market, pick out the freshest greens and the best fish, and carry home two big bags full.
