Thinking and speaking are “cooking the food”. You wash, you chop, you season, you put it in the pan, and the aroma fills the whole kitchen.

Doing is “eating the food”. You pick it up with your chopsticks, put it in your mouth, chew it, swallow it, and let it go into your stomach and your bloodstream until it becomes your own flesh and bone.

A very simple picture, yet it hides a truth that cuts deep. Let’s look at three situations.

The first: only buying the food

There is a kind of person who only sees and listens. He buys food every day and his fridge is crammed full, yet he never cooks a meal.

He has plenty of knowledge, but no life. His bookshelf is full of spiritual books, his phone is full of sermons, his notes are neat and tidy — and then what? The food in the fridge rots day by day, and he goes hungrier day by day.

That sounds absurd, but psychology gives us a very sobering figure. The nineteenth-century German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, in his work On Memory, published in 1885, used himself as the subject of his experiments and recorded the famous “forgetting curve”: without any review or application, within just one day of learning something a person forgets more than half of it, and the forgetting is fastest in the first few hours.

Brothers and sisters, what does that mean? It means that the wonderful sermon you heard on Sunday — if you don’t think about it, speak it or do it — by Tuesday it has most likely gone from you. You think you bought the food, but in fact it fell out of the bag on the way home.

The Lord Jesus told us long ago how such a person ends up: “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand” (Matthew 7:26). Notice: this man did “hear”. It wasn’t that he didn’t buy the food; he bought the food and starved to death in his own kitchen.

The second: buying the food and cooking it

The second kind of person goes a step further: he sees, he listens, he thinks, and he speaks too. He buys the food and he cooks it, and the whole house is filled with a wonderful aroma — but he doesn’t eat it.

This kind of person can share, can teach, can explain the truth with complete fluency, can lead deep discussions in a small group, can move people to tears from the pulpit. But he has not lived it out, and so his life is still unchanged.

There is a passage in Ezekiel that sends a chill down the spine. God said to the prophet Ezekiel: “They come to you as the people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear your words, but don’t do them; for with their mouth they show much love, but their heart goes after their gain. Behold, you are to them as a very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument; for they hear your words, but they don’t do them” (Ezekiel 33:31–32).

“A very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument” — they enjoyed God’s word like a concert. When it was over they applauded and cheered; out the door they went, and life carried on as before.

Brothers and sisters, aren’t we often just the same today? After a good sermon we say, “That was so good,” “So moving,” “Amen” — and then we go home and carry on treating our spouse the way we always have, carry on with the same attitude to money, carry on wearing the same face towards the person we don’t like. The food is cooked and smells delicious, and we haven’t taken a single bite.

The third: buying the food, cooking it and eating it too

The third kind of person goes the whole way. He sees, he listens, he thinks, he speaks, he does. He buys the food, cooks it, and eats it too.

And so the truth enters his life, and his life truly grows.

Physiologically, absorption is far more intricate than we imagine. The inner wall of the human small intestine is covered with folds, villi and microvilli, which multiply its absorbing surface to an astonishing degree. According to a measurement study by Helander and Fändriks published in the Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology in 2014, the absorptive surface of the adult small intestine is about thirty square metres — roughly half a badminton court. God designed the human body with an interface the size of half a badminton court for one purpose alone — to turn food into you.

Brothers and sisters, God has designed just such an interface in your life too, and it is called “doing”. Doing is the moment the truth enters your bloodstream.

The Lord Jesus said: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock” (Matthew 7:24). Notice: the wise man and the foolish man heard the same sermon and met the same storm; the only difference was one thing — doing.

The key is not how much you know, but how much you live out

The great German writer Goethe wrote in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years: “Knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do.”

And the German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer put it even more sharply in The Cost of Discipleship: “Only he who believes is obedient, and only he who is obedient believes.” When he wrote these words, he was walking a road of obedience that would take him to the gallows. On 9 April 1945 he was martyred in Flossenbürg concentration camp, only thirty-nine years old. He did not just cook the word until it smelled good for others; he ate it himself and digested it with his life.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 Path of Serving is: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God — the Holy Spirit is my guide (Spirit), the Bible is my standard (Understanding), Jesus is my role model (Life), let Jesus be King (Service), let Jesus receive all the glory (God).

You see, this path also runs from “receiving” to “living out”, and finally gives the glory to God. Stop at “Understanding”, and you have only bought the food and cooked it; only when you reach “Life” and “Service” have you really eaten it.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people have the order reversed — ministry first, then relationships, and life only as an afterthought. The result is “a lifetime spent cooking for others, while starving to death in the kitchen”. Brothers and sisters, remember: people matter more than tasks, and life matters more than ministry.

sections.heading: 5. Why Do So Many People Fail to Grow?
sections.html:
Scripture

“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

“For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did, but the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.” (Hebrews 4:2)

Two common stopping points

Why do so many people fail to grow? The answer is actually very simple: they have stopped. And they usually stop in one of two places.

The first stopping point is at “seeing” and “listening”. These people are great at hearing sermons. Wherever there is a special conference, they rush there; whichever speaker is popular, they listen to him. They have a collector’s passion for truth, but no heart to practise it.

The second stopping point is at “speaking”. These people are great at sharing. In the small group they talk the most, in the prayer meeting they pray the longest, and they have an answer for everyone else’s problems. But when it comes to their own lives, not one of those answers gets used.

Great at hearing sermons, great at sharing, but not doing the word — a life like that is spiritual malnutrition.

“Mixed”: one crucial word

Hebrews 4:2 gives us the most precise diagnosis: “the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.”

“Mixed” in Greek is συγκεράννυμι (synkerannymi), which originally means to pour two liquids together and stir them until they are thoroughly blended — like mixing wine, like making a soup — so blended that you can no longer tell them apart.

Brothers and sisters, this word tells us that once the word has entered you, it must be stirred together with your faith, stirred together with your real daily life; otherwise it floats on top, like oil on water — visible, but unable to get in.

That is exactly what happened to the generation of Israelites who came out of Egypt. They heard the promises, saw the Red Sea part, saw manna come down from heaven, saw the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire — when it comes to “seeing” and “hearing”, few generations in all of human history have been richer than they. Yet they fell dead in the wilderness, because the word was not mixed with faith.

Deluding your own selves

James 1:22 uses a very severe expression: “deluding your own selves.” The Greek is παραλογίζομαι (paralogizomai), which literally means “to deceive yourself with a false calculation”, like someone who has added up his accounts wrongly and thinks he is rich.

What kind of self-deception is this? It is miscounting “I’ve heard it” as “I’ve got it”, miscounting “I agree” as “I’ve changed”, miscounting “I was moved” as “I’ve obeyed”.

James then uses a brilliant picture: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was. But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does” (James 1:23–25).

What is a mirror for? It is for showing you what needs adjusting, so that you go and adjust it. If a man looks in the mirror in the morning, sees that his hair is a mess and his collar is crooked, and then turns and walks away without doing a thing — what use is that mirror to him?

God’s word is that mirror. Look in the mirror without lifting a hand, and however clearly it shows you, the looking was for nothing.

Psychology confirms it: the gap between knowing and doing

In 2006 the psychologists Webb and Sheeran published a meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin, bringing together a number of experimental studies, and its conclusion is well worth our reflection: even when experiments succeeded in raising participants’ “intention” to act by a medium to large amount, the change in actual “behaviour” was only small to medium. Researchers call this phenomenon the “intention–behaviour gap”.

In other words, resolve is not the same as action. This is a fact of human nature that has been confirmed again and again.

Brothers and sisters, this explains exactly the sister who went to more than thirty special conferences and wept and made a commitment every time. Each time her “intention” was raised to the highest pitch, yet her “behaviour” never took that step. The stirring in the meetings was real, the tears were real — it’s just that being moved is not obeying.

Another psychologist, Peter Gollwitzer, put forward the concept of “implementation intentions” in the journal American Psychologist in 1999: when someone does not merely resolve, “I will do such-and-such,” but sets a concrete plan — “If situation A arises, I will do action B” — the rate at which the behaviour is actually carried out rises significantly.

This is exactly the wisdom of “doing”. Don’t say vaguely, “From now on I’ll love my family more.” Say concretely, “Tonight, as soon as I come through the door, I’ll go into the kitchen and give my wife a hug.” Vague resolutions evaporate; concrete actions land.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 speaks of the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Those who stop at “seeing and listening” have reached only the first stage, “Information”. Those who stop at “speaking” may have reached the second and third stages, “Revelation” and “Conviction” — they understand, and they agree — but they have not stepped into the fourth stage, “Implementation”.

And if the truth never enters “Implementation”, then “Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication” after it never get the chance to happen. The eight stages are like a chain, and the fourth link is the crucial one; if the fourth link isn’t joined, the whole chain breaks off in mid-air.

321 also reminds us: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. Many people won’t do the word because their focus has slipped — their eyes are fixed on “I can’t do it”, on “nobody else is doing it either”, on “my circumstances won’t allow it”. Brothers and sisters, turn your focus back to Jesus, and you will find that he never commands anything without preparing the grace for you to accomplish it.

sections.heading: 6. Action Is the Doorway into Life
sections.html:
Scripture

“Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

“If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)

“Doing” is not the last step but the most crucial step

We tend to put “doing” at the bottom of the list, as if it were a finishing touch. Wrong. Brothers and sisters, “doing” is not the last step; “doing” is the most crucial step.

Because without “doing”, nothing that came before counts as finished.

It’s like an operation. The surgeon’s diagnosis is precise, the scans are clear, the team is in place, the instruments are all ready, the theatre lights are bright — but if that incision is never made, the patient is not healed. All the preparation was for that one incision.

Or it’s like a seed. Breeding, choosing the ground, turning the soil, fertilising, watering — all of it done; but if the seed is never put into the ground, it will never sprout. “Doing” is the act of putting the seed into the soil.

The Lord Jesus said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17). He said this just after washing the disciples’ feet. He did not say, “Since you know these things, you are blessed.” What he said was, “if you do them”. The blessing is not in knowing; the blessing is in doing.

The Lord also asked a question no one can sidestep: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46)

“Perfect” comes not by knowing, but by living it out

Matthew 5:48 says: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.”

“Perfect” in Greek is τέλειος (teleios), from τέλος (telos, purpose, end). It means not “without any flaw” but “having reached the purpose for which it was made, grown into the maturity it should have”. A fruit that is fully ripe and ready to be picked is called teleios.

So the Lord is not telling us, “You must become sinless, flawless people.” He is saying, “You must grow into what you are meant to grow into — grow until you love the way your heavenly Father loves.” Notice the verses just before this one: the Lord has just said, “love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44), and then says the Father “makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5:45).

The Father’s perfection shows itself in his “action” — continually, unceasingly showing grace to the undeserving. The sun shines every day, the rain falls year after year — this is the Father’s perfection.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Perfection is not a state of knowledge; it is a pattern of action. Perfection comes not by knowing, but by living it out.

Once or twice is not enough — keep on doing it

The lesson has one very precious sentence: doing the word once or twice is not enough; we must keep on doing it. What is done becomes habit, and habit becomes life.

This is exactly the teaching of the Bible. Paul says to Timothy: “Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come” (1 Timothy 4:7–8). “Exercise” in Greek is that same word again, γυμνάζω (gymnazō) — training in the gym. No one builds muscle from one visit to the gym, and no one grows character from reading the Bible once.

Modern research supports this too. Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London, in a study published in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2010, followed participants as they formed new daily habits and found that it took on average sixty-six days for a behaviour to become “automatic”, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

Sixty-six days. Brothers and sisters, this gives us two reminders. First, don’t rush — if you’ve done it for three days and feel nothing, that is normal; don’t give up. Second, don’t stop — real change happens on day forty, day fifty, day sixty, in those days that seem to show no progress at all.

Neuroscience also tells us that repeated practice gradually thickens the myelin sheath around neural circuits, making signals travel faster and more reliably. This is why an accomplished pianist can play scales without thinking. Spiritual life is the same: at first you have to grit your teeth to forgive someone; keep doing it long enough, and forgiveness becomes a reflex.

What is done becomes habit; habit becomes life.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Why can’t we live it out? Because that “self” is stuck in the middle. “I can’t do it” is “self”; “I’ll lose face” is “self”; “Why should I be the first to back down?” — that is “self” too.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. The first act of doing the word is very often laying down that “self”.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). When you move the “self” out of the way, what is lived out is no longer your effort but the life of Christ.

Brothers and sisters, if you can’t live it out, it may well not be because you aren’t trying hard enough, but because you are trying too hard — you keep relying on the brain and yourself instead of relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit. 321 says: rely on the heart and you are glad; rely on the brain and you are troubled. Hand over the “self”, let the Holy Spirit be your guide, and you will be able to take that step.

sections.heading: 7. True Disciples: Not Just People Who Preach
sections.html:
Scripture

“but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.” (1 Corinthians 9:27)

“My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)

Those who preach may also fail to grow

Brothers and sisters, this is the point today that takes the most courage to hear, and the most humility to receive.

The lesson gives us a very important reminder: those who preach may also fail to grow.

Why? Because they are only “cooking the food”, not “eating the food”.

Being able to speak doesn’t mean being able to live; being able to teach doesn’t mean having life.

This is not a jibe at anyone; it was the apostle Paul’s deepest warning to himself. He said: “but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

“Beat” in Greek is ὑπωπιάζω (hypōpiazō), literally “to strike under the eye”, a term from the boxing ring — to hit your opponent until his eye is bruised black. Paul used such a violent word to describe how he governed himself. This apostle, who wrote thirteen letters, founded countless churches and received visions in the third heaven, still said soberly: I am afraid that after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected.

Brothers and sisters, if even Paul needed to be this watchful, how much more do you and I?

The Lord Jesus’ sternest rebukes were for “people who could talk”

Read the four Gospels and you notice something: the Lord Jesus was gentle with tax collectors, gentle with prostitutes, gentle with lepers, gentle with the Canaanite woman. His sternest rebukes he kept for the group of people who could talk about the Scriptures best of all.

He said: “The scribes and the Pharisees sat on Moses’ seat. All things therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do, but don’t do their works; for they say, and don’t do” (Matthew 23:2–3).

“They say, and don’t do” — these few words are the Lord Jesus’ diagnosis of the religious professionals.

He also said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 7:21). What follows is even more startling: on that day many will say, didn’t we prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? But the Lord will say to them: “I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matthew 7:22–23).

Prophesying, casting out demons, doing mighty works — these are the very peak of “speaking” and “working”. Yet what the Lord looks at is not the results on the platform but the reality in the life.

The picture of a chef

I know a head chef at a restaurant. Every day he prepares meals for hundreds of guests, perfect in colour, aroma and taste. But he has one habit: at the end of the rush he just shovels down a couple of mouthfuls of cold rice and calls it a meal. After a few years, the guests who eat his cooking glow with health, while he himself has developed stomach trouble.

Brothers and sisters, doesn’t this picture look a lot like some preachers, small-group leaders, Sunday school teachers — perhaps even ourselves? We prepare a lavish spiritual feast for others, while for years we ourselves eat cold rice. We study the Bible in order to lead Bible studies, we read Scripture in order to write sermons, we pray because it’s on the order of service — the truth passes through us but never gets into us.

True spiritual influence has never come out of the mouth; it shines out of the life. When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, the skin of his face shone, and that light was not because of anything he had said but because he had been with God (Exodus 34:29).

True disciples are people who live out the truth

The Lord Jesus defines a disciple very clearly: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples” (John 8:31).

“Disciple” in Greek is μαθητής (mathētēs), from the verb μανθάνω (manthanō, to learn). But in the Jewish rabbinic tradition, “learning” was never copying the teacher’s knowledge into a notebook; it was living with the teacher and imitating his every move. A disciple watched how the teacher prayed, how he ate, how he treated people, how he faced his enemies — and then did the same.

So in the biblical sense, a “disciple” was always a “person who lives out the truth”. Someone who could recite but would not imitate would not even have counted as a disciple in the rabbinic tradition.

That is also why the last line of the Great Commission is worth chewing on all our lives: “teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). The Lord did not say “teaching them to know”; the Lord said “teaching them to observe”.

The goal of discipleship training has never been to produce more people who know a lot, but to produce more people who can live it out.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 has a very practical exercise called “the 920 practice”: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; with each “2” we are to practise living out a selfless life (0) and bear the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice this: fruit is not spoken into being; fruit grows. No tree ever grew apples by giving a speech.

The 920 practice is the training ground for “doing”. It nails abstract truth to one concrete person. Who is your “2” today? Your spouse, your child, your colleague, that neighbour who gives you headaches. If the truth doesn’t enter your relationship with them, the truth is still in the kitchen and hasn’t yet reached your bloodstream.

321 also speaks of “235 relationships”: becoming a “2”, spiritual companions, with someone selfless; establishing a “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5”, spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team. The role of a spiritual companion is precisely to support each other, evaluate each other and correct each other at this checkpoint of “doing”. One person easily deceives himself; two people find it much harder.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. True disciples have the order right. They first let the truth happen in their own life, then let it flow out in their relationships, and only then does it become ministry. Reverse the order, and the bigger the ministry, the emptier the life.

sections.heading: 8. Integrating the 321 Vision: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do and 3-2-1
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s five actions in fact correspond perfectly with the 321 vision. Please keep this in your heart.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

“See” — Jesus is my role model. The Lord said: “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). The Lord himself was the one who acted by watching the Father. We too must look to him every day. What we look at, we become.

“Listen” — the Bible is my standard. We hear too many voices: the voice of the world, the voice of public opinion, the voice of our own desires. Only God’s word is the standard. “Be careful therefore how you hear” (Luke 8:18).

“Think” — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Thinking is not reasoning with the brain; it is letting the Holy Spirit shine his light in the heart. “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

“Speak” — let Jesus be King. Confessing with our mouth that Jesus is Lord is the very declaration that hands over the throne. “For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation” (Romans 10:10). Revelation also says: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11).

“Do” — let Jesus receive all the glory. For the Lord said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). What people see is not our doctrine but our deeds; and the glory goes to the Father in heaven.

Finally, all of this flows together into the Goal: establish God’s system. A community that sees together, hears together, thinks together, proclaims together and acts together is exactly what 1 Timothy 3:15 speaks of — the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.

A shift in perspective

321 says: we must move from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from what is of the world to what is of God.

Man’s perspective says, “Knowing is enough — why take it so seriously?” God’s perspective says, “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17).

The earthly perspective says, “First show some results.” The heavenly perspective says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

The temporary perspective says, “Let it go this time; we’ll see next time.” The eternal perspective says: those sixty-six days, those small, unremarkable acts of obedience one after another, are forging a life that will last for eternity.

The worldly perspective says, “If you can talk, you’ll have influence.” God’s perspective says, “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22).

sections.heading: 9. Putting It into Practice: Eating the Truth
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper, one by one.

Practice one: Examine yourself — at which stage have I stopped?

Face your spiritual condition honestly: do I only see and only listen? Or have I already begun to do?

Information: today you have received the five links, See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. Copy them onto the first page of your notebook.

Revelation: be still and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: “Lord, please show me which link I am stuck at.” Don’t guess for yourself; let the Holy Spirit speak.

Conviction: when the Holy Spirit points it out, don’t argue. Admit it: “Lord, it’s true — I’ve stopped at speaking and haven’t gone on to doing.”

Implementation: write it down today, on a piece of paper you will see every day.

Evaluation: at the end of this week, look back: did I actually move, or do I merely know I ought to move?

Correction: if you didn’t move, don’t condemn yourself; adjust your method — shrink the goal until it is something you are sure you can do.

Repetition: examine yourself once a month, so that self-examination becomes a habit.

Multiplication: explain these five links to someone, and invite them to examine themselves too.

Practice two: Put at least one truth into practice every day

From the word you hear today, choose the simplest thing and do it, so that the truth enters your life.

Notice that word “simplest”. This is not lowering the standard; it is spiritual wisdom. Remember Gollwitzer’s research mentioned earlier: concrete, clear plans are far more likely to be carried out than vague resolutions.

So don’t say, “From now on I’ll be more loving.” Say, “At lunchtime today I’ll phone that older friend I haven’t been in touch with for three months.”

Don’t say, “I want to be better at forgiving.” Say, “Tonight I’ll pray for three minutes, by name, for the person who hurt me.”

Don’t say, “I want to read the Bible more.” Say, “Tomorrow at half past six in the morning I’ll sit in this chair and read Mark chapter 1.”

Information and Revelation: after your morning devotion each day, ask yourself one question — “What does this passage want me to do today?”

Conviction: believe that this small thing is a big thing in God’s eyes. “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10).

Implementation: do it the same day; don’t let it sit overnight.

Evaluation and Correction: spend one minute before bed going back over the day. If you did it, thank God; if you didn’t, make it smaller and more concrete tomorrow.

Repetition: forty days in a row. Remember that sixty-six-day study — habits take time to grow.

Multiplication: find a spiritual companion, and each day report to each other in one sentence: “Here’s what I did today.”

Practice three: Build the complete cycle of See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do

Don’t just read the Bible; meditate on it, share it, and finally be sure to live it out, so that your life is fed.

Here is a suggested way to arrange each day:

See and Listen: in the early morning, do your morning devotion — read a passage of Scripture and listen to a message. This is buying the food.

Think: after reading, be still for five minutes. Chew one verse over and over, like the lion that clamps on to its prey and won’t let go (the “growling” in Isaiah 31:4 is the very same Hebrew word as “meditates” in Psalm 1:2). Ask three questions: What does this passage say about what kind of God he is? What does it say about what kind of person I am? How does it want me to act today?

Speak: write down what you have received and send it to a spiritual companion, or share it in your small group. This is cooking the food.

Do: set one concrete action and complete it that day. This is eating the food.

Evaluation, Correction, Repetition: look back once a week, adjust once a month, and keep going without stopping.

Multiplication: bring someone along to do this cycle with you. When you bring someone onto this road, you will find you walk it more steadily yourself — because “Multiplication” is itself the strongest form of “Repetition”.

A Gentle Reminder

It isn’t how many sermons you have heard, but how much of the word you have lived out.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the growth of life is not a change in an instant, but “living it out” one time after another.

No one is changed in a single special conference. People are changed in one small, unremarkable act of obedience after another: in the harsh word you held back and never said, in the phone call you made first, in the moment when you could have kept score but chose to let it go, in that early morning when you wanted to stay in bed but got up and knelt down instead.

When you begin truly to do it, you will discover — the truth is no longer just knowledge; it becomes life.

One day you will be surprised to find that you no longer have to grit your teeth to forgive, because forgiveness has become your nature; you no longer have to force yourself to love, because love has become your breath. That is being “perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect”.

So this morning I want to issue you a call.

Not a call to hear more sermons, not a call to buy more books, not a call to attend more meetings.

I want to call you — to do one thing.

Just one. Today. Something concrete.

Let Jesus be King in that one thing. Let the “self” step down in that one thing. Let the truth, in that one thing, move from your head into your bloodstream.

Then tomorrow, one more. The day after, one more.

Once you’ve bought the food, cook it; once it’s cooked, eat it. Let us go through the whole process, live a life that is truly like Jesus, and give all the glory to him.

For the Lord said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

keyVerses: but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. (1 Timothy 3:15)
Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect. (Matthew 5:48)
The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you. (Philippians 4:9)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:
Lord, I don’t only want to hear your word — I want to live out your word! Help me to move from “knowing” to “doing”. Let your truth become my life, and make me more like you day by day!
practices: Put at least one truth into practice every day
Build the complete cycle of See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

You have given us your word, not for us to store away, but for us to eat and live out. Lord, we confess that we often buy a great deal of food and cook a great deal of food, yet never eat it. We know so much, and live out so little. Please forgive us.
Holy Spirit, shine your light on me, and show me which link I am stuck at. Have I stopped at seeing and listening? Have I stopped at speaking? Give me courage to take that step.

Lord Jesus, reign as King in me. Move my “self” out of the way, so that it is no longer I who live, but you who live in me. Give me perseverance — not to do it once or twice, but day after day, until the truth becomes my habit, and the habit becomes my life.
Make me a pillar and ground of the truth — not in word, but in deed and truth — so that people, seeing my good works, will give the glory to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Of the five links — See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do — at which do you most often stop? What makes you stop there? Share a specific example with your group. (James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”)

Write down one specific thing you “can go and do today” — the smaller the better — and arrange with a spiritual companion to ask each other about the result in a week’s time. How do you think living it out consistently will change your relationship with God and with others? (John 13:17: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”)
l117.title: Why Seeing, Listening, Thinking, Speaking and Doing Matter
l117.subtitle: The Cycle of Life from Knowing to Doing
l117.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: Why We Follow the Steps and Still Don’t Break Through
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning.

In the last lesson we saw two things together: the growth of life lies in cultivation, and the key to cultivation lies in “See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do.” These five words are like five doors. Every single day, something comes in through these five doors, settles inside us, and then grows within us into the shape of a person.

But this morning we have to face a deeper, and more honest, question.

There was a sister who had been a believer for fifteen years. She never missed a meeting. She had filled seven notebooks with Bible-reading notes. She could recite the order of the five books of Moses, and she could quote whole passages of the Sermon on the Mount. One day in her small group she suddenly broke down in tears. She said, “I’ve read the Bible for all these years, and I’m still the mother who comes home and screams at her children. What on earth is wrong with me?”

Brothers and sisters, that question isn’t only hers. It may well be ours too. We followed the steps. We saw, we listened, we thought, we spoke — we even did. So why is there still no breakthrough in our lives? Why is the old self still there? Why haven’t the old things passed away?

When I was young I saw something in the countryside that I’ve never forgotten. An old gardener was transplanting a fruit tree. He dug the tree up from one plot and carried it to another. Because he was in a hurry, he simply stood the tree in the hole, threw a loose layer of soil over it, and rushed off to water it and fertilise it. For the next three months he watered it every day and fertilised it every day — bag after bag of fertiliser, bucket after bucket of water. After three months, the tree was dead.

The old gardener said something I have remembered all my life: “It wasn’t the fertiliser. The roots never took hold of the soil.”

Brothers and sisters, that is the very heart of today’s lesson. What changes our lives has never been method; it is position. It isn’t how much we do; it is whether or not we are in him. If the roots haven’t taken hold, all the water and all the fertiliser in the world will only make the tree die a little faster.

So today’s answer is a key that goes even deeper: are you “in Christ”?

In this lesson we will climb five steps together. May the Holy Spirit, this morning, plant his word deep within us.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Declaration of a New Creation, from the Lips of a Deeply Misunderstood Apostle
sections.html:
Let’s first stand where the text was written. The author of 2 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. It is generally thought to have been written between AD 55 and 56, in Macedonia, during his third missionary journey. The letter was addressed to the church in Corinth.

Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, an extraordinarily prosperous commercial port city. It sat on a narrow isthmus: the port of Cenchreae on the east opened towards Asia, and the port of Lechaeum on the west opened towards Italy. Goods, crowds and religions from right across the Mediterranean passed through this one city. On the heights of the Acrocorinth, south of the city, stood the temple of Aphrodite; in those days the name Corinth was almost a byword for loose morals.

In other words, the believers in the Corinthian church didn’t come to faith in a monastery. They came to faith in a great city given over to sensual pleasure, money and idols. Their old life was just around the corner; their old friends lived next door; their old habits came knocking at the door every day.

The setting of this letter is heavier still. Paul wrote 2 Corinthians in the aftermath of deep misunderstanding and hurt. Some people questioned whether he was an apostle at all, saying “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (see 2 Corinthians 10:10); others brought in a different gospel. All the way through to chapter 5, he is describing how a man who has been completely gripped by the Lord’s love sees himself, sees other people and sees the world.

When we read the context of chapter 5, we understand the weight of verse 17 all the more. In verses 1 to 10, Paul says that our earthly tent will be torn down, but we have an eternal house in heaven, and so “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). In verses 14 and 15 he names the driving force of the whole chapter: “For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died. He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15) In verse 16 he says that from now on we know no one after the flesh. And then, only then, the great declaration of verse 17 rings out like thunder: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.”

Brothers and sisters, please notice the order. First the love of Christ constrains us; then we “no longer live to ourselves”; and only then comes “a new creation.” This is exactly what 321 says — the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless. A new creation is not the old self who has got better at handling people; it is a person who no longer lives for himself.

John 15 is a completely different scene. It is the night on which the Lord Jesus was betrayed. The Last Supper is over, and on the way to the garden of Gethsemane the Lord speaks his farewell words to his disciples (John 13–17). The author is the apostle John; the Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 85 and 90, possibly in Ephesus. Throughout the Old Testament the vine had always been a symbol of Israel (see Psalm 80:8–9; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21), and the vine of Israel had produced wild grapes. Now the Lord says, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). He is the true Israel who bears fruit, and if we are to bear fruit, the one and only way is to be joined to him.

On one side, the bustling streets of Corinth; on the other, a night road outside Jerusalem. One speaks of a renewed standing; the other speaks of a living connection. Put the two passages together and you have today’s message: you are already a new creation — the question is, where do you live?

sections.heading: 1. The Foundation of Life: In Christ
sections.html:
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

1. What changes a life is not method but position

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to where the stress falls in this verse.

Paul didn’t say, “If anyone works very hard.” He didn’t say, “If anyone has the right method.” Still less did he say, “If anyone is naturally gifted.” What he said was, “If anyone is in Christ.”

“In Christ” in Greek is ἐν Χριστῷ (en Christō). This phrase, together with its equivalents — in him, in the Lord — is one of the most frequent expressions in Paul’s letters; it is generally reckoned to occur more than a hundred and sixty times. It isn’t a pious catchphrase. It is the most fundamental coordinate Paul uses to describe who a Christian is.

It is a word of position, not a word of degree.

A person cannot be “a little bit in Christ,” any more than a baby can be “a little bit born.”

Either you are in, or you are out.

So the lesson puts it with great precision: what changes a life is not method but position. In Christ, you are a new creation; outside Christ, you are still the old life.

There is a very important spiritual discernment here. Many believers today don’t lack methods; they lack position. We have Bible-reading plans, prayer charts, devotional apps and a calendar packed with ministry. Yet we are like that old gardener — watering and fertilising, watering and fertilising — without ever stopping to ask: have this tree’s roots taken hold of the soil?

2. So what does “in Christ” mean?

The Lord himself gave the answer.

“If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.” (John 15:7)

“Remain” in Greek is μένω (menō). It means to settle, to stay, not to move away. It isn’t “visiting”; it is “taking up residence.” In the short span of John 15:1–11 — just eleven verses — this word occurs more than ten times. The Lord says it again and again: remain in me, remain in me.

And the Lord immediately sets “remaining in him” side by side with “his words remaining in us” — notice, these are two halves of one sentence.

So: to be in Christ is to live in his word.

If someone says he remains in Christ, yet there is almost no word of God in his daily living, he is deceiving himself. If someone says he reads God’s word every day, yet there is no Christ in his life, what he has is knowledge. To be truly “in Christ” is for his word to become my dwelling place — the place where I eat, sleep, make decisions and face conflict.

3. Not only knowing, but obeying

The Lord then put it even more concretely:

“If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and remain in his love.” (John 15:10)

Brothers and sisters, notice the Lord’s own example: “even as I have kept my Father’s commandments.” The Lord Jesus isn’t asking us to do anything he hasn’t done himself. He is our role model — and that is the first of 321’s foundations: Jesus is my role model.

So obedience isn’t an optional extra-credit question. Obedience is what “remaining in Christ” actually looks like.

James, the Lord’s brother, says it even more bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) And the Lord himself said, “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24)

Here we must guard against a misunderstanding: obedience is not using our own strength to earn that position. The American Christian writer Dallas Willard said something of great weight: “Grace is not opposed to effort, it is opposed to earning.” We don’t obey in order to purchase being “in Christ”; we are able to obey because we are already in Christ. And every act of obedience makes that connection deeper, truer and more alive.

4. And “See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do” is the very way to live in Christ

This joins the last lesson to this one.

“See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do” are not five techniques. They are five channels through which the word of Christ comes into us, remains in us, and then is lived out from within us.

See him — looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith (see Hebrews 12:2).

Listen to him — faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ (see Romans 10:17).

Think on him — set your mind on the things above, not on the things on the earth (see Colossians 3:2).

Speak of him — for out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks (see Matthew 12:34).

Do his word — everyone who hears these words of mine and does them (see Matthew 7:24).

Five actions, one object: Christ. Without that object, See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do is nothing more than a five-step process of self-improvement. With that object, they become five arteries through which we remain in Christ.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: the Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? These Three Foundations are precisely the three dimensions of being “in Christ.”

Jesus is my role model: he kept his Father’s commandments and remained in his Father’s love; that is the pattern for my remaining in him.

The Bible is my standard: his words remain in me, and my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing now have a standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: apart from the Lord we can do nothing; it is the Holy Spirit who makes the life of Christ real within us.

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll worry, rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice. That sister who had read the Bible for fifteen years and still lost her temper every day — her problem wasn’t that she hadn’t read enough. It was that she had been using her brain to “manage” herself, instead of using her heart to “remain” in the Lord.

sections.heading: 2. The Process of Life: From New Creation to Renewal
sections.html:
“The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

1. A common misunderstanding

Many people assume that the moment you believe, you are completely changed on the spot.

So three months after coming to faith they discover that the temper is still there, the weakness is still there, the old habits are still there — and they begin to wonder: was I ever saved at all?

Brothers and sisters, this is a mindset that needs to be corrected by Scripture.

“New creation” in Greek is καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis). The word for “new” here is καινός (kainos), which means new in nature and in quality, not νέος (neos), which is new in time. It doesn’t mean “the old thing given a makeover”; it means “a whole new kind of creature.” So Paul isn’t talking about improvement; he is talking about creation — creation like Genesis chapter 1.

And if it is creation, then it is something God accomplished once and for all, not something we bring about slowly. So your standing today is this: you are already a new creation. It is a completed act, an established fact, and it cannot be shaken.

2. The standing is settled; the process is under way

Yet the second half of the very same verse points to an ongoing process: “all things have become new.”

Paul says it even more clearly elsewhere:

“That you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:22–24)

“But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

“From glory to glory” — those words are the process.

So we must hold on to two things at the same time:

We are already a new creation. That is our standing, and God gave it.

We are being made new. That is the process, and it happens every day.

A newborn baby is fully and completely a human being from the moment of birth — that is standing. But the baby still has to learn to walk, learn to talk, learn to eat — that is process. Standing doesn’t have to be fought for; process can’t be skipped.

3. The key in between: letting the old things pass away

Between standing and process there is a key phrase, and the lesson grasps it precisely: let the old things pass away.

Notice that Paul didn’t say “the old things have vanished automatically.” He said “the old things have passed away.” On the cross of Christ the old things have already been dealt with; but in our daily living the old things often hang around and refuse to leave — because we keep feeding them.

We have to admit it: there are some old things we can’t bear to let go of. The memory of being wronged — we take it out and polish it every day. The wound we suffered — we can’t bring ourselves to hand it to the Lord. The old habit — we pray for God to take it away, and then we give it a good meal every night.

Neuroscience has a well-known saying, generally attributed to the neuroscientist Carla Shatz as a summary of the theory of the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb (1949): “Neurons that fire together wire together.” It means that the more often you repeat a particular response, the thicker, faster and more automatic that neural pathway becomes. And the reverse is true: the longer you leave a pathway unused, the weaker it grows.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly how “letting the old things pass away” works in practice. The old things don’t disappear because you hate them. The old things gradually lose their power because you stop feeding them — and start feeding the new.

4. Not only a change of identity, but a change of the way we live

The lesson puts it well: it is not only a change of identity, but a change of the way we live.

Paul says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10) We are created new in order to walk in a new way.

Picture a man who has been pardoned and released from prison. His status is now that of a free man. But if, after his release, he still lives right next to the prison, still keeps a prisoner’s routine and still looks at people through a prisoner’s eyes, then his status has changed but his life has not.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: there is a fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living.

“Already a new creation, being made new” — that is the first of the five changes: mindset.

Many people are stuck where they are, not because they haven’t tried hard enough, but because their mindset hasn’t been renewed. They think that believing in Jesus should make them perfect overnight, and the moment they see themselves stumble, they condemn themselves. The more they condemn themselves, the weaker they become; the weaker they become, the further they slide back.

321 also speaks of a shift in perspective — from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. When we look at ourselves through God’s eyes, what we see is not “a failure who keeps on losing,” but “a child of God who has already been made a new creation and is being transformed from glory to glory.”

Once the mindset changes, the life is set free; once the life is set free, the daily living begins to move too.

sections.heading: 3. The Key Breakthrough: It Begins with “See” and “Listen”
sections.html:
“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

1. Transformation of life begins at the source

Brothers and sisters, we often try to change the outcome, but we rarely touch the source.

We want to change our temper — temper is “Do.” We want to change the way we talk — that is “Speak.” We want to change our thoughts — that is “Think.” But where does “Think” come from? It comes from “See” and “Listen.”

The lesson puts it exactly: what you see shapes your thinking; what you hear shapes your beliefs.

On this point, Scripture and science agree. The human brain handles an enormous volume of information every day, and sight and hearing are its two main entrances. The optic nerve of a single eye carries more than a million nerve fibres sending signals into the brain. Our eyes are not a passive camera; they are an intake. Our ears are not a passive tape recorder; they are a conveyor belt.

The Lord Jesus spoke very solemnly about both these entrances.

About the eye: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” (Matthew 6:22)

About the ear: “Take heed what you hear.” (Mark 4:24)

If a lamp is dirty, the whole house grows dim. If an entrance is polluted, the whole life turns murky with it.

2. What we see, and what we hear

The lesson sets out two clear paths:

If what we see is the world and what we hear is the flesh, then our thinking, speaking and doing will all drift away from God.

If what we see is Christ and what we hear is God’s word, then our thinking, speaking and doing will be renewed.

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

The original behind “conformed to this world” carries the sense of being pressed into the same mould as this age. The world doesn’t use force; the world uses a mould. You soak in it every day, and without even noticing it you are pressed into its shape.

King David understood this well. He made a vow: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes. I hate the deeds of faithless men. They will not cling to me.” (Psalm 101:3)

Paul also gave us a list: “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)

Brothers and sisters, of these two verses, one closes a door and the other opens one. Spiritual growth has always needed both hands: one hand closing the doors that shouldn’t be open, the other opening the doors that should.

3. Evidence from psychology: we are far more easily shaped than we imagine

In his famous “Bobo doll experiment” of 1961, the psychologist Albert Bandura found that children who had merely “seen” an adult attacking a doll would afterwards imitate the very same aggressive behaviour on their own. In Social Learning Theory (1977) he pointed out that a great deal of human behaviour is learned not from lectures but from observation.

In other words: what you look at, you slowly become. That isn’t religious language; it is a fact about human beings that has been confirmed again and again.

That is also why the Lord said, “Take heed what you hear.” Taking heed isn’t about guarding against other people; it’s about guarding your own entrances.

4. So the starting point is not “Do” but “See” and “Listen”

Brothers and sisters, here is the most practical sentence in this whole lesson: the starting point of transformation is not “Do”; it is “See” and “Listen.”

How many people, the moment they resolve to change, go straight for the last link in the chain — gritting their teeth to change their behaviour. The result? Three days of enthusiasm, a collapse on day five, and then self-condemnation: “I knew it. I just can’t do it.”

It’s like a polluted river. Every day you stand downstream fishing out rubbish, but you won’t walk upstream and shut off the waste pipe. You can fish all your life, and the river will still be dirty.

The real breakthrough is upstream. And what is upstream? It is the content on your phone, the voices in your earphones, the last fifteen minutes of what you watch before you sleep, the very first thing you touch when you open your eyes in the morning.

The fact that we are sitting here this morning for our morning devotion is itself an upstream decision.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, “what we see and what we hear” comes down in the end to the question of where we put our focus. Focus on yourself, and the more you look the more you pity yourself. Focus on other people, and the more you look the more bitter you become. Focus on your circumstances, and the more you look the more afraid you grow. Only when the focus is on Jesus does the looking fill you with more and more hope.

321 also says: out of the heart flows the whole outcome of a life. So what we keep is not just our behaviour but our heart. And the way to keep the heart is not to stand guard by willpower, but to make our choices at the entrance.

And 321 says: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If your first look in the morning is at God, the order of your day is right. If your first look in the morning is at the news and your messages, the day begins with “things,” and your heart is thrown into disarray.

sections.heading: 4. The Process of Life Transformation
sections.html:
“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.” (Joshua 1:8)

1. A complete path of spiritual growth

The lesson maps this path out very clearly. Let’s walk through it step by step:

See and Listen are the entry of Information.

Think and Speak are the stages of Revelation and Conviction.

Do is Implementation.

And then —

Repeated practice becomes habit.

Habit becomes character.

Character becomes life.

This is the practical road map for how “a new creation” lives out “a whole new life.”

2. See and Listen are Information; Think and Speak are Revelation and Conviction

Brothers and sisters, please notice: information is not the same as revelation.

Many people’s spiritual lives stop at the level of “See and Listen.” Plenty of information, very little revelation. They’ve heard a hundred sermons and can repeat ninety of them, yet not one has become revelation to them.

To move from information to revelation, you have to pass through “Think.” Joshua 1:8 says “meditate on it day and night.” The Hebrew word for “meditate” is הָגָה (hagah), the same word that appears in Psalm 1:2. Its root meaning carries the sense of “murmuring under one’s breath, chewing over and over” — like a cow chewing the cud, bringing up the grass it has swallowed and slowly chewing it again.

Brothers and sisters, we often read the Bible the way a duck gulps its food, swallowing it whole. God wants us to be like the cow chewing the cud, chewing slowly. Chew long enough, and information turns into revelation.

And “Speak”? “Speak” is the confirmation of conviction. The Lord said, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) You speak to the degree that you believe. When a person begins to say God’s word with his own mouth, the truth finally drops from the head into the heart. So sharing in a small group, retelling it at home, bearing witness in the workplace — none of this is a performance. It is the process of pressing revelation into life.

3. Do, habit, character, life

Next comes “Do.” Practising something once is only an action; practising it again and again is what makes it a habit.

There is reliable research to confirm this. In a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London found that it takes an average of about sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit — and that it varies widely from person to person and from behaviour to behaviour, anywhere from eighteen days to more than two hundred.

In other words, a habit isn’t formed on day three, nor on the day you “feel like it.” It is formed on the fortieth day, the fiftieth day, when you feel nothing at all and do it anyway.

Once a habit has taken shape, its power is enormous. Research by Professor Wendy Wood of the University of Southern California and her colleagues (2002) showed that a very large share of what people do each day — the study estimated more than forty per cent — consists of habitual actions repeated automatically in familiar settings, not rational decisions made in the moment.

Brothers and sisters, what does this mean? It means that most of our life is actually being driven by our habits. And habits are formed by repeated practice; practice is brought about by conviction; conviction is born of revelation; revelation comes from information; and information comes in through seeing and hearing.

One chain, link joined to link, running all the way from the eyes and ears to life itself.

There is a widely circulated saying, generally attributed to the American businessman Frank Outlaw: “Watch your thoughts; they become words. Watch your words; they become actions. Watch your actions; they become habits. Watch your habits; they become character. Watch your character; it becomes your destiny.” Its origin is debated, but the saying is strikingly consistent with the order of Scripture. Only Scripture said it earlier, and says it more deeply — it tells us that the source lies in “seeing” and “hearing,” and that the destination is not destiny but the life of Christ.

4. This is how a new creation lives out a whole new life

So “a new creation” is not a label. It is a road you can walk.

Our standing God gives once for all; our life God grows day by day.

He has already placed new life within us. Now, through this path, he wants to grow that life from the inside out — into our thoughts, our mouths, our hands, our homes and our workplaces.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that the process in this lesson corresponds almost exactly to 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset?

Information — See and Listen.

Revelation — Think.

Conviction — Think and Speak.

Implementation — Do.

Evaluation, Correction, Repetition — repeated practice becoming habit.

Multiplication — habit becoming character, character becoming life, and then that life going on to influence the next person.

321 also speaks of the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do changes the mindset; the mindset changes the life; the life changes the daily living; the daily living changes relationships; and only relationships can bear the weight of ministry.

That is why 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people turn the order upside down and charge into ministry first. The result is that the bigger the ministry grows, the drier the life becomes and the stiffer the relationships. Brothers and sisters, don’t be in a hurry to bear fruit. First let the branch be firmly joined to the vine.

sections.heading: 5. The Key Principle: Choose the Right Cultivation
sections.html:
“I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

1. “See” and “Listen” are in themselves neutral

The lesson makes a very important observation: “See” and “Listen” are in themselves neutral.

The eye is not sin; the ear is not sin. God made the eye to behold his glory; God made the ear to hear his voice.

The problem has never been the organ. The question is: what are you choosing to let into your life?

It’s like a field. A field is neutral. Sow wheat and you get wheat; sow tares and you get tares; sow nothing at all and you get weeds. A field never stays empty — every farmer knows that.

So: wrong seeing and hearing cultivate a wrong life; right seeing and hearing cultivate a right life.

2. The white dog and the black dog

The lesson mentions a parable we know well, a widely told Native American story. An old man tells his grandson that inside us two dogs fight every day — one good, one evil. The grandson asks, “Which one wins?” The old man answers, “The one you feed.”

In 321 we put it like this: to feed the white dog is to feed our spiritual life; to starve the black dog is to stop feeding the old, self-centred life.

Brothers and sisters, please notice: we don’t overcome by “beating the black dog to death.” How many people spend their whole lives wrestling with their old self until they are utterly exhausted! Scripture’s method is not wrestling; it is cutting off one food supply and switching to another.

Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) The old self has already been dealt with on the cross. What we have to do today is stop providing for someone who has already been sentenced to death.

3. What you feed is what grows

This is a spiritual law, and it is a natural law too.

A farmer doesn’t stand in his field shouting, “No weeds!” A farmer sows, waters and weeds. If a fruit grower planted his trees in salty ground and prayed every day for God to make them bear sweet fruit, that wouldn’t be faith; it would be defying the very laws God himself has set.

The law God has set is this: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” (Galatians 6:7)

So, what you feed is what grows; what you choose is what you become.

This morning I want to ask a very honest question, and I ask you, brothers and sisters, to answer it honestly for yourselves: over the past seven days, what was the ratio between the time I spent on screens and the time I spent in God’s word?

That ratio is the direction of our life. It doesn’t lie.

And this choice is not made once and for all. At the end of his life Joshua said, “As for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15) That was a decision he was making again every single day. Even if you fed the wrong dog yesterday, this morning you can choose again.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

What is the self-centred life? The self-centred life is that black dog. And what does it eat? It feeds on being exalted, being noticed, being affirmed, being served. So much of what we watch and listen to every day is feeding that very dog — comparison, showing off, sarcasm, complaint. Mouthful after mouthful, it’s all the food it loves.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. That is precisely the declaration of Galatians 2:20.

321 also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. A person who feeds the black dog every day speaks in barbs, and strife breaks out at home and in church. A person who feeds the white dog every day speaks words of grace, and relationships are healed.

Brothers and sisters, this is the 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” Before them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

What you feed is what grows. Feed on God’s word and the fruit of the Spirit grows; feed on this world and the lusts of the flesh grow. Between the two there is no third way.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s gather this lesson up into the vision of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he kept his Father’s commandments and remained in his Father’s love. The Bible is my standard — his words remain in me. The Holy Spirit is my guide — apart from the Lord we can do nothing. These Three Foundations are the three pillars of being “in Christ.”

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — wherever the King is, there is his kingdom. To let him reign as King is to hand back to him, one by one, the sovereignty over our eyes, our ears, our thoughts, our tongues, our hands and feet. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when the branch bears fruit, the glory goes to the vine. If the renewal of our lives turns into a ledger of our own achievements, the fruit turns sour.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Only a person whose seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing have all been renewed can become a living stone that stands firm in God’s system.

The 235 relationships: become a “2” with someone who is selfless, reminding each other whether we are feeding the white dog or the black dog today; build your “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing this path of life transformation on; and become part of a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together.

The shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s — no longer looking at ourselves by asking “Have I done enough?” but by asking “Am I in him?”; from the earthly, the temporary and the worldly to the heavenly, the eternal and the godly — every mouthful we take in today is shaping the life that is yet to be revealed.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them deeper using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1. Adjust the source: what am I seeing and hearing every day?

Information: This week, take a sheet of paper and honestly record, for three days, how much time you spend each day on video, social media and news, and how much time you spend in God’s word.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you through Psalm 101:3 and Philippians 4:8, and to show you which entrance needs to be closed and which needs to be opened.

Conviction: Admit that this isn’t “being too strict”; it is the Lord’s mercy — he wants to protect the hearts of those he loves.

Implementation: This week, set one concrete subtraction and one concrete addition. For example: no phone for the thirty minutes before bed — read a passage of Scripture instead; no complaint-filled programmes on the commute — listen to worship songs or a Bible reading instead.

Evaluation: Each evening, take three minutes and ask yourself: today, how many mouthfuls did I feed the white dog, and how many did I feed the black dog?

Correction: Don’t condemn; just adjust. If you fall, choose again tomorrow morning.

Repetition: Keep it up for at least sixty-six days. Remember, habits are formed on the days when you feel nothing and do it anyway.

Multiplication: Find a “2” partner, and give each other an account once a week.

Practice 2. Practise the life of being “in Christ”

Information: Each day, after you read the Bible, pick just one verse and write it on a card or set it as your phone’s home screen.

Revelation: Be still for three minutes and chew on that verse again and again, like a cow chewing the cud. Ask the Lord: what do you want this word to accomplish in me today?

Conviction: Say to the Lord, “Lord, I believe. I am willing to live by this word.”

Implementation: That same day, find one concrete opportunity to obey it — a word of apology, a phone call to check in on someone, one moment of holding back instead of answering back.

Evaluation: In the evening, look back: did I obey today? At what moment did I choose myself?

Correction: Hand the moment of failure to the Lord, ask his precious blood to cleanse you, and set a smaller, more workable step.

Repetition: One verse a day, seven verses a week — in a year, more than three hundred verses will truly be remaining in you.

Multiplication: In your small group, share the one verse you “lived out” this week. No theory, only experience.

Practice 3. Build a cycle of life renewal

Information: Write out the five words “See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do” and put them somewhere you’ll see every day.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you that these aren’t five assignments; they are five channels for remaining in Christ.

Conviction: Believe that a changed life comes not by bursts of effort but by the power of a cycle.

Implementation: Design a daily cycle of your own — in the early morning, see and listen (read the Bible, listen to Scripture); during the day, think (meditate on one verse); in the evening, speak (share one sentence with your family or your partner); and at any moment, do (one concrete act of obedience).

Evaluation and Correction: Every Sunday evening, spend ten minutes reviewing the week. Whichever link breaks most easily, make that link simpler and smaller.

Repetition: Allow yourself to go slowly, but don’t allow yourself to stop.

Multiplication: Bring someone along to do it with you, and your cycle becomes someone else’s starting point.

A Gentle Reminder

A changed life doesn’t begin with effort; it begins with “what you let into you.”

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the old gardener’s words: it wasn’t the fertiliser; the roots never took hold of the soil.

You are already a new creation — God accomplished that for you once and for all on the cross, and it can’t be altered or shaken. But whether you live out the new life depends on your choices every day: what you let into your eyes, what you let into your ears, and whom you let reign as King within you.

When you keep remaining in Christ, letting his word come into you and living it out, the old things will pass away naturally, and the new life will be truly revealed. It isn’t that you drove the old things out; it’s that the new life grew, and the old was left with no room.

You are not only a new creation — you will live out a whole new life!

So this morning I want to issue a call to you, brothers and sisters: give your eyes to Jesus, give your ears to Jesus, and let him be King over your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Not so that we can become better people, but so that he may receive all the glory.

When the branch is joined to the vine, the fruit comes; and when the fruit comes, the glory goes to the Lord who planted it.

keyVerses: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
“If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.” (John 15:7)
declarations: Lord, I am willing to remain in you, and to let your words remain in me.
Help me to choose the right things to see and hear, so that my thoughts, my words and my actions are all renewed, and I live out the new life you have given me.
practices: Adjust the source: what am I seeing and hearing every day?
Practise the life of being “in Christ”
Build a cycle of life renewal
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you, because on the cross you have already made us a new creation. Our standing is not something we earned; it is the grace you have freely given.

Lord, we confess that we often put method in place of position, busyness in place of connection, and knowledge in place of obedience. Every day we feed the old, self-centred life, and then we ask you to drive it out for us. Please forgive us.

Cleanse our eyes, and cleanse our ears. Teach us to close the doors that shouldn’t be open and to open the doors that should. May what we see be Christ, and what we hear be your word, so that our thoughts, our words and our actions are all renewed by you.
