Lord, may your word remain in us this very day and become our standard. May the Holy Spirit guide us, so that we do not rely on the brain and ourselves but on the heart and the Holy Spirit. May Jesus reign as King in our lives and receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17) Do you believe that you are already a new creation? Is there an “old thing” that, even today, you still can’t bear to let pass away? Are you willing to hand it to the Lord today?

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Be specific: this week, which entrance of “seeing” or “hearing” will you close, and which will you open? Pray for one another in your small group, and agree to come back next week and report.
l118.title: Living Out New Life in Christ
l118.subtitle: Why Seeing, Listening, Thinking, Speaking and Doing Matter (Part 2)
l118.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: That Little Patch of “Nothing” in the Sky
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

In December 1995 a group of astronomers made a decision that many of their colleagues at the time considered “a waste of telescope time.” They pointed the priceless Hubble Space Telescope at a tiny patch of night sky near the Great Bear that seemed to contain nothing at all — a patch so small it was about the size of a grain of sand held at arm’s length. Seen through ground-based telescopes, it had always been simply black, completely empty.

Yet they kept the shutter open, building up exposure over ten days.

When the image was developed, the whole world was stunned. That dark patch of “nothing” was crammed with some three thousand galaxies, and each galaxy held hundreds of billions of stars. The image came to be called the Hubble Deep Field, and it became one of the most famous photographs in the history of astronomy.

Brothers and sisters, notice one thing: that night, the patch of sky didn’t change. Those three thousand galaxies had always been there — they had been there for billions of years. What changed was not the sky; it was the “ability to see.”

Our lives are just the same.

So often we think the problem lies in our circumstances, in other people, in what has happened to us. We say, “If only my husband would change a bit,” “If only my health were a little better,” “If only the economy picked up, the children were a bit more sensible, the brothers and sisters at church were a bit more considerate — then my faith would be fine.” We spend half our lives trying to rearrange the sky outside.

But the Bible tells us that the real key isn’t out there. It lies in how we see.

The same event, seen differently, leads to completely different outcomes in life. In the same wilderness, ten spies saw giants, while two spies saw God’s promise. In the same city surrounded by the Syrian army, the servant saw the enemy, while Elisha saw chariots and horses of fire. At the same cross, some see defeat and some see the power of salvation. On the same ordinary morning, some see another day of worry about to begin, and some see God’s compassion, new every morning.

The French writer Proust wrote a line in In Search of Lost Time that has been quoted for a century: the real voyage of discovery consists not in seeking new landscapes, but in having new eyes.

Brothers and sisters, we haven’t come today to trade in our sky for a different one. We’ve come to ask the Lord to give us a new pair of eyes.

So the beginning of revival is not only outward change; it is the changing of the “eyes” within us. This is exactly what the 321 vision calls the fivefold change: change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and the daily living changes; change the daily living, and relationships change; change relationships, and ministry changes. The starting point of it all is “mindset” — and mindset is simply how you see.

In this lesson we are going to learn together how to “see rightly.” We’ll see the two kinds of eyes; we’ll see how wrong seeing leads people away from God; we’ll see how right seeing brings people back to God; we’ll see how, once the eyes are opened, a life is turned around; and finally we’ll take hold of one key truth: as you see, so you live.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Hunted Man Asks God to Open His Eyes
sections.html:
Our theme verse today is Psalm 119:18: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.”

Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with 176 verses. It is a carefully woven acrostic poem: the whole psalm is divided into 22 stanzas, matching the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet; each stanza has 8 verses, and every verse begins with that stanza’s letter. This structure isn’t a scholar showing off. It is a spiritual discipline — the writer wants to use the entire alphabet, every resource of language, to praise God’s word from beginning to end.

The psalm is unsigned. From its content, the writer was someone holding tightly to God’s word in the midst of trouble: he was derided by the proud (verse 51), persecuted by princes without cause (verse 161), his soul was “weary with sorrow” (verse 28), and he even said he had become “like a wineskin in the smoke” (verse 83). Many commentators think it may have come from an Israelite during or after the exile; some link it to a scribe steeped in the law, someone like Ezra. Whoever the writer was, one thing is very clear: this was a man writing in darkness, under pressure and amid injustice.

Notice that in such circumstances his prayer in verse 18 is not “Change my circumstances,” nor “Destroy my enemies,” but — “Open my eyes.”

The Hebrew for “open” here is gālāh, whose basic meaning is “to uncover, to lift off a covering.” It is often used for drawing back the curtain of a tent or lifting a veil from a face. In other words, the psalmist is saying: Lord, it isn’t that your word isn’t wonderful enough; it’s that there’s a cloth over my eyes. Please lift that cloth away.

And the Hebrew for “wondrous things,” nip̄lā’ôṯ, is the word most often used in the Old Testament to describe God’s earth-shaking acts — the ten plagues in Egypt, the parting of the Red Sea. The psalmist is saying: God, there are wonders on the scale of the Red Sea in your law, yet I read it every day and memorise it every day, and all I see are words. Open my eyes.

Brothers and sisters, what an honest prayer this is. It admits something we are often unwilling to admit: the problem isn’t that God’s word is too shallow; it’s that my eyes are too dim.

In the New Testament, Ephesians 1:18 is the echo of this very prayer. Paul wrote to the church in Ephesus around AD 60 from prison in Rome. Ephesus was then the great city of the province of Asia; in it stood the temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and the city teemed with religions, magic and idols. Paul prays for these believers living in spiritual darkness — and what does he ask for? He doesn’t first ask that they would prosper, be healthy and have everything go smoothly. He asks: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened” (Ephesians 1:17–18).

“The eyes of your hearts” — in the original, literally “the eyes of the heart.” Paul acknowledges that there is a pair of eyes within a person, and if those eyes have not been enlightened by the Holy Spirit, a person can know the Bible backwards and forwards and still see nothing at all.

Fifteen hundred years later, the Reformer John Calvin used a famous image in Book One, chapter six, of his Institutes of the Christian Religion: Scripture is like a pair of spectacles. An old man with failing sight, he said, sees nothing but a blur even when the book in front of him is clearly printed; but once he puts on spectacles, the words stand out sharp and clear before his eyes. God’s word is the pair of spectacles God has prepared for us.

And what we want to say today is this: God has already given us the spectacles. The question is whether we are willing to let the Lord first heal our eyes.

sections.heading: 1. Two Kinds of Eyes: Worldly Eyes and Spiritual Eyes
sections.html:
From the very beginning, Scripture reveals that human beings have two completely different ways of “seeing.”

1. Worldly eyes: wrong seeing

Genesis 3:7: “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.”

This is the first time in human history that “eyes were opened.” But brothers and sisters, please notice: this “opening of the eyes” was not the opening of physical eyes. Before they sinned, Adam and Eve were not blind. They could see every tree in the garden, they could see the birds of the air, and Adam had given names to every living creature. Their physical eyes had always been fine.

So what was opened? What was opened was a way of looking that had turned away from God.

This is exactly what the serpent had promised. In Genesis 3:5 the serpent said, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Satan never blinds people directly. His method is far subtler — he gives you a new pair of eyes, eyes that are “like God,” eyes that put yourself at the centre and judge good and evil for yourself.

And the result? When those eyes opened, what was the first thing they saw?

Not God’s glory, not the beauty of the garden, but this — “they knew that they were naked.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the first mark of worldly eyes: they make people start staring desperately at themselves.

Seeing their own inadequacy; seeing their own shame and weakness; seeing their own problems and lack.

And then the second mark follows immediately. Genesis 3:10: “The man said, ‘I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.’”

Look at the three actions in this verse: afraid, naked, hid. What worldly eyes bring is fear; what fear brings is distance from God; and once they are far from God, people have no option but to start covering themselves by their own efforts — taking fig leaves and sewing themselves a covering.

That fig-leaf covering was humanity’s first “image project.” Leaves wither, split and fall off, yet people keep on sewing. We don’t sew fig leaves any more. We sew academic degrees, job titles, performance figures, our children’s achievements, photos we’ve retouched, other people’s good opinion of us. We use anything we can lay our hands on to cover up the self we don’t dare to face.

That is worldly eyes — they make people live in “self,” away from God.

In the language of 321: worldly eyes are self-centred eyes. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. The essence of that bite of fruit wasn’t appetite; it was “I want to be God myself.” And the moment a person sits down on God’s throne, the first thing he feels isn’t freedom but fear — because that seat is far too big; no human being can sit in it.

Helen Keller is generally credited with saying that the only thing worse than being blind is having sight but no vision. That was exactly the tragedy of Adam and Eve that day: their eyes were “opened,” yet from then on they could no longer see God.

2. Spiritual eyes: right seeing

Thank God, Scripture doesn’t stop at Genesis chapter 3.

Ephesians 1:18: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints,”

The Greek for “enlightened” is phōtizō, meaning “to make shine, to give light.” Its subject is not us; it is God. This is a passive action — we have no way of opening the eyes of our own hearts by straining, by gritting our teeth, or by reading more books. It is the work of the Holy Spirit.

This is precisely what the third of 321’s foundations says: the Holy Spirit is my guide. We do not rely on the brain and ourselves; we rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit. Rely on the brain and you’ll worry; rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice. Spiritual eyes are not the privilege of the clever; they are the grace given to the obedient.

So what do spiritual eyes see? Paul lists it clearly in this prayer: they see what is the hope of God’s calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance, and how exceedingly great is his power towards us who believe.

They see God’s glory. They see God’s promises. They see God’s heart.

Notice the contrast. When worldly eyes open, what they see is “their own nakedness.” When spiritual eyes open, what they see is “the riches of God’s glory.” The same person, the same pair of eyes — yet two entirely different worlds.

In Luke 24:31, the two disciples on the road to Emmaus give us a beautiful picture: “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him.”

Brothers and sisters, there is something about these two disciples well worth pondering. From the moment they left Jerusalem, the risen Jesus walked with them the whole way. He walked with them for seven miles; he listened to their complaints; he explained to them the words of Moses and all the prophets, until their hearts burned within them. Yet Scripture says that before this, “their eyes were kept from recognizing him” (Luke 24:16).

Jesus was right beside them, and they couldn’t recognise him.

Isn’t that a picture of so many Christians? The Lord has been there all along; he has never left. It is our eyes that are clouded. And at the moment Jesus took the bread, gave thanks, broke it and handed it to them — that act of breaking bread, those nail-pierced hands — their eyes were opened.

When spiritual eyes are opened, people recognise Jesus. That is the most important thing of all. The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The purpose of spiritual eyes has never been to let us see more doctrine; it is to let us recognise him.

This also shows us an important principle: spiritual eyes are often opened in the course of walking with the Lord, listening to the Lord’s word and sitting at table with the Lord. Their hearts burned as they listened on the road; their eyes were opened as he broke bread at the table. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what our daily 321 Morning Devotion is for — we haven’t come to complete an assignment; we’ve come to walk with the Lord and let him open our eyes.

sections.heading: 2. Wrong Seeing: It Leads People Away from God
sections.html:
Genesis 3:6: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.”

Brothers and sisters, the fall of humanity began with a single word: “saw.”

The text says “the woman saw that the tree…” It wasn’t the first day she had seen that tree — it stood in the middle of the garden and had been standing there a long time. She passed it every day, saw it every day, and nothing had ever gone wrong. What went wrong was this particular act of seeing, because this time she was looking with the serpent’s words in her head.

This reminds us of something extremely important: our eyes are always shaped by the words we listen to. Whoever you listen to, that is the angle from which you’ll see the world. Listen to the serpent, and you’ll look at that tree with the serpent’s eyes; listen to God, and you’ll look at the whole of life with God’s eyes. That is also why the 321 vision makes “the Bible is my standard” one of the Three Foundations — not one standard among others, but the only standard. Whatever you take as your standard is what you see through.

From this verse we see that wrong seeing has three layers:

1. Looking at the outward appearance: a delight to the eyes

“A delight to the eyes” — the first layer is being drawn by outward appearance.

The eye is the organ most easily moved. Physiologically, the human retina has roughly 120 million rod cells and more than six million cone cells; the optic nerve has about a million fibres; and a sizeable proportion of the brain’s cortex is involved in processing visual information. What an intricate gift of grace God has given us in our eyes! Yet the very same intricate eyes, fixed on the wrong focus, become the quickest breach in our defences.

1 John 2:16 says it precisely: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” The lust of the eyes stands in the middle of the list, yet it is the one that most often opens the door.

2. Looking at the gain: good for food

“Good for food” — the second layer is calculating the gain: what’s in it for me?

Brothers and sisters, look at the scene in Genesis 13. Abram’s herdsmen and Lot’s herdsmen were quarrelling, and Abram let Lot choose first. Scripture says: “Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere … as you go to Zoar” (Genesis 13:10). Lot’s seeing was the seeing of self-interest — he saw water and pasture, he saw rich land, he saw prospects. He chose the best land, then moved his tent step by step until he was living in Sodom, and in the end he lost everything in fire and sulphur.

But in verses 14 and 15 of the same chapter: “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever.’”

Both men “lifted up their eyes and looked.” Lot lifted his eyes and chose for himself; Abram lifted his eyes because God told him to look. Lot saw a plain; Abram saw forever.

Brothers and sisters, when you make decisions today, is it Lot’s kind of seeing or Abram’s kind? Do you pick for yourself first, or do you wait for God to tell you to lift up your eyes?

3. Looking at yourself: to be desired to make one wise

“To be desired to make one wise” — the third layer, and the deepest: I want to be capable on my own, to manage on my own, to be my own master.

Put these three layers together and they have only one essence: self-centred seeing.

And self-centred seeing always produces four results: wanting to be our own master; no longer relying on God; living in the system of the self-centred life; and finally ending up in fear and separation.

The second half of Genesis chapter 3 acts out these four results with perfect clarity. They made themselves master and ate the fruit; they no longer waited for God to speak; they began sewing coverings to hide themselves; and finally they hid among the trees — humanity separated from God, and then people began to be separated from one another as well. Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it” (Genesis 3:12). In a single sentence he shifted the blame onto his wife and onto God at the same time.

Brothers and sisters, this is how terrible pride is: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. When I look at you with self-centred eyes and you look at me with self-centred eyes, all that’s left between us is defensiveness, comparison and blame. Only humility inspires humility, and then both sides win.

Here I want to share a scientific fact with you, one that can really help us understand ourselves.

Each human eye has a “physiological blind spot” on the retina — the point where the optic nerve leaves the eyeball, where there are no light-sensitive cells at all. In other words, in every one of our fields of vision there is a patch where we genuinely see nothing. And yet, remarkably, we never feel that there’s a black hole in our vision, because the brain automatically “fills it in” with the surrounding image, so that we believe what we see is complete.

Brothers and sisters, what an accurate spiritual picture this is: we all have blind spots, and our minds are very efficient at telling us, “You don’t have any blind spots.”

Psychology confirms this too. In research in 1960, the cognitive psychologist Peter Wason described what is now called “confirmation bias”: when gathering information, people unconsciously lean towards looking for evidence that supports what they already think, and ignore the evidence against it. In other words, we don’t first see and then believe; very often we first believe, and only then see.

So the most frightening thing about wrong seeing is not that it sees wrongly, but that it sees wrongly and feels it sees perfectly clearly.

That is what lies behind the stern words the Lord Jesus spoke to the Pharisees. John 9:39: “Jesus said, ‘I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.’”

Brothers and sisters, the only way out is to come back before God and confess: “Lord, there are places I cannot see. Please open my eyes.”

sections.heading: 3. Right Seeing: It Brings People Back to God
sections.html:
Psalm 119:18: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.”

Right seeing does not look at ourselves or at our circumstances. It sees God, sees the truth, sees heavenly reality.

Notice that this verse is a prayer. Right seeing has never been a technique; it is a grace. It isn’t “I must try harder to think positively”; it is “Lord, please open my eyes.” This is the posture of laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. That is humility. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

Scripture gives us three very concrete pictures to help us understand what “heavenly reality” means.

First, 2 Kings 6:17. The chariots, horses and soldiers of the king of Syria had surrounded the city of Dothan by night. Elisha’s servant got up early, took one look and was terrified. He said, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?” Elisha answered, “Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” And then Scripture says: “Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.”

Brothers and sisters, notice: Elisha didn’t pray, “Please remove the Syrian army.” He prayed, “Please open his eyes.” At that moment, the chariots and horses of fire on the mountain weren’t suddenly created — they had been there all along. Only one thing changed: the servant’s eyes.

That is heavenly reality: it has always been there; we just haven’t seen it.

Second, Hebrews 11:27 describes Moses: “By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.”

“As seeing him who is invisible” — this is one of the most precise definitions of faith there is. Faith isn’t charging ahead with your eyes shut. Faith is opening the eyes of the heart and seeing the God who truly exists but whom physical eyes cannot see.

Here I want to mention a scientific fact. The visible light that the human eye can see has wavelengths of roughly 380 to 750 nanometres. But in the whole electromagnetic spectrum — from radio waves whose wavelengths are measured in kilometres to gamma rays — that narrow band is only a minute fraction. Right now, in this very room, radio waves, infrared and microwaves are passing through our bodies, and we feel nothing at all.

Brothers and sisters, if more than ninety-nine per cent of even the material world is invisible to our physical eyes, what grounds do we have to say, “I haven’t seen it, so it doesn’t exist”?

2 Corinthians 4:18 says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”

The Greek word for “look at” is skopeō, the root of the English “scope,” as in telescope. It means “to fix one’s gaze on, to make something one’s aim.” Paul is saying: it isn’t that we don’t look; we point the telescope in a different direction.

This is exactly the shift in perspective the 321 vision speaks of: from man’s perspective to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

Third, Acts 26:18. Before King Agrippa, Paul testifies to the commission the Lord gave him: “to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.”

Brothers and sisters, look at the order in this verse. It is a very clear spiritual pathway: their eyes are opened; then they turn from darkness to light; then from the power of Satan to God; then they receive forgiveness of sins; and finally they share in the inheritance.

The starting point of it all is “eyes opened.”

This also tells us what evangelism is at heart. We don’t go out to persuade people or to win arguments; we ask the Holy Spirit to open people’s eyes. 2 Corinthians 4:4 says: “in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, that the light of the Good News of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not dawn on them.” So when we pray for family members who don’t yet believe, the most powerful prayer isn’t “Lord, change his temper,” but “Lord, open the eyes of his heart.”

When spiritual eyes are opened, a person passes from darkness into light. This isn’t gradual persuasion; it is an instant of illumination.

sections.heading: 4. Once the Eyes Are Opened, the Life Is Turned Around
sections.html:
Paul’s own experience is the clearest example in the whole Bible.

Acts 9:18: “Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.”

Brothers and sisters, let’s look carefully together at the whole picture.

Who was Saul to begin with? He was a star pupil of Gamaliel, a Pharisee of the Pharisees, one of that group of people who were the best at “seeing” Scripture in the Judaism of his day. He knew the law thoroughly, he served zealously, and he believed he was burning with zeal for God. Yet this very man was travelling to Damascus, armed with letters from the high priest, to arrest those who believed in the Lord.

It wasn’t that he didn’t read Scripture. He read Scripture and still couldn’t see Jesus.

On the road to Damascus, a light from heaven flashed all around him. Notice the deep paradox here: after that light shone on him, Scripture says, “Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one” (Acts 9:8).

His eyes were open, yet he was blind.

Brothers and sisters, those three days of blindness were one of the greatest graces God ever gave Paul. For those three days he neither ate nor drank. In the darkness, the man who all his life had judged right and wrong by his own sight could, for the first time, see nothing whatsoever. God had to shut down his worldly eyes before he could open his spiritual ones.

Then Ananias came and laid his hands on him. At that moment, “something like scales fell from his eyes.”

The original word for “scales” describes something flaky, like the scales of a fish. Luke the physician uses this word to record an outward, visible miracle; but through it the Holy Spirit lets us see a spiritual reality — the thick, hard crust over Paul’s eyes, formed of legalism, religious zeal and self-righteousness, fell away.

Outwardly, it was the restoring of sight; in essence, it was the opening of spiritual eyes.

And the result?

From persecuting Jesus, he became a man who lived for Jesus. From opposing God, he became completely obedient to God.

Later he himself explained this turnaround in “seeing.” Philippians 3:8: “Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ”

Brothers and sisters, notice that Paul uses the word “count” twice. He isn’t saying that those things had gone bad; he’s saying that the way he “counted” them had changed. His education was the same education, his pedigree the same pedigree, his credentials the same credentials. The things hadn’t changed; the eyes that valued them had. Once he treated those things as treasure; now he treated Christ as his treasure and counted everything else as refuse.

One change in “seeing” brought about the change of an entire life.

Here I want to mention a very important insight from psychology. In the 1960s the American psychiatrist Aaron T. Beck developed cognitive therapy. From a great deal of clinical observation he found that people’s emotional distress is often caused not directly by events themselves, but by their “automatic thoughts” about those events and the way they interpret them. With the same event, if a person’s interpretation is “I’m finished, I’m worthless,” depression sets in; if the interpretation changes, the emotions change with it. Albert Ellis’s rational emotive behaviour therapy, put forward in the 1950s, describes the same thing using the framework of A (the activating event), B (the belief) and C (the consequence): what really determines C is not A, but B.

Brothers and sisters, psychology can describe this phenomenon, but it has no way of giving anyone a new pair of eyes. Psychology can tell you to “look at it from another angle,” but who can make those scales fall away? Only Jesus.

That is why the 321 vision says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living. But this change isn’t self-hypnosis, and it isn’t positive thinking; it is the illumination of the Holy Spirit. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. When Paul’s eyes were opened, the first thing he did was not to rush off and build a great ministry. First he was baptised — first there was life. Then Barnabas took him under his wing and there was the team at Antioch — that was relationships. Only last came the three missionary journeys — that was ministry.

Get the order wrong, and service becomes just another set of fig leaves.

sections.heading: 5. The Key Truth: As You See, So You Live
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus said something that makes the core of this lesson as clear as it could possibly be. Matthew 6:22–23: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness.”

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: Jesus didn’t say, “The eye is the window of the body.” He said the eye is the “lamp” of the body. A window only lets light in; a lamp decides whether the whole house is light or dark. However your eyes see, that is how your whole self will live.

Let’s compare honestly:

Look at yourself, and you’ll produce inferiority, shame and fear. That was Adam’s condition in the garden. The more you stare at yourself, the more you feel you’re not enough; the more you feel you’re not enough, the more you need to cover up; and the more you cover up, the further you drift from God.

Look at your circumstances, and you’ll produce anxiety, unease and pressure. That was Peter’s condition on the water. Matthew 14:30: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” Brothers and sisters, Peter didn’t sink that day because the wind grew stronger — the wind was strong already; it had been strong when he stepped out of the boat. He sank because he “saw” that the wind was strong. His eyes had moved from Jesus’ face to the crest of the waves.

Look at other people, and you’ll produce comparison, envy and hurt. That was the condition of the ten spies. Numbers 13:33: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.” Notice the astonishing phrase in this verse — “and so we were in their sight.” Did the sons of Anak ever say anything of the kind? Scripture never records it. The spies imagined it themselves. Brothers and sisters, we often spend an enormous amount of energy bearing a verdict that nobody ever actually pronounced on us. Once you’ve seen yourself as a grasshopper, you’ll assume the whole world sees you as a grasshopper too.

On the other hand —

Look at Jesus, and you’ll receive peace. Hebrews 12:2: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” The Greek for “looking to” is aphoraō, meaning “to turn one’s gaze away from everything else and look intently at one thing.” To look to him, you first have to stop looking at certain other things.

Look at the truth, and you’ll receive freedom. John 8:32: “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.”

Look at God, and you’ll receive victory. In 2 Chronicles 20:12, with a powerful enemy before him, Jehoshaphat prayed: “We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” And God fought the battle for them.

Here I want to share a famous psychology experiment with you. In 1999, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris of Harvard University published a study in the journal Perception. They had participants watch a short video, with the task of counting how many times the people in white shirts passed a ball. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the scene, beat their chest and walked out again — about nine seconds in all. The result was astonishing: almost half the participants never saw the gorilla at all.

This phenomenon is called “inattentional blindness.” It tells us something: what people see depends on what they are paying attention to. When you are wholly absorbed in counting passes, a gorilla can walk right in front of you and you won’t see it.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly the condition of many Christians. All our lives we’re busy counting our own passes — counting our results, counting our income, counting what others owe us, counting our own grievances — and so God’s works pass right in front of us, and we don’t see a thing.

So the problem isn’t out there. It’s in your “eyes.”

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: From Self-Centred Eyes to Selfless Eyes
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set this lesson within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations are really the three focal lengths of a new pair of eyes. Jesus is my role model — I learn how to see by following how he sees. The Bible is my standard — I no longer use feelings, public opinion or experience as my eye chart; I correct my vision by God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — I admit I have no power to open my own eyes, and every day I ask him to enlighten them.

The Two Core Values are the centre that these new eyes see. Let Jesus be King: wherever the eyes look, that is where the throne is; when my eyes are fixed only on myself, I am my own king. Let Jesus receive all the glory: when spiritual eyes are opened, the first thing they see is glory — and that glory doesn’t belong to me.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, what the eyes of Genesis chapter 3 established was a self-centred system — with self at the centre, comparing with one another, covering up from one another, shifting blame onto one another. What spiritual eyes establish is God’s system — in which God is God and man is man; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

Going from the old self to the new self is exchanging self-centred eyes for selfless eyes. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When “self” no longer stands in front of our eyes, the view opens up. Have you ever had this experience? A tiny coin, held right up against your eye, can block out the whole sky. “Self” is that coin. It isn’t big; it’s just too close to you.

Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Proud eyes look up at their own seat; humble eyes look up at God’s throne. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

The fivefold change is the very skeleton of this lesson. The mindset changes — I no longer think the problem is my circumstances; I admit the problem is how I see. Then the life changes — fear recedes and faith comes in. Then the daily living changes — facing the same difficulty, I no longer react the same way. Then relationships change — the way I look at my spouse, my children and my co-workers changes, and love begins to flow. Then ministry changes — I no longer serve to prove myself, but so that Jesus may receive glory.

The priority of relationships is also the priority of seeing. First with God — whom do I see first each day? Then with myself — seeing myself through God’s eyes, no longer through a grasshopper’s. Then with others — seeing people through the eyes of grace. And only last of all, with things.

In the 920 practice, brothers and sisters, everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” Today’s lesson gives us a very concrete assignment: when you face your “2” — your spouse, your child, your parents, your colleague — are you looking at them with worldly eyes or with spiritual eyes? Worldly eyes see their faults, what they owe you, the ways they’ve let you down. Spiritual eyes see someone God loves, someone Christ died for, someone in whom God means to work. Which pair of eyes you look at them with determines whether you can live out selflessness (0) towards them and bear the ninefold (9) fruit of the Spirit.

2 Corinthians 5:16–17 says: “Therefore we know no one after the flesh from now on … Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” Knowing no one after the flesh means not looking at people with worldly eyes.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared three practices for us. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset to put them into action.

Practice 1: Discern where your way of seeing is coming from

When you’re feeling emotional or under pressure, stop and ask yourself one question: am I looking at this right now with worldly eyes, or with spiritual eyes?

Brothers and sisters, emotions are an excellent alarm system. When anxiety shows up, it usually means I’m looking at my circumstances; when envy shows up, it usually means I’m looking at other people; when shame shows up, it usually means I’m looking at myself. Don’t rush to suppress the emotion. First use the emotion to find out where your eyes are pointing.

Practice 2: Deliberately shift your focus

When you start looking at the problem or at yourself, practise turning: look at Jesus, look at the promises, look at what God is doing.

Notice that the key word here is “deliberately.” A shift of focus won’t happen automatically — just as those participants counting passes didn’t automatically see the gorilla. You have to say it out loud, on purpose: “Lord, right now I am taking my eyes off this matter. I want to look at you.”

A very practical way to do this: prepare three verses you know best to be your “turning keys.” For example, Hebrews 12:2, 2 Corinthians 4:18, and Psalm 121:1–2: “I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from? My help comes from Yahweh, who made heaven and earth.” The moment emotions rise, read those three verses out loud.

Practice 3: Pray every day for your eyes to be opened

Pray using Psalm 119:18: Lord, open my eyes, that I may see your truth.

Brothers and sisters, this one prayer moves God’s heart more than most of our prayers do. Solomon asked for wisdom, and God added to him what he hadn’t asked for as well. The prayer for opened eyes is just the same.

Going deeper with the eight stages of changing our mindset

Stage one, Information. Today’s lesson is the information: people have two kinds of eyes; the problem isn’t my circumstances but how I see. Please write that sentence somewhere you can see it.

Stage two, Revelation. Information stays in the head; revelation reaches the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to point out one specific thing in your life: “Lord, what matter, what person, am I looking at with worldly eyes right now?” Be still for one minute and wait for him to speak.

Stage three, Conviction. When the Holy Spirit points it out, don’t argue, and don’t explain, “But he really has gone too far.” The first words of surrender are: “Lord, you are right.”

Stage four, Implementation. This week, choose one specific person and one specific matter, and deliberately look at them with new eyes. Look at your husband, your wife, that co-worker who is hardest to work with — and ask yourself: how does Jesus see this person?

Stage five, Evaluation. Every evening, spend three minutes looking back over the day: how many times did I look with worldly eyes, and how many times did I manage to turn? Don’t condemn yourself; just keep an honest record.

Stage six, Correction. Find the moments when your focus is most easily stolen — is it scrolling on your phone late at night? Is it when you see other people’s achievements? Is it when you’re misunderstood? For that moment, prepare one specific action for turning.

Stage seven, Repetition. Restoring sight isn’t a one-time event. Although Paul’s scales fell off all at once, he spent his whole life practising “not looking at the things which are seen.” Spiritual eyes need to be enlightened every day.

Stage eight, Multiplication. Once your eyes have been opened, go and pray for your “2”: “Lord, please open the eyes of his heart.” Then share this lesson with him. One person whose eyes have been opened will bring out a whole company of people whose eyes are opened.

A Gentle Reminder

It isn’t your circumstances that determine your life; it’s “how you see” that determines your life.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that patch of sky we began with.

Those three thousand galaxies had been there all along. The chariots and horses of fire had been there all along. The risen Lord had been walking with his disciples on the road to Emmaus all along. And God’s faithfulness and loving kindness are surrounding you, right now, all along.

When the eyes are wrong, life goes off course; when the eyes are right, life lights up.

The man born blind, after he was healed, faced a barrage of questions from the Pharisees, and he answered with one sentence — the simplest and most powerful of all. John 9:25: “He therefore answered, ‘I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.’”

Brothers and sisters, may this become our testimony too.

Let us no longer look with the eyes of “self,” but with eyes the Holy Spirit has opened — seeing Jesus, fixing our eyes on Jesus, living out Jesus.

Seeing Jesus is the beginning of grace; fixing our eyes on Jesus is the secret of victory; living out Jesus is the purpose of our whole life.

This morning I want to invite you to make a decision: take off that pair of glasses you’ve been wearing for so long. Perhaps they’re called “I’m not good enough.” Perhaps they’re called “He’ll never change.” Perhaps they’re called “There’s no hope in this situation.” Take them off, put them in the Lord’s hands, and say, “Lord, please open my eyes.”

Let Jesus reign as King over the way we see, and let all the glory go to him.

This is the beginning of entering the victorious life.

Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, we confess that we often think the problem lies in our circumstances, in other people, in what has happened to us. Today you have shown us that the real key is how we see. We also confess that there are many blind spots within us that we cannot see for ourselves.

discussion: Genesis 3:6: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.” Wrong seeing has three layers: looking at the outward appearance, looking at the gain, and looking at yourself. Share a recent situation: which layer did you find yourself seeing through? What was the result?

2 Kings 6:17: “Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.” In your present situation, is there something where you see only “the Syrian army” and haven’t yet seen “the chariots and horses of fire”? Name it specifically, and let your small group pray for you, asking the Lord to open your eyes.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Gorilla in the Middle of the Picture
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we open the Bible, I’d like you to join me in a small experiment.

In 1999 two psychologists, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, published a paper called “Gorillas in Our Midst” in the journal Perception. They asked volunteers to watch a very short video: two teams passing basketballs in front of the camera, one team in white shirts, the other in black. The researchers’ instruction was very simple — just one sentence: please count how many passes the white team makes.

The volunteers concentrated hard. Their eyes stayed glued to the ball, darting back and forth with it, not daring to miss a single pass. Halfway through the video, a person in a gorilla suit strolled in from the right of the screen, walked to the very centre, stopped, turned to the camera and thumped its chest — staying there a full nine seconds — and then ambled unhurriedly out to the left.

When the video ended, the researchers first asked: how many passes did the white team make? Almost everyone answered quickly and accurately. Then came the second question: tell me, did you see a gorilla?

Nearly half of the volunteers — about 46 per cent in the experiment — stared back wide-eyed and asked blankly, “What gorilla?”

Brothers and sisters, notice this: their eyes were fine, their sight was normal, the lighting was bright, and the gorilla stood right in the middle of the picture thumping its chest for a full nine seconds. Yet they truly did not see it. Psychology has a name for this: “inattentional blindness.” It means that when your attention is completely taken up with one thing, you become entirely blind to something else that is right in front of you.

The most startling thing about the experiment isn’t that “some people didn’t see the gorilla.” It is this — every one of those who missed it was convinced they had seen perfectly clearly. They’d even argue with you: there was no gorilla in that video at all.

In our last lesson we saw a truth together: people have two kinds of eyes — worldly eyes and spiritual eyes. Today we’re going to take one step further and face a truth that is even more decisive, and even more piercing —

These two kinds of eyes cannot be open at the same time.

If you’re counting passes, you won’t see the gorilla; if you’re fixed on the world, you won’t see God. Whether your life is full of light or full of darkness is, most of the time, not decided by your circumstances, but by which kind of “seeing” you choose. Your circumstances are only the video; what really decides the ending is what you’ve been told to count.

This morning, may the Holy Spirit himself speak to us, rescue us from “thinking we see,” and enable us truly — to see God.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Lamp in the Sermon on the Mount
1. Author, Date and Readers
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by Matthew, one of the Lord Jesus’ twelve disciples, also called Levi, who had been a tax collector in Capernaum. Before the Lord called him, he looked at people, at money and at profit every day with eyes well trained in keeping accounts; once the Lord called him, he left the tax booth behind and followed Jesus with a brand-new pair of eyes. That a man who once could see nothing but silver later wrote down “the lamp of the body is the eye” is a testimony in itself.

Matthew’s Gospel is generally thought to have been written in the 60s AD, chiefly for Jewish Christians scattered in many places. These people had just come out of the traditions of Judaism and were facing a hard question: what is true righteousness, really? Is the righteousness the Pharisees could see the righteousness God wants? Matthew answers them with his whole book: Jesus is the King who brings the kingdom of heaven, and the righteousness of the kingdom begins on the inside.

sections.heading: 2. The Surrounding Context
sections.html:
Matthew 5 to 7 is the familiar “Sermon on the Mount,” the rule of life for the people of the kingdom. Our theme passage sits right in the middle of chapter 6, with a clear context on every side.

In Matthew 6:1–18 the Lord Jesus speaks about three religious disciplines: giving, prayer and fasting. These three sections share a common refrain: don’t do your good deeds before people in order to be seen by them; “your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:4). Right from the start the Lord Jesus is dealing with one question: whose eyes are you living for?

In Matthew 6:19–21 the Lord Jesus speaks about treasure: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth … but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven … for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:19–21).

Matthew 6:22–23, our theme passage, says that the eye is the lamp of the body.

Matthew 6:24 says no one can serve two masters.

Matthew 6:25–34 says do not worry, but seek first God’s kingdom and his righteousness.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Treasure, the eye, two masters, worry — these four passages aren’t four separate sermons; they are one chain, link fastened to link. Where your treasure is, there your heart is; where your heart is, there your eyes look; where your eyes look decides which master you serve; and which master you serve decides whether you worry every day or rest every day. The eye is the link in the middle of the chain.

sections.heading: 3. Laodicea, Ephesus, Dothan
sections.html:
Today we’ll also step into the setting of three other passages, so let’s prepare a little.

Laodicea, in Revelation 3, lay in the Lycus valley in Asia Minor and was a famous, wealthy city of its day. It was a centre of banking and finance; after an earthquake in AD 60 the Laodiceans even refused help from the Roman Empire and rebuilt their homes with their own money. It was known for a glossy black woollen cloth. It also had a well-known medical school that produced a salve for treating eye disease. But it had one fatal weakness: the city had no good water source of its own, so water had to be piped in from far away, and by the time it reached the city it was lukewarm. So every word the Lord spoke to them — lukewarm, buy white garments, buy eye salve — was nothing casual; each one pierced precisely the thing they were proudest of.

The letter to the Ephesians was written by the apostle Paul around AD 60–62, during his first imprisonment in Rome. Ephesians 1:15–23 is a great prayer. Paul didn’t pray about their circumstances; he didn’t pray for their health, their careers or their safety; he prayed for their “eyes.”

The setting of 2 Kings 6 is the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century BC, in the days of the prophet Elisha. The king of Aram sent out raiding parties against Israel again and again, and Elisha, by revelation from God, kept telling the king of Israel where the Aramean ambush lay. The king of Aram was furious and sent a great army by night to surround Dothan, the city where Elisha was. At daybreak a young servant pushed open the door and saw horses, chariots and soldiers all around the city.

Three places, three kinds of people, one shared problem: the eyes.

sections.heading: 1. The Eye Is the Lamp of the Body
sections.html:
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

Here the Lord Jesus sets out an enormously important principle — simple enough for a child to understand, deep enough that a theologian could never finish preaching it:

If the eye is clear, the whole body is full of light; if the eye is dim, the whole body is full of darkness.

sections.heading: 1. The Key Word: Not “Eyesight” but “Single”
sections.html:
The word translated “sound” is the Greek haplous (ἁπλοῦς). Its literal meaning isn’t “perfect twenty-twenty vision” but “single, simple, unfolded, undivided.” In the New Testament and in Jewish writings of the time, the word was also often extended to mean “generous, not grudging.”

Its opposite is ponēros (πονηρός), which literally means “evil.” In everyday Hebrew speech, “a bad eye” was an idiom for someone stingy, envious and greedy. Proverbs 28:22 says, “A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn’t know that poverty waits for him” — the Chinese Union Version renders it “a man with an evil eye.”

So, brothers and sisters, what the Lord Jesus is talking about here is never, from start to finish, a problem for the eye doctor; it is a problem of the heart. He isn’t asking, “Can you see clearly or not?” He is asking, “Are your eyes fixed on one single direction, or are they split in two?”

A divided eye is a divided heart. And a divided heart brings a divided life.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Lamp Is Not the Light Source but the Window
sections.html:
Some people read “the lamp of the body is the eye” and mistakenly think the eye gives off light. In fact, in the imagery of the ancient world, the saying means this: the eye is to the body what a window is to a house. The house itself gives no light; whether it is bright or dark depends entirely on which way the window faces, how big it is and how clean it is.

That is why the Lord Jesus’ next sentence is so frightening: “If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:23) He didn’t say “it is dark outside”; he said “the light that is in you is darkness.”

Brothers and sisters, please hear this distinction clearly:

It isn’t dark outside; it’s dark inside.

It isn’t the world that shapes you; it’s “how you see” that shapes you.

Solomon says in Proverbs 4:23, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The heart is the source; the eyes are the floodgate. Whichever way the floodgate opens, that is the water that fills the source; and whatever fills the source, that is what flows out of your whole life.

sections.heading: 3. Science and Life: One Lens Can Change the Whole World
sections.html:
The human eye is a breathtakingly precise piece of work. The retina of a single eye holds about 120 million rod cells and about 6 million cone cells. These cells turn light into electrical signals and send them through the optic nerve into the brain. But notice this: put just one thin tinted lens in front of so precise a system, and the whole world instantly changes colour.

Put on a pair of yellow-tinted sunglasses, and the blue sky turns khaki, the white clouds turn cream, your wife’s face looks sallow, and you can’t help asking her, “Are you feeling unwell?” The problem isn’t the sky, and it isn’t your wife; it’s the two pieces of plastic on the bridge of your nose.

The Reformer John Calvin, in Book One of his Institutes of the Christian Religion, used a beautiful image: the eyes of the human heart have grown dim through sin, and Scripture is like a pair of spectacles God has given us; put them on, and a world that was blurred and confused shows its clear outlines. Calvin reminds us that the question has never been “Should I wear lenses or not?” — everyone looks at the world through some kind of lens. The question is which pair you are wearing.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight: Change the Mindset and You Change the Life
sections.html:
The 321 vision says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. That order cannot be reversed, and the first link is mindset.

What is a mindset? A mindset is “how you see.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living; change your daily living and you change your relationships; change your relationships, and only then is there genuine ministry.

So, brothers and sisters, if today there’s a place in your daily living where you’re stuck, a relationship that won’t open up, a corner of your service that is dry and powerless, don’t rush to repair the ministry, and don’t rush to change other people. 321 tells us: life first, then relationships, then ministry. And the door to life opens with one key — the mindset.

The second of the Three Foundations says: the Bible is my standard. That standard is the pair of glasses that corrects our sight. When you open your Bible every morning, it isn’t just to “finish the reading plan”; it is so that God can correct the lenses you’ll be wearing today.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Kinds of Eyes Cannot Coexist
sections.html:
“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

Notice that this verse follows straight on from “the lamp of the body is the eye,” in one breath. The Lord Jesus speaks first about the eye and then about two masters, because these are really two sides of the same thing.

sections.heading: 1. Who Is Mammon?
sections.html:
“Mammon” is a transliteration of the Aramaic-derived word mamōnas, and the Chinese Union Version adds a small note here: “Mammon: meaning wealth.” What’s interesting is that the Lord Jesus personifies wealth and calls it a “master.” Money itself is not a master, but once money becomes the focus of your eyes, it automatically takes the master’s seat and starts giving orders — deciding what time you get up, whom you spend time with, what you fear and what you chase.

The Lord Jesus didn’t say “you may not have money”; he said “no one can serve two masters.” Because the eye has only one focal length. You can own two things at once, but you can’t focus on two things at once.

sections.heading: 2. Light and Darkness Cannot Coexist
sections.html:
At the very beginning of Genesis 1, the first separation God makes is to divide light from darkness: “God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness” (Genesis 1:4). Light and darkness can’t be mixed; they can only take turns. In the same way:

When the worldly eyes open, the spiritual eyes close; when the spiritual eyes open, the worldly eyes close.

The apostle Paul says it even more directly: “for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). And again: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

Moses’ life is a footnote to those words: “By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible” (Hebrews 11:27). Brothers and sisters, Moses wasn’t unafraid of Pharaoh because he didn’t see Pharaoh, but because he saw Someone greater.

sections.heading: 3. Science Bears It Out: Dark Adaptation Is a Long Wait
sections.html:
The human retina has two systems. The cone cells work in bright places and handle colour and detail; the rod cells work in dim places and are far more sensitive. These two systems aren’t fully switched on at the same time: when you walk out of blazing sunlight into a pitch-dark room, at first you can’t see a thing, and you have to wait while your eyes slowly “dark-adapt.” The cones adapt fairly quickly, but the rods need roughly twenty to thirty minutes to reach full dark adaptation.

But — and this is the crucial sentence — if someone suddenly switches on a lamp, or you glance down at your phone screen, within a few seconds all twenty minutes of hard-won dark adaptation is reset to zero, and you have to wait all over again. That’s why serious astronomers, whether in an observatory or stargazing up a mountain, use only red-light torches and never switch on a white light.

Brothers and sisters, how much this picture looks like our spiritual life. To grow quiet before God and see the One who is unseen takes time, takes waiting, takes an early morning that isn’t interrupted. Yet a single blast of worldly glare — a news item, a bit of gossip, a comparison, a scroll through your phone — can wreck half an hour of stillness in a few seconds.

This isn’t saying how strong the world’s light is; it’s saying how precious our spiritual eyes are, and how much they need protecting.

sections.heading: 4. Psychology Bears It Out: Attention Is Zero-Sum
sections.html:
As early as 1953, the British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry carried out his famous “dichotic listening” experiments and discovered what later came to be called the “cocktail party effect”: at a noisy party a person can focus on hearing one speaker clearly, but the price is that they hear almost nothing of what’s being said on the other side. Attention is like a spotlight: light it up here, and over there goes dark.

The gorilla at the start is exactly the same principle. Human attention is limited; it is zero-sum. You cannot “look at everything.” You think you’re keeping everything in view, but really you’re only switching; and every time you switch, something is going dark.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: You Must Choose a Side
The first of the 321 vision’s Two Core Values is this: let Jesus be King.
sections.html:
Being King is an exclusive position. A country can’t have two kings, and a heart can’t have two focal points. People’s deepest pain often isn’t “I don’t love God” but “I love God, and I can’t let go of Mammon either,” and so they live as divided people: on Sunday they look like spiritual people, on Monday like worldly people; with their mouths they speak of faith, in their hearts they go by sight.

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When we insist on keeping both sets of eyes under our own control, that is the self-centred life; when we are willing to close one of them and let God reign, that is selflessness.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, which side will you choose?

sections.heading: 3. Wrong Seeing: Thinking You See, When You Are Actually Blind
sections.html:
“Because you say, ‘I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing;’ and don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked.” (Revelation 3:17)

These are words the risen Lord spoke personally to the church in Laodicea, in the revelation generally held to have been received by the apostle John on the island of Patmos around AD 95.

sections.heading: 1. The Most Frightening Distance: Our Self-Assessment and God’s Assessment
sections.html:
Compare the two assessment reports in this verse.

Laodicea’s self-assessment: rich, have gotten riches, need nothing. Three descriptions, each more satisfied than the last.

The Lord’s assessment: wretched, miserable, poor, blind, naked. Five descriptions, each more desolate than the last.

The same church, at the same moment — how far apart are those two reports? Brothers and sisters, the most dangerous place in a person’s spiritual life isn’t being very weak; it’s being very weak and feeling very strong.

Then the Lord prescribes three remedies: “I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, that you may become rich; and white garments, that you may clothe yourself, and that the shame of your nakedness may not be revealed; and eye salve to anoint your eyes, that you may see” (Revelation 3:18).

Laodicea was proud of its banking and finance; the Lord says, buy real gold from me. Laodicea was proud of its black woollen cloth; the Lord says, buy white garments from me. Laodicea was famous for its eye salve; the Lord says, buy the real eye salve from me. What they held in their hands was precisely what they lacked most on the inside. They could heal the eyes of all Asia, but they couldn’t heal their own.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Those Who See Become Blind
sections.html:
John 9 records that after the Lord Jesus healed the man born blind, he said, “I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.” Those of the Pharisees who were with him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?” Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains” (John 9:39–41).

Brothers and sisters, these are some of the most piercing words in the whole Bible. The one who admitted he was blind was healed; those who insisted they could see — their sin remained. It wasn’t that God wouldn’t open their eyes; it was that they never felt any need for them to be opened.

Paul says too: “in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, that the light of the Good News of the glory of Christ … should not dawn on them” (2 Corinthians 4:4). There are two kinds of spiritual blindness: one is being blinded by deception, the other is refusing to look. The second is harder to heal.

sections.heading: 3. Science: You Really Do Have a Blind Spot
sections.html:
Here is a solid physiological fact. In each of your eyes there is a place on the retina where the optic nerve passes out, called the optic disc. That spot has no light-sensitive cells at all; it is a real, physical blind spot. In other words, there is already a hole in your field of vision.

But have you ever noticed a black hole in your field of vision? No. Why not? Because your brain automatically “fills in” that hole with the surrounding image, so you think you’re seeing one whole, complete picture.

Brothers and sisters, please take this to heart: not only do you have a blind spot, but your brain will invent a picture that “looks complete” to cover it. The most dangerous thing has never been a blank; it’s an illusion.

sections.heading: 4. Psychology: Those Who Know Least Are Most Confident
sections.html:
In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger of Cornell University published research in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology showing that the people who did worst on tests of grammar, logic and humour tended to rate themselves far above their actual scores. The reason is simple, and cruel — to recognise that you’re doing badly requires exactly the ability you lack.

Laodicea’s problem was a spiritual version of this kind of self-overestimation. They “looked at the outside and thought they were fine; looked at the world and thought they were rich.” Worldly eyes create an illusion: they make people think they’re doing well when they have actually drifted away from God.

This is the condition of many people today: they have Jesus but don’t know Jesus; they have a faith but no life; they have meetings but no encounter. Why? Because they’re still looking at spiritual things with worldly eyes.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: The Self-Centred Life Keeps Us from Seeing Our Own Poverty
The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.
sections.html:
Pride’s most powerful move isn’t making you bad; it’s making you unable to see that you are bad. A self-centred person has a home-made mirror that reflects only the image he wants to see. Laodicea wasn’t without a mirror; its mirror was broken.

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Only when our focus returns to Jesus do we see our true selves — not a self that is condemned, but a self lit up by grace and able to be healed.

That is why, after the rebuke, the Lord says, “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten. Be zealous therefore, and repent” (Revelation 3:19). When the Lord points out our blindness, it is never to humiliate us; it is to heal us.

sections.heading: 4. Right Seeing: We Need God to Open Our Eyes
sections.html: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.” (Ephesians 1:18)

sections.heading: 1. Spiritual Sight Is Not Learned; It Is Revealed by God
sections.html:
Look at the verse just before this part of Paul’s prayer: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him” (Ephesians 1:17).

“Enlightened” is phōtizō in the original, meaning “to give light, to illuminate”; “the eyes of your hearts” is a literal rendering. Paul knew very well that the Ephesian believers were not short of brains, information or teaching — Ephesus was a great city, and the church there had had three whole years of Paul’s teaching. What they lacked was the light of revelation.

So, brothers and sisters, remember: spiritual sight isn’t something people learn; it is something God reveals. You can build up knowledge by reading books, but you can’t manufacture revelation by reading books. The psalmist says, “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). He didn’t say, “Give me more law”; he said, “Open my eyes.” The Word was there all along; it was the eyes that needed opening.

sections.heading: 2. Morning in Dothan: Three Parties, Three Ways of Seeing
sections.html:
“When the servant of the man of God had risen early, and gone out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was around the city. His servant said to him, ‘Alas, my master! What shall we do?’ He answered, ‘Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.’ Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.” (2 Kings 6:15–17)

The same morning, the same city, the same hills.

What the Aramean army saw: one prophet, one small town, victory in the bag.

What the young servant saw: horses, chariots and soldiers surrounding the city — and so he cried out “Alas!”, trembling from head to foot.

What Elisha saw: the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire — and so he said, perfectly calmly, “Don’t be afraid.”

Pay special attention to Elisha’s prayer. When his servant was afraid, Elisha didn’t pray, “Lord, drive the Arameans away,” nor did he say, “Lord, let us escape safely today.” His prayer was a single sentence: “Please open his eyes, that he may see.”

God answered. And then? Did the Aramean army withdraw? No. The horses were still there, the chariots were still there, the soldiers were still there; not one piece of the siege had gone.

The circumstances didn’t change, but the “seeing” did. And so fear turned into faith.

Brothers and sisters, what a great comfort this is. The way God most often answers our prayers isn’t by moving the mountain at once, but by first opening our eyes, so that we see, on the other side of the mountain, whole ranks of horses and chariots of fire.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Moment the Eyes Are Opened
sections.html:
The Bible has several moments when “eyes are opened,” and each one is a turning point in a life.

The two disciples on the road to Emmaus walked the whole way with the risen Lord and listened to him explain the Scriptures the whole way, yet they didn’t recognise him. Not until, at the table, the Lord took the bread, gave thanks, broke it and handed it to them — “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him” (Luke 24:31).

Saul of Tarsus was struck down by a blazing light on the road to Damascus and could not see for three days; after Ananias laid his hands on him, “Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight” (Acts 9:18). A Pharisee who thought he saw better than anyone first had to be truly blind for three days before he learned what seeing means.

sections.heading: 4. Science: Even the Best Eyes Need Light
sections.html:
How sensitive is the human eye? Modern vision research tells us that, when fully dark-adapted, a single rod cell can respond to just a handful of photons — clear evidence of the Creator’s precise design.

But, brothers and sisters, think about this: put someone with perfect eyes and better-than-perfect vision into a room with absolutely no light — what can he see? Nothing at all. Because seeing has never been only a matter of the eye; it is even more a matter of light. Without light, the best eyes are blind.

The psalmist said it long ago: “For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light” (Psalm 36:9).

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: The Holy Spirit Is My Guide
sections.html:
The third of 321’s Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Of the eight stages of changing our mindset, the first is Information and the second is Revelation. Information you can find for yourself; Revelation you must ask God for. Many brothers and sisters are rich in Information — they’ve heard hundreds of sermons and read dozens of books — yet they’ve stayed stuck at stage one, because they’ve never once knelt down and said, “Lord, please open my eyes.”

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. The young servant relied on his brain and did the arithmetic: a great Aramean army against two men, and the answer came out as “Alas!” Elisha relied on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and the answer he saw was “Don’t be afraid.” The same problem, different eyes, different answers.

sections.heading: 5. The Key to Opening Spiritual Eyes: Humility
sections.html: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (James 4:6)

sections.heading: 1. Spiritual Eyes Are Grace, and the Entrance to Grace Is Humility
sections.html:
If spiritual sight is God’s revelation and God’s grace, then the next question is a very practical one: to whom does God give grace?

The Bible’s answer is entirely consistent from the Old Testament to the New. Proverbs 3:34 says, “Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.” James quotes it, and Peter quotes it too: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5).

Notice the word “resists.” In Greek it is antitassomai, originally a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” God isn’t merely a little cool towards the proud; he draws up his ranks and stands against them. How serious that is.

sections.heading: 2. Four Passages, One Promise
sections.html:
“He will guide the humble in justice. He will teach the humble his way.” (Psalm 25:9) The humble are guided and taught.

“The humble have seen it, and are glad. You who seek after God, let your heart live.” (Psalm 69:32) The humble see — and seeing, they are glad.

“For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: ‘I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.’” (Isaiah 57:15) The God who dwells in the high and holy place has a second address: the heart of the humble.

“At that time, Jesus answered, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.’” (Matthew 11:25)

Look carefully: the very same “these things” are hidden from the wise and understanding and revealed to infants. It isn’t that God plays favourites; it’s that the posture is different. When someone holds his chin up, the light can’t get into his eyes; when someone bows his head, the light comes in.

So the conclusion is very clear: the humble have their eyes opened by God; the proud have their eyes covered by God.

sections.heading: 3. The Marks of an Infant
sections.html:
The word “infants” in Matthew 11:25 is the Greek nēpios, meaning a little child who can’t yet talk. Why does the Lord Jesus single out infants? Infants have three marks:

First, simplicity. An infant doesn’t listen to you while calculating your motives in his heart.

Second, dependence. An infant never thinks, “I can manage on my own.” When he’s hungry he cries; he knows he has nothing.

Third, not being self-opinionated. An infant has no position to defend, no face to save, no foregone conclusion to prove.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the selfless life. Selflessness isn’t childishness, and it isn’t having no thoughts of your own; the Lord Jesus himself said, “be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Matthew 10:16). Selflessness is this: I no longer treat my own opinion as the final verdict.

sections.heading: 4. Psychology: Only the Humble Can Tell True from False
sections.html:
In recent years psychology has developed a field of research called “intellectual humility,” meaning a person’s willingness to admit that their beliefs might be wrong. In 2017 Mark Leary of Duke University and his colleagues published research in the Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin showing that people higher in intellectual humility were better at telling strong arguments from weak ones when evaluating them, and more willing to revise their position in the light of new evidence.

In other words, even at the natural level, science has observed the same principle: humble people see more accurately. How much more in spiritual things.

sections.heading: 5. An Illustration and a Famous Saying
sections.html:
In ancient times there was often a small door beside the city gate, low and narrow; a man leading a camel couldn’t get through until he had unloaded the goods and made the camel kneel and lower its head. Spiritual sight is like that: if you don’t put down your load and bend your knee, the door is right there, but you simply can’t get in.

The English writer C. S. Lewis, in his 1944 address “Is Theology Poetry?”, said something that is often quoted: “I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen: not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the essence of spiritual eyes. It isn’t that you study the sun; it’s that the sun lights up your whole field of vision.

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: Humility Overcomes Pride
sections.html:
