The 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. It also says: pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win.

This holds not only in our relationships but even more in this matter of “seeing.” Proud people argue with others over who sees rightly, and in the end neither of them sees; a humble person says, “I may have seen it wrongly — Lord, open my eyes,” and in the end both are lit up by the light.

321 says the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Humility is the password for all four layers of relationship. Humble before God, I can see God; humble before myself, I can see my true self; humble before others, I can see the worth of my brothers and sisters; humble in the things I do, I can see God’s timetable rather than my own.

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: Only Selflessness Can See Rightly
sections.html: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

sections.heading: 1. Two Equations
sections.html:
Having come this far, we can gather the whole lesson into two simple equations:

Pride equals the self-centred life, and the self-centred life means wanting to see with my own eyes.

Humility equals selflessness, and selflessness means letting God lead my seeing.

And so: in the self-centred life, the worldly eyes stay open; only in selflessness can the spiritual eyes be opened.

This is also the truth behind the first tragedy in the whole Bible. The serpent said to the woman, “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). Humanity really did eat, and their eyes really were “opened” — “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked” (Genesis 3:7). Satan didn’t lie; he just didn’t finish the sentence: their eyes were opened, but it was the worldly pair that opened. Humanity gained the right to see for itself, and the price was losing the ability to see God.

From that day on, humanity’s problem has always been the same one: I want to see for myself.

sections.heading: 2. Selflessness Is Not Having Nothing; It Is Entering into the Fullness
The 321 vision puts it very precisely: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out.
sections.html:
Selflessness doesn’t mean wiping yourself out, or becoming someone with no opinions, no feelings and no worth. Selflessness means letting Jesus become my eyes.

No longer seeing with myself, but letting Christ see in me.

The apostle Paul says it like this: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Notice that Paul didn’t disappear. He went on writing letters, travelling, shepherding and suffering. What he lost was not himself, but that “self-centred way of seeing.”

sections.heading: 3. The Most Fitting Illustration: The Lens of a Telescope
sections.html:
You’re looking at the stars through a telescope. Tell me — do you see the lens, or the stars?

If what you see is the lens — dust, fingerprints, scratches — then the telescope has failed. The greatest achievement of a good lens is to make you forget it exists altogether, so that you see only the stars.

Our eyes are more wonderful still. You can go a whole day with healthy eyes and never be aware of them at all. When do you become keenly aware that you have eyes? When they’re inflamed, when there’s grit in them, when they’re dry and sore.

Brothers and sisters, “selflessness” works the same way. The healthiest state of the self isn’t self-inflation, nor self-destruction, but a self that is no longer in the way. When I’m no longer intensely aware of “me,” I begin to see “him” clearly.

This is exactly what the Lord Jesus said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). A pure heart is haplous — a single heart, an undivided heart, a lens with no fingerprints and no scratches.

sections.heading: 4. Jesus Is Our Role Model of Selflessness
sections.html:
The first of 321’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model.

Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

“Emptied himself” is the most perfect definition of selflessness. And how did the Lord Jesus “see” while he ministered on earth? He said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19).

Listen: even the Son of God, on earth, didn’t see by himself, but looked at what the Father was doing. How much more should we?

sections.heading: 5. Seeing from Four Perspectives
sections.html:
321 says that our perspective must shift from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, and from the worldly to the godly.

Seen from the human perspective, the young servant saw two against ten thousand; seen from God’s perspective, Elisha saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.

Seen from the earthly perspective, Laodicea saw banks, wool and eye salve; seen from the heavenly perspective, the Lord saw the wretched, the miserable and the poor.

Seen from the temporary perspective, the world sees only what is seen; seen from the eternal perspective, Paul looked at the things which are not seen.

Brothers and sisters, these four pairs of perspectives are four pairs of glasses that today’s lesson wants to give you.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From Seeing to Being Built Up
1. The Three Foundations Are Three Lights
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model — he is the Lord who “emptied himself,” and the Son who didn’t see by himself. To see rightly, first look at how he sees.

The Bible is my standard — Scripture is the pair of glasses God has given us, correcting all our sight that sin has distorted. Any “seeing” that doesn’t fit the Bible, however beautiful, moving or reasonable, doesn’t count.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — revelation isn’t the result of human effort; it is the work of the Holy Spirit. So every day we must pray: Lord, enlighten the eyes of my heart.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values Are One Focal Point
sections.html:
Let Jesus be King — the eye has only one focal length, and the heart can have only one King. Whom you choose to let reign as King today decides which eyes you’ll use to look at the world today.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when our spiritual eyes are opened, the first reaction isn’t “How wonderful I am, I have spiritual gifts,” but falling down in worship. Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Therefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5–6). Anyone who has truly seen God will give the glory to God.

sections.heading: 3. The Goal: Establish God’s System
sections.html:
Why does God want to open our eyes? Not just so we’ll feel a little better and a little less anxious. God opens our eyes in order to establish God’s system.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Only a group of people whose eyes have been opened, gathered together, can establish God’s system; a group of people who only think they see, gathered together, will just build another Tower of Babel.

sections.heading: 4. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships
sections.html:
The 920 practice says: every person we’re in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, this is the very training ground for “seeing.” How do you see your spouse? How do you see the co-worker who is always late? How do you see the person who once hurt you? Look with worldly eyes, and what you see is faults, debts and unpaid bills; look with spiritual eyes, and what you see is someone for whom Christ laid down his life. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” Only when you see rightly can the fruit be borne.

The 235 relationships say: become a “2” with a selfless person — your spiritual companion; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Notice Elisha’s relationship with that young servant. Elisha didn’t laugh at him for being a coward, didn’t scold him for unbelief, and didn’t show off with “I saw it long ago.” He did what a spiritual father ought to do — he prayed for his son and asked God to open his eyes.

Brothers and sisters, is there a “servant” beside you, standing at the city gate in the early morning, trembling? The best thing you can do for him isn’t to analyse the situation for him; it’s to pray for him: Lord, please open his eyes, that he may see.

sections.heading: 5. The Fivefold Change
sections.html:
A change of mindset: I no longer believe “seeing is believing”; I believe that faith is my evidence.

A change of life: from fear to faith, from complacency to humility.

A change of daily living: the first thing in the morning is no longer scrolling my phone, but asking God to enlighten the eyes of my heart.

A change of relationships: I begin to look at every “2” around me with heaven’s eyes.

A change of ministry: I no longer work out of my own zeal; I see what the Father is doing, and then I do it.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Practices, Eight Stages
sections.html:
This lesson has three practices for daily living. We keep the practices from the lesson text and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Make one choice every day — which eyes will I use?

Look at your circumstances? Or look at God? In the first three minutes after you open your eyes each morning, you have to make this choice.

Information: first fix today’s truth firmly in your memory — the two kinds of eyes cannot be open at the same time. Copy the theme verse somewhere you’ll see it.

Revelation: don’t stop at knowing. Kneel down and pray: Lord, let these words become light inside me, not just knowledge in my head.

Conviction: say one honest sentence to God in your heart: I admit that for most of my days I’ve been living with worldly eyes.

Implementation: start today. Change your first words on waking to: “Lord, today I want to see with your eyes.”

Practice 2: Practise “closing the worldly eyes”

Compare less, worry less, judge by feelings less; don’t let the world’s values take charge of you.

Implementation: this week, pick one specific thing to close off. For example: no social media in the hour before bed; or whenever you catch yourself comparing in your heart — income, children, the fruit of your ministry — stop at once and quietly recite 2 Corinthians 5:7: “for we walk by faith, not by sight.”

Evaluation: every evening take three minutes to look back: at what moment today did my worldly eyes suddenly snap open? What was I looking at?

Correction: identify your own personal “glare.” Just as astronomers know they mustn’t switch on a white light, you need to know what most easily wrecks your dark adaptation, and then set a boundary against it.

Practice 3: Practise “humbling yourself so God can open your eyes”

Pray every day: “Lord, I won’t rely on my own seeing; let me see what you see.”

Repetition: 321 says a change of mindset isn’t a one-off event; it is a matter of repetition. This prayer isn’t one you pray once today; you pray it every day for forty days, a hundred days. God often doesn’t open our eyes all the way at once; it’s like the blind man at Bethsaida, who the first time saw people “like trees walking,” and only when the Lord laid his hands on him again did he see everything clearly (see Mark 8:24–25). Don’t give up because you can’t see clearly yet.

Multiplication: learn from Elisha. When someone near you is trembling with fear, be the one who prays for them and asks God to open their eyes. Anyone who has truly learned to see will bring others to see as well.

A Gentle Reminder

It isn’t that you can’t see; it’s which eyes you choose to use.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: You Will Begin to See God
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we’re nearly at the end. Let me distil today’s message into one sentence:

The spiritual life doesn’t lie in how much you know, but in how much you see.

Those who know a great deal but cannot see are Laodicea; those who see and are glad are the humble of Psalm 69. Knowledge can be piled up; sight has to be given. And from creation until now, God’s condition for giving sight has been only one — humility.

When you’re willing to lay yourself down and let God open your eyes, three things will happen:

Darkness turns to light — because when the eye is sound, the whole body is full of light.

Fear turns to faith — because what you see is no longer horses, chariots and soldiers, but a mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.

Confusion turns to clarity — because you no longer serve two masters; your heart has become single.

This morning the Lord’s invitation is very concrete. He doesn’t want you to become cleverer; he wants you to let him reign as King. He doesn’t want you to try harder to see; he wants you to humble yourself and let him become your eyes.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. When one day we truly see, we will never say, “I’ve finally figured it out.” We will only fall down like Job and say: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.

Brothers and sisters, you will no longer just look at the world — you will begin to see God!

keyVerses: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)
declarations: Lord, I choose to humble myself before you and lay down my own views and judgements! Open my eyes, and let me see your truth, your works and your glory! Let me live in the light and no longer in darkness!
practices: Make one choice every day — which eyes will I use?
Practise “closing the worldly eyes”
Practise “humbling yourself so God can open your eyes”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you that this morning you have shone on us through your Word. Lord, we confess that we are often like Laodicea, thinking ourselves rich when we are poor, thinking we see when we are blind. And we are often like that young servant: the moment we open our eyes we see only the horses, chariots and soldiers surrounding us, and we begin to be afraid.

Lord, enlighten the eyes of our hearts. Give us a spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that we truly know you. Take away the pride and the self-centred life within us, and make us like infants — simple, dependent and not self-opinionated. Teach us to close our worldly eyes, so that our spiritual eyes can be opened.

Lord, from today on we will no longer see by ourselves. Would you see in us and live in us. Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our workplaces, reign as King in our church. May all the glory be yours, for ever and ever. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 6:24 says, “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” Take three minutes of quiet and think honestly: this week, what specific thing is your “Mammon” using to steal your focus? How do you plan to close that eye?

2 Kings 6:17 says, “Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.” Share a time when “your circumstances didn’t change, but what you saw did.” Right now, is there someone near you who is afraid, someone God wants you to pray for, asking him to open their eyes?
l120.title: Let God Open My Eyes
l120.subtitle: Seeing Rightly (Part 2) — Two Kinds of Eyes Cannot Be Open at Once
l120.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: You Have to See It Before You Receive It
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this morning I’d like you first to answer a question that is very simple, and very hard: over this past week, where have your eyes rested most often?

On your phone screen? On the figures in your bank account? On what other people think of you? On your own aches and illnesses, your children’s grades, the look on your boss’s face? Or on God’s kingdom, God’s righteousness, God’s eternal purposes?

We often assume life runs in this order: first you “receive,” then you “see.” Once I have money, I’ll be able to see a future; once my health is better, I’ll be able to see hope; once my circumstances change, I’ll be able to see God. But the order the Bible gives us is exactly the opposite — first you “see,” and then you “receive.”

This isn’t chicken soup for the soul; it is a consistent truth of Scripture. What you see is what you pursue; what you pursue is what you receive. Your eyes decide your steps, and your steps decide your whole life. So the key isn’t how much you own right now; it is this — what are you actually looking at?

There is a deeply moving scene in Genesis 13. When Abram and Lot parted ways, Lot “lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere … as you go to Zoar” (Genesis 13:10), and he chose the land that looked richest. But the Bible goes on: “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever’” (Genesis 13:14–15).

Both of them “lifted up their eyes and looked.” Lot saw the water and pasture in front of him; Abram saw God’s promise. Lot gained Sodom; Abram gained the whole land of Canaan, for ever. Brothers and sisters, two men lifted their eyes at the same time, looked in different directions, and came to completely different ends.

A psychologist’s experiment changed the way I think about “seeing” for good. In 1999 the American psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris published a famous study in the journal Perception called “Gorillas in Our Midst.” They asked volunteers to watch a video and count how many times the players in white passed the ball. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the picture, stopped in the very centre, thumped its chest and then slowly walked off — nine seconds in all. And the result? About half of the volunteers didn’t see the gorilla at all.

Their eyes were plainly open, the light was plainly entering their eyes, the image was plainly landing on their retinas — yet they did not “see.” Psychology calls this “inattentional blindness.” The experiment tells us something frightening: people don’t see everything in front of them; people see only what they pay attention to.

Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of the spiritual world. God’s grace surrounds us every day, God’s glory fills the whole earth, God’s kingdom is right in front of our eyes — but our attention is on other things, so we “can’t see.” It isn’t that God isn’t there; it’s that we aren’t looking.

The theme of today’s lesson is this: what we see, we shall surely receive. Together we’re going to adjust our vision — from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly, from the human perspective to God’s perspective. Because “what you see is what you will receive.”

sections.heading: Scripture Background: How a Crushed Man Saw Eternal Glory
sections.html:
Our theme verse comes from 2 Corinthians 4. To understand it rightly, we need to know who said it and in what situation.

Second Corinthians was written by the apostle Paul, around AD 55–57, most likely in Macedonia. It was addressed to the church in Corinth. Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, sitting on the isthmus that links the Aegean and the Adriatic; it was the richest, busiest and most licentious commercial city of its day. It had a temple to Aphrodite (Venus), and in the Greek world of the time “to live like a Corinthian” had almost become a byword for debauchery and luxury.

The Corinthian church grew up in a city like that. They had gifts, eloquence and knowledge — but they also had factions, quarrels and pride. Worse still, a group calling themselves “super-apostles” had come into the church. They had a fine appearance, polished speech and a fondness for credentials, and they turned round and criticised Paul: “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10). In a city that worshipped appearances, success and an impressive presence, Paul — a weathered old apostle covered in scars — really did look “not successful enough.”

So in chapter 4 Paul says something that has rung down the centuries: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7). “Clay,” in the Greek, is ὀστράκινος (ostrakinos), the cheapest, most ordinary earthenware, the kind that breaks the moment you drop it. Paul admits: I am a clay jar. But what the clay jar holds is a priceless treasure.

Then he lists four contrasts in one breath: “We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not to despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:8–9). This isn’t theory; it is Paul’s CV. Second Corinthians 11 records that he received forty lashes minus one from the Jews five times; he was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, and spent a night and a day in the open sea.

How can a man beaten black and blue still not lose heart? Paul gives the answer in verses 16–18: “Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory, while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”

Notice two astonishing contrasts. The first is a contrast of time: “light … for the moment” against “exceedingly … eternal weight.” The second is a contrast of objects: “the things which are seen” against “the things which are not seen.”

The word for “look at” is the Greek σκοπέω (skopeō). It doesn’t mean a casual glance; it means “to fix your gaze on, to take careful aim.” The English word “scope” (as in telescope, or a rifle scope) comes from the same root. Paul means: my life has a scope, and what I’ve trained that scope on isn’t the circumstances I can see but the glory I can’t.

“Temporal” in the original is πρόσκαιρος (proskairos), literally “for a season, lasting only as long as the time lasts” — when the time is gone, so is it. “Eternal” is αἰώνιος (aiōnios), belonging to the ages, not bound by time.

Brothers and sisters, the same lashes, the same prison cells, the same shipwrecks — seen with worldly eyes, they are utter defeat; seen with heavenly eyes, they are “working an eternal weight of glory.” The circumstances didn’t change; the way of seeing did. And when the way of seeing changes, the whole of life changes.

This is exactly the fivefold change the 321 vision speaks of: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Everything starts with mindset — and mindset is “how you see.”

sections.heading: 1. Two Kinds of Seeing: The Temporary and the Eternal
sections.html:
“while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

In this verse the Bible divides everything in the universe, cleanly and neatly, into two kinds: what can be seen is temporary; what cannot be seen is eternal.

Notice that Paul doesn’t say, “What can be seen is bad, and what cannot be seen is good.” The Bible never despises the material world; God made all things and saw that they were good. What Paul is talking about is how long things last: what can be seen will pass away; what cannot be seen will remain.

Let’s set them side by side. The body can be seen, but the body wastes away — Paul himself says “our outward man is decaying.” Money can be seen, but money disappears — “where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal” (Matthew 6:19). Status can be seen, but status changes — high up today, perhaps forgotten tomorrow.

But what about the other side? Spiritual life can’t be seen, yet it is eternal; our relationship with God can’t be seen, yet it is eternal; heavenly reward can’t be seen, yet it is eternal. The apostle John says, “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:17).

Here is a fascinating scientific fact that can help us. The visible light the naked human eye can see has wavelengths of only about 380 to 700 nanometres — a share of the whole electromagnetic spectrum so small it is almost negligible. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays — all of them really exist, and not one of them can our naked eyes see. At this very moment countless electromagnetic waves are passing through your body and mine, and we have no idea.

More astonishing still, according to the observations released in 2013 from the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite, ordinary matter in our universe — the stuff that makes up stars, the earth, your body and mine — accounts for only about 5 per cent; the rest is about 27 per cent dark matter and about 68 per cent dark energy, all of it invisible to us.

Brothers and sisters, even in the natural world what can be seen is only 5 per cent. What makes you think that in the spiritual world “what can be seen” is all there is?

This is just what Hebrews says: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Faith isn’t imagining something out of thin air; faith is connecting to a reality that is greater and more real. Of how Moses was able to leave the palace of Egypt, the Bible says: “By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible” (Hebrews 11:27).

“As seeing him who is invisible” — how beautiful those words are. The physical eye can’t see him, but the eye of the heart sees him perfectly clearly.

Second Kings 6 paints a wonderful picture. The king of Aram sent a great army by night to surround the city of Dothan. Elisha’s servant got up early, looked out — and there were horses, chariots and soldiers surrounding the city. In panic he said, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?” Elisha said, “Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” Then Elisha prayed: “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha (2 Kings 6:17).

Brothers and sisters, notice: the horses and chariots of fire had been there all along. They didn’t appear after the prayer; it was after the prayer that the servant saw them. From beginning to end the circumstances never changed; all that changed was a pair of eyes.

I often think that our morning devotion is really that one prayer, every morning: “Yahweh, please open my eyes, that I may see.” The psalmist asked the same: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).

In the 321 vision, this is the most fundamental shift of perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective; from the earthly perspective to the heavenly; from the temporary perspective to the eternal; from the worldly perspective to the godly. These four shifts are really one thing — changing your eyes.

And the way to change your eyes is the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — I learn how he sees; the Bible is my standard — I see as the Bible sees; the Holy Spirit is my guide — I ask the Holy Spirit to open my eyes. Once the Three Foundations stand firm, your way of seeing naturally turns around.

Brothers and sisters, remember this sentence: if you look at the temporary, you’ll live in the temporary; if you look at the eternal, you’ll live out the eternal.

sections.heading: 2. Wrong Seeing: Living for “Zero”
sections.html:
“For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.” (1 Timothy 6:7)

“‘Vanity of vanities,’ says the Preacher; ‘Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.’” (Ecclesiastes 1:2)

These words Paul wrote to Timothy are very plain, and very sharp. Naked we came from our mother’s womb, and naked we shall return. In the few decades in between we grab for all we’re worth, and in the end we can’t take a single thing with us.

The word “vanity” in Hebrew is הֶבֶל (hebel), which originally means “breath, vapour, a puff of white mist.” Ecclesiastes opens with “vanity of vanities,” the Hebrew way of expressing the superlative — like “King of kings” or “Holy of Holies” — meaning “vanity to the uttermost.” The white breath you puff out on a winter morning: reach out to grab it, and all you catch is air — Solomon says that is what everything people chase under the sun is like.

I want to use a very true-to-life illustration from the lesson text to show this.

On the day you were born, you received the first piece of paper of your life — a birth certificate. You went to school and received certificate after certificate: diplomas, degree certificates, all sorts of licences. You went to work and every month received a payslip. You worked hard for half a lifetime and finally got the title deed to a house, a car’s registration, a savings book, investment statements. You filed these papers away in a drawer one by one; they were the report card of your life.

And then one day, the last piece of paper arrives — a death certificate.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed something? What’s written on all those earlier papers is “numbers”: marks, salary, square footage, savings. But on that last piece of paper there are no numbers at all. In that moment, every number is reset to zero.

If all our lives we live only for those numbers, then we are — living for “zero.”

Jesus told a parable about a rich fool. The man’s land produced a bumper crop, and he said to himself: “This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. I will tell my soul, ‘Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.’” But God said to him, “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared — whose will they be?” (Luke 12:19–20). Jesus drew the conclusion: “So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God” (Luke 12:21).

Pay attention to what the rich man says. In just two short verses, “I” and “my” come up eight times: I will, my barns, my grain, my goods, my soul. His problem wasn’t that he had money; his problem was that there was only one person in his world — himself.

This is what the 321 vision calls the self-centred life. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. In the Garden of Eden, “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6). You see, the fall began with “seeing” — the eyes looked wrongly, the hand reached wrongly, and human history went wrong.

In psychology, there are two studies worth thinking quietly about.

The first: in 2010 the Nobel laureate in economics Daniel Kahneman and the economist Angus Deaton published a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in America, analysing more than 450,000 survey responses from Americans. They found that income does raise people’s emotional well-being, but that beyond an annual income of about 75,000 US dollars the effect clearly levels off. In other words, money can relieve the pain that poverty brings, but it can’t buy a matching increase in happiness.

The second: the Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed more than seven hundred men through the whole course of their lives — one of the longest-running studies of happiness in human history. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, sums up decades of findings in one sentence: what keeps people healthy and happy isn’t wealth, and it isn’t fame; it is good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, these two studies can’t prove the Bible, and the Bible doesn’t need them to prove it. But they are like two mirrors reflecting a fact: humanity has used its most rigorous methods to look for the answer, and the conclusion it finally reached is what the Bible said three thousand years ago — “all is vanity.” And what God has always valued is relationships: first our relationship with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and only last with things.

This is what 321 means by: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Brothers and sisters, worldly eyes have one distinctive feature: they can see only the present, never eternity. They can see this quarter’s financial report with perfect clarity, yet not see the judgement seat of eternity; they can spot every last one of other people’s faults, yet not see their own pride.

Lord, have mercy on us. Don’t let us be busy all our lives, only to discover at the end that we were living for “zero.”

sections.heading: 3. Right Seeing: Investing the Temporary in the Eternal
sections.html:
“but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal.” (Matthew 6:20)

If everything that can be seen is going to pass away, should we then flee the world, hide in a cave and want nothing at all?

No. Brothers and sisters, please pay special attention to this: Jesus never rejected earthly resources. He didn’t say, “Don’t have treasure”; he said, “Don’t lay up your treasure on earth; lay it up in heaven.” What he teaches isn’t about “having or not having” but about “how you use it.”

Matthew 6:19–21 is one complete passage: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”

In Jesus’ day wealth came mainly in three forms: grain, clothing, and gold and silver. Grain gets eaten by pests, clothing gets eaten by moths, gold and silver get dug through and stolen by thieves. In one breath Jesus names the fate of all three kinds of wealth — not one of them can be kept safe.

But he doesn’t stop there. He says: there is a bank that no pest can get into, that rust cannot touch, that no thief can break into. That bank is called “heaven.” And the way to transfer funds into that bank is to invest the temporary resources of this life in eternal things.

So, brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: money isn’t the problem; the problem is how you see money. The same hundred dollars, if it’s for yourself, goes to zero along with you; if it’s for God, it goes into eternity along with God.

Here there is a crucial watershed, and the difference comes down to just two words: “for whom.”

Use your time to love people — and that time enters eternity. For the Lord says, “because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

Use your money to bless people — and that money enters eternity. For “He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh” (Proverbs 19:17).

Use your life to serve God — and that life enters eternity. For “whoever will lose his life for my sake, will save it” (Luke 9:24).

Paul puts it even more clearly to Timothy: “Charge those who are rich in this present world that they not be arrogant, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share; laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life” (1 Timothy 6:17–19).

Notice the phrase “laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come.” So giving isn’t a loss; it’s moving house. It isn’t a reduction; it’s a transfer. You move your earthly savings into an account that can never go bankrupt.

On 28 October 1949 the missionary Jim Elliot wrote a sentence in his journal that later became the motto of countless missionaries: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Seven years later, in 1956, he and four co-workers were killed in Ecuador while taking the gospel to the Waodani people (then known as the Auca); he was just twenty-eight. Seen with worldly eyes, it was a total waste; but that people later turned to Christ, and his wife, Elisabeth Elliot, went back and lived among the very tribe that had killed her husband. Brothers and sisters, this is investing the temporary in the eternal.

C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, also said something profound: “If you read history you will find that the Christians who did most for the present world were just those who thought most of the next.” Those words overturn a common misunderstanding. People assume that anyone who thinks about heaven won’t bother with earthly things. The truth is the exact opposite: Wilberforce, who brought about the abolition of slavery; Müller, who opened hospitals and orphanages; Nightingale, who founded the spirit of the Red Cross — it was precisely people with eternity in their hearts who left the deepest footprints on earth.

Psychology also gives us some sidelong confirmation. From the late 1960s the Stanford psychologist Walter Mischel ran his famous “marshmallow experiments”: researchers put a marshmallow in front of a young child and told them that if they could wait until the researcher came back before eating it, they would get two. Some children ate it at once; others tried every trick they could — covering their eyes, turning their backs, singing — and held out to the end. Mischel’s core finding was that the children who managed to delay gratification mostly didn’t do it by sheer willpower; they did it by “diverting their attention” — by not looking at the sweet.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Even a four-year-old understands that the way to overcome the temptation in front of you isn’t to grit your teeth; it’s to take your eyes off it and look somewhere else.

Hebrews taught us this long ago: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2). How did Jesus endure the cross? He saw “the joy that was set before him.” His eyes looked beyond the cross and saw the resurrection; beyond the shame, and saw the glory.

This is what 321 calls the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — he opens my eyes; the Bible is my standard — it tells me what has eternal value; Jesus is my role model — however he invested the temporary in the eternal, that is how I will do it; so I let Jesus reign as King and put all my resources in his hands; and finally, I let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, temporary things can be turned into eternal value. What do you have in your hands today? Some time? A little money? A phone call you could make? A word of comfort you could speak? These are all “temporary,” but the moment you use them for the Lord, they become “eternal.”

sections.heading: 4. Your Eyes Decide Your Master
sections.html:
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus places these three sayings — about “treasure,” “the eye” and “masters” — tightly side by side, and that is no accident. He is describing a chain that runs through life: what you look at, you love; what you love, you serve; what you serve becomes your master.

The word “sound” is the Greek ἁπλοῦς (haplous), which originally means “single, unfolded, undivided in devotion.” Its opposite isn’t “not bright” but “divided, double.” In Jewish idiom a “good eye” (a single eye) meant generosity, while an “evil eye” meant greed and stinginess. Proverbs says, “A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn’t know that poverty waits for him” (Proverbs 28:22) — in the Chinese Union Version, “a man with an evil eye.”

So what Jesus means is this: if your eyes look single-mindedly at God, your whole body is full of light; if your eyes want to look at God and at Mammon too, split in two, your whole body is full of darkness.

“Mammon” in the original is μαμωνᾶς (mamōnas), from Aramaic, meaning wealth or money. Notice that Jesus personifies Mammon here, speaking of it as a “master.” He didn’t say, “You can’t serve God and manage money”; the word he uses is “serve.” Once money is set on the throne, it stops being a tool and becomes a master — and a brutally harsh master at that, one that will never say to you, “That’s enough.”

Brothers and sisters, look at this chain: look at money, and money becomes your master; look at the world, and the world becomes your master; look at yourself, and you become your own master; look at God, and God becomes your Master.

An everyday illustration comes to mind. Have you ever driven at night? Every driver knows one thing: the car goes where your eyes look. Driving instructors say that when you take a bend, don’t stare at the barrier at the side of the road, because wherever you stare, the steering wheel will turn without your meaning it to. This is called “target fixation.” Many accidents happen because the driver stared fixedly at the very thing he least wanted to hit.

Life is the same. If you spend all day staring at what you lack, you’ll keep driving into lack; if you spend all day staring at what others owe you, you’ll keep driving into bitterness; if you look up to Jesus, your life will naturally turn towards him.

Here is a very important reminder: you are not “without a master.” No one has ever been “without a master.” If you don’t let Jesus be King, something else will certainly be king — perhaps money, perhaps reputation, perhaps what other people think of you, perhaps your own pride and face.

Augustine says at the opening of his Confessions: “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The human heart is a throne made for God, and that seat never stays empty. Drive God out, and something else will sit down in his place.

The 321 vision puts it very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Self-centred people put themselves on the throne, and so spend their whole lives running around for their own kingdom; selfless people put Jesus on the throne, and so live their whole lives in God’s kingdom.

And the difference between the two often begins the moment you open your eyes in the morning: what do you look at first? Your phone, or God’s Word?

Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that you have no master; you are choosing who will be master. And the way you choose is by choosing what you look at.

sections.heading: 5. The Key Practice: Trading the Fleeting for the Eternal
sections.html:
“He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?” (Luke 16:10–11)

Once we understand the principle, next comes the practice. Jesus spoke these two verses after the parable of the dishonest manager, tying “money” and “trust” together.

Notice two expressions. The first is “a very little.” Promotion in God’s kingdom works completely differently from the world. The world looks at how big the things you’ve achieved are; God looks at whether you are faithful in the very least of things. The second is “the unrighteous mammon” — the Chinese Union Version says “unrighteous wealth,” but the original literally reads “the mammon of unrighteousness,” meaning the money of this present age. Jesus is saying that money is a “quiz” God sets us, and what it tests is faithfulness; only when you pass that little quiz does God entrust you with “the true riches” — that is, eternal, spiritual wealth.

Brothers and sisters, what a serious and what a glorious mindset this is! How you spend your salary this month has a bearing on whether God will put a family, a flock, a harvest field into your hands.

So the lesson gives us three very concrete practices:

First, use money to bless people. Not waiting until you’re well off before you give, but starting now. Of the widow’s two small coins the Lord said she “gave all that she had to live on” (Mark 12:44). In God’s ledger, what counts isn’t the amount but the proportion; not how much you gave, but how much you kept back.

Second, use resources to build people up. Your connections, your expertise, your experience, your home, a meal you cook — these are all resources. Using resources to “build people up” is an eternal investment. Because houses get torn down, but people last for ever.

Third, use your life to glorify God. This is the highest level. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

And Jesus condenses all of this into one overarching principle: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33).

The word “first” in “seek first” is the Greek πρῶτον (prōton). It means not only first in time but first in order of priority, first in value. Not “finish everything else first, and seek God’s kingdom when you have a spare moment,” but “God’s kingdom comes first, and everything else comes after.”

Brothers and sisters, there is a beautiful division of labour here. When you see God’s kingdom —

God takes care of your needs, and you take care of God’s kingdom.

It’s the best bargain in the whole world. You hand over to God your small, perishable “needs” that you can never hold on to anyway, and God hands over to you his imperishable “kingdom.” And the result? Earthly provision, plus heavenly reward, will all be given to you as well.

Some people worry: if I seek God’s kingdom first, what about my children? What about my job? What about my old age? Brothers and sisters, listen to the Lord’s words: “all these things will be given to you as well.” The word behind “given … as well” is προστίθημι (prostithēmi), meaning “to add on as an extra.” God isn’t asking you to choose one or the other; God is saying: just take care of that “first,” and he himself will take responsibility for adding on everything else.

This is the practical substance of what 321 calls the 920 practice. Every person we’re in relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise the “0” — the selfless life; and the result is the ninefold fruit of the Spirit, the “9”: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

The person you bless with money is your “2”; the person you build up with your resources is your “2”; the phone call you make, the meal you bring, the tears you sit through with someone — all of it is living out the life of “0” towards your “2.”

And from among these “2”s God will raise up some to become your spiritual companions. That’s where the 235 relationships begin: first a “2,” a spiritual companion; then a “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, trading the fleeting for the eternal — this isn’t a losing deal; it’s the smartest investment in the kingdom of heaven.

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: What You See Is What You Live Out
sections.html:
The five key points so far have covered the truth about “seeing.” Now, in the light of 321, we’re going to draw it all together into one sentence: what you see is what you live out.

Look at yourself, and you’ll live out yourself; look at the world, and you’ll live out the world; look at Jesus, and you’ll live out Christ.

This sentence is really an enormously important spiritual principle of the Bible. Paul says, “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Notice the order: first “seeing,” then “transformed.” Not transformed first and then seeing, but seeing first and then transformed. Whatever we gaze at is what shapes us. Human life has a wonderful power of “assimilation” — whatever you look at day after day, you slowly become.

Numbers 13 records the twelve spies returning from the land of Canaan. The same land, the same forty days, the same descendants of Anak — yet they brought back two completely opposite reports. Ten of the spies said, “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33). They looked at themselves and saw grasshoppers; seeing grasshoppers, they lived like grasshoppers; living like grasshoppers, they died in the wilderness.

But Caleb was different. God said, “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and has followed me fully, him I will bring into the land into which he went. His offspring shall possess it” (Numbers 14:24). Where the Chinese Union Version reads “a different resolve,” the Hebrew literally says “another spirit.” Forty-five years later, eighty-five-year-old Caleb stood before Joshua and said, “Now therefore give me this hill country, of which Yahweh spoke in that day” (Joshua 14:12). The mountain he had “seen” all those years before, forty-five years later he really “received.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the theme of our lesson — what we see, we shall surely receive.

So why do people see wrongly? The 321 vision gives the deepest diagnosis: because of the self-centred life.

The self-centred person will always look at the temporary. Why? Because “self” lives in time. The self’s lifespan is limited, its field of vision is limited, its capacity is limited. However wide a self-centred person opens their eyes, they can only see as far as their own lifetime, their own generation, their own little patch.

Only the selfless can see eternity. Because they no longer have “self” at the centre of their circle; their centre is God. And God is eternal, so their field of vision enters eternity too.

That is why 321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Brothers and sisters, there is a huge misunderstanding to clear up here. Some people hear “selflessness” and think it means erasing yourself, denying your worth, belittling yourself, becoming a person of no value. No! Selflessness isn’t becoming a zero. Selflessness is that small, limited centre stepping aside, so that the infinite God becomes the new centre. The radius stays the same; change the centre, and the circle goes from finite to infinite.

So the selfless don’t live for themselves; they live for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom.

Living for Jesus — because he is my role model, and he laid down his life for me.

Living for others — because every person is my “2,” a lesson and a blessing God has placed in my life.

Living for God’s kingdom — because it is the only kingdom that can never be shaken.

And these three “fors” are exactly 321’s Two Core Values and the Goal: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory, establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, quietly ask yourself one question: whom is the lens of my life trained on?

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s place this lesson’s message within the complete framework of 321, so we can see it more clearly.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. These three are exactly the three pairs of glasses for our “seeing.” Jesus is my role model: on the cross he saw “the joy that was set before him,” and I learn to see as he did. The Bible is my standard: it tells me what is temporary and what is eternal, and I tell them apart by it. The Holy Spirit is my guide: it is by him that we have “the eyes of your hearts enlightened” (Ephesians 1:18), so that I truly see.

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The fourth key point of this lesson, “your eyes decide your master,” is really about exactly this. Whatever you look at becomes king. So every day we must adjust the lens, so that Jesus grows bigger and bigger in our eyes, and we grow smaller and smaller. John the Baptist said, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

The Goal — establish God’s system. When one person sees eternity, he himself is saved; when a whole group of people see eternity, God’s system is established. That system isn’t held together by institutions; it is held together by a group of people whose eyes are looking in the same direction.

From the self-centred life to selflessness — the self-centred life looks at the temporary; selflessness looks at the eternal. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. What the devil is best at is zooming the lens in, so close that all you can see is your own grievances, your own lack, your own face. He doesn’t need to get you to commit some monstrous sin; he only has to keep you staring at yourself, and you’ll naturally live in the temporary. And the way to break it is simple: zoom the lens out — out to eternity, out to the cross, out to the throne.

Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win. It’s the same at home. When a husband and wife quarrel, both are “looking at” the other’s faults, and the more they look, the bigger those faults grow; if one of them is willing to turn their eyes to the Lord, the whole home turns around.

The fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This lesson deals with the very first link: mindset. Mindset is “how you see.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living. So don’t underestimate this morning’s lesson: if you truly change the way you see, your whole life will begin to turn.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry — people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. So the order of “using time to love people, using money to bless people and using our lives to serve God” is always first our relationship with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and only last with things.

The shift of perspective — from the human to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. These four lines are the 321 version of 2 Corinthians 4:18.

The 920 practice — every person we’re in relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise the “0,” living out selflessness; and we bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit, the “9.” This lesson’s practice, “do one thing of eternal value every day,” worked out in real life, is 920.

The 235 relationships — become a “2” with a selfless person, build a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. When you begin to see people with eternal eyes, you’ll no longer think only, “Is this person useful to me?” but, “What does God want to do in this person?”

Finally: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain, and you’ll keep calculating gains and losses, and you’ll be troubled; rely on the heart, and you’ll simply entrust things to God, and you’ll be glad. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices for daily living. We’re going to combine them with 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Re-examine your “seeing.” Ask yourself every day: what do I pay most attention to? Money? Achievement? Or God’s kingdom?

Information: read 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 and Matthew 6:19–34, and make two lists, “temporary” and “eternal.”

Revelation: pray quietly and ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you: “Lord, where is my real treasure?” Ask him to point out the thing you’d find hardest to let go of.

Conviction: acknowledge from your heart — the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal. Not just saying it, but truly believing it.

Implementation: this week, spend three minutes every evening taking an “eye inventory”: today, which three things took most of my attention?

Evaluation: at the weekend, look back over the seven days of notes and see which category took up the biggest share.

Correction: move whatever came first to a place behind God’s kingdom — not throwing it away, but changing its position.

Repetition: keep practising for forty days in a row, until the new mindset becomes a new habit.

Multiplication: share what you’ve discovered with a spiritual companion, and help them do an “eye inventory” too.

Practice 2: Invest deliberately in eternity. Do one thing of “eternal value” every day — caring for someone, sharing the gospel, serving someone.

Information: read Matthew 6:20 and 1 Timothy 6:17–19, and understand what it means to “lay up treasures in heaven.”

Revelation: ask the Lord to give you a name. Not a crowd of people, but one name — the person God wants you to love today.

Conviction: believe that a small thing isn’t small in God’s eyes. “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10).

Implementation: do it today; don’t put it off until tomorrow. A phone call to see how someone is, a prayer for someone, a gift, some time spent with someone.

Evaluation: in the evening, write it down: what did I do? How did the other person respond? What did I feel inside?

Correction: if you couldn’t do it, ask yourself whether it was a problem of time or a problem of the heart, and then adjust.

Repetition: do it for twenty-one days running, until “one eternal thing a day” becomes the rhythm of your daily living.

Multiplication: invite a family member or companion to do it with you and report to each other. This is the 920 practice brought down to earth.

Practice 3: Adjust your life’s priorities. Put “God’s kingdom” first, and let everything else follow naturally.

Information: memorise Matthew 6:33: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.”

Revelation: ask the Lord to shine on you: what is really “first” in my life? Your diary and your accounts don’t lie.

Conviction: believe that God takes care of my needs, and I take care of God’s kingdom. This is a division of labour, not a gamble.

Implementation: this month, in your diary, first block out time with God, time for relationships with people and time for serving, and then schedule everything else after that.

Evaluation: at the end of the month, check: was there any day when “first” got squeezed out? Why?

Correction: adjust your time, adjust your budget, adjust your friendships, until the order is put right again.

Repetition: rearrange it once every month, and keep going for a year.

Multiplication: teach this order of “seeking God’s kingdom first” to your children, your small group and your co-workers.

Brothers and sisters, the eight stages look like a long list, but really they have only one core: don’t stop at “knowing.” Knowing isn’t the same as changing. Information has to become Revelation, Revelation has to become Conviction, Conviction has to become Implementation, Implementation has to be repeated until it becomes life, and finally it has to be multiplied into other people. Only then is the change complete.

A Gentle Reminder

The lesson text closes with a very short but very powerful sentence:

It isn’t that you haven’t received; it’s that you haven’t been looking at the right thing.

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is worth keeping in your heart all day long. We often complain to God: why haven’t I received it yet? But what God wants to ask us is: what are you looking at?

Esau saw a bowl of red stew and sold his birthright. Solomon asked for wisdom, and God added the riches and honour he hadn’t asked for as well. Mary chose to sit at Jesus’ feet and listen to his word, and the Lord said, “Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

What you see is what you will receive.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we began today with a question: what are you actually looking at? Now we’re going to finish with an answer.

The most important thing in life isn’t how much you own, but “what you see.”

Look at the temporary, and you’ll receive the temporary; look at the eternal, and you’ll receive the eternal.

Abram lifted up his eyes, saw God’s promise and received the whole land of Canaan. Caleb lifted up his eyes, saw that mountain, and at eighty-five could still take hold of it. Moses lifted up his eyes, as seeing him who is invisible, and left Egypt. When Stephen was being stoned, he, “being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55) — so while the stones struck his body, he saw heaven opened.

Brothers and sisters, when you begin to see God’s kingdom, your life will no longer be reset to zero; it will enter into eternal value and glory.

So this morning I want to give you three calls.

First, let Jesus be King. Hand him the steering wheel of your eyes. No longer “whatever I see is what I do,” but “whatever he sees is what I see.” Pray this one sentence to the Lord every day: “Please open my eyes, that I may see.”

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When you invest your temporary resources in eternity, remember that it isn’t to make yourself look good, and it isn’t to win people’s praise; it is so that Jesus is glorified.

Third, starting today, do one thing of eternal value. You don’t need to wait until you’re more mature, better off or less busy. Today — this very day.

Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

Brothers and sisters, what you see is what you will receive. May we lift up our heads together and see Jesus seated on the throne, and together, in this generation, establish God’s system, until his kingdom comes.

keyVerses: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

“Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory.” (2 Corinthians 4:16–17)
declarations: Lord, adjust the way I see.
Let me no longer see only fleeting things,
but see what has eternal value.
Let me live my whole life for your kingdom,
and live out eternal meaning in this fleeting life.
practices: Re-examine your “seeing”
Invest deliberately in eternity
Adjust your life’s priorities
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Lord, we confess that our eyes are often filled up with the things right in front of us. We see the bills, but not your provision; we see the difficulties, but not the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire; we see our own weakness, but not your grace.
Lord, open our eyes, as you opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant. May your Holy Spirit enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that we may know what is the hope of your calling.

Lord, take away the self-centred life within us. We no longer want to live for numbers that will all end up as zero. Make us selfless people who don’t live for ourselves, but for you, for others and for your kingdom.
Lord, from today on, teach us to use our time to love people, our money to bless people and our lives to serve you, investing every temporary thing in eternity.
We declare: you are our King, and we will seek first your kingdom and your righteousness. All glory be to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 2 Corinthians 4:18 says, “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Share honestly: this week, on what kind of things did you spend most of your time, money and attention? Is there one “visible thing” that is taking up too much of your gaze?

Matthew 6:33 says, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” If “seeking God’s kingdom first” were to show up for real in your diary and your budget, what one concrete adjustment would you make this month? Name one action your small group can follow up with you on.
l121.title: What We See, We Receive
l121.subtitle: What We See, We Shall Surely Receive (Part 1)
l121.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: What Are You Looking At?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. This morning, let’s first be still for three seconds, and then open our eyes and look at the room in front of us.

What do you see? Some see a table not yet cleared, dishes not yet washed, a pile of bills. Others see a lamp left on for them, an open Bible, a new morning given by God. The same room, the same light, the same twenty-four hours — and yet we see completely different worlds.

In the last lesson we saw a key truth together: what you see is what you pursue, and what you pursue is what you obtain. A person’s eyes are, in fact, the steering wheel of his life. Today God wants to take us one layer deeper. He wants to tell us this: the “value you see” determines the direction and the ending of your life.

Please pay special attention to this sentence: it is not how hard you try, but what you treasure.

We often think the differences between lives come down to how much effort we put in, how much ability we have, how good or bad our opportunities are. But the Bible shows us a more fundamental fact: two people can work equally hard, be equally clever, stand in exactly the same place — and end up worlds apart. The reason lies not in the feet but in the eyes; not in the hands but in the heart. For what you chase in life will never exceed what you see, and what you gain will never exceed what you treasure.

There is a famous experiment in psychology that can help us understand this. In 1999, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, then teaching at Harvard University, published a study in the journal Perception called “Gorillas in Our Midst.” They asked participants to watch a short video in which two teams were passing basketballs, and the task was to count the passes made by the team in white. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit strolled right through the middle of the screen, even stopping to beat its chest — nine seconds in all. And the result? About half of the participants never saw the gorilla at all.

Their eyes were fine, the light was good enough, and the gorilla was real. They didn’t see it simply because they were busy counting something else. The researchers gave this phenomenon a name: inattentional blindness. It isn’t that we cannot see; it’s that we “only see what we are paying attention to.”

Brothers and sisters, this is a true picture of the spiritual life of many Christians. God is right there among us, grace is right before our eyes, his works are made plain every day — but we are busy counting our own balls: counting our losses, counting what others owe us, counting the difficulties of our circumstances. And so we miss God.

So today’s lesson is not meant to rebuke our weakness but to renew our eyes. God wants to set six lights before us, to turn us from worldly eyes to spiritual eyes; from man’s point of view to God’s point of view; from what is earthly and temporary to what is heavenly and eternal.

Because what you see today determines what you receive tomorrow.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Histories of “Seeing”
sections.html:
The two main passages we are entering today are Genesis 13 and Exodus 14. According to the unanimous tradition of the Jewish people and the church for two thousand years, both books were written by Moses. Moses was writing for the people of Israel, who had just been brought out of the land of slavery in Egypt, were walking through the wilderness and were about to enter Canaan. What was the greatest problem of this people? Not a lack of miracles, but an inability to see. They had seen the ten plagues, seen the Red Sea part, seen the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire — and still in the wilderness they complained, drew back and were afraid. So Moses took up his pen and wrote first how their forefather Abraham “saw,” and then how they themselves “saw” at the edge of the Red Sea. This is a textbook about the eyes.

The background of Genesis 13 is a family dispute over property. Abram (God had not yet renamed him Abraham) came back from Egypt to Bethel, and the Bible says he “was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold” (Genesis 13:2). His nephew Lot had also grown rich. With so much wealth, the land was no longer enough. The text says: “The land was not able to bear them, that they might live together; for their possessions were so great that they couldn’t live together … The Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land at that time” (Genesis 13:6–7). Notice that last sentence: the Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land. In other words, this quarrel was taking place before the eyes of unbelieving outsiders. The family shame of God’s household was being watched by the world.

Abram was the elder, the one who had been called. By custom, by law and by seniority, the first choice was his. But he did something that in the world’s eyes was utterly foolish: he gave the choice to the younger man.

The background of Exodus 14 is a national crisis. Israel had only just come out of Egypt, yet God did not lead them by the short road through the land of the Philistines; instead, “God led the people around by the way of the wilderness by the Red Sea” (Exodus 13:18). God even told them to turn back and camp by the sea, in order to lure Pharaoh out in pursuit (Exodus 14:2–4). In other words, the dead end at the Red Sea was no accident; God himself had arranged it. Water in front, soldiers behind, wilderness on either side — a deadlock no human calculation could solve and no one could escape.

In both of these histories God is doing the same thing: he places two people, two groups of people, in exactly the same circumstances, and then lets us see how different ways of “seeing” lead to utterly different endings.

Brothers and sisters, this is also what God wants to do with us this morning. He may not change your circumstances straight away; first he wants to change your eyes.

sections.heading: 1. Two Ways to Live: For Yourself, or for God
sections.html:
“Abram said to Lot, ‘Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives. Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.’” (Genesis 13:8–9)

This is the most beautiful “giving way” in the whole Bible. Abram and Lot faced the same situation and the same choice — how to divide the gains. But they “saw” in different ways, and so their endings were completely different.

How Lot Saw: Worldly Eyes

“Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar.” (Genesis 13:10)

“Lifted up his eyes, and saw” — Lot raised his eyes, but his eyes could do only three things.

First, he looked at the environment. He saw that it was “well-watered,” a fertile plain. The Hebrew word is “the whole plain” (kikkar) — a round, lush lowland. What he saw was water and grass, harvests, a place where livestock could grow fat.

Second, he looked at advantage. The question he asked was: which piece is best for me? He did not ask God, nor did he ask his elder, and the Bible records not a single prayer from him.

Third, he looked at the present. Here the Bible adds a very important aside: “before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.” When Moses wrote this, he already knew the ending. That land, which looked like the garden of Eden, became a scorched waste of sulphur and fire a few decades later. Lot saw what was in front of him; the Holy Spirit saw how it would end.

And the result? “So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one other” (Genesis 13:11). Then the Bible records his slide in one very quiet yet very frightening verse: “Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom” (Genesis 13:12).

The Chinese Union Version puts it this way: he “moved his tent little by little” — words we should remember all our lives. Lot did not move into Sodom in a single day. First he gazed at it from afar, then he lived on the plain, then he moved his tent a little closer each time, and in the end he was sitting in the gate of Sodom (Genesis 19:1). Spiritual decline is never one leap off a cliff; it is a move of an inch a day.

And the next verse of the Bible coldly adds: “Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners against Yahweh” (Genesis 13:13). Lot saw the pasture but did not see the sin. His eyes measured only altitude, never depth.

And the final ending? When God’s judgement came, Lot lost almost everything. His sons-in-law treated the warning as a joke (Genesis 19:14), and his wife “looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). Later the Lord Jesus reminded his disciples in just three words: “Remember Lot’s wife!” (Luke 17:32)

Brothers and sisters, that “looking back” was not a movement of the neck; it was the direction of the heart. Where a person looks, the heart goes; where the heart goes, the person stops. Her body left Sodom, but her heart stayed in Sodom, and so she stopped forever halfway, a pillar of warning.

There is a famous experiment in psychology that can help us understand Lot. In the 1960s and 70s, Professor Walter Mischel of Stanford University in the United States carried out the “marshmallow test.” He put a marshmallow in front of a child and told the child that if they could wait until the researcher came back before eating it, they would get two. Some children ate it immediately; others tried every way they could to distract themselves and waited for the double reward. Mischel’s later follow-up studies found that the children who were able to delay gratification often did better in adolescence. And his key finding was this: the children who could wait did not have stronger willpower; they simply knew “not to keep staring at the marshmallow.”

What you see is what you crave; what you crave is what you grab. Lot’s tragedy was that he kept staring at that plain.

How Abram Saw: Spiritual Eyes

Abram did three things that were the exact opposite of Lot: he did not contend, he gave way, and he did not live for himself.

He did not contend — he said, “let there be no strife between you and me,” because what he saw was not a piece of land but the reputation of God’s testimony before the nations. He gave way — he handed over the right to choose first. He did not live for himself — he gave up the visible gain and held on to the invisible God.

And the result? How beautifully the text puts it: “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever’” (Genesis 13:14–15).

Brothers and sisters, please notice two details.

First, the time when God spoke was “after Lot was separated from him.” Abram let go first, and only then did God speak. While our hands are still clenched tight, God often says nothing; when we let go, heaven opens.

Second, the action God spoke of was the same as Lot’s: “lift up your eyes, and look.” Lot lifted his own eyes and saw one plain; Abram was told by God to lift his eyes and saw the whole land, north, south, east and west. Lot used his own eyes to pick the best piece; God used his eyes to give Abram all of it. The very land Lot chose was later included within the borders God promised to Abram.

This is the great dividing line between the worldly and the spiritual: those who live for themselves lose; those who live for God gain everything.

The Lord Jesus put this principle even more plainly: “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25).
