The 321 vision tells us: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? It is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? It is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Lot seized the right to choose; he sat in God’s seat and made himself lord of his own life. Abram laid down the right to choose; he returned to his originally intended position as a creature and let God be Lord for him. One grasped, one let go; one contended, one gave way. Looking back thirty years later, the man who grasped lost everything, and the man who gave way became a blessing to all nations.

Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. This is not a slogan; this is the history of Genesis 13.

sections.heading: 2. The Value You See Is the Life You Live
sections.html:
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

These words of the Lord Jesus come in the Sermon on the Mount, and the surrounding context is about “laying up treasures in heaven” and “no one can serve two masters.” In other words, the “eye” the Lord is speaking of here is not eyesight but values. The original word for “sound” (haplous) carries the sense of “single, pure, undivided”; the word for “evil” (ponēros) carries the sense of “bad, wicked, greedy.” A person whose eye is single is full of light; a person whose eye is greedy is full of darkness.

So what the Lord is saying is this: whatever you see as valuable is what your whole being will be lit up by — or swallowed up by.

Let’s lay this principle out point by point.

Those who look at themselves live for themselves. Their world is very small, small enough to hold only one person, and everything revolves around “I feel, I need, I’ve been hurt, I’ve been short-changed.” It isn’t that they don’t work hard — they work very hard — it’s just that all that effort goes to feeding themselves.

Those who look at advantage live for advantage. Before doing anything they reach for the calculator; even in serving God they ask, “What’s in it for me?” It isn’t that they bear no fruit; it’s just that their fruit has no eternal weight.

Those who look at God live for God. Their world is very large, large enough to hold a kingdom. They know they are not the main character, and precisely because of that they have found true freedom.

The same principle applies between the church and the kingdom.

Those who look at “my church” will breed competition. Whose congregation is bigger, whose church building is larger, whose speaker is more famous — once the comparisons start, conflict follows. Those who look at “God’s kingdom” will move towards unity. Because the kingdom has only one King, and all the glory goes to him alone, there is nothing left for us to fight over.

Worldly seeing says, “I want to get”; spiritual seeing says, “I want to give.” Paul wrote the difference between these two kinds of eyes into a passage of great depth: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:3–4). Notice that in the Chinese Union Version Paul again uses the word “see”: each one sees others as better than himself. Unity is not something we grit our teeth to endure; it is something we learn to see.

Brothers and sisters, here we must say something very important: denying of self is not a loss; it is entering into a greater gain.

The Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24). Many people hear “deny yourself” as a losing bargain, as if believing in Jesus means having things taken away again and again. But the 321 vision makes this very clear: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Paul bore witness to this himself: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Think about it: put a drop of water in the palm of your hand, and in half a day it has dried up; put a drop of water into the ocean, and it will never dry up — and from then on it has the power of the whole ocean. What has that drop lost? It has lost the shape of its own “self.” What has it gained? It has gained the ocean.

This is selflessness. Selflessness is not becoming zero; it is placing that “self” into the infinity of God.

From the standpoint of psychology, too, there is evidence for this. Viktor Frankl, the Austrian psychiatrist and a survivor of the Nazi concentration camps, recorded his observations in his book Man’s Search for Meaning: in an environment as extreme as the camps, those who held on were often not the physically strongest, but those who could still see a meaning in their hearts, who still had an unfinished mission, who still had someone waiting for them to come home. Frankl quoted Nietzsche, whose words are commonly taken to mean that a person who knows “why” he lives can bear almost any “how.”

People who see meaning have the strength to go on living. And the meaning a Christian sees is not some vague ideal, but a Lord who is true and living.

The fivefold change of 321 says: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. The first link in the whole chain is mindset — that is, how you see. That is why we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

This is exactly how Abram saw things in that dispute over the land: Lot the man mattered more than that pasture; the testimony of God’s household mattered more than my rights. He kept the relationship, and God gave him the land.

sections.heading: 3. Same Circumstances, Different Sight, Different Endings
sections.html:
“Moses said to the people, ‘Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today; for you will never again see the Egyptians whom you have seen today.’” (Exodus 14:13)

Now we move from Genesis to Exodus, from the choice of one family to the crisis of a whole nation.

The scene is the Red Sea. In front, fathomless water; behind, Pharaoh’s six hundred chosen chariots. God’s people are caught in between. Notice that at this moment everyone’s situation is exactly the same: the same sea, the same pursuers, the same sand, the same night. Yet they “saw” differently, and so their endings were different.

How the Israelites Saw: A Dead End

“When Pharaoh came near, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them; and they were very afraid. The children of Israel cried out to Yahweh.” (Exodus 14:10)

“Lifted up their eyes” — that phrase again. What did they see? The Red Sea in front, the pursuers behind. Their conclusion was perfectly reasonable: it’s over. So they said to Moses, “Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness? Why have you treated us this way, to bring us out of Egypt?” (Exodus 14:11)

Brothers and sisters, listen to those words — the day before they were cheering their freedom, and today they would rather go back and be slaves. That’s what the human heart is like: whatever we see, we speak; whatever we speak, we become. What they saw was a threat, and what they reaped was fear and complaint.

Psychology can explain this. In 1998 the psychologist Barbara Fredrickson of the University of North Carolina in the United States put forward the “broaden-and-build theory.” Her research shows that negative emotions, especially fear, “narrow” a person’s attention and range of possible actions, leaving only two roads — flight or fight; whereas positive emotions, such as joy, hope and gratitude, “broaden” a person’s field of attention and flexibility of thought, enabling them to see more possibilities.

That is why the frightened Israelites could think of only two options: drown, or go back to Egypt. Their eyes had been narrowed by fear. God’s third way was right in front of them, and they could not see it.

How Moses Saw: God

Moses stood on the shore of the very same sea. What did he see?

He saw the works of God — “see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today.”

He saw the promises of God — God had said, “I will bring you into Canaan,” so Moses knew this sea could not be the end of the road.

His conclusion was: God will save. And the result? A miracle happened.

“Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. The children of Israel went into the middle of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.” (Exodus 14:21–22)

Brothers and sisters, please take hold of this order — it is the most important sentence of today: the circumstances did not change first. The “seeing” changed first, and then the miracle appeared.

When did the sea part? After Moses had finished saying, “Don’t be afraid. Stand still.” When Moses made his declaration, the sea was still there. He did not have faith because he saw the sea part; he saw the sea part because he had faith.

We often get the order backwards. We say to God, “Lord, part the sea first, and then I’ll believe you.” God says to us, “Child, see me first, and the sea will part.”

There is a beautiful parallel passage here, the story of Elisha and his servant. The Aramean army surrounded the city of Dothan by night. The servant got up early in the morning, saw horses and chariots and soldiers besieging the city, and panicked. “Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17).

Notice that Elisha did not ask God to “drive the enemy away”; he asked God to “open his servant’s eyes.” The horses and chariots of fire had been there all along; the servant just could not see them. God did not change the circumstances. God changed the eyes — and for the servant, the circumstances were completely different.

From a scientific point of view, the human eye is itself a lesson in humility. Every eye of every person has a physiological blind spot on the retina — the place where the optic nerve leaves the eyeball. There are no light-sensitive cells there, so nothing at all is seen. The reason we don’t normally notice it is that the brain automatically “patches” the hole using the surrounding image. In other words, a small piece of the world we see every day is made up for us by our brain — and we are convinced it is the truth.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t our spiritual life just the same? Every one of us has blind spots, and our minds are very good at making up stories to cover them. That is why we need God to open our eyes. The psalmist prayed, “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). This should also become our very first prayer every morning.

The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. It also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you will worry, rely on the heart and you will rejoice. The Israelites relied on their brains and calculated all night, and what they came up with was a grave; Moses relied on the heart and looked to God, and what he saw was dry ground.

sections.heading: 4. A Spiritual Principle: What God Lets You See, He Will Bring to Pass
sections.html:
“By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.” (Hebrews 11:27)

The first three points showed us how people see. The fourth point is to show us how God works.

There is a spiritual order that recurs again and again in the Bible: God first gives you “sight,” and then leads you into “experience.”

He first had Abram lift up his eyes and look north, south, east and west, and only then gave him the land. He first gave Joseph dreams, in which he saw the sheaves and the stars bow down to him, and only after thirteen years in the pit and the prison did he set him as ruler over Egypt. He first let Moses see at Horeb a bush burning with fire yet not consumed, and only then sent him to Pharaoh. He first let Joshua and Caleb see the fruit of the land, and only then gave the land into their hands.

Brothers and sisters, what a great comfort this is: you do not need to know “how” first. You only need to see, believe and obey; the responsibility for bringing it to pass lies with God, not with you.

Hebrews 11:8 says: “By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went.” Not knowing where he was going, he still went — because he had seen the One. What he saw was not a route map; it was God himself.

This is the essence of faith. The definition of faith that Hebrews gives is: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). The original word for “assurance” (hypostasis) carries the sense of “base, foundation, substance”; the word for “proof” (elenchos) carries the sense of “evidence, credentials.” Faith is not shutting our eyes to the facts; faith is seeing a higher fact — that the invisible Lord is more real than the visible Red Sea.

So we must hold this firmly: faith is not a feeling; faith is seeing “what cannot be seen.”

Feelings rise and fall with blood sugar, sleep, the weather and a single remark from someone else; but God’s word never changes. Paul says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

This is precisely the change of perspective 321 speaks of: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

Here is a good picture of it. At the foot of a mountain, what you see is a wall blocking the way; ride the cable car to the summit, and you see a winding path that goes round the wall and straight on to the other side of the mountain. The wall was there all along, and so was the path. What changed was not the terrain but the height. Prayer is the cable car God gives us; God’s word is the height God gives us.

In 1948 the sociologist Robert K. Merton put forward the concept of the “self-fulfilling prophecy”: the way a person defines a situation affects his behaviour, and his behaviour in turn makes that originally false definition come true in the end. The ten spies saw themselves as grasshoppers, and they really did fall dead in the wilderness; Caleb “had another spirit with him” (Numbers 14:24), and at the age of eighty-five he really did receive the hill country of Hebron.

Of course, we must make a clear distinction here: this is not what the world calls the “law of attraction,” as though whatever a person imagines in his heart he can create. The Bible never says that human faith can create reality. What the Bible says is this: God speaks first, God gives the sight first, and our faith is our “Amen” to God’s word. It is God who brings things to pass, not our thoughts. We do not use faith to command God; we use faith to respond to God.

So, brothers and sisters, the question to ask this morning is not “Can I do it?” but “What has God said?” You don’t need to know how. You only need to see, believe and obey. God takes responsibility for bringing it to pass.

sections.heading: 5. Weakness Is Not the Problem — Seeing Wrongly Is
sections.html:
“He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)

Brothers and sisters, this part is for those of you who, this morning, feel in your heart that you are not good enough.

When Paul wrote 2 Corinthians 12, he was dealing with something very painful. There was “a thorn” in his flesh. The Bible does not say plainly what it was — perhaps an illness, perhaps persecution. Paul pleaded with the Lord three times to take this thorn away from him. God’s answer was not to remove the thorn, but to give him a word: “My grace is sufficient for you.”

The tone of the original is beautiful. “Is sufficient” (arkei) is in the present tense, meaning continually, unceasingly enough. God did not give Paul a one-off deposit of grace; he gave him a stream of living water supplied every day.

Then God spoke the sentence that turns everything around: my power is made perfect in weakness. “Made perfect” (teleitai) means “brought to completion, reaching fullness.” God’s power does not reach its fullness when we are at our strongest, but when we are at our weakest.

So please hear this sentence clearly today: God is not afraid of your weakness; God is afraid of your seeing wrongly.

Look at yourself, and you are weak; look at God, and you are strong. Paul goes on: “Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

This is not a trick of positive thinking; it is spiritual physics. A cup filled with itself has no room for anything else; only an emptied cup can be filled. Weakness is the empty space God clears in your heart.

Let’s look at an example. Gideon was threshing wheat in the winepress, afraid the Midianites would see him. The angel appeared to him and said, “Yahweh is with you, you mighty man of valor!” (Judges 6:12) Gideon immediately replied, “My family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house” (Judges 6:15). You see, what the angel saw and what Gideon saw were completely different. The angel saw a Gideon of whom it could be said, “Yahweh is with you”; Gideon saw himself as “the least.” God did not argue with him. God simply said, “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man” (Judges 6:16).

The problem was never how small Gideon was, but whom he was looking at.

The psychologist Carol Dweck, a professor at Stanford University in the United States, has spent many years researching people’s “mindset.” Her research distinguishes between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset”: people with a fixed mindset believe ability is fixed, so they treat failure as a verdict on their self-worth and tend to give up when they meet difficulties; people with a growth mindset believe ability can grow through effort and learning, so they treat failure as information and become more engaged when difficulties come. The same setback, two ways of seeing it, two different lives.

Brothers and sisters, Christians have an even higher way of seeing than the “growth mindset.” We might call it “the eyes of grace”: I do not grow by my own strength; I am filled by grace. My weakness is not my sentence of condemnation; it is my letter of invitation — inviting the power of Christ to rest on me.

Helen Keller is commonly credited with saying something like this: the only thing worse than being born blind is having sight but no vision. Helen Keller herself was blind and deaf, yet she saw things that many people with bright eyes never see in their whole lives.

So the problem is not how strong you are; the problem is whom you are looking at. Stop staring at your thorn. Lift up your head and look at the Lord who says, “My grace is sufficient for you.”

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: The Selfless See the Works of God
sections.html:
When we gather the previous five points together, we see a clear spiritual law:

The self-centred look at themselves, and the result is that they limit God; the selfless look at God, and the result is that they experience God.

This is not to say that God’s power can be limited by man — God is almighty. It is to say that a heart full of itself leaves no room for God to work; just as with the Lord Jesus in Nazareth, “He didn’t do many mighty works there because of their unbelief” (Matthew 13:58).

What is the self-centred life? The self-centred life puts “self” at the centre and measures everything by “me”: my face, my rights, my feelings, my plans. Self-centred people do not necessarily do evil; they may be hard-working, zealous, even very spiritually busy — but their eyes keep circling around themselves, and so the world they see all their lives is no bigger than themselves.

What is selflessness? Selflessness is not having no self-worth; it is not being negated or trampled on. 321 puts it very clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Selfless people bear three marks:

First, they do not contend for themselves. They know their inheritance is in God’s hands, and no one can take it away. Abram was just such a person.

Second, they do not live for themselves. “For the love of Christ constrains us; … He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).

Third, they do not gain for themselves. It is not that they receive nothing; it is that they do not treat what they receive as private property. They know they are stewards, not landlords.

So for whom do such people live? For three: for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom.

This is exactly the order 321 speaks of: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

And such people experience three things: they see God, they experience God, and they gain God.

Notice that these three things form one line. Seeing is the starting point, experiencing is the process, gaining is the outcome. And what is gained is not “things” but God himself. What Abraham finally gained was not only the land of Canaan, but God himself saying to him, “I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward” (Genesis 15:1).

In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). To be “pure in heart” is to be single-hearted, without impurity, without a divided mind — in other words, selfless. The pure in heart shall see God. This is the Lord’s promise.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s walk through today’s message once more, this time within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Jesus is my role model — he is the Lord “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). What he saw was the Father’s will, not his own rights. Abram’s giving way is only a shadow of him.

The Bible is my standard — our eyes are far too easily deceived by our circumstances, so we need a standard that does not move. When the Red Sea is in front of you, the question to ask is not “What does this look like?” but “What has God said?” Let God’s word replace what the eye sees; let the promises replace feelings.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who opens the eyes of our hearts. Paul prayed for the church in Ephesus: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Ephesians 1:18). Only the Holy Spirit can enlighten the eyes of the heart.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Lot’s problem was not that he chose the wrong land, but that he made the choice sitting on the throne himself. When Jesus reigns as King, we are set free from the burden of choosing — because the right to choose has been handed back to the Lord who is wisest and who loves us most. And when the miracle happened, Moses did not take the credit for himself; the glory of the Red Sea went wholly to Yahweh.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

When Abram gave up that land, it looked as though he had lost a round; in fact, God was using him to establish a new system — a family that did not rely on grabbing or on calculating, but trusted in God alone. Four thousand years later, we still call him “the father of faith.”

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s lesson starts precisely with the first link. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. How you see determines what kind of person you become; what kind of person you become determines how you live your days; how you live your days determines your relationships with others; your relationships with others determine the fruitfulness of your service. That is why we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

If a person does not change in how he “sees,” then changing churches, changing positions or changing methods is only moving the same play to a different stage.

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” Before them we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the nine (9) fruits of the Holy Spirit — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, think about it: the person you will face today — the colleague who often makes you uncomfortable, the stubborn elder, the rebellious child — the way you “see” them will determine your attitude towards them, and your attitude towards them will determine your relationship. If you look at them with Lot’s eyes, you will see a threat and a loss; if you look at them with Abram’s eyes, you will see someone God loves and wants to bless through you.

The 235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, as spiritual companions to one another; build a “3,” becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. One person’s eyes tire easily; when a group of people remind one another, they can see further and walk longer. Elisha prayed for his servant, and the servant’s eyes were opened — this is the value of a spiritual companion.

The change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Paul says: “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

Brothers and sisters, this is the summary of the whole lesson: lift your eyes a little higher.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive each of them deep, one by one.

Practice 1: When facing a choice, ask yourself, “What am I looking at?”

Information: First put the truth into your heart — Lot looked at the plain, Abram looked at God; one lost, the other gained the whole land.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you and bring to mind the most recent major choice you made. What was your real reason that time? Advantage, or God’s will?

Conviction: Say to God in your heart, “Lord, I believe your view is more reliable than my calculations.” Without conviction, knowledge is just data.

Implementation: Starting today, before making any choice that takes more than three minutes to decide, stop and ask one question: “Lord, how do you see this?”

Evaluation: Every evening spend three minutes thinking back over the day: was there a choice I made with Lot’s eyes?

Correction: If there was, confess it in prayer, and immediately think of a concrete action that can put it right.

Repetition: Practise this for forty days in a row. Psychology reminds us that forming a habit takes time and repetition; spiritual renewal all the more so — Paul tells us to “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2), and in the original this is an ongoing process.

Multiplication: Teach this question to your family, your companions and your small group, so that they too learn to ask God before they choose.

Practice 2: When facing difficulty, change what you see

Information: Remember Moses’ order — the circumstances did not change first; the “seeing” changed first, and then the miracle appeared.

Revelation: Write your greatest difficulty right now on the left side of a sheet of paper; then quietly ask God, and write his power and his promises on the right side.

Conviction: Acknowledge that your difficulty is real — but God is more real than your difficulty.

Implementation: Don’t look at the size of the problem; look at the power of God. Whenever you notice yourself replaying that problem over and over again, open your mouth and declare one of God’s promises.

Evaluation: At the end of the week, look at that sheet of paper: how many of the difficulties on the left were imagined, and how many were real?

Correction: Add one more promise on the right.

Repetition: Every time a difficulty comes, make the sheet again.

Multiplication: When God opens a way for you, tell that testimony, so that someone else standing at the edge of their own Red Sea can also stand firm.

Practice 3: Practise “the seeing of faith” every day

Information: Let God’s word replace what the eye sees; let the promises replace feelings.

Revelation: Each morning as you read the Bible, ask God to give you one verse as “today’s promise.”

Conviction: Copy that verse onto your phone’s wallpaper and onto a sticky note, and put it where you will see it ten times a day.

Implementation: Whenever you feel low, don’t analyse the feeling first; read that verse first.

Evaluation: In the evening, write down how God fulfilled it for you today, or how he comforted you.

Correction: If you didn’t think of that verse all day, move it somewhere more visible tomorrow.

Repetition: One verse a day, and in a month you will have thirty verses in your heart.

Multiplication: Each week share one verse with a friend who has not yet believed, or who is going through a weak time.

Brothers and sisters, there is one more little reminder — please keep it in your heart: it is not that you have no opportunities; it is that you have not seen God’s opportunities.

God’s grace is never absent; what is often absent is our eyes. Just like the half of the participants who could not see the gorilla — God is right there in the middle of the picture, and we are busy counting our own balls.

keyVerses: “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever. I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if a man can count the dust of the earth, then your offspring may also be counted. Arise, walk through the land in its length and in its width; for I will give it to you.’” (Genesis 13:14–17)
“By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.” (Hebrews 11:27)
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord, open my eyes! Let me no longer look only at myself and my circumstances, but see your works and your promises! Make me live by faith, obey your leading, and experience your wonderful power!
Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s road once more.
Lot saw the plain, and what he received was destruction; Abraham saw God, and what he received was the promise.
The Israelites saw the Red Sea and lived in fear; Moses saw God and experienced a miracle.
The same land, the same sea, the same day. The difference was not in the circumstances, but in the eyes.
So please take this sentence home with you: what you see today determines what you receive tomorrow.

When you choose to see with spiritual eyes, crisis becomes opportunity, weakness becomes power, and the impossible becomes possible. Not because you are capable, but because the One you see is capable. For what you see, God will surely bring to pass for you.

Dear brothers and sisters, this morning God wants to do something in your heart: he wants to take your eyes off yourself and set them on him. He wants you no longer to be Lot, clinging tightly to the plain, but Abraham, who opened his hands and lifted up his eyes to look. He wants you no longer to be the one at the seashore counting the pursuers, but the one who stands firm, declares, and sees the salvation of the Lord.
Let Jesus be King over your eyes, let Jesus be King over your choices, let Jesus be King over your weakness. May all the glory go to him.
practices: When facing difficulty, change what you see
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. You are the God who opens the eyes of the blind, and the God who shows us your works every day.

Lord, please forgive us — so often, like Lot, we see only the advantage in front of us and do not see your heart; so often, like the Israelites at the Red Sea, we see only the pursuers and the great waters and do not see your arm.

Enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that we may know the hope of your calling. Take away the “self” in our hearts, so that we no longer contend for ourselves, live for ourselves or gain for ourselves, but live only for Jesus, for others and for your kingdom.
Lord, today we hand the right to choose back to you, entrust our difficulties to you and offer our weakness to you. May your power be made perfect in our weakness.
May all that we see today be you; may all that we receive tomorrow be what you have promised.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Genesis 13:10–11: “Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere … So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one other.” Please share: in the most recent major choice you made, what did you “see” at the time? If you could do it again, what question would you want to ask God first?

2 Corinthians 12:9: “He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’” Please share: what is the one weakness you currently dislike most? If God wanted to display his power through this weakness, how do you think he might do it? What kind of prayer are you willing to pray about it this week?
l122.title: What You See Is What You Receive
l122.subtitle: The Value You See Determines the Direction and the Ending of Your Life
l122.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: The Ending of a Life Begins with a Single “Look”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning.

Let me begin with a question. Picture the same heavy rain on the same morning. One person pushes open the window, frowns and says, “What a wretched day.” Another pushes open the very same window, takes a deep breath and says, “How clean the air is today.” The same rain, the same window, the same morning — yet two moods, two days, and as the days add up into months and years, two lives. The rain didn’t change; the window didn’t change. What changed was the pair of eyes.

We often think the outcome of our lives is decided by our circumstances. When the economy is good, things go well for me; when my health is good, I’m joyful; when people treat me well, I’m loving. Circumstances are the cause, life is the effect, and we are merely passive recipients. But the Bible shows us a deeper, truer spiritual path:

Seeing determines thinking; thinking determines doing; doing determines the outcome.

How you see determines how you think; how you think determines what you do; what you do determines how your life ends. These four links are like a chain, each link fastened to the next, with no break in between. You cannot spend years looking at everything through the wrong eyes and yet live the right life; nor can you fix your eyes on Jesus every day and find your life entirely unchanged. This is cause and effect in the spiritual world, more reliable than gravity.

So the key is not “how things happen,” but this: how you see what happens.

Humanity has in fact been groping towards this truth for a long time. As early as the first and second centuries AD, the Stoic philosopher Epictetus wrote in the fifth section of his Handbook (Enchiridion): “People are disturbed not by things themselves, but by their views about things.” In the twentieth century, in 1955, the American psychologist Albert Ellis put forward Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT), the best-known part of which is the “ABC model”: A is the Activating event, B is the Belief — how a person interprets that event — and C is the Consequence, the emotions and behaviour that follow. Ellis pointed out that most people assume it is A that determines C — that event made me angry, that event made me depressed; but in fact it is B that determines C — it is my view of that event that makes me angry and depressed. Later, the cognitive therapy that Aaron T. Beck developed at the University of Pennsylvania was built on the same insight.

Brothers and sisters, psychology took a detour of nearly two thousand years to arrive where the Bible had long since been: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). However the heart sees, so the outcome flows.

And there is an even more piercing discovery. In 1999 the American psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris carried out an experiment at Harvard University that later became famous around the world, known as “the invisible gorilla.” They asked participants to watch a short video, and the task was simple: count how many times the people in white passed the ball to one another. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked in from the right of the screen, stopped in the very centre to beat its chest, and walked out on the left — nearly nine seconds in all. After the experiment the researchers asked, “Did you see the gorilla?” About half of the participants had not seen it at all. Their eyes were plainly open, the light had plainly entered their retinas, the image had plainly reached the visual cortex of the brain — but they “did not see.”

Psychology calls this phenomenon “inattentional blindness.” It turns out that seeing has never been only a matter of the eyes; it is a matter of attention, a matter of the heart. What you pay attention to, you see; what you see, you think about; what you think about, you do; what you do, you become.

Today’s lesson is to take this chain apart link by link, so that we can see: different ways of seeing bring completely different outcomes.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Eye and the Focus
1. Matthew 6:22–23
sections.html:
The author of Matthew’s Gospel is Matthew, also called Levi, who was originally a tax collector at the tax office in Capernaum. The Lord Jesus said to him, “Follow me,” and he left everything and followed the Lord (Matthew 9:9). It is generally thought that the book was written in the AD 60s, chiefly for Jewish Christians, which is why the whole book quotes the Old Testament so heavily, showing again and again that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the King of the kingdom of heaven.

The saying “The lamp of the body is the eye” comes from the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). We often read this passage as a stand-alone proverb, but in fact it sits between two very practical teachings. Before it, verses 19–21 say: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth … but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven … for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:19–21). After it, verse 24 says: “No one can serve two masters … You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

When the Lord Jesus places “the eye” between “treasure” and “Mammon,” he is not suddenly changing the subject; he is pointing out the hinge of the whole passage: where your treasure is, there your eye is; where your eye is, there you go.

The word translated “sound” is the Greek ἁπλοῦς (haplous), meaning “single, simple, undivided,” and in Jewish usage it also carries the sense of “generous, holding nothing back.” Its opposite, “evil,” is πονηρός (ponēros), whose basic meaning is “wicked”; in Jewish idiom “an evil eye” means greed, envy, stinginess. So what the Lord Jesus is talking about here is not a problem of eyesight at all but a problem of loyalty: are your eyes fixed singly on one Master, or are you glancing left and right, with a foot in two boats?

Notice also the picture of the “lamp.” Houses in ancient Palestine had very small windows and were dim inside all day long; the light or darkness of the whole house depended on one small oil lamp. If the lamp was bright, the whole room was lit; if the lamp went out, the whole room was dark. The eye is to a person what that lamp is to the whole house.

sections.heading: 2. 2 Corinthians 4:18
sections.html:
The author of 2 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. It was written in about AD 55–56, to the church in Corinth. Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, a great, wealthy, proud seaport city that prized eloquence and appearances. At the time, some in the church were questioning Paul: he was unimpressive in person, crude in speech, persecuted everywhere, his body covered in scars — how could someone like that be a servant God was using mightily?

Paul’s answer is written in 2 Corinthians 4. He says, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7). He also says, “Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:16–17). Immediately after comes verse 18, the summing up.

The word translated “look at” is the Greek σκοπέω (skopeō), the very root of the English word “scope” (as in telescope or rifle scope), meaning “to aim at, to gaze at intently, to make one’s target.” Paul is not saying Christians shut their eyes to reality; he knew reality better than anyone. He is saying: what we aim at is not what is in front of us, but what is eternal. Wherever you aim the gun of your life, that is what you will hit.

Put these two passages together and you have the skeleton of this lesson: the eye determines the whole body, and the focus determines the ending.

sections.heading: 1. Wrong Seeing Brings Sin and Destruction
sections.html:
“At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at.” (2 Samuel 11:2)

Before the Fall Comes Slackness

When we read this verse, we often jump straight to “he saw,” and overlook the verse before it: “At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroyed the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed at Jerusalem” (2 Samuel 11:1).

The Holy Spirit took care to record one sentence: David stayed at Jerusalem. When he should have gone out to battle, he stayed in the palace; when he should have been up, he was still in bed; only when the sun was going down did he get up. Brothers and sisters, a spiritual fall never happens suddenly. Before the fall comes slackness; before failure comes leaving one’s post. A person who has left his originally intended position will find his eyes beginning to wander.

The Chain Reaction of One “Look”

The Hebrew word for “saw” is רָאָה (ra’ah), and the original behind “very beautiful to look at” is טוֹבַת מַרְאֶה (tovat mar’eh), where mar’eh means precisely “what is seen, the outward appearance.” In other words, the Bible tells us with great precision: what David saw was “appearance.” He did not see God, nor did he see that behind this appearance was a married woman, the home of a loyal officer.

What follows is a clear downward chain:

He saw beauty — this step is not sin; a person’s eyes will inevitably fall on beautiful things.

He did not turn his eyes away — at this step, the door to sin opened.

He began to think — he sent to inquire about her (2 Samuel 11:3).

Desire arose — imagination turned into longing.

He put it into action — he sent messengers and had the woman brought to him.

The book of James describes exactly the same chain: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:14–15). John also says, “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16). Notice that John lists “the lust of the eyes” on its own, because the eyes are the front door of the heart.

One wrong look brought a whole series of destruction: adultery, then murder by another’s hand — he wrote to Joab, “Send Uriah to the forefront of the hottest battle, and retreat from him, that he may be struck, and die” (2 Samuel 11:15). Finally, the breaking of his family — God declared through the prophet Nathan: “Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised me, and have taken Uriah the Hittite’s wife to be your wife” (2 Samuel 12:10). The later disgrace of Amnon, the rebellion of Absalom, the bloodshed within the family — all of it began with that one look from the palace roof.

Let’s set beside him a man who saw rightly. Job said, “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1) Job did not wait until he had seen before he struggled; before he ever saw, he had already made a covenant with his own eyes. What wisdom that is.

An Example from Daily Life: Where You Look, the Bike Goes

Anyone who has had motorcycle or racing training knows a term called “target fixation.” The instructor’s first lesson is often: don’t stare at the thing you’re afraid of. When a rider on a mountain road sees a large rock by the roadside and thinks, “Whatever I do, I mustn’t hit it,” yet keeps his eyes fixed hard on that rock, nine times out of ten the bike heads straight for it. That’s because the body unconsciously follows the line of sight. So the right thing to do is: look where you want to go, not at what you’re afraid of.

Psychology confirms this too. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published the famous “white bear experiment” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. The researchers asked participants not to think of a white bear for the next five minutes, and to ring a bell whenever they did. The result was that those told “don’t think of a white bear” actually thought of white bears more than those who had not been told. This is called the “ironic rebound effect.”

Brothers and sisters, this is why simply gritting our teeth and saying, “I won’t look, I won’t think about it,” nearly always fails. The Bible’s method has never been “don’t think about it”; the Bible’s method is “turn your eyes and fix them”: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2a). The way to overcome the darkness is not to glare at the darkness with all your might, but to switch on the light.

Thank God: Repentance Also Begins with a “Look”

But the story does not end in destruction. Nathan came and told a parable about a poor man and his little ewe lamb. David burned with anger, but Nathan said, “You are the man!” And so —

“David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against Yahweh.’ Nathan said to David, ‘Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.’” (2 Samuel 12:13)

Brothers and sisters, please notice: David’s fall began with a wrong look; David’s restoration also began with a right look — at last he saw his own sin. In Psalm 51 he says, “For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me” (Psalm 51:3).

That is why he could pray like this: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

The Hebrew word for “search” is חָקַר (chaqar), whose basic meaning is “to dig deep, to explore,” like a miner with a lamp digging down layer by layer. David is asking God: Lord, I cannot see myself; please bring your light and dig down to the very bottom of my heart.

Only when we see ourselves rightly can we enter into repentance and restoration.

Applying the 321 Vision

In the light of 321 we say: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. David standing on the palace roof and looking down — this was precisely a look that had “left its originally intended position”: he was king, he had power, and whatever he saw he could take. When a person looks with his own eyes, the eyes become servants of desire; when a person lets Jesus become his eyes, the eyes become a window of worship.

When the focus is on ourselves, the ending is failure. Of the fivefold change, the first is mindset — because how you see is your mindset. Only a change of mindset can change the life, and only a changed life can change daily living.

sections.heading: 2. Wrong Seeing Brings Fear and Sinking
sections.html:
“But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:30)

The Background: The Sea in the Fourth Watch

This took place right after the miracle of the five loaves and two fish. “Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, and to go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away” (Matthew 14:22). The Lord himself went up the mountain to pray. Then “in the fourth watch of the night” — that is, between three and six in the morning, when the sky is darkest and people are most exhausted — “Jesus came to them, walking on the sea” (Matthew 14:25). The disciples thought it was a ghost and cried out in terror. “But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, ‘Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid’” (Matthew 14:27).

Then comes one of the bravest sentences in the whole Bible: “Peter answered him and said, ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.’ He said, ‘Come!’ Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus” (Matthew 14:28–29).

Brothers and sisters, please don’t be too quick to laugh at Peter. In that boat, he was the only one who got out; in all of human history, apart from the Lord Jesus, he is the only one who has walked on water. To begin with, Peter was this: looking at Jesus, he walked on the water.

What Changed Was Not the Circumstances but the Focus

Then the text says: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid.” The word “saw” here is the Greek βλέπω (blepō), meaning seeing with the physical eye.

Here is a vitally important detail: the wind and waves did not arrive at that moment. The wind and waves had been there before he got out of the boat — indeed, even earlier, the disciples had been tossed about on them for most of the night. What changed was not the circumstances; what changed was the focus. At first he looked past the wind and waves and saw the Lord; now he let the wind and waves block his view of the Lord.

So Peter did not sink because his ability fell short, nor because his faith was too small to get out of the boat — he had already got out of the boat! He sank because he “saw wrongly.”

When the Lord pulled him up, he said, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:31) The Greek word for “doubt” is διστάζω (distazō), whose root carries the idea of “two,” meaning “to stand on two sides, to have a heart split in half.” Half looking at the Lord, half looking at the wind — and a person sinks. This is exactly what the Lord Jesus said in Matthew 6:22: when the eye is not sound, not single, the whole body is full of darkness.

Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology

Physiologically, our balance depends not only on the vestibular system of the inner ear but very heavily on sight as well. You can try it right now: stand on one foot, and many people can stay there for a long time; but close your eyes, and most people start wobbling within a few seconds. Where the eyes look, there the body steadies itself. That is why tightrope walkers never look down at their feet; they fix their eyes on one point on the far side.

Psychologically, research on anxiety has repeatedly confirmed a phenomenon called “attentional bias.” In 1986 Colin MacLeod, Andrew Mathews and Philip Tata published a study in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology which found that the attention of highly anxious people is involuntarily drawn to threatening information, whereas that of ordinary people is not. In other words, the more afraid people are, the more they stare at frightening things; and the more they stare, the more afraid they become — a vicious circle.

The Bible gave us the way out long ago. The word “looking” is the Greek ἀφοράω (aphoraō), made up of apo (away from) and horaō (to see). Its literal meaning is: first take your eyes off everything else, and only then can you fix them on the One. So the act of faith has two halves: first look away, then fix your gaze. If you don’t look away, you can’t fix your gaze.

Here is another picture. When Elisha was surrounded by the Aramean army, his servant got up early in the morning, saw horses, chariots and soldiers all around the city, and cried out: “Alas, my master! What shall we do?” “He answered, ‘Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.’ Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:16–17).

Brothers and sisters, please notice: those horses and chariots of fire were there all along. Elisha did not ask God to conjure up horses and chariots of fire; he only asked God to open his servant’s eyes. God’s resources are never lacking; what is lacking is our seeing.

Applying the 321 Vision

When the focus is on our circumstances, we waver. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will rejoice, rely on the brain and you will worry. The moment Peter stepped out of the boat, he was relying on the heart; the moment he began calculating amid the wind and waves, he was relying on the brain. As soon as he started calculating, he started sinking.

Look at your circumstances, and you are afraid; look at Jesus, and there are miracles. The key to faith has never been how hard you try, but this: whom you are looking at.

sections.heading: 3. Right Seeing Brings Promise and Blessing
sections.html:
“For I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever.” (Genesis 13:15)

How Abram Saw, and How Lot Saw

The background of this passage is a family dispute. Abram and his nephew Lot both had large flocks and herds, and their herdsmen quarrelled with each other. As the elder, as the one who had been called, Abram could easily have exercised his authority. But he said: “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives. Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left” (Genesis 13:8–9).

What humility this is — laying down his rights and returning to his originally intended position; letting man be man and letting God be God.

Then Lot also “lifted up his eyes”: “Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar. So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one other” (Genesis 13:10–11).

Brothers and sisters, Lot also lifted up his eyes and also saw, but what he saw was “well-watered” — immediate, worldly, temporary gain. Right after, in verse 13, the Holy Spirit adds a sentence: “Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners against Yahweh” (Genesis 13:13). Lot saw the water and grass of Sodom, but did not see the wickedness of Sodom. And the result? He lost his property, lost his testimony, lost his sons-in-law, and in the end lost even his wife — “But Lot’s wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). Even while fleeing for her life, she looked back at the wrong place.

And Abram? “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward’” (Genesis 13:14).

Please notice two things. First, he gave way first, and only then did he see. Humility comes first; then comes spiritual vision. Second, it was God who told him to look. Human seeing is something we choose for ourselves; spiritual seeing is God opening your eyes. Lot’s seeing was his own choice; Abram’s seeing was God’s gift. Two kinds of seeing, two endings.

God also said: “Arise, walk through the land in its length and in its width; for I will give it to you” (Genesis 13:17). After seeing, you must step out — the seeing of faith inevitably brings forth the steps of faith.

Interestingly, Abraham never actually possessed that land in his lifetime. Stephen said before the Council: “He gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on” (Acts 7:5a). All he ever bought in the land of Canaan in his whole life was a single burial plot for Sarah. But Hebrews says: “For he looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:10). And again: “These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13a).

What he saw was further and truer than the ground beneath his feet.

Elisha: To See Is to Receive

“Elijah said to Elisha, ‘Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.’ Elisha said, ‘Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.’ He said, ‘You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be so for you; but if not, it will not be so.’” (2 Kings 2:9–10)

Why was “seeing” the condition? This was not a magic show or an eyesight test. It was a spiritual verification. That day, fifty of the sons of the prophets stood watching at a distance (2 Kings 2:7), but only Elisha followed closely: from Gilgal to Bethel, from Bethel to Jericho, from Jericho to the Jordan. Three times Elijah told him to stay behind, and three times he answered, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you” (2 Kings 2:2, 4, 6).

In other words, “seeing” was the fruit of following to the very end. You cannot stand at a distance watching and expect to receive a double anointing.

“As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha saw it, and he cried, ‘My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!’” (2 Kings 2:11–12a) He saw, and so he received. From that day on, the waters of the Jordan parted in his hands, and the sons of the prophets said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha” (2 Kings 2:15a).

See spiritual things, and you inherit spiritual power.

An Example from Science: That Seemingly Empty Patch of Sky

In December 1995 astronomers made a decision that many at the time thought was a waste: they pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a tiny patch of sky in Ursa Major that appeared completely empty, and exposed it continuously for ten days, taking more than three hundred images in all. How small was that patch of sky? Roughly the area you would cover with the head of a pin held at arm’s length.

And the result? Out of that tiny patch of “nothing” emerged nearly three thousand galaxies. This is the famous “Hubble Deep Field.”

Brothers and sisters, what seems completely empty is in fact full of glory — it just takes a long enough, focused enough gaze. Does your situation today look like a blank? God’s glory may be right there, waiting for you to fix your eyes on it.

Applying the 321 Vision

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. This is exactly what Abram did. He dealt with the relationship first — he would rather lose out himself than quarrel with his own flesh and blood; once the relationship was right, God gave him the inheritance. Lot did it the other way round, grabbing things first, and in the end he lost both the things and the relationship.

321 also speaks of the 235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, build a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Abram and Lot could have been each other’s “2,” but they were separated because of Lot’s way of seeing; Elijah and Elisha, on the other hand, became the most beautiful “3” in the Bible — a spiritual father and son. The first thing Elisha cried out was “My father, my father!” This was not the handing on of an office; it was the handing on of a life.

sections.heading: 4. The Seeing of Faith Brings Eternal Reward
sections.html:
“By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.” (Hebrews 11:27)

Moses: Faith Is a Revaluation

Hebrews 11 has been called “the roll of honour of the heroes of faith.” About Moses, the writer says: “By faith, Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to share ill treatment with God’s people than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a time, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked to the reward” (Hebrews 11:24–26).

The word “considering” is the Greek ἡγέομαι (hēgeomai), meaning “to judge after weighing things up, to assess.” So please notice: faith is not blind; faith is a revaluation. It is not that Moses had never done the sums — he did them more clearly than anyone. He put the treasures of Egypt on one side of the scales and the reproach suffered for Christ on the other, and then said: the second weighs more.

“As seeing him who is invisible” is, in the original, ὡς ὁρῶν τὸν ἀόρατον — literally, “as seeing the unseeable.” The same root for “see” (horaō) is used twice in a single phrase, once positively and once negatively, forming a beautiful contrast. The essence of faith is to see, in an unseen way, the God who cannot be seen.

Supporting Evidence from Science: What We Can See Is Only a Tiny Part

Here I want to draw your attention to a wonderful fact, brothers and sisters. The visible light the human eye can see has wavelengths of only about 380 to 700 nanometres — an extremely small slice of the whole electromagnetic spectrum. Infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, radio waves — we cannot see any of them, yet they are really there every moment, even passing through our bodies.

Even more staggering is the make-up of the universe. According to the observations published in 2013 by the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite, the universe is made up of roughly 68% dark energy and 27% dark matter, while the ordinary matter we can see accounts for only about 5%.

Brothers and sisters, even science is telling us: what can be seen is only a tiny part. How narrow, then, is a life that judges entirely by the naked eye; how poor is a person who believes only what he can see.

So Hebrews goes on: “But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them” (Hebrews 11:16). See eternity, and you will not be bound by this life. A person with a homeland in his heart will not quarrel himself red in the face over a scrap of land while he is a sojourner.

Paul: A Recalculated Profit-and-Loss Statement

“Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ.” (Philippians 3:8)

The Greek word for “refuse” is σκύβαλον (skybalon), meaning kitchen scraps, leftovers, rubbish and dung thrown out of the door. It is a very strong word.

But please notice that Paul is using the language of accounting here. In the previous verse he says: “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ” (Philippians 3:7). Gain and loss — this is a profit-and-loss statement. Paul’s pedigree, education, zeal and righteous deeds had all been entered in the “assets” column; after he came to know Christ, he did the accounts again and moved every one of them to the “liabilities” column.

It was not that those things had gone bad in themselves; it was that he “looked” at them again, and their value was completely revised.

Because he saw rightly, he lived rightly.

The Crown: See Eternity, and You Gain Eternity

When Paul wrote 2 Timothy, he was in prison in Rome, about to be martyred for the Lord. He said, “For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come” (2 Timothy 4:6). And then he said:

“From now on, the crown of righteousness is stored up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing.” (2 Timothy 4:8)

To the naked eye, it was a cold cell, a sword about to fall, an ending in failure. To the eye of faith, it was a crown of righteousness, a Lord who gives the crown in person, a glorious beginning. The same scene, two ways of seeing, two conclusions.

Help from Psychology: Seeing the Reward Not Yet in Hand

From the late 1960s to the early 1970s, the Stanford University psychologist Walter Mischel and his colleagues carried out the famous “marshmallow test.” The researcher put a marshmallow in front of a preschool child and told the child that if they could wait a while without eating it, they would get two when the researcher came back. Later follow-up studies (Shoda, Mischel and Peake, 1990) found that the children who had been better able to wait showed better self-control and academic results in adolescence. It should be said that a large-sample replication study by Tyler Watts and others in 2018 found that this link was weaker than originally reported and was influenced by family socio-economic background; but the basic principle — “those who can see a reward not yet in hand can let go of the immediate pleasure in their hand” — is still widely affirmed.

Brothers and sisters, faith is in fact the highest form of delayed gratification: because we see the unseen reward, we can let go of the temporary sweet in our hand. Moses let go of the throne of Egypt, Paul let go of his prospects in Judaism, and the Lord Jesus himself, “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2b).

Helen Keller is commonly credited with saying: “The only thing worse than being blind is having sight but no vision.” A person can have excellent eyesight and yet see nothing at all.

Applying the 321 Vision

321 speaks of a change of perspective: from man’s point of view to God’s point of view, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. These four changes can be seen plainly in Moses and in Paul.

See eternity, and you gain eternity.

sections.heading: 5. Key Summary: Two Ways of Seeing, Two Ways of Living
sections.html:
Let’s gather these four parts together.

Worldly Seeing

Look at desire, and you sin — that was David.

Look at circumstances, and you fear — that was Peter.

Look at yourself, and you are weak — that was the ten spies.

The result: failure, destruction, sinking.

Spiritual Seeing

Look at God, and you have faith — that was Elisha.

Look at the promise, and you obey — that was Abraham.

Look at eternity, and you overcome — that was Moses and Paul.

The result: blessing, power, glory.

The Same Land, Two Reports

Numbers 13 is the most vivid example of this truth. Twelve spies explored the same land of Canaan, walked the same roads, looked at the same city walls, met the same descendants of Anak — and came back with two completely opposite reports.

The ten spies said: “There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33).

Brothers and sisters, please notice the second half of this verse — “and so we were in their sight.” They imagined that for themselves; the Bible never records a single descendant of Anak saying any such thing. A person who sees himself as a grasshopper will assume the whole world sees him as a grasshopper. A sense of inferiority is also a kind of seeing wrongly.

But Caleb and Joshua said: “Only don’t rebel against Yahweh, neither fear the people of the land; for they are bread for us. Their defense is removed from over them, and Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them” (Numbers 14:9).

The same giants were, through one pair of eyes, a wall too high to scale; through another, “bread for us.” We all know the outcome: the ten spies and that whole generation aged twenty and over fell dead in the wilderness, and only the two who saw rightly entered the promised land.

Supporting Evidence from Psychology: The Frame Determines the Choice

In 1981 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman published their famous study of the “Asian disease problem” in the journal Science. The researchers told participants that a disease was expected to kill 600 people, and that there were two programmes to choose from. The first group heard it described this way: “Programme A will save 200 people; with Programme B there is a one-third chance that all 600 will be saved and a two-thirds chance that no one will be saved.” Most chose the cautious A. The second group heard it described this way: “With Programme A, 400 people will die; with Programme B there is a one-third chance that nobody will die and a two-thirds chance that all 600 will die.” This time most chose the risky B.

But brothers and sisters, the numbers for the two groups were exactly the same! The only difference was that one looked at it in terms of “saving” and the other in terms of “dying.” This is the famous “framing effect.” The facts were identical; only because the frame through which they were seen was different, the choices were completely reversed.

This is precisely what the Lord Jesus said: “The lamp of the body is the eye” (Matthew 6:22a).

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: The Focus Determines the Outcome
sections.html:
Three Focal Points, Three Endings

When the focus is on ourselves, the ending is failure.

When the focus is on our circumstances, the ending is wavering.

When the focus is on Jesus, the ending is victory.

The self-centred look with their own eyes; the selfless let Jesus become their eyes.

Brothers and sisters, please notice that selflessness is not shutting our eyes, not looking at nothing. 321 puts it very clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. It is the same with the eyes — it is not that we stop looking, but that we look with a different pair of eyes.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Asking God to Enlighten the Eyes of the Heart

Paul’s prayer for the church in Ephesus was for exactly this: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Ephesians 1:17–18).

So it turns out we also have a pair of eyes in our hearts, and those eyes need to be enlightened by the Holy Spirit. The physical eye is lit by light; the eye of the heart is lit by the Holy Spirit. This is the third of the Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Humble Seeing and Proud Seeing

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

David looking down from the palace roof was seeing from outside his originally intended position: I am king, and whatever I see I can take.

Abram saying to Lot, “If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right,” was seeing from within his originally intended position: I am not the owner of this land; God is.

And the result? Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. From then on the sword never left David’s house, while Abram’s offspring became like the dust of the earth.

Change Your Position, Change Your Life

In 1987 the writer Frank White coined a term, “the Overview Effect.” He interviewed many astronauts and found that the moment they looked back at the earth from space, their values were often permanently changed: there was a blue planet hanging in the darkness, without a single national border, fragile, beautiful, whole. Looking down from that height, many of the rivalries of the human world suddenly seemed very small.

Brothers and sisters, we too have a position. God “raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6). Our seat is not beside our problems; it is in Christ, in the heavenly places. That is why Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

This is how the selfless see the heart of God, experience the power of God and receive the promises of God.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s string the light of 321 together from beginning to end.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — the Lord himself is the One who “saw rightly”: he, “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2b). The Bible is my standard — “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). The eyes need a lamp, and the lamp is God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who enlightens the eyes of our hearts.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — where the King is, there the eyes are; where the eyes are, there the person goes. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when we look at Jesus alone, human glory naturally fades away.

The Goal. Establish God’s system — when a group of people who see rightly gather together, that is God’s system; when a group of people who each see their own way gather together, they are merely a crowd.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This lesson works on precisely the first. How you see is your mindset. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Many brothers and sisters want to change their daily living or their ministry directly, but are unwilling to change their mindset — and so after all their effort they are still going round in circles in the same place.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. David’s tragedy was that he turned this order completely upside down — he looked first at a “thing” (a beautiful appearance), and as a result he ruined his relationship with God, his relationship with himself and his relationship with others.

The 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” Brothers and sisters, think about it: when you look at your “2” with worldly eyes, what do you see? Their faults, their threat, what they owe you, how they have wronged you. But when you practise selflessness (0) and let Jesus be your eyes, you see someone God loves, someone for whom Christ laid down his life. Then the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit naturally grow: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23a).

How you see your “2” determines how many of those fruits you can bear.

The 235 relationships. Elijah and Elisha were the most beautiful “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children. Elisha was able to inherit a double anointing not because he had some outstanding talent, but because he followed all the way, kept his eyes fixed all the way, and in the end “saw.” Spiritual inheritance has never depended on courses; it depends on seeing.

The Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit guides me, the Bible enlightens me, Jesus is my role model, and so I rise up to serve, until in the end Jesus receives all the glory. Every step of this path requires a renewed pair of eyes.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. We’ll keep them, and deepen them using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Check your “seeing” on the spot

Whenever your emotions surge, immediately ask yourself one question: What am I looking at right now? My circumstances? Myself? Or God?

Emotions are the most honest dashboard there is.
