When you’re angry, you’re looking at “my rights”; when you’re jealous, you’re looking at “how well others are doing”; when you’re anxious, you’re looking at “what hasn’t happened yet”; when you feel inferior, you’re looking at “this grasshopper that is me.” Behind every negative emotion stands a focal point.

A suggestion: put a small card on your phone’s home screen or on your desk with five words on it — “What am I looking at?”

Practice 2: Practise turning your eyes to Jesus

Whenever anxiety or temptation comes, don’t argue with it, don’t play tug-of-war with it; turn to the Lord at once, and let Scripture replace what your eyes see.

This is exactly the reminder the white bear experiment gives us: telling yourself “don’t think about it” only makes you think about it more. So the Lord’s method is “looking to” — first look away, then fix your gaze.

A suggestion: prepare three “turn-your-eyes verses” and learn them by heart, so you can say them at any moment. For example:

“looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2a)

“Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2)

“while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen.” (2 Corinthians 4:18a)

Practice 3: Ask the Lord every day to search your sight

Every night before you sleep, use David’s prayer to ask God to shine his light on the way you see inside, and to correct the wrong ways of seeing.

“Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

Information: First fix the content of this lesson in your memory — seeing, thinking, doing and the outcome form a chain; David, Peter and Lot saw wrongly; Abraham, Elisha and Paul saw rightly. Information is the foundation; without the right information, there is no right seeing.

Revelation: Information is in the head; revelation is in the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn “knowing” into “seeing,” just as God opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant. Pray: Lord, enlighten the eyes of my heart.

Conviction: Do you really believe that “I am not defeated by my circumstances; I am defeated by seeing wrongly”? Conviction means handing over sovereignty, admitting that your way of seeing needs to be governed by God. Without conviction, practice turns into performance.

Implementation: Starting tomorrow morning, put the three exercises above into practice. Don’t make ten resolutions at once; start with one — start with the question, “What am I looking at?”

Evaluation: Set aside three minutes every evening to review today’s “seeing.” At what moment today did I see wrongly? What was I feeling at that moment? What did I do afterwards?

Correction: Identify the situation in which you most often see wrongly — it might be when you open your phone, when you look at your bank account, or when you face a particular family member. Prepare a verse for that situation, like a soldier posting extra guards on the stretch of wall most easily breached.

Repetition: A habit is not formed all at once. Give yourself forty days, every day without a break. Spiritual sight is like a muscle: the more you use it, the stronger it gets; and like a mirror: the more you polish it, the brighter it shines.

Multiplication: Find one of your “2”s and practise together, asking each other one question every week: “What have you been looking at this week?” 321 says that if change does not multiply, it stops with us. Those who have received must become those who give.

A Gentle Reminder

You are not defeated by your circumstances; you are defeated by “seeing wrongly.”

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look once more at what we have seen today:

David saw wrongly, and he sinned.

Peter saw wrongly, and he sank.

Lot saw wrongly, and he lost.

Abraham saw rightly, and he received the land.

Elisha saw rightly, and he received power.

Paul saw rightly, and he received the crown.

Different ways of seeing bring completely different outcomes.

This morning the Lord sets this choice before us. He has not promised us that there will be no wind and waves — on the night Peter stepped out of the boat, the wind was already strong. He has not promised us that there will be no temptation — every one of us stands on David’s roof once a day. He has not promised that we will receive the land straight away — to the day he died, Abraham bought only a burial plot.

But the Lord does promise: what you look at, you become.

So when you choose not to look at the world, not to look at yourself, but to look at Jesus alone, your life will never be the same again; instead it will enter into the victory and glory God has prepared!

Brothers and sisters, letting Jesus be King begins with letting Jesus be your eyes. When he reigns as King in your eyes, he reigns as King in your thoughts; when he reigns as King in your thoughts, he reigns as King in your actions; when he reigns as King in your actions, he reigns as King over your whole life.

On that day, everything we have received will be laid at his feet. Because we saw rightly, we lived rightly; because we lived rightly, all the glory goes to him.

May all the glory go to our Lord Jesus Christ alone.

keyVerses: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

“while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)
declarations: Lord, guard my eyes! Do not let me look at everything with worldly eyes, but with your eyes! In every choice, let me see you and walk in the way that pleases you!
practices: Practise turning your eyes to Jesus
Ask the Lord every day to search your sight
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we worship you before your face.

Lord, thank you for reminding us this morning that the outcome of our lives is no accident; it begins with a single “look.” Please forgive us — so often we are like David, seeing and yet refusing to turn our eyes away; so often like Peter, plainly walking on the water and yet letting the wind and waves steal our focus; so often like Lot, seeing only the well-watered plain in front of us and not the danger behind it.

Lord, guard our eyes. Do not let us look at people, at things or at ourselves with worldly eyes, but with your eyes. Just as you opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant, open our eyes, so that we see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, and see that your presence has never left us.
We ask that the Holy Spirit would enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that we may see the hope of your calling. Let us see you in every choice, and walk in the way that pleases you.
May the focus of our whole lives be not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances, but on Jesus alone. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Think back to the most recent event that sent your emotions surging. At that moment, where was your focus — on your circumstances, on yourself, or on God? If you had been able, like Peter, to cry out, “Lord, save me!”, how might things have turned out differently? Read Matthew 14:30–31 together.

Abram gave way first, and only then did God tell him to lift up his eyes and look (Genesis 13:8–9, 14–15). In your relationships at present, is there something in which God wants you first to lay down your rights and return to your originally intended position? What price are you willing to pay first, so that you can see further? Read Genesis 13:14–17 together.
l123.title: Different Seeing, Different Outcomes
l123.subtitle: Focus Decides the Outcome; Vision Decides the Life
l123.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: What Sets the Direction of a Life Is Not Only the Eyes, but Also the Ears
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. In our last lesson we thought together about “seeing rightly.” We saw that the direction our eyes look is very often the direction our feet will walk. Today we take one more step and look at another key that just as surely sets the direction of a life — what are you listening to?

Let me begin with a story from the sea. Late on the night of 14 April 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. Many people think it was a disaster that came without warning. It wasn’t. According to the inquiries held afterwards in both Britain and the United States, the Titanic’s wireless room received at least six ice warnings from nearby ships over the course of that day. The warnings kept coming; the signals were in the air all along. The problem was not that no one spoke; the problem was that what was said was not taken seriously. That evening the wireless operator was busy sending private telegrams for first-class passengers, and when the Californian sent its final warning, he even snapped back: “Shut up, I am busy.” Forty minutes later the ship hit the iceberg.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? It wasn’t that there was no warning; it was that no one listened. It wasn’t that the message didn’t arrive; it was that the ears weren’t open.

Our lives are very often like that. Many people’s problem is not that they don’t try hard enough, not that they aren’t zealous enough, not that they aren’t clever enough. Many people’s problem is that they are listening to the wrong voice.

Let’s keep this order in our hearts: how you listen shapes what you believe; what you believe shapes how you live. Listening is the source, believing is the middle of the road, living is the outcome. Let the source be off by one degree, and by the end of the road you are a thousand miles astray.

Have you ever wondered why God gave us two ears but only one mouth? There is a widely quoted saying usually attributed to the ancient Greek philosopher Epictetus: “We have two ears and one mouth so that we can listen twice as much as we speak.” That is a piece of wisdom about human relationships; but in the spiritual world the matter is far more serious — because what we listen to is not only the words of people, but also the word of God; and there is yet another kind of voice, the voice of the world, of our own self, even of Satan.

The Bible makes this plain from its very first pages. Humanity’s first fall did not begin with “seeing”; it began with “listening.” The serpent spoke to the woman, and the woman listened; the woman spoke to the man, and the man listened. God’s sentence on Adam does not begin, “Because you ate”; it begins, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life.” (Genesis 3:17)

Brothers and sisters, notice this: the first thing God called to account was “whom did you listen to?” The doorway of sin is not the mouth; it is the ear.

And the doorway of salvation is the ear as well. Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17) The ear can cost a person paradise, and the ear can bring a person eternal life. One and the same door opens onto two utterly different endings.

So in this lesson we must honestly ask ourselves three questions. First, what am I actually listening to every day? Second, after I have listened, have I changed? Third, when God speaks in a still small voice, can my heart grow quiet enough to hear?

May God himself open our ears this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Jeremiah’s Sermon at the Temple Gate
sections.html:
The theme text of this lesson comes from Jeremiah chapter 7. To really feel the weight of this verse, we first need to stand where Jeremiah stood.

Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin. He was called around the thirteenth year of Josiah king of Judah, that is, about 627 BC, and his ministry spanned five kings — Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah — continuing until after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. He is called “the weeping prophet,” because his forty-odd years of ministry were almost nothing but speaking, and speaking, and being rejected.

Jeremiah 7 is usually called “the Temple Sermon.” Yahweh told Jeremiah to stand in the gate of the temple and speak to all the people of Judah coming in to worship. It is a startling scene: crowds walking devoutly into the temple to offer sacrifice, and a prophet standing at the gate crying out God’s word to them.

The people of that day had a slogan, recorded in chapter 7, verse 4: “Yahweh’s temple, Yahweh’s temple, Yahweh’s temple, are these.” They treated the temple as a lucky charm. Their logic was this: the temple is here, so God will never abandon Jerusalem; the sacrifices have never stopped, not one step of the worship is missing, so God is bound to be on our side.

But through Jeremiah God showed that their worship was empty. For what God wanted from the very beginning was never that whole routine. Listen to verses 22 and 23: “For I didn’t speak to your fathers or command them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices; but this thing I commanded them, saying, ‘Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. Walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.’” (Jeremiah 7:22–23)

“This thing I commanded them” — brothers and sisters, God says there was one thing. Not seventy things, not seven things, but one: listen to my voice.

Notice the three layers here. The first is “Listen to my voice” — that is the starting point. The second is “I will be your God, and you shall be my people” — that is the relationship. The third is “Walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you” — that is the outcome. The order could not be clearer: first we listen, and then there is relationship; once there is relationship, there is true walking in his ways and true blessing.

The Hebrew verb for “listen” here is shama. It is an enormously important word. The passage that Jews recite every morning and evening, “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.” (Deuteronomy 6:4), begins with this very word, shama. It does not mean merely that the ear picks up a sound; it carries in itself the sense of “paying heed, responding, obeying.” In the Hebrew mindset, to hear without obeying is not to have heard at all. What Chinese needs two characters to say — “to hear” and “to follow” — Hebrew says in a single word.

So when Jeremiah says, “Listen to my voice,” he is not saying, “Please lend me your ears for five minutes.” He is saying: hand your whole self over to this word, and let this word be master.

Chapter 7, verse 24 goes on to record how Israel actually responded: “But they didn’t listen or turn their ear, but walked in their own counsels and in the stubbornness of their evil heart, and went backward, and not forward.” That sentence pierces straight to the nature of “wrong listening” — it isn’t that the ears are broken; it’s that people “walk in their own” way.

The same theme runs through every biblical example we will look at today. Saul, Abraham, Rehoboam — none of them was deaf. They all heard; they simply chose to listen to other voices.

sections.heading: 1. Wrong Listening Brings Deviation and Loss
sections.html:
The Bible is the most honest book there is. It records not only successes but failures too, in detail. On the consequences of “listening wrongly,” it gives us three very concrete examples.

1. Saul: Listening to the Voice of People over the Voice of God

In 1 Samuel 15, God gave Saul a crystal-clear command through Samuel: strike the Amalekites and utterly destroy all they had. This was not a judgement call left to Saul; it was God’s explicit order.

Here is how the Bible records what happened: “But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, of the cattle, and of the fat calves, and the lambs, and all that was good, and were not willing to utterly destroy them; but everything that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.” (1 Samuel 15:9)

Notice the detail in that verse: what they killed was the “vile and refuse”; what they kept was “the best.” On the surface it looks like thrift; underneath it is picking and choosing. Saul treated God’s command as a list of suggestions he could carry out selectively.

When Samuel arrived, how fine Saul’s first words sounded! He said, “You are blessed by Yahweh! I have performed the commandment of Yahweh.” (1 Samuel 15:13) But Samuel’s reply was sharper still: “Then what does this bleating of the sheep in my ears, and the lowing of the cattle which I hear mean?” (1 Samuel 15:14)

Brothers and sisters, that is a remarkable sentence. With his mouth Saul said, “I have performed it,” while in Samuel’s ears came the bleating of sheep and the lowing of cattle. Your mouth can dress things up, but your life makes its own sound. Whom you have truly obeyed, your life will cry out by itself.

What was the consequence? God himself said: “It grieves me that I have set up Saul to be king; for he has turned back from following me, and has not performed my commandments.” (1 Samuel 15:11)

And in the end Saul himself admitted the real reason: “I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of Yahweh, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” (1 Samuel 15:24)

The reason comes down to one word: fear. He feared the people, so he listened to the people. Whomever we listen to is whomever we fear; and whomever we fear becomes our king.

There is a very famous confirmation of this from psychology. In 1951 the social psychologist Solomon Asch ran his well-known “line conformity experiment” at Swarthmore College. He showed participants a card with three lines of clearly different lengths and asked them which one matched a standard line. The answer was so simple it was almost impossible to get wrong. But the other “participants” in the room were all confederates planted by the researchers, and they would deliberately give the same wrong answer in unison. The result: about 75 per cent of the real participants went along at least once with an answer they plainly knew was wrong.

Asch’s experiment tells us something: when people go against their own judgement, it is very often not because they have been persuaded, but because they don’t want to be shut out. Saul did not fail to know what God had said; he did not want to be shut out by the people.

This is what it looks like when the outside seems obedient but the substance is rebellion.

Seen through the 321 vision, this is exactly the self-centred life. In the end the self-centred person listens to whichever voice protects his own face, position and sense of security. The real king in Saul’s heart was not Yahweh but Saul himself; the people’s voice drowned out God’s voice because Saul wanted to keep his throne. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. Saul left his originally intended position as “the anointed servant,” seized on “public opinion” as his prop, and so God took his position back.

2. Abraham: Listening to Human Advice and Losing God’s Timing

The second example comes closer to our everyday lives. This time the one who listened wrongly was not a rebellious king but the father of faith.

“Sarai said to Abram, ‘See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.’ Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” (Genesis 16:2)

Brothers and sisters, look closely: Sarai’s suggestion was not idolatry, not lustful adultery. In the culture of the ancient Near East it was a legal, understandable and reasonable course. The Nuzi texts and the Code of Hammurabi from the eighteenth century BC both record that a wife who could not bear children might give her maidservant to her husband, and the child born would be counted as the mistress’s own. Sarai broke no law; she was simply being practical.

So where was the problem? The problem was this: it was a human method used to bring about God’s promise.

God’s promise had already been given: “He who will come out of your own body will be your heir.” (Genesis 15:4) God hadn’t said when. And so ten years went by, and Sarai could wait no longer. The greatest temptation in waiting is to “give God a hand.”

And the result? The text goes on: “He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.” (Genesis 16:4) Trouble broke out in the household at once. Of Ishmael, God said, “He will be like a wild donkey among men. His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him. He will live opposed to all of his brothers.” (Genesis 16:12) Family turmoil and long-running conflict that has continued to this day.

For thirteen years the Bible records no further word from God to Abram, until Genesis 17:1, when God appeared to him again. Brothers and sisters, one time of listening wrongly may bring thirteen years of silence.

There is a spiritual principle here worth noticing: the more hurried you are, the more easily you hear human voices; the quieter you are, the more easily you hear God’s voice. Impatience amplifies human advice; only stillness amplifies God’s word.

The Nobel laureate in economics Daniel Kahneman, in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), distinguishes two systems of thinking: System 1 is fast, intuitive and automatic; System 2 is slow, effortful and requires concentration. He points out that under stress and fatigue, people almost always hand control over to System 1. The spiritual lesson is similar: when we are anxious, worn out and chased by the clock, we most easily react by instinct instead of growing quiet and waiting for God’s guidance. Sarai’s suggestion landed at precisely the point where Abram was most weary.

The 321 insight here is very clear: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. In that moment Abram’s focus fell on “circumstances” — ten years, and still no child; and on “other people” — this is what Sarai is saying. Once our focus leaves God, the human voice becomes the loudest voice.

3. Rehoboam: Listening to the Wrong People and Losing a Kingdom

The third example carries the greatest cost of all — a nation.

After Solomon died, his son Rehoboam took the throne. The people asked him to lighten the heavy yoke his father had laid on them. Rehoboam first consulted the old men, and the old men advised him to treat the people with kindness. But the text says: “But he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him.” (2 Chronicles 10:8)

Notice the words “who had grown up with him.” These young men were no outsiders; they were his echo chamber. They were his age, had lived what he had lived, and saw things the way he saw them. The voice we take in most easily is very often not the wisest voice but the voice most like our own.

In 1960 the psychologist Peter Wason first put forward what came to be known as “confirmation bias”: the tendency to seek out, notice and remember information that supports what we already think, while automatically ignoring evidence to the contrary. In other words, we are often not looking for an answer; we are looking for agreement. Rehoboam was not asking for advice; he was looking for people to endorse him.

And the result? 2 Chronicles 10:16 records that all Israel said to the king: “What portion do we have in David? We don’t have an inheritance in the son of Jesse! Every man to your tents, Israel! Now see to your own house, David.” A kingdom that had been united for some eighty years split in two from that day; the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah formally divided around 931 BC and never came back together.

Brothers and sisters, what Rehoboam rejected was wisdom; what he embraced was the flesh. It wasn’t that he lacked information; it was that he didn’t listen.

Listening to the wrong people can destroy a nation. Listening to the wrong people can also destroy a home, a marriage, the calling of a lifetime.

Wrong Listening Brings a Threefold Loss

Put these three examples side by side, and we see what wrong listening brings:

Saul listened to the people — spiritual failure, rejected by God. Abram listened to Sarai — a fractured family, long-running conflict. Rehoboam listened to the young men — a life’s loss, a nation divided.

From the spiritual, to the family, to the achievement of a lifetime — every line fell.

And these three men had one thing in common: none of them asked God first.

sections.heading: 2. Right Listening Brings Blessing and Life
sections.html:
Having looked at failure, we return to the heart of God. What God asks of us is, in fact, astonishingly simple.

“This thing I commanded them, saying, ‘Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. Walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.’” (Jeremiah 7:23)

Brothers and sisters, God says, “This thing I commanded them.” God isn’t asking us to do a hundred things; God is asking us to do one thing right — listen to his word, and obey.

Listen, then obey. These two are really one. For the Hebrew shama already contains obedience; and the Greek word for “obey,” hupakouō, literally means “to listen from beneath” (hupo is “under,” akouō is “to hear”). Whether in Hebrew or in Greek, the obedience the Bible speaks of is at heart a “posture of listening” — placing ourselves beneath the word and listening.

Samuel put this most penetratingly. In the very chapter of Saul’s failure, Samuel left us one of the most important principles in the Old Testament:

“Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.’” (1 Samuel 15:22)

Notice that Samuel did not say sacrifice was bad. Burnt offerings and peace offerings were instituted by God himself. What Samuel was talking about was order: obedience first, sacrifice after. Turn that order upside down, and no amount of sacrifice will be accepted.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the predicament of many zealous Christians. God doesn’t want a great deal of ministry from you; God wants you to listen to his word. Not doing a lot, but doing what is right.

I often use this illustration. Suppose you hire a decorator to work on your house and tell him: paint the master bedroom wall off-white. You come home from work and find he has very diligently painted the living room, the kitchen and the hallway all navy blue. He is dripping with sweat, and he says to you, “Boss, I got so much done today!” Would you be moved? You would probably be heartsick. Not because he was lazy, but because he worked all day long and didn’t do the one thing you asked.

God is like that too. What he values is not our workload but our obedience.

Isaiah describes the perfect Servant so beautifully: “The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught. The Lord Yahweh has opened my ear. I was not rebellious. I have not turned back.” (Isaiah 50:4–5)

“He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear” — brothers and sisters, this is exactly what morning devotions mean. It isn’t that we wake God up every morning; it is that God wakes up our ears every morning.

The Lord Jesus himself lived out this very pattern. He said, “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.” (John 5:30)

The Lord of the universe became flesh and came to earth, and the principle of his service was, of all things, “As I hear, I judge.” Jesus is my role model — he listened first, then acted.

From the 321 perspective, this is the first and second of the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, and the Bible is my standard. What is a standard? A standard is a measuring rule. If a craftsman won’t lay his work alongside the rule, however hard he works he won’t know how far off he is. Every morning when we open the Bible, we are laying our lives alongside the rule.

sections.heading: 3. Two Kinds of Service: Busyness and Listening
sections.html:
The third key point brings this principle into a household scene — Martha and Mary of Bethany.

“She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word.” (Luke 10:39)

“Sitting at Jesus’ feet” — in first-century Jewish culture, this was the place of a disciple. Paul says he was “brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers” (Acts 22:3). And in that era, those who sat at a rabbi’s feet to be taught were usually men. Mary sitting there was a rather bold act; and the Lord Jesus not only didn’t stop her, he defended her.

Meanwhile, what was Martha doing? The text says she “was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). The Greek word is perispaō, which literally means “to be pulled off in every direction.” How vivid! Being frazzled isn’t having a lot to do; being frazzled is having your heart torn apart.

Finally Martha couldn’t hold it in any longer. She said to the Lord, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.” (Luke 10:40)

The Lord’s answer is the key to the whole passage:

“Jesus answered her, ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.’” (Luke 10:41–42)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the Lord’s words: “One thing is needed.” This echoes Jeremiah 7:23 exactly — “this thing I commanded them.” So it is in the Old Testament, and so it is in the New; God has only ever asked for one thing.

Notice too that the Lord did not rebuke Martha for serving. Serving is good; the Lord himself said, “even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28) What the Lord pointed out was that the order was wrong — not that she was doing the wrong thing, but that she had it in the wrong sequence.

Listen first, then act; align first, then move.

Here I’d like to quote a martyr. The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in Life Together (1939): “The first service that one owes to others in the fellowship consists in listening to them.” He goes on to say that whoever can no longer listen to his brother will soon no longer be listening to God either. Bonhoeffer put “listening” at the very front of all service — because those who cannot listen end up serving only themselves.

We can see something fascinating from brain science as well. In 1953 the British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry published a study in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America that described the famous “cocktail party effect”: in a room buzzing with voices, a person can somehow focus on and clearly hear one speaker while filtering out every other sound. What does this tell us? That “hearing” has never been the work of the ears alone; it is a choice of attention.

In 2012 Polly Dalton and Nick Fraenkel of Royal Holloway, University of London, published an experiment in the journal Cognition. Participants were asked to listen closely to one conversation while, on the soundtrack, a man walked through the scene repeating “I’m a gorilla” for a full nineteen seconds. The result: about 70 per cent of those concentrating on the demanding task never noticed him at all. The researchers called this phenomenon “inattentional deafness.”

Brothers and sisters, what a fitting picture that is. God’s voice may have walked through your life for nineteen seconds, and because you were frazzled, you didn’t hear a single word.

Martha wasn’t a bad person; Martha was simply too busy. One of the greatest dangers in the church today is not that people won’t serve, but that people serve until they can no longer hear the Lord’s voice.

The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Martha put the “task” first; Mary put the “relationship” first. And the Lord said that the part Mary chose would not be taken away from her.

sections.heading: 4. Right Listening Brings Faith and Repentance
sections.html:
Right listening bears two fruits you can see at once: the first is faith, the second is repentance.

Look first at faith.

“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17)

Brothers and sisters, faith isn’t something you grit your teeth to produce; faith is something you hear your way into.

This matters enormously. We often think faith is a kind of willpower: clench your jaw and force yourself to believe. The harder we force it, the more exhausted we become; the more we strain, the emptier we feel. Paul says no. Faith “comes by hearing” — the Greek is akoē, meaning “the message that is heard.” Faith is fed into being by the word of God.

So when your faith feels weak, the right prescription isn’t “believe harder” but “listen more quietly.” No one gets strength by frantically telling himself, “I must be strong”; he needs to eat. And the food of faith is the word of God.

Now look at repentance.

“Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, ‘Brothers, what shall we do?’” (Acts 2:37)

The Greek word behind “cut to the heart” is katanussomai, which originally means “to be pierced, to be stabbed through.” This isn’t hearing something and thinking it makes sense; this is being pierced to the core.

On the day of Pentecost Peter preached, and he preached the crucified Jesus. And the Bible records: “Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.” (Acts 2:41)

Three thousand. The same sermon, the same preacher. What made the difference? The difference was that those who heard received it.

Brothers and sisters, true listening is not only the ears hearing; it is the heart being changed.

You can do an honest check: in the past year, has there been a single time when reading the Bible or hearing a sermon actually led you to change one thing? If so, you are listening. If all you ever think is, “That was well preached,” perhaps it’s only your ears that are moving.

James puts it very bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) In the original, the word for “deluding” carries the sense of deceiving yourself with false accounts. A person who only hears and never does is cooking the books of his own spiritual life.

The Lord Jesus also said, “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24) Notice that the wise man and the foolish man heard the very same sermon. The difference was not in the hearing; the difference was in “does them.”

This is precisely the fivefold change the 321 vision speaks of: change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes; change daily living, and relationships change; change relationships, and ministry changes. And the starting point of all of it is God’s word entering our mindset. Listening is the doorway into a change of mindset.

sections.heading: 5. God’s Voice Is Often Found in Stillness
sections.html:
The fifth key point addresses a confusion many of us share: I want to listen, but I can’t hear.

Look at what happened to Elijah. He had just won a great victory on Mount Carmel, and in the blink of an eye Jezebel was hunting him down. He fled to Mount Horeb and hid in a cave, asking to die. And right there God spoke to him:

“He said, ‘Go out, and stand on the mountain before Yahweh.’ Behold, Yahweh passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains, and broke in pieces the rocks before Yahweh; but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.” (1 Kings 19:11–12)

Brothers and sisters, the structure of this passage is exquisite. Wind, earthquake, fire — all three are earth-shaking spectacles, and God was in none of them. Where was God? In the “still small voice.” The Hebrew is qol demamah daqqah, literally “a thin, silent sound”; some translate it “a gentle whisper.”

Of course God can speak in thunder. He did so on Mount Sinai. But far more often, he chooses to speak in a still small voice. Why? Because a still small voice can be heard only by those who draw near. A father speaking to his baby never uses a loudspeaker.

So we need to adjust our mindset: very often the problem isn’t that God hasn’t spoken; the problem is that we haven’t been quiet enough to listen.

In physics, for a sound to be heard, two conditions are needed: enough volume, and low enough background noise. The relationship between the two is what engineers call the “signal-to-noise ratio.” When the background noise is loud enough, even the clearest signal is drowned out. The spiritual principle is exactly the same. God doesn’t need to raise his volume; we need to lower the noise.

A 2022 World Health Organization report states that more than a billion young people worldwide aged twelve to thirty-five are at risk of hearing loss because of prolonged exposure to loud recreational sound. The human cochlea holds roughly fifteen thousand hair cells, and once these hair cells are damaged, they never grow back. As it is in the body, so it is in the spirit: ears that are steeped in din year after year slowly lose the ability to hear a quiet voice.

The psalm says: “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10) The Hebrew word for “be still” is raphah, which originally means “to relax, to let go, to stop straining.” God says: let go, and then you will know that I am God.

The 321 vision has a wonderful saying: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain and everything is noise; rely on the heart and you hear. Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. For “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Brothers and sisters, how long has it been since you let your morning grow quiet? Not a morning without sound, but a morning without noise.

The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) Sheep recognise the shepherd’s voice not because sheep are clever but because they follow the shepherd every day. Familiarity is the secret of hearing.

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: Only the Selfless Can Hear God
sections.html:
Having come this far, we must ask a deeper question: why do some people hear, and others don’t?

The 321 vision gives us a very sharp answer: the key is whether we are living the self-centred life or living in selflessness.

The self-centred person listens to his own voice. The self-centred person also listens to the voices of others — because he wants their approval. Only the selfless person can hear the voice of God.

Why? Because the proud person already has the answer in his heart. Someone who already has the answer has no need to listen. When he asks your opinion, he only wants you to agree with him. That was Rehoboam exactly.

The humble person is different. The humble person is willing to wait; the humble person is willing to obey. Because he knows he is not God.

Remember the 321 definition: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When a person returns to his originally intended position as a human being, he will naturally lift his head to listen; when a person wants to take God’s place, he will only bow his head and listen to himself.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Nowhere is this clearer than in listening. Put two proud people together, and neither listens to the other; the words get louder and the relationship drifts further apart. Put two humble people together, and each listens first — and in the end both are understood.

Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) When the voice of “I” grows quieter, the voice of Christ grows louder. This is not loss; it is enlargement. For my cleverness is limited and God’s wisdom is limitless; to switch off a limited voice and gain limitless guidance is the best bargain there is.

Young Samuel gives us the most beautiful example. That night he heard the call again and again, and finally, at Eli’s direction, he spoke the words: “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10)

Brothers and sisters, notice the shape of that sentence. Not “Listen, for your servant will speak,” but “Speak; for your servant hears.” Whoever speaks is the master. The selfless life gives the speaking seat to God and takes the listening seat for itself.

This is the Two Core Values of the 321 vision: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. At the most everyday level, letting Jesus reign as King means letting Jesus speak while I listen.

And the 321 Path of Serving starts with listening too: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. The first step is Spirit, being led by the Holy Spirit; and the precondition for being led is being able to hear.

Only when we hear God can we live out God.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set what we have seen today within the whole picture of the 321 vision.

First, all Three Foundations are directly tied to listening. Jesus is my role model — he said, “As I hear, I judge” (John 5:30); the Bible is my standard — “faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10:17); the Holy Spirit is my guide — “and when you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” (Isaiah 30:21) Three Foundations, three kinds of listening.

Second, the Two Core Values are the purpose of our listening. We listen not to add to our knowledge but to let Jesus be King; we obey not to show how spiritual we are but to let Jesus receive all the glory. Saul listened to the people, and the glory went to Saul’s face; Mary listened to the Lord, and the glory went to the Lord.

Third, the Goal is to establish God’s system. What is a system? A system is a body of people who use the same standard, listen to the voice of the same Head, and fit together. A body can move in harmony because every member listens to the same head. If everyone in a church listens to his own voice, that isn’t a body; it’s a heap of spare parts.

Fourth, a shift of perspective. Wrong listening mostly comes from standing in a human, earthly, temporary, worldly perspective. Saul looked from the human perspective — what will the people think? Sarai looked from the temporary perspective — I’ve already waited ten years. Rehoboam looked from the worldly perspective — I must assert my authority. Right listening shifts our perspective to God’s, the heavenly, the eternal, the godly. Look at the same matter from eternity, and the conclusion is often the very opposite.

Fifth, the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. This lesson is that priority put into practice. Only when I listen to God first do I know who I am; only when I know who I am will I not be held hostage by human voices; only when I am not held hostage by human voices can I do things rightly.

Sixth, the 920 practice. Every person connected to us is our “2.” As we practise living a selfless (0) life, we will bear the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit. And listening is the most practical entry point into 920 — because the first act of love is listening, and the first act of patience is hearing someone out before you speak. Proverbs says: “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.” (Proverbs 18:13) James says: “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Do you want to know whether the fruit of the Spirit is growing in you? See whether today you truly listened to someone until they had finished speaking.

Seventh, 235 relationships. With selfless people we become each other’s “2,” spiritual companions; we build “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children; and we become “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Rehoboam’s tragedy was that he had no “3” — he had old men he could have listened to, but he would not have them. A person with no spiritual parents easily ends up with nothing but an echo chamber. Brothers and sisters, make sure you have one or two people in your life whose hard truths you are willing to hear.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work them through, solidly and thoroughly.

Practice 1: Check What You Listen to Every Day

Is it the voice of the world, or the word of God?

Information: Today, start with an honest tally. Take out your phone, look at your screen time, and count the hours you spent this week on short videos, news and social media; then count the hours you spent reading the Bible, praying and listening to sermons. Write the two numbers down side by side.

Revelation: Ask God to show you how those two numbers have shaped your moods, judgements and decisions this past year. Ask him to bring to mind a time when your emotions were clearly dragged down by some particular voice.

Conviction: Admit it sincerely — the shape of my life today is the sum of what I have listened to all these years.

Implementation: Make one concrete adjustment this week. For example: the first thing you do when you open your eyes in the morning is not scroll your phone but read a passage of Scripture; and in the last half hour before bed, turn off the news.

Evaluation: Spend ten minutes at the weekend looking back. On how many of these seven days did you manage it? On which day did you slip? What was going on at the time?

Correction: Don’t condemn yourself; adjust your method. If you can’t manage it in the morning, leave your phone outside the bedroom; if you slip before bed, keep your Bible on the bedside table.

Repetition: Keep practising for four weeks in a row. Neuroscience tells us that building a habit takes sustained repetition; a 2009 study by Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London, published in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that a new habit takes on average about sixty-six days to become automatic, with wide variation between people and behaviours. So please don’t give up because you failed on day five.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister, share this practice with them, and hold each other accountable.

Practice 2: Build the Habit of “Listen First, Then Act”

Before every decision, seek God first.

Information: Learn one principle — don’t make major decisions when you are exhausted, angry or impatient. Saul decided in fear, Sarai decided when she couldn’t wait any longer, Rehoboam decided when he wanted to assert his authority; all three times they were wrong.

Revelation: Ask God to point out one unresolved matter in your life right now — work, marriage, money, a relationship, ministry.

Conviction: Admit that you had originally planned to settle this matter by your own judgement.

Implementation: This week, set aside a time of prayer devoted to this one matter. Don’t ask God to do things your way; ask only that God would speak. Write down in a notebook the impressions, verses and reminders God gives you in your heart, and date them.

Evaluation: Is this impression in line with Scripture? Is there peace? Has it grown clearer with time? All three checks are needed; none can be skipped.

Correction: If it isn’t clear, wait. Waiting isn’t wasting time; waiting is refusing to use human methods to bring about God’s promise. Had Abram been willing to wait a little longer, the storm over Ishmael would never have happened.

Repetition: Make “pray first, then decide” your default setting for everything, starting practice with the smallest matters.

Multiplication: Teach this habit to your family. Before your household makes a decision, be quiet together for three minutes first.

Practice 3: Practise Quietly Listening for the Lord’s Voice

Set aside time every day; pray, meditate, wait.

Information: Stillness is not emptying your mind. Christian meditation has a definite object — the word of God. Psalm 1 says of the blessed man: “his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” (Psalm 1:2)

Revelation: Choose a passage of Scripture and read it slowly three times. The first time, read for the content; the second time, ask, “God, what do you want to say to me?”; the third time, grow quiet and say nothing.

Conviction: Believe that God truly wants to speak to you today. Not because you deserve it, but because he is a God who speaks.

Implementation: Begin with ten minutes a day. Same place, same time, with your phone in another room.

Evaluation: Write down the one sentence God gives you each day. Look back at those thirty sentences after a month, and you will be amazed.

Correction: If you keep getting distracted, write down on paper the stray thoughts that float up; once they are written down, set them aside and return to stillness.

Repetition: Do it day after day. Isaiah says, “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear” (Isaiah 50:4) — every morning, not once a year at a special conference.

Multiplication: Share what you receive in the stillness with your small group. What you share is what truly becomes your own.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please take this sentence home with you: it isn’t that you don’t know what to do; it’s that you haven’t first listened to the right voice.

We often think we lack methods, when what we really lack is the right voice.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s road once more.

Saul listened wrongly, and he was rejected; Abraham listened wrongly, and he suffered; Rehoboam listened wrongly, and the kingdom was divided.

Mary listened rightly, and received the good part; the disciples listened rightly, and received life; the church listened rightly, and received revival.

The same ears, the same voices — different ways of listening bring utterly different outcomes.

This morning the Lord extends an invitation to us. When you choose not to listen to the world, not to listen to yourself, but to listen to God alone, your life will enter a road that is clear, steady and victorious.

Clear — because you have God’s direction and no longer rely on guesswork. Steady — because your foundation is not other people’s opinions but the word of God. Victorious — because a life that lets Jesus reign as King is, by its very nature, a victorious life.

Seven times Revelation says the same words to the seven churches: “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies.” (Revelation 2:7) In the last days the voices will only grow more numerous and more noisy. May we be the people who can still hear the still small voice.

Today, let Jesus be King. Not tomorrow, not when I’m ready — today.

“Today if you will hear his voice, don’t harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15).

May all the glory go to Jesus.

keyVerses: “This thing I commanded them, saying, ‘Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. Walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.’” (Jeremiah 7:23)
“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17)
declarations: Please declare with me:
Lord, open my ears! Let me no longer listen to the voice of the world, nor to my own voice, but to your word alone! Through your word give me faith, and let me walk in the way that pleases you!
practices: Check what you listen to every day
Build the habit of “listen first, then act”
Practise quietly listening for the Lord’s voice
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We confess before you that we have often listened to the wrong voice. Like Saul, we fear what people think; like Sarai, we cannot wait for your timing; like Rehoboam, we listen only to what we like to hear. Lord, please forgive us.
This morning, open our ears yourself, just as every morning you awaken the ear of your servant. Take away the noise in our hearts, and let us recognise you in the still small voice.
Lord, we are willing to lay down our own voice, our own plans and our own pride. Work the selfless life in us, so that it is no longer we who live, but Christ who lives in us.
Make us people who listen first and then act, people who hear and then go and do. May our families, our small groups and our church all become communities that can hear your voice.
Lord, we say: Speak; for your servant hears.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 1 Samuel 15:24 says: “Saul said to Samuel, ‘I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of Yahweh, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.’” In your present situation, whose voice — one person’s or a group’s — is louder to you than God’s voice? What is it that you fear?

Luke 10:41–42 says: “Jesus answered her, ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.’” Share honestly: in your schedule this week, where does “the one thing needed” rank? What one concrete adjustment are you willing to make this week?
l124.title: Listening Only to God’s Voice
l124.subtitle: 321 Morning Devotion · Lesson 124 · Listening Rightly (Part 1): Right Listening and Wrong Listening
l124.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: What You Hear Is Shaping You
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this early morning. Today let’s think together about something utterly ordinary and yet supremely important — listening.

Let me begin with a true picture. In 1953 Colin Cherry, a scientist at Imperial College London, carried out a famous experiment. He placed participants among a noisy crowd, with voices coming at them from every side, and asked them to concentrate on just one person speaking. What he found was that people have an astonishing ability: even with dozens of voices pouring into their ears at once, they can still lock on to one voice and push all the rest into the background. Researchers later called this phenomenon the “cocktail party effect.”

That experiment tells us something very important: the ear is not a passive radio receiver; the ear is an organ that chooses. Every day you are choosing whose voice to listen to. You think you’re “just half-listening,” but in fact you are selecting who gets to shape you.

We often think “listening” is just receiving information — a sound comes in, you know something, and that’s the end of it. Not so. Brothers and sisters, please keep this sentence in your heart this morning: listening is where a changed life begins.

Why? Because there is an invisible chain: what you listen to decides what you believe; what you believe decides what you become. No one changes first and then starts to listen; every person who has changed first heard, and then began to change.

So Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17) Faith doesn’t sprout out of thin air; faith grows out of the ear. Wherever your ears lead, that is the shape your life will grow into.

This also explains a puzzling thing we see in the church. Many people have believed in the Lord for ten or twenty years. They can recite verses, sing the hymns, share in small group — and yet their lives have barely moved. The same temper, the same fear, the same bondage. Where is the problem?

The problem isn’t a lack of truth. If there is one thing this age doesn’t lack, it is information about the truth — sermons a tap away, verses a search away, more commentaries than any generation before us. The problem is that there is no “listening rightly.”

The truth goes into the ears but not into the heart; it is heard but not received; it is known but it doesn’t change us. It’s like someone who stands at the dining table every day reading the menu but never eats a mouthful. Of course he’s still hungry.

The Lord Jesus spoke very sternly about this. He said, “Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has.” (Luke 8:18) He didn’t say, “Be careful what you hear”; what he said was, “Be careful how you hear.” The same sermon, the same verse — one person hears it and receives life, another hears it and feels nothing. The difference isn’t in the word; it’s in “how you hear.”

The Lord also said, “Take heed what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you, and more will be given to you who hear.” (Mark 4:24) However large the vessel you bring to listen with, that is the size of vessel God will fill for you. Small ears receive small grace; large ears receive large grace.

Brothers and sisters, in this lesson we will learn seven things together: true change begins with hearing God; right listening brings renewal of life; the key strategy of replacing the wrong with the right; right listening brings an expanding blessing; how to discern whom you are listening to; how you listen decides how you live; and finally a 321 insight — only the selfless can hear God.

May the Lord himself tune our ears this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Setting and Context of Ephesians 4
sections.html:
Before we come to the key points, let’s get clear on the background of our theme text. When a text has its background, the exposition stands on solid ground.

The author of Ephesians is the apostle Paul. The letter begins: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus.” (Ephesians 1:1) When Paul wrote this letter he was in prison; he calls himself “the prisoner in the Lord” (Ephesians 4:1). It is generally thought to come from his first Roman imprisonment, around AD 60–62. The same group of letters includes Philippians, Colossians and Philemon, which church tradition calls the “Prison Epistles.”

Ephesus, the city receiving the letter, was the capital of the Roman province of Asia and a great port on the eastern shore of the Aegean, with a population at the time of perhaps more than two hundred thousand. The city was most famous for the Temple of Artemis, which the ancients counted among the Seven Wonders of the World. Acts 19 records that Paul lived in Ephesus for more than two years, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus, “so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks” (Acts 19:10). Notice the verb — “heard.” The Ephesian church was a church born of listening.

And precisely because of that, the believers in Ephesus lived with an enormous tension. Most of them came from Gentile backgrounds, steeped from childhood in a culture of idol worship, sorcery and sensual indulgence. Acts 19:19 says that many who had practised magic brought their books and burned them, books worth “fifty thousand pieces of silver.” They had come to faith, but the old world still spoke in their ears every day — the hawkers in the marketplace, the music from the temples, the neighbours’ gossip, the memories of the past.

So Paul wrote Ephesians with its first three chapters on “who you are in Christ” — chosen, redeemed, reconciled to God, fellow members of God’s household — and its last three chapters on “how you should walk.” Chapter 4 is the pivot: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.” (Ephesians 4:1)

At 4:17, Paul begins to deal head-on with the problem of the “old life”: “This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind, being darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts.” (Ephesians 4:17–18)

Notice Paul’s diagnosis: “darkened in their understanding,” “the hardening of their hearts.” The original uses νοῦς (nous), which means mind, understanding, mindset. The Gentiles’ problem was not outward behaviour but inward mindset; it wasn’t their hands that were sick, it was their thinking.

Then comes our theme text: “But you didn’t learn Christ that way, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man … and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man.” (Ephesians 4:20–24)

There are three actions here, each wonderfully vivid in the Greek. “Heard” is ἀκούω (akouō), simply hearing; “were taught” carries the sense of being personally instructed, of becoming a disciple; and “learned” Christ means being taught, being shaped. Paul is saying: true listening has layers — from hearing, to receiving, to being taught until you take shape.

The pair of verbs “put away” (ἀποτίθημι, apotithēmi) and “put on” (ἐνδύω, endyō) were originally everyday words for taking off and putting on clothes. Paul uses the most down-to-earth picture to teach the deepest truth: the old self is like a garment worn for decades and caked with filth; the new self is like a white robe. You don’t give the old clothes a wash and keep wearing them; you take them off, throw them away, and put on the new.

The sentence in the middle is the key: “be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” That is a literal rendering of the original — the renewal takes place not in behaviour but in the mind, in the mindset. This is exactly the starting point of the fivefold change the 321 vision speaks of: only when the mindset changes does the life change; only when the life changes does daily living change.

And where does mindset come from? From the ears. That is why Paul puts “hearing” first. Brothers and sisters, this is the logic of the whole passage: hearing → mindset → putting off the old self → putting on the new self → living out Christ.

sections.heading: 1. True Change Begins with Hearing God
sections.html:
“He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” (Acts 9:4)

Let me begin with a man. Saul — later Paul.

Before he met the Lord, he was the most promising young man in the Judaism of his day. He says himself, “I advanced in the Jews’ religion beyond many of my own age among my countrymen, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.” (Galatians 1:14) He was taught at the feet of Gamaliel, a Pharisee of the Pharisees. His zeal went so far that he personally hauled Christians off to prison and personally stood at the scene of Stephen’s martyrdom.

Acts 9:1 says he was “still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord.” He wasn’t a cold-blooded killer; he was a man full of religious passion, heading completely the wrong way. He thought he was burning with zeal for God.

Then, on the road to Damascus, everything was turned upside down.

“As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him. He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ He said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.’” (Acts 9:3–5)

Brothers and sisters, notice what the key to Saul’s turnaround was.

It wasn’t that his circumstances changed. He was still on the same road, still carrying the high priest’s letters, still the same man with the same standing.

It wasn’t that he gained more doctrine. Saul knew the Old Testament better than anyone else there. His problem was never a lack of knowledge.

It wasn’t that he met with setbacks. He was at the very height of his success; he wasn’t a failure, he was a winner.

The key was this — he heard the voice of the Lord.

One act of “hearing” changed a whole life. From persecuting Christ to following Christ; from opposing God to suffering for God. The Lord later said to Ananias, “For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.” (Acts 9:16) The man who once made others suffer for the Lord would from then on suffer for the Lord himself.

And this “hearing” has one very tender detail. In Acts 26:14, Paul himself adds, “I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language.” The Lord didn’t use Greek, didn’t use the official tongue; the Lord called him by name in his mother’s language, the language of his childhood. And he called him twice: “Saul, Saul!”

In the Bible, when God calls a name twice, it is often the most intimate and most urgent of calls. “Abraham, Abraham!” (Genesis 22:11) “Moses! Moses!” (Exodus 3:4) “Samuel! Samuel!” (1 Samuel 3:10) “Martha, Martha” (Luke 10:41). When God calls a person, he never calls out a number; he calls a name.

Science gives us a beautiful picture too. In 1980 the American researchers Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer published a study in the journal Science showing that newborns only a few days old can already recognise, and prefer, their own mother’s voice. Before a person can speak, before he can see clearly, he already knows the voice that loves him most. Brothers and sisters, this is the mark the Creator has placed within us: we are born to recognise the voice of the One who loves us.

The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27)

So if this morning you feel you are “hard to change,” let me say a word of comfort to you: what you need may not be more effort, but one true hearing of God.

The 321 vision says that the first of the Three Foundations is “Jesus is my role model,” and the third is “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” Where does guidance begin? With hearing. The Holy Spirit cannot guide a person who won’t listen; but for a person who is willing to listen, one word from God can turn his whole life around. The moment Saul fell to the ground was the moment Paul was established in heaven — because at last he was no longer the one doing the talking; instead he asked, “Who are you, Lord?”

sections.heading: 2. Right Listening Brings Renewal of Life
sections.html:
“If indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:21–24)

Brothers and sisters, Paul speaks of “listening” here with great precision.

He doesn’t say, “It’s enough that you’ve heard of it.” In the Chinese Union Version his words unfold as three progressive verbs: heard, received, learned.

The first layer is “heard” — the sound has entered the ears.

The second layer is “received” — the truth has entered the heart and become mine.

The third layer is “learned” — the life is shaped and grows into the likeness of the truth.

Many people get stuck at the first layer. Hearing is information; receiving is revelation; being shaped is life. In what the 321 vision calls the eight stages of changing our mindset, the first stage is precisely “Information,” the second is “Revelation,” and only the third is “Conviction.” Information stays in the head; revelation enters the heart; conviction grows into life.

So what does true listening bring? Paul makes it very clear: it brings three processes.

First, putting off the old self. “That you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit.” (Ephesians 4:22) Notice the words “grows corrupt.” The old self didn’t go bad in a day; it was deceived by desire day after day, eaten away bit by bit. Like clothes left in a cupboard — you don’t touch them, and they go mouldy all by themselves. So putting off the old self isn’t waiting until it has rotted through before dealing with it; it’s taking it off today.

Second, the renewal of the mind. “And that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” (Ephesians 4:23) The emphasis of the original is on νοῦς — mind, mindset. This is the most crucial sentence of the whole passage. Behaviour is the fruit; mindset is the root. If you change your behaviour without changing your mindset, that’s called suppression, and it won’t hold for long. Paul says the same thing in Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

Third, putting on the new self. “And put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:24) The new self is not an improved version of the old self; it is created anew in the likeness of God. We take off in order to put on; we are emptied in order to be filled.

Psychology gives us a very apt confirmation here. In 1949 the Canadian neuropsychologist Donald Hebb proposed a principle later known as “Hebb’s rule”: neurons that fire together wire together. That is, the more often you repeat a particular thought or reaction, the thicker, faster and more automatic that neural pathway in the brain becomes. That’s why a habitual complainer hardly needs to think before complaining — that road has already been worn into a motorway.

But the same principle brings enormous hope: neural pathways can be laid down anew. This is called “neuroplasticity.” If you keep walking a new road, the new road will widen too. When God made us, he built “the capacity to be renewed” right into our design.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Even your brain bears witness to being “renewed in the spirit of your mind.”

This is the very route of the fivefold change in the 321 vision: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. And the renewal of the mindset begins with “listening rightly.”

James says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) “Deluding your own selves” — the greatest victim of a person who only hears and never does is himself, because he thinks he already has it.

So remember this sentence: listen rightly, and your life will change.

sections.heading: 3. The Key Strategy: Replace the Wrong with the Right
sections.html:
“Putting off the old self” sounds easy. Why is it so hard to do?

Because many people use the wrong method. Their method is — suppression. Grit your teeth so you won’t lose your temper; clench your fists so you won’t look at that website; tell yourself desperately, “Don’t think about it, don’t think about it.” And the result? The more you suppress it, the more you think about it; the more you think about it, the wearier you get; and in the end everything collapses.

Brothers and sisters, here is a vitally important strategy: putting off the old self is not straining to suppress; it is replacing the old with the new.

The Bible never just tells us “don’t.” In the Bible, “don’t” is always followed straight away by “but.”

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” (Romans 12:2)

“Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18)

“Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29)

Do you see it? Every time, it is “don’t … but …” God’s method isn’t to create a vacuum; God’s method is replacement.

The Lord Jesus told a very sobering parable. An unclean spirit goes out of a man and wanders through waterless places, then says it will return to where it came from; “when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order,” and so it brings along seven other spirits more evil than itself, and “the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matthew 12:43–45). A house swept clean but left empty is more dangerous than one never swept at all. After being emptied, we must be filled.

So our practice is replacement on five levels:

Wrong seeing becomes right seeing.

Wrong listening becomes right listening.

Wrong thinking becomes right thinking.

Wrong speaking becomes right speaking.

Wrong doing becomes right doing.

These five levels form a chain. What you see affects what you listen to; what you listen to affects what you think; what you think decides what you say; what you say brings out what you do. If you only try to change the last link — behaviour — without touching the four before it, it’s labour in vain. Solomon says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

There is a widely told Native American fable about two dogs fighting inside a person’s heart, a white dog and a black dog. Someone asks: which one will win? The answer: the one you feed.

That picture fits here perfectly. The white dog is the spiritual life; the black dog is the self-centred life. What we must do is this — nourish the white dog, and starve the black dog.

Notice: not “beat the black dog to death.” You can’t kill it; the more you beat it, the fiercer it gets. What you must do is stop feeding it. What does it eat? Negative information, complaining conversations, accusing words, indulgent images. Cut off the supply, and day by day it grows thin.

And what does the white dog eat? The word of God, praise, thanksgiving, fellowship with spiritual companions. Keep up the supply, and day by day it grows strong.

Paul puts it even more positively: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8) Paul doesn’t say, “Don’t think bad things”; Paul gives you eight good things to think about. When your mind is full of good things, there is no room left for the bad.

This is the practical outworking of what the 321 vision calls “selflessness.” Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is giving up the place the self-centred life has occupied and letting Christ fill it. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Not becoming empty, but changing masters.

Brothers and sisters, whatever you feed is what you will live out.

sections.heading: 4. Right Listening Brings an Expanding Blessing
sections.html:
“All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.” (Genesis 22:18)

This verse is the most glorious promise in the Bible attached to “listening.”

The setting is Mount Moriah. God said to Abraham, “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” (Genesis 22:2)

This is the heaviest command in human history. Isaac was the son of promise, the son awaited for twenty-five years, the very one of whom God himself had said, “For your offspring will be named through Isaac” (Genesis 21:12). It was as though God were tearing down his own promise.

How did Abraham respond? The Bible says, “Abraham rose early in the morning.” (Genesis 22:3) No arguing, no delaying, no bargaining. He heard, and he obeyed.

Three days’ journey. Three days is long enough for a man to change his mind a hundred times. Yet step by step he climbed. On the mountain, with the knife already raised, the angel of Yahweh called to him from heaven: “Abraham, Abraham!” (Genesis 22:11) — once again, a name called twice. Then God said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God.” (Genesis 22:12)

And then comes that astonishing blessing: “All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.” (Genesis 22:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice the “because” clause: “because you have obeyed my voice.” The Hebrew literally reads, “because you listened to my voice.” The Hebrew word for “listen” is שָׁמַע (shama), which carries both senses at once — “to hear” and “to obey.” In the Hebrew mindset, to hear without obeying is not to have listened at all. That is why the confession of faith Israel recites every day begins with this very word: “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.” (Deuteronomy 6:4)

That is why Samuel said to King Saul, “To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22) King Saul kept back the sheep and cattle for sacrifice; it looked very spiritual, but it was really not listening. What God wants is not your offering; what God wants is your ear.

And how great is the result of one person obeying God? As great as “all the nations of the earth.”

When Abraham raised the knife on Mount Moriah, he did not know he was foreshadowing what would happen on another mountain two thousand years later — “For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son” (John 3:16). Nor did he know that Paul would one day say, “Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring … which is Christ.” (Galatians 3:16)

One man’s obedience became the blessing of the nations.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision calls “Multiplication.” The last of the eight stages of changing our mindset is not “Repetition”; it is “Multiplication.” If your change truly comes from God, it will surely flow outward. When one person truly hears God, his home will be different, his small group will be different, his workplace will be different.
