This is also the spirit of the 920 practice: every person connected to us is our “2.” When we live out the “0” of selflessness, the nine fruits of the Spirit — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23) — will grow in those relationships. And so the blessing spreads outward, ring after ring.

So right listening affects not only you but the people around you. The day you obey may be the day your children’s blessing begins.

sections.heading: 5. Discerning the Voices: Whom Are You Listening To?
sections.html:
“The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out.” (John 10:3)

There is deep meaning in the Lord Jesus comparing us to sheep. Sheep have poor eyesight, can’t run fast and have no claws or fangs; their only way to survive is to recognise the shepherd’s voice.

The Lord goes on: “They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers.” (John 10:5)

Brothers and sisters, here is a fact we must admit: every one of us is listening to some voice at every moment. Nobody lives in a vacuum.

Broadly speaking, there are four voices in our ears:

The voice of God.

The voice of Satan.

Our own voice.

The voice of the world.

The question isn’t whether there are voices — the voices are always there; the question is which one you listen to.

So how do we tell them apart? The most practical way is to look at the results. A tree is known by its fruit, and so is a voice. The Lord said, “By their fruits you will know them.” (Matthew 7:16)

Listening to Satan’s voice produces four kinds of fruit: discouragement, condemnation, anger and despair.

One of Satan’s names is “the accuser.” Revelation 12:10 says, “The accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night.” His voice has one hallmark: it presses you down — down until you can’t lift your head, down until you feel you are beyond help, down until you don’t want to pray and don’t dare come before God. His aim is to “steal, kill, and destroy” (John 10:10).

Listening to God’s voice produces four kinds of fruit: humility, repentance, peace and change.

God will also point out our sin, but his correction brings hope, not despair. Paul draws the line very clearly: “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.” (2 Corinthians 7:10)

It’s the same words — “You are wrong.” When God says them, you want to run towards him; when the enemy says them, you want to hide from him. After Adam sinned he hid among the trees — that was the enemy’s voice in his ears. After David sinned he wrote Psalm 51 — that was God’s voice in his heart.

James gives us another measuring rule: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.” (James 3:17)

There is one more principle of discernment: God’s voice will never contradict God’s word. The Bible is our standard. Any voice, however pleasant, however moving, however much it fits your wishes, is not from God if it goes against Scripture. The second of the Three Foundations is “the Bible is my standard.”

We also need to watch out for our own voice and the voice of the world. These two are often the hardest to discern, because they say exactly what we want to hear. Paul warned Timothy: “For the time will come when they will not listen to the sound doctrine, but having itching ears, will heap up for themselves teachers after their own lusts.” (2 Timothy 4:3) “Itching ears” — what a vivid phrase. People with itching ears aren’t looking for truth; they are looking for agreement.

And God’s voice is often quiet. On Mount Horeb, the great wind, the earthquake and the fire all passed Elijah by, and then? “After the fire, there was a still small voice.” (1 Kings 19:12) God doesn’t need to shout, because he isn’t competing with anyone. He waits for you to grow still.

“Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10)

Brothers and sisters, different voices bring utterly different results. This morning, whom are you listening to?

sections.heading: 6. How You Listen Decides How You Live
sections.html:
This is the most practical point of the whole lesson.

We have talked about “whom we listen to”; now we need to talk about “how we listen.” Because the very same sentence can be heard as two completely different voices.

Take the most common example: criticism from others.

Someone says to you, “You didn’t handle this very thoroughly.”

Listen with worldly ears, and what you hear is: he looks down on me, he’s got it in for me, he’s embarrassing me in front of everyone. The result: hurt, anger, defensiveness, a broken relationship.

Listen with spiritual ears, and what you hear is: perhaps God is using this person to show me something I can’t see. The result: growth, change, and a relationship that actually goes deeper.

One sentence, two kinds of ears, two kinds of life.

So the Bible says, “The ear that listens to reproof lives, and will be at home among the wise.” (Proverbs 15:31) And again, “Don’t reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you. Reprove a wise person, and he will love you.” (Proverbs 9:8) The difference between the wise and the scoffer isn’t who gets rebuked but how each one listens to rebuke.

David takes this to its very limit: “Let the righteous strike me, it is kindness; let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head; don’t let my head refuse it.” (Psalm 141:5) “Don’t let my head refuse it” — what humble ears those are.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: very often the problem isn’t the sentence itself but how you hear it.

Next I want to speak about a more hidden danger: “replaying.”

Wrong listening keeps replaying negative voices.

Have you ever had this experience? Someone says something unkind; the person who said it has long since forgotten it, but you have been playing it in your heart for three months. Lying in bed at night, that sentence starts up again by itself; you go over the scene again and again, and get hurt all over again each time. The person who said it hurt you once; you have hurt yourself a hundred times.

Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania, the founder of cognitive therapy, put forward the idea of “automatic negative thoughts” in the 1960s. He observed that in people who are depressed, negative verdicts keep popping up automatically in their minds; these thoughts come uninvited and loop over and over, and in time they are taken as fact. His treatment was not to tell people “don’t think about it,” but to help them identify these thoughts and then replace them with thoughts that match reality.

Brothers and sisters, God’s method came earlier, goes deeper, and has more power.

Right listening means meditating on God’s word again and again.

“His delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” (Psalm 1:2)

“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.” (Joshua 1:8)

The Hebrew word for “meditate” is הָגָה (hagah), which originally carries the sense of murmuring under one’s breath and chewing over again and again. Some compare it to a cow chewing the cud — swallowing, bringing it back up and chewing slowly, again and again, until it is fully digested into its own flesh and blood.

Your heart is a player, and it will always be playing some recording. The only question is: which tape will you put in?

Paul gives us a very powerful picture: “throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:5) “Bringing into captivity” — that is the language of war. Your thought life is a battlefield; either it is occupied by the enemy, or it is taken captive for Christ.

So whatever you meditate on again and again, that is what you are shaped into.

This is what the 321 vision calls a shift of perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) And again, “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Listen from a new perspective, and you will live a new way.

sections.heading: 7. A 321 Insight: Only the Selfless Can Hear God
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, having come this far, we must ask the most fundamental question: why is it that some people simply can’t hear God?

The answer lies at the heart of the 321 vision: because of the self-centred life.

The self-centred person hears only what he wants to hear.

It isn’t that he has no ears; it’s that he has a sieve. Whatever suits him, he takes in; whatever doesn’t, he automatically filters out. When he listens to a sermon, he isn’t asking, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” He is assessing, “Was that a good preacher or not?” When he reads the Bible, he isn’t looking for God’s heart; he’s looking for verses to back up his own position.

The self-centred person resists the voice of God.

Because God’s voice so often asks us to let go — let go of our rights, let go of our face, let go of our plans, let go of whatever we are clutching so tightly. And the instinct of the self-centred life is to hold on.

The 321 vision puts it very penetratingly: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Go back to Eden, and you will find that humanity’s first fall was precisely a case of “listening wrongly.” The serpent said, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Eve listened. Afterwards God said to Adam, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you …” (Genesis 3:17) Notice the words: “Because you have listened …” Humanity’s catastrophe began with listening to the wrong voice.

And humanity’s salvation also began with one Man’s perfect listening. The Lord Jesus said, “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.” (John 5:30)

“As I hear, I judge” — this is selflessness at its height. The life of the Son of God on earth was a life of perfect hearing and perfect obedience. “Though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” (Hebrews 5:8) “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:8)

Paul sets these two side by side with perfect clarity: “For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous.” (Romans 5:19)

One man would not listen, and all humanity fell; one Man listened, and all humanity was offered salvation.

So what does a selfless person look like?

The selfless person is willing to hear the truth — even when the truth stings.

The selfless person is willing to be adjusted — even when the adjustment is humiliating.

The selfless person hears God, obeys God and lives out God.

The Lord Jesus said, “He who is of God hears the words of God. For this cause you don’t hear, because you are not of God.” (John 8:47) Being able to hear God’s words is itself a sign.

Brothers and sisters, this is where the Two Core Values of the 321 vision come in:

Only selflessness can let Jesus be King. Because as long as “I” am still on the throne, Jesus can only stand at the side as an adviser. You can ignore an adviser; you cannot ignore a King.

Only selflessness can be led by the Holy Spirit. Because the Holy Spirit guides; he does not coerce. He speaks in a “still small voice,” and a noisy self cannot hear a still small voice.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

And selflessness is not having nothing. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) When you turn your own voice down, you hear the voice of the One who created the universe. That isn’t loss; that is the greatest gain of all.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set what we have learned today within the framework of the 321 vision and look at it once more.

The Three Foundations are, in fact, three kinds of right listening.

Jesus is my role model — he said, “As I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). If we want to learn how he lived, we first learn how he listened.

The Bible is my standard — “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Every voice must be brought before Scripture to be tested.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — “and when you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” (Isaiah 30:21) The Spirit’s guidance is something received with the ears.

The Two Core Values decide how we listen.

Let Jesus be King — the King’s word is a command, not a suggestion. To hear and then go and do it: that is what it means for him to be King.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — we don’t listen to sermons to add to our knowledge or to our stock of conversation, but so that his name may be lifted high.

The Goal — establish God’s system. One person who listens to God will influence a household; one household that listens to God will influence a small group; and a community that listens to God is what God’s system looks like on earth.

The fivefold change can be seen especially clearly in this lesson.

A change of mindset: from “listening is receiving information” to “listening is where a changed life begins.”

A change of life: putting off the old self, being renewed in mind, putting on the new self.

A change of daily living: stop replaying negative voices, and start meditating on God’s word day and night.

A change of relationships: hear criticism with spiritual ears and rebuke with humble ears, and relationships move from breakdown towards repair.

A change of ministry: “All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring” (Genesis 22:18) — one person’s obedience becomes the blessing of the nations.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people’s service bears no fruit because they have skipped the first two steps. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Nor can the priority of relationships be jumbled: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. The order of listening is the same — first listen to what God says, then honestly listen to the voice in your own heart, then patiently listen to others, and only last deal with the task. Get the order right, and things will go right.

The 920 practice: every person connected to us is our “2.” When we live out the “0” — the selfless life — the nine fruits of the Spirit grow in those relationships. Notice that not one of the nine fruits is “eloquence,” yet several of them have to do with how we listen: patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control. A person who knows how to listen is bound to be a person who bears fruit.

235 relationships: with selfless people we become each other’s “2,” spiritual companions who remind each other, “Did I just hear that wrongly?”; we build “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing right listening down the generations; and we become “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, standing together on the truth.

Finally, the shift of perspective: from the human to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

Brothers and sisters, when all is said and done, to change your ears is to change your perspective, and to change your perspective is to change your life.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html: The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work them through, solidly and thoroughly.

sections.heading: 1. Build the Habit of “Right Input”: Listen to God’s Word Every Day (Scripture Reading, Sermons, Hymns).
sections.html:
Information: First, face a fact — on average, how much time do you spend each day listening to God’s word, and how much listening to other voices? Write it down honestly.

Revelation: Ask God to show you that the present state of your life is the result of what you have taken in over the past. This isn’t condemnation; it is light.

Conviction: Resolve to believe that Romans 10:17 is true — faith really does come by hearing.

Implementation: Make a plan that is concrete, small and doable. For example, every morning read a passage of Scripture, read it once aloud, and then be still for three minutes. 321 Morning Devotion itself is the best training ground.

Evaluation: After a week, look back. On which days did you manage it? On which days did you break off? Why?

Correction: Don’t make the penalties stiffer; make the threshold lower. If you can’t manage twenty minutes, start with five. The German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus’s research on the forgetting curve in 1885 showed that memory fades fastest at the beginning, but that if you review it again before it is forgotten, it can be kept for a long time. Little and regular beats a lot and broken off.

Repetition: Let it become as much a part of everyday life as brushing your teeth, so that you don’t have to decide afresh every day.

Multiplication: Bring someone along to do morning devotions with you. When you teach others, you yourself hear most clearly.

sections.heading: 2. Stop Feeding the Wrong Voices: Cut Down on Negative Information, Complaining and Accusation.
sections.html:
Information: Make a list of your “voices” — the channels you regularly watch, the social media you regularly scroll, the chat groups you regularly talk in.

Revelation: Ask God to point out which of them is feeding the black dog.

Conviction: Believe that “whatever you feed is what you live out” is not a slogan but a spiritual law.

Implementation: This week, cut off one of them first. Just one. At the same time, add a positive replacement — leave a complaining group and join a group that prays for one another. Remember: emptying must go hand in hand with filling.

Evaluation: After three days, have your emotions changed? Has your sleep changed?

Correction: If you can’t cut it off, find a spiritual companion to walk with you; don’t fight alone.

Repetition: Keep it up for four weeks, until the new pathway becomes the main pathway.

Multiplication: Share your experience so that others can be set free too.

sections.heading: 3. Practise “Listening with the Heart”: Not Just Having Heard, but Receiving, Meditating and Doing.
sections.html:
Information: Learn a simple method — after hearing a sermon or reading a passage of Scripture, write down three sentences: What did God say? What does God want me to change? What one thing will I do this week?

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. Without the Holy Spirit, Scripture is only words on a page; with the Holy Spirit, the words become living water.

Conviction: You must believe that God still speaks today, and that he wants to speak to you.

Implementation: This week choose one verse, say it aloud three times every day, and meditate on it whenever you can.

Evaluation: At the weekend ask yourself: did this verse help me in some specific situation?

Correction: If not, perhaps the verse you chose was too abstract; switch to one closer to where you are right now.

Repetition: Build up verse by verse. Fifty-two verses a year means that in ten years more than five hundred verses will be written on the tablet of your heart.

Multiplication: Share in your small group how this verse has changed you.

The 321 vision reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Listening with the brain means analysing, comparing, judging; listening with the heart means receiving, surrendering, responding.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please take this sentence home with you:

It isn’t that you can’t change; it’s that you haven’t kept on “listening rightly.”

It isn’t that you are weaker than others, or that your personality is especially stubborn, or that your circumstances are especially hard. It is a problem of input.

Change the input, and you change the output; change the input for long enough, and you change a lifetime.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Let’s walk today’s road once more.

Saul heard the Lord, and his life was turned around. The man who persecuted Christ became a man who suffered for Christ.

Abraham obeyed God, and the nations were blessed. One man’s obedience on a mountain became a blessing to the whole earth.

The sheep listen to the shepherd’s voice, and they have life. “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

Three figures, three situations, one principle:

What you listen to is what you become.

So when you begin to listen to God’s word constantly — not now and then, but every day;

when you begin to listen to God’s word with the heart — not analysing it with the brain, but receiving it with the heart;

when you begin to obey God’s word — not hearing and leaving it there, but hearing and then doing;

your life will not merely change; it will enter into a life that is abundant, victorious and like Christ.

This morning the Lord Jesus still stands outside the door and knocks. “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me.” (Revelation 3:20) He doesn’t break the door down; he only knocks. He is waiting for someone who can hear, and who is willing to open the door.

And he is still speaking to the churches: “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies.” (Revelation 2:7)

Brothers and sisters, may each of us answer as the boy Samuel did: “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10)

May we be, every morning, like the one who is taught: “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4)

Let us offer up our ears and let Jesus be King; let us offer up our changed lives and let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: Ephesians 4:20–24 (WEB):

“But you didn’t learn Christ that way, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.”
Romans 10:17 (WEB):
“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.”
practices: Build the habit of right input — read Scripture, hear sermons and sing hymns every day; just start with five minutes.
Stop feeding the wrong voices — this week cut off one negative source, and add a positive replacement in its place.
Practise listening with the heart — afterwards write down three sentences: What did God say?
prayer: Lord, tune my ears.

Let me no longer listen to the wrong voices, nor let negative words linger in my heart. Lord, I confess that the reason my life has not yet changed is not that you have not spoken, but that I have not listened rightly.

Help me listen to your word alone. Cleanse my ears, and remove from me the self-centred life that hears only what it wants to hear. Make me humble, willing to be adjusted; make me selfless, able to be led by the Holy Spirit.

Lord, let your truth change my life. Teach me to put off the old self, to be renewed in my mind, and to put on the new self. Teach me to nourish the white dog and starve the black dog; teach me to replace everything wrong with right seeing, right listening, right thinking, right speaking and right doing.
May I, like Saul, turn to you as soon as I hear you; like Abraham, obey you as soon as I hear; like the sheep, recognise the voice of the Shepherd.
May my obedience become a blessing to my family, and a blessing to the people around me.
Reign as King in my life, and receive all the glory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has.” (Luke 8:18) Think back over the past week: what kind of voice did you spend the most time listening to? What fruit has that voice produced in you — discouragement, condemnation, anger and despair, or humility, repentance, peace and change?

“That you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man … and put on the new man.” (Ephesians 4:22, 24) Name one specific thing you are trying hard to “suppress” but can’t keep down. If you switched to the strategy of “replacement,” what right input would you use to take its place? Who could be your spiritual companion and walk this stretch with you?
l125.title: Listen Rightly and Life Changes
l125.subtitle: Listening Rightly (Part 2): Right Listening and Wrong Listening
l125.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: God Is Not Silent — We Have Gone Deaf
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, let’s begin by being still for thirty seconds. Don’t do anything. Just listen.

What did you hear? Perhaps the low hum of the air conditioner, perhaps birdsong outside the window, perhaps your own breathing, perhaps a car passing somewhere in the distance. Those sounds were there all along. They didn’t appear in these thirty seconds; it was only in these thirty seconds that you “heard” them.

And that is the first spiritual fact we have to face today: the sound has been there all along. The problem lies with the one who is listening.

The human ear is a design of awe-inspiring precision. A healthy ear can pick up sound waves from roughly twenty hertz to twenty thousand hertz; inside the cochlea some fifteen thousand hair cells translate the vibrations of the air into nerve signals. And yet at this very moment countless waves are passing straight through your body — radio waves, mobile phone signals, the high-pitched song of insects — and you hear not one of them. Not because they don’t exist, but because your receiver isn’t tuned to that frequency.

In 1953 Colin Cherry, a cognitive scientist at Imperial College London, carried out a famous experiment; later generations would call what he found “the cocktail party effect.” He discovered that in a noisy banquet hall a person can focus on the friend in front of him and automatically filter out the conversations of dozens of people all around. But here is the remarkable thing: let someone at the far end of the room softly mention his name, and he turns his head at once. Cherry’s conclusion was this: we do not hear every sound; we hear the sounds we care about.

Brothers and sisters, please remember that sentence: we do not hear every sound; we hear the sounds we care about.

Our God has never been a silent God. From Genesis 1, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’” to the last chapter of Revelation, “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” — the whole Bible is a book about a God who speaks. In Knowing God the theologian J. I. Packer points out that the very foundation of the Christian faith is this: God is a self-revealing God. He takes the initiative and speaks, and only so can anyone know him. If God did not speak, all human religion would be nothing but guesswork.

Yet many believers today live in a kind of spiritual dullness. They attend meetings, read the Bible, pray, even serve for years — and never once have they clearly sensed: God has just spoken to me. Their faith is knowledge about God, not conversation with God. They are like the Israelites in Samuel’s day, of whom Scripture says, “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.” (1 Samuel 3:1)

Notice that the verse says Yahweh’s word was rare — and yet in that very same chapter we see God calling, four times over, in a single night. God was not stingy with his voice at all. What was rare was not God’s word; it was people who heard it.

So in this lesson the question we ask is not “Is God speaking?” but “Am I listening?”

Here is an important 321 Insight; brothers and sisters, please take it to heart: it is not that God doesn’t speak — it is that we rely on the brain and not on the heart. It is not that God doesn’t guide — it is that we set our minds on the flesh and not on the Spirit.

Rely on the brain, and you worry; rely on the heart, and you rejoice. The brain is an organ of analysis; the heart is an organ of reception. When we spend our whole lives using our brains to calculate God, evaluate God and argue with God, we tune ourselves to a frequency on which God can never be received. God’s voice is not a puzzle waiting to be solved; it is the heart of a Father.

Today God wants to open our ears. May every one of us leave this lesson changed — from “someone who knows God can speak” into “someone who really hears God speak.”

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Night Servants Became Friends
sections.html:
Our key verse is John 15:15. To understand it we first have to stand in the place where those words were spoken.

John’s Gospel was written by John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. It is generally dated somewhere between AD 85 and 95, very probably written in Ephesus in Asia Minor, to churches scattered across the Greco-Roman world. By then most of the first generation of apostles had been martyred, heresies were starting to rise, and believers needed to be reminded afresh that the Jesus they believed in is the Word who was with God from the beginning. That is why John opens his book with these words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” (John 1:1)

“Word” in Greek is λόγος (logos), meaning “speech, a spoken word.” With this term John announces something astonishing: God does not merely speak — God himself is that Word. And this speaking God in the end became a Word that human beings could hear: “The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14)

Our key verse falls within the long section of John 13 to 17. It is often called the Upper Room Discourse: the farewell words the Lord Jesus spoke to the eleven disciples on the night he was betrayed, after the Last Supper. Judas had already gone out, the cross was at the door, and the Lord had only a few hours left. What a man says in the last hours of his life is always what matters most to him.

What did the Lord say that night? He washed the disciples’ feet, he gave them a new commandment, he promised that the Holy Spirit would come, he told the parable of the vine and the branches. And then he said this: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” (John 15:15)

There are two key Greek words here. “Servant” is δοῦλος (doulos), a bondservant, a slave. What marks a slave is not that he does little but that he is not told. A master owes his slave no explanation; the slave simply carries out orders. “Friend” is φίλος (philos), from φιλέω (phileō, to love dearly): someone the master holds in his heart, someone who is let into the master’s inner thoughts.

So what the Lord Jesus proclaims here is a revolution in relationship. He is saying: from now on I will not treat you as slaves who can only take orders; I will treat you as friends who can know my heart.

Pay special attention to the reason the Lord gives: “for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” On what basis does the Lord call us friends? Not because we are so good, but because he has told us everything he heard from the Father. The evidence of friendship is speech.

Brothers and sisters, this is the Bible’s deepest definition of “God speaking to people”: God speaks not in order to issue commands, but in order to share his heart.

Look at how the Lord Jesus himself lived. He said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” (John 5:19) And again, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.” (John 7:16) Through his thirty-three years on earth the Lord Jesus was a man who listened to the Father every day and acted on the Father’s word every day.

This is exactly the first of the 321 vision’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model. We learn to hear God’s voice not in pursuit of some mystical experience, but in order to live the very life the Lord lived on earth — a life constantly connected to the Father, constantly hearing the Father’s heart.

From the Old Testament to the New there is a clear line of development in the way God speaks. Hebrews draws that line in its very first sentence: “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2) “At many times and in various ways” — the phrase shows how astonishingly rich God’s ways of speaking are. He has spoken by a voice, by visions, by dreams, by the Law, by prophets, by nature, by the events of history. And in these last days he has spoken by his Son; and since the Lord’s ascension he has gone on speaking to everyone who belongs to him by the Holy Spirit and by the Scriptures.

In this lesson we will look at three of the most basic and most common ways: God speaking in person, God speaking through the Bible, and God speaking in our hearts.

sections.heading: 1. God Speaks in Person: He Is a God Who Will Speak to You
sections.html:
Scripture says, “Yahweh called Samuel. He said, ‘Here I am.’” (1 Samuel 3:4)

Scripture also says, “He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” (Acts 9:4)

These two passages show us one and the same truth: God is able to speak to people directly, with a “voice.”

Take Samuel first. It was the close of the period of the judges, around the eleventh century BC, and the ark of the covenant rested in the tabernacle at Shiloh. Eli the high priest was old and his eyes were dim; his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were wicked men. All Israel lay in spiritual darkness, which is why Scripture says, “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.” (1 Samuel 3:1)

In just such an age, God spoke. And the one he called was not the seasoned high priest but a boy who “didn’t yet know Yahweh” (1 Samuel 3:7). Samuel was probably about twelve years old. At God’s first call he ran to Eli; at the second he ran to Eli again; at the third, once more he ran to Eli. It is a lovely detail, and a very true one — he heard the voice, but he didn’t know it was God.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had that experience? A prompting comes, and you think you’re overthinking it. A word pierces you deeply, and you put it down to emotion. A burden weighs on you for days, and you call it stress. In fact it was God calling your name — you just didn’t yet recognise his voice.

The turning point that night came when Eli finally discerned what was happening. He said to Samuel, “Go, lie down. It shall be, if he calls you, that you shall say, ‘Speak, Yahweh; for your servant hears.’” (1 Samuel 3:9) And so, the fourth time, “Yahweh came, and stood, and called as at other times, ‘Samuel! Samuel!’ Then Samuel said, ‘Speak; for your servant hears.’” (1 Samuel 3:10)

“Here I am” in Hebrew is הִנֵּנִי (hineni). It is one of the weightiest words in the Bible. Abraham said “Here I am” on Mount Moriah (Genesis 22:1); Moses said “Here I am” before the burning bush (Exodus 3:4); Isaiah, in his vision in the temple, said “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8). The word is not answering a roll call; it is an act of surrender. It means: Lord, all of me is here before you — do with me whatever you will.

Now take Saul. Some time in the AD 30s the Pharisee Saul was on the road to Damascus, carrying letters from the high priest and breathing out murder. He was certain he was burning with zeal for God. Suddenly a light from heaven flashed all around him; he fell to the ground and heard the Lord say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4)

Notice the Lord’s words. It was Christians that Saul was persecuting, yet the Lord said, “Why do you persecute me?” That one sentence overturned Saul’s entire theology at a stroke — the church is Christ’s own body, and to touch the church is to touch the Lord himself. Years later this same Paul would write, “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually” (1 Corinthians 12:27), and the root of it lies in that one sentence on the Damascus road.

One word from God can rewrite a person’s whole life.

To Samuel that voice was as real as a person speaking; for Saul that voice shook the direction of his entire life. This tells us that it isn’t only prophets and apostles who can hear God’s voice. God is willing to speak to people — that has always been his heart.

But where is the key? The key is that Samuel said those words: “Here I am!”

That is the response of the heart, not the analysis of the brain. Samuel didn’t ask, Where did that voice come from? Could it be a hallucination? Is there any scientific evidence? He simply gave himself over completely.

I often use the radio as an illustration. Right now this room is full of the signals of dozens of stations: news, music, traffic — all of them here, without a moment’s pause. But you can’t hear them, because you have no receiver; and even with a receiver, if it isn’t tuned to the right frequency, all you hear is static. Tune it right, and you hear; tune it wrong, and there is nothing but silence.

What is God’s frequency? Humility.

Scripture says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) The Greek word for “resists” here is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” In the spiritual world, the proud are people against whom God has drawn up his battle lines. It isn’t that they can’t pick up the signal; they are shut outside the door.

This is what the 321 vision means when it says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — wanting to take God’s place. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When someone says, “Here I am; speak, for your servant hears,” he has returned to his originally intended position: God is Lord and I am servant; God speaks and I listen. In that moment, heaven opens.

The proud, on the other hand, hear only themselves. In 1999 the Harvard psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris ran a famous experiment that later became widely known as “the invisible gorilla.” They asked participants to watch a video of people passing a ball and to concentrate on counting how many passes the players in white made. Partway through, someone in a gorilla suit strolled into the frame, beat his chest and walked out again — nine seconds in all. The result? Roughly half the participants never saw the gorilla at all.

The phenomenon is called “inattentional blindness,” and it reveals a sobering fact: when people are wholly absorbed in their own task, even the most obvious thing in front of their eyes gets automatically deleted. Brothers and sisters, the spiritual world has its own “inattentional deafness.” When we are wholly absorbed in our own plans, our own grievances, our own achievements, God can stand right in front of us and speak, and we will not hear.

So the first condition for hearing God’s voice is not technique; it is posture. It is that one sentence: “Lord, here I am.”

321 Insight: the humble hear God easily; the proud hear only themselves.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, will you say to the Lord, as Samuel did, “Lord, here I am. Speak, for your servant hears”?

sections.heading: 2. God Speaks Through the Bible: His Word Is Alive
sections.html:
Scripture says, “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12)

This is one of the most powerful verses anywhere in the Bible about the Bible itself. Notice its two descriptive words.

“Living” in Greek is ζῶν (zōn), quite simply “alive.” Applied to Scripture, it means that the Bible is not a finished ancient document, sealed and put away. It is a living thing. Open it today, and it will speak to you.

“Active” in Greek is ἐνεργής (energēs), the root of the English word “energy.” It means “at work, in operation, exerting its power.” The Bible is not an object lying there waiting for you to study it; it is a power actively at work in you.

And the most arresting part of the verse is its second half: “able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” The picture in the original is of a surgeon’s scalpel opening up the deepest places in a person. Brothers and sisters, when we read the Bible, the Bible also reads us. We think we are analysing the text, when in fact the text is laying us open.

Why, then, do some people read the Bible every day and never once hear God’s voice in it?

Paul gives the answer: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6)

The word translated “spirit” here is πνεῦμα (pneuma), and the Chinese Union Version even notes in its margin that it may be rendered “the Holy Spirit.” Paul is not saying the words of Scripture don’t matter — his letters quote the words of the Old Testament from beginning to end. He is saying that words without the breath of the Holy Spirit are just letters carved on a gravestone; but words the Holy Spirit breathes into become God’s living word, spoken to you.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: the Bible is my standard, and the Holy Spirit is my guide. These two foundations must be held together as one.

A standard without a guide turns faith into legalism — correct, but lifeless, like the Pharisees. The Lord said to them, “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.” (John 5:39–40) What a frightening sentence: a group of people who knew the Scriptures inside out, and who walked straight past the very One the Scriptures point to.

A guide without a standard turns faith into mysticism — lively, but rootless, ready to be blown away at any moment. That is why Scripture says, “test the spirits, whether they are of God.” (1 John 4:1)

Standard plus guide — only that is truly hearing God.

So when God really does speak to us through the Bible, what are the signs?

Luke’s Gospel gives us the loveliest of answers. On the afternoon of the resurrection, two disciples were trudging dejectedly to Emmaus. The Lord walked with them and explained the Scriptures to them. Then, when he made himself known in the breaking of the bread and immediately vanished, they said this: “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32)

“Burning” in Greek is καιομένη (kaiomenē), “being on fire, ablaze.” And notice — they only understood afterwards. At the time all they felt was an inexpressible burning in their hearts; they didn’t know it was the Lord.

Brothers and sisters, this is the sign that God is speaking through the Bible: not merely “I understand,” but “my heart has been set on fire.”

Throughout church history this fire has blazed up again and again.

In the summer of AD 386 a North African named Augustine sat weeping in a garden in Milan. He was a man of brilliant learning and broken morals; at thirty-two he was bound by his own sin and could not break free. Suddenly he heard a child’s voice from a neighbouring house, chanting over and over, “Take up and read, take up and read.” He rushed back, picked up Paul’s letters, opened them at random and read: “Let’s walk properly, as in the day; not in reveling and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and lustful acts, and not in strife and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.” (Romans 13:13–14) In his Confessions he later wrote that as he finished that sentence, every shadow of doubt in his heart vanished at once. A passage he had read who knows how many times became, that day, God speaking to him in person.

More than thirteen hundred years later, on the evening of 24 May 1738, at a small meeting in Aldersgate Street in London, a discouraged English clergyman named John Wesley listened as someone read aloud Martin Luther’s preface to the Epistle to the Romans. In his journal he wrote the words still quoted today: “I felt my heart strangely warmed.” In that moment he was assured that Christ had taken away his sins. Wesley had been reading Romans for half his life, but that night the words became a voice.

I often put it like this: the Bible is like a letter, the Holy Spirit is like the one who reads the letter aloud to you, and your heart is the receiver. Without the Holy Spirit, the Bible is just print; with the Holy Spirit, the Bible becomes a voice.

That also explains a common experience. You have read the same verse twenty times and felt nothing, and then one morning it suddenly pricks your heart like a needle. The verse hasn’t changed. What has changed is that in that moment the Holy Spirit has aimed it squarely at your situation.

So the way we read the Bible has to change. Don’t read only with your brain; listen with your heart.

Church history has an ancient tradition called lectio divina, “sacred reading.” It had already taken shape among the Benedictines in the sixth century, and a twelfth-century monk later summed it up in four steps: read, meditate, pray, contemplate. Its spirit is very simple — reading the Bible is not gathering information; it is keeping an appointment.

We can turn it into an even simpler practice: as you read, stop at any point and ask the Lord, “Lord, what do you want to say to me today?” Then be still, and wait.

Here is a very practical reminder. Brain science tells us the human brain has a “default mode network,” proposed in 2001 by the American neuroscientist Marcus Raichle of Washington University. Research found that when people stop performing a task and become quiet, certain regions of the brain actually grow more active — and this is the crucial moment when people integrate meaning and arrive at insight. In other words, even physiologically, stillness is not wasted time; stillness is when deep understanding actually happens.

Brothers and sisters, when God made us he had already written “only in stillness can you hear” into our very bodies. No wonder the psalm says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10) The Hebrew word here, רָפָה (raphah), means “to let go, to let your hands drop.” Let go first — and then you will know that he is God.

321 Insight: the Bible is the standard and the Holy Spirit is the guide; only when the two are one do we truly hear God.

From a 321 point of view, this is a change of mindset. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. When your mindset about the Bible shifts from “a book to get through” to “a Lord to meet,” your daily habit of reading Scripture changes; when that habit changes, your life changes. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living.

sections.heading: 3. God Speaks in Our Hearts: The Holy Spirit’s Prompting Is the Most Common Way
sections.html:
Scripture says, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)

Scripture also says, “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13)

Brothers and sisters, where does God speak most often? Not outside you, but inside you.

This is the greatest grace of the New Testament age. In Old Testament times the Spirit of God “came upon” certain people — upon judges, upon kings, upon prophets — and he could depart. That is why David prayed after his sin, “don’t take your Holy Spirit from me.” (Psalm 51:11) But in the New Testament the Lord promised, “he lives with you, and will be in you.” (John 14:17) From the day of Pentecost onwards, the Holy Spirit has come to live inside everyone who belongs to the Lord.

The Greek word for “led,” ἄγω (agō), is passive in Romans 8:14, meaning “to be brought along.” It is used of a shepherd leading his sheep and of a person being shown the way. It does not mean “to be pushed along” but “to be taken along” — a walking together that needs you to be willing to keep up.

The Greek for “works” is ἐνεργέω (energeō). Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? It shares its root with “active” (energēs) in Hebrews 4:12. The same divine energy is at work in Scripture and at work in your heart. The word outside you and the prompting within you come from the same God, and so they will never contradict each other.

So in what ways does God speak in our hearts? At least four: promptings, thoughts, conscience, and peace or the lack of it.

The first is promptings. While Peter, on the rooftop in Joppa, was still puzzling over his vision, “the Spirit said to him, ‘Behold, three men seek you.’” (Acts 10:19) That one prompting opened the door for the gospel to reach the Gentiles.

The second is thoughts. God often places a thought within us: call so-and-so, visit so-and-so, deal properly with a certain matter. These thoughts are often very light and unremarkable, yet they tend to be remarkably accurate.

The third is conscience. Paul says, “I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit.” (Romans 9:1) Notice Paul’s wording — his conscience bears witness “in the Holy Spirit.” Conscience in itself is not the Holy Spirit, but the Holy Spirit uses a conscience he has cleansed to speak.

The fourth is peace or the lack of peace. Paul says, “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” (Colossians 3:15) The Greek for “rule” is βραβεύω (brabeuō), originally meaning “to act as umpire, to arbitrate.” Like the referee in a match, peace blows the whistle in your heart: this step is fine, that one is not.

But here comes the question — the one more brothers and sisters ask me than any other: how do I tell whether this is God’s voice or just my own thinking?

Scripture gives us a clear measuring rod: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:6)

The Greek for “mind” is φρόνημα (phronēma), the bent of a person’s thinking, the direction the whole person is facing. So this verse is not about a thought that occasionally flickers past; it is about the orientation of your whole self.

From this verse we can draw out three tests.

First, look at the fruit. God’s voice brings life and peace; the voice of the flesh brings confusion and unrest. Note that peace does not mean things going smoothly. When Jonah was running from God he found a ship, paid his fare and slept soundly; everything went smoothly all the way — but there was no peace in his heart. On the other hand, Paul was compelled by the Holy Spirit to go up to Jerusalem, knowing full well that chains were waiting for him, and yet he said, “nor do I hold my life dear to myself.” (Acts 20:24) Outside, a storm; inside, peace.

Second, see whether it agrees with Scripture. The Holy Spirit will never lead you to do what the Bible plainly forbids. Any “prompting” that goes against the clear teaching of Scripture, however strong it feels, is not the Holy Spirit. This is the standard standing guard.

Third, see whether it lifts up Jesus. The Lord said that when the Holy Spirit comes, “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). Any voice that puffs you up, that makes you feel more spiritual than others, that makes you want to control other people, is not from the Holy Spirit. This is precisely the second of the 321 Two Core Values: let Jesus receive all the glory.

Here I need to draw a very important distinction. The Holy Spirit lives in the “heart,” not in the “brain.”

Of course God has given us reason, and reason is good; God wants us to love him with all our mind. But the organ that receives the things of the Spirit is the heart, not the brain. Proverbs says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) A person’s life does not flow out of the brain; it flows out of the heart.

Rely on the heart, and things become clear; rely on the brain, and things become confused. The brain is forever calculating gains and losses, projecting risks, weighing advantages, and it can never work out the item called “God’s will.” But the heart is the altar God has placed within us, and there the Holy Spirit lights the fire.

The French mathematician and thinker Blaise Pascal wrote a famous line in his Pensées: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” He also said that all of humanity’s unhappiness comes from one single thing — not being able to sit quietly alone in a room. An observation made more than three hundred years ago is even truer today. On average we unlock our phones dozens of times a day; we fear silence more than we fear busyness. Yet God’s voice is very often found in the very ten minutes we are least willing to give him.

Elijah’s experience at Mount Horeb gives us the best picture. “Behold, Yahweh passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains, and broke in pieces the rocks before Yahweh; but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.” (1 Kings 19:11–12) God was not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire. God was in that still small voice.

Brothers and sisters, God’s voice is not necessarily loud, but it is always clear. He usually doesn’t rush to speak; he waits for you to be still.

321 Insight: rely on the heart, and things are clear; rely on the brain, and things are confused — because the Holy Spirit lives in the heart, not in the brain.

This is also the lesson of what the 321 vision calls selflessness. The old self lives the self-centred life; everything revolves around “me,” so inside there is always one very loud voice talking, and that voice is “I.” When the voice of “I” is that loud, of course God’s still small voice is drowned out. The new self is selfless — not by reducing the self to empty nothing, but by giving up the throne so that Christ may reign as King within. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When “I” fall silent, God’s voice becomes clear.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Hearing God Is a Road Back to Our Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
Let’s set today’s three key points within the 321 framework and look at them again; a complete picture will emerge.

The Three Foundations correspond exactly to the three ways God speaks. Jesus is my role model — the Lord himself is the Son of God who said, “everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you”; on earth he lived a life of constantly listening to the Father. The Bible is my standard — God speaks through Scripture, and every prompting must come back to this measuring rod to be tested. The Holy Spirit is my guide — God speaks in our hearts, turning the word outside us into life within us. Brothers and sisters, these Three Foundations are not three separate things; they are one and the same God saying one and the same thing to you on three levels.

The Two Core Values determine our motive for listening. Let Jesus be King — when we seek God’s guidance, it is not to get God to approve our plans but to hand over the throne and let him give the orders. Many people pray for God to speak when in their hearts they have already decided; they just want God to endorse it. That isn’t listening; that’s holding a vote. Let Jesus receive all the glory — every voice that truly comes from God will in the end give the glory to Jesus, not to the person who “heard” it.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. God has never spoken to people merely to soothe their personal feelings, but to build his kingdom. God spoke to Noah so that the ark would be built; God spoke to Abraham so that a nation would be founded; God spoke to Moses so that the tabernacle would be built; God spoke to Peter so that the door to the Gentiles would be opened. When God speaks to you today, it will surely have something to do with his kingdom on earth too.

Now look at the core message. The self-centred life and selflessness are precisely the watershed between not hearing and hearing. The old self is self-centred: the self sits on the throne within, so the loudest voices inside are its own desires, its own fears, its own face. The new self is selfless: it yields the throne to Christ, and then everything inside grows quiet, and God’s still small voice can be heard. So we say: only selflessness can hear God; only selflessness can let Jesus reign as King.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. This principle is especially true when it comes to listening. A proud person can’t even take in what his spouse, his children or his co-workers say — so how could he possibly hear what God says? Only someone who has learned to listen quietly before people will listen quietly before God. So the practice of listening to God begins with the practice of listening to people.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people are in a hurry to ask God, “What ministry should I be doing?” But God often asks first, “Will you be with me first?” God’s first purpose in speaking is to build a relationship with you, not to hand out jobs. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. God’s voice reaches us along exactly that order.

A change of perspective. When we truly hear God, our perspective is turned upside down — from man’s perspective to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. On the Damascus road Saul had all four perspectives overturned by a single sentence. He went from “zeal for his own religion” to “suffering for the name of Christ,” and from pursuing a position on earth to pursuing a reward in heaven.

The 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; live the life of “0” (selflessness), and you will bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Of the nine, the first is love, one is gentleness, and another is self-control. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that these fruits all have to do with listening? Someone without self-control always has a mouth faster than his ears; someone without gentleness only wants to persuade, never to listen. So “hearing God” is not an isolated devotional technique; it bears fruit directly in your relationships with your family, your colleagues and your co-workers.

The 235 relationships. When you begin to hear God, you need a “2” — a selfless spiritual companion who can discern with you and confirm with you. For Scripture says, “Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counselors they are established.” (Proverbs 15:22) God often puts half of what you have heard with someone else. Next come the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — to pass on what you have heard; and then it widens into the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together.

Finally, there is the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. First the Holy Spirit’s guidance (Spirit), then understanding from Scripture (Understanding), then the life lived out (Life), then entering into service (Service), and at last giving all the glory to God (God). You see, the starting point of this whole road is listening. If you don’t listen, nothing happens.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Practices, Eight Stages
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. I want to take them deeper using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Practise listening quietly for God’s voice every day

Set aside ten minutes every day. Don’t talk, don’t analyse; just be still before God and say to the Lord, “Lord, here I am; please speak to me.” Learn to turn from busyness to listening, and let your heart tune in to God’s frequency.

Information: first know a fact — God is a God who speaks, and he often speaks in a still small voice (1 Kings 19:12).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you that part of your busyness over these years has really been a way of avoiding stillness.

Conviction: truly believe in your heart that “these ten minutes are not wasted; they are the most important ten minutes of my day.”

Implementation: starting tomorrow morning — a fixed time, a fixed place, a fixed posture, and your phone in another room. For the first five minutes do only one thing: breathe, and say to the Lord, “Lord, here I am.”

Evaluation: after a week, ask yourself — did I really become still? Or did I just move my thinking to a different place?

Correction: if ten minutes is too hard, start with three; if early morning is impossible, switch to bedtime. What matters is not the time slot but that you don’t break the chain.

Repetition: keep it up for forty days in a row. A study published in 2010 by the psychologist Phillippa Lally and her team at University College London found that a new habit takes on average sixty-six days to become automatic — and that missing a day or two along the way does not ruin the whole habit. So don’t give up just because you missed a day.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister and invite them to do these forty days of stillness with you, sharing with each other once a week.

Practice 2: Read the Bible prayerfully, and let Scripture become God’s voice

When you read the Bible, don’t just aim to understand the content; pray as you go: “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” Turn the text into a conversation, and let the Holy Spirit turn the words into life.

Information: know that the Bible is “living and active” (Hebrews 4:12); it will speak to you of its own accord.

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you that your Bible reading in the past has often stopped at “I understand” and never reached “my heart is on fire.”

Conviction: believe that reading the Bible is keeping an appointment, not handing in homework.

Implementation: read only a short passage each day, and when you finish, do three things. First, ask: what does this passage show me about who God is? Second, ask: Lord, what do you want to say to me today? Third, write down in a notebook, in a single line, the one thing the Lord said to you.

Evaluation: at the weekend, look back over those seven lines and see what theme God has been speaking to you about this week. You’ll be surprised how often it’s the same thing.

Correction: if a whole week goes by and you can’t write a single line, halve the amount you read. Hearing one sentence is better than finishing a whole chapter.

Repetition: let this way of reading replace your old method, and keep it up for three months.

Multiplication: share your “one-line notes” in your small group, and draw the whole group into reading the Bible this way.

Practice 3: Pay attention to the promptings of your heart and obey at once

When a peaceful leading, a reminder or a rebuke arises in your heart, don’t delay and don’t analyse — obey at once. Obey once, and it becomes easier to hear the next time.

Information: know that the Holy Spirit’s most common ways are promptings in the heart, thoughts, conscience and peace.

Revelation: think back over the past year. Was there a prompting you ignored at the time and regretted afterwards?

Conviction: believe that obedience is not a burden; it is the way we walk with God. The Lord said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) Notice the order — first they hear, then they follow.

Implementation: begin with the smallest act of obedience. If today a thought comes telling you to phone someone, make the call within three minutes. Don’t put it off till the afternoon, and don’t analyse it first.

Evaluation: before you sleep at night, spend two minutes looking back: what did God say to me today? Did I obey?

Correction: if you find yourself delaying again and again, name the reason for the delay. More often than not it’s the fear of losing face, or the wish to control the outcome. Hand both of those over to the Lord.

Repetition: do this two-minute review every evening for a month.

Multiplication: as your stories of obedience start to pile up, tell them. Your testimony will become a doorway through which others hear God.

A Gentle Reminder

First, God is always speaking; the question is whether you are listening.

Second, God’s voice is not necessarily loud, but it is always clear.

Third, God’s voice is not confused; it brings life and peace.

That is why Scripture reminds us, “Don’t quench the Spirit.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19) The Greek word for “quench” is σβέννυμι (sbennymi), originally “to put out a fire by pouring water on it.” Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit’s prompting is like a candle flame just lit, easily put out by three things: delay, analysis, and other people’s idle talk. May the Lord guard that little flame within us.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Lord, Here I Am — I Am Willing to Listen
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, everything we have said today can really be gathered into one sentence: God is not a distant God; he is a God who speaks, who guides and who leads.

The question has never been whether God is speaking, but whether you are listening with your heart.

When you begin to rely on the heart, you will discover that the Bible is speaking to you, that the Holy Spirit is speaking within you, that God is speaking in every moment of your life. You will find that the things you took for coincidences were in fact arranged; that the promptings you dismissed as emotion were in fact a call; that the verses you have read for ten years suddenly open their mouths and speak to you.

Brothers and sisters, please remember our two sentences for today: only selflessness can hear God; only selflessness can let Jesus reign as King.

For as long as “I” sit on the throne, the voice of “I” will drown out everything else. When “I” step down and let Jesus take the throne, everything inside grows quiet. At that point it isn’t that you have become better at listening; it’s that you have finally returned to your originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

The purpose of all this is not to make us spiritual experts who can go and set others straight; it is to let Jesus be King and to let Jesus receive all the glory. Someone who has truly heard God won’t have “I heard him” written on his face, but “He is worthy.”

From today on, let’s learn one thing, and it comes down to a single sentence:

Lord, here I am. I am willing to listen.

keyVerses: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” (John 15:15)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I believe you are a God who speaks.
I am not someone who cannot hear; I am your sheep.
I will learn to rely on the heart and not the brain; I will set my mind on the Spirit, not on the flesh.
I will become someone who hears your voice, understands your heart and obeys your leading.
In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare it. Amen!
practices: Practise listening quietly for God’s voice every day
Read the Bible prayerfully, and let Scripture become God’s voice
Pay attention to the promptings of your heart and obey at once
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that you are not a silent God. You spoke at creation, you spoke on the cross, and you are still speaking this very morning.

Lord, forgive us. All these years we have been too busy, too noisy, too full. We have relied on the brain and not on the heart; we have set our minds on the flesh and not on the Spirit. We have often asked you to speak, yet we were not ready to listen.
Lord, open our ears, and open our hearts too. Remove the loud, talking “I” within us, and reign as King in us.
When we read your word, set our hearts on fire; when we are still, help us discern your still small voice; and whenever we are prompted, help us obey at once.
Make us people who hear your voice, understand your heart and obey your leading; and use us, we pray, to carry your voice to those who are still in darkness.
May all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: Three times in a row Samuel heard God calling, yet thought it was Eli. Look back over your own life: was there a time when “it was really God speaking, but you took it for something else”? How did you come to recognise it later? Read it alongside the verse: “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.” (1 Samuel 3:1)

Question 2: Do you find it easier to “rely on the brain” or to “rely on the heart”? In a decision you are facing right now, do you have real peace? Read it alongside the verse: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:6)
l126.title: Hearing God’s Voice
l126.subtitle: The Ways God Speaks to People (Part 1)
l126.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: You Heard It — You Just Weren’t Listening
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

In 1953 Colin Cherry, a cognitive scientist at Imperial College London, carried out a study of what would later be called “the cocktail party effect.” He discovered something remarkable: in a banquet hall full of voices, clinking glasses and loud music, a person can somehow pick out, from dozens of sounds, the one voice he is concentrating on. More remarkable still, even while you are deep in conversation with the person in front of you, if someone at the far side of the room calls your name, your ears turn towards it instantly.

Cherry concluded that human hearing is never a passive radio; it is an active choice. It isn’t that we can’t hear; it’s that we aren’t listening.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what this lesson wants to say to us today.

In the last lesson we saw that God is a God who speaks. He spoke on the very first day of creation: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:3) And the first thing he did after making man was to speak with him. The sixty-six books of the Bible are, from beginning to end, the record of “God speaking to people.”

But today we want to see something further: God does not speak in only one way. He is the God who created heaven and earth and all things, and his speaking is rich, varied and beyond all limits. He speaks through prophecy, through visions and dreams, through angels, through circumstances, through an open Bible — and through a casual word of greeting.

The Bible shows us a truth of the utmost importance: God not only speaks — he speaks in all kinds of ways.

But the key has never been the method. The key is this — are you listening? Are you discerning?

A picture often comes to my mind. The radio is broadcasting, but the dial isn’t tuned properly, and the whole room fills with hissing static. The problem isn’t the station; the station has been transmitting all along. The problem is the reception. That is so often our condition: God is speaking all the time, but we are tuned to the wrong channel; we turn the volume right up, and all we hear is the echo of our own voice.

So in this lesson God wants to lead us deeper into two things: first, how God speaks to people in all kinds of ways; and second, how we can discern whether something really comes from God.

Here the 321 vision gives us its first ray of light: the focus is not the “method”; the focus is Jesus.

Some people spend their whole lives chasing dreams; some spend their whole lives chasing miracles; some spend their whole lives chasing one word from a particular prophet. But Jesus never told us to chase methods. He simply said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) What the sheep recognise is not the shepherd’s gestures, nor the shepherd’s staff, but the shepherd’s voice. Recognising the voice is the fruit of a relationship, not the product of a technique.

And here is the second ray of light: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and things are clear; rely on the brain and ourselves, and things are confused.

The brain is an organ of analysis; the heart is an organ of reception. When we use the brain to take every prompting apart, it is like trying to grip a gust of wind with tweezers — the harder you try, the less you hold, until all that’s left is a heap of theories and a tired heart. When we rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit, God’s voice comes like the light of early morning: it doesn’t dazzle, yet it makes everything plain. Scripture says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Rely on the heart, and you rejoice; rely on the brain, and you worry. Brothers and sisters, this is not a slogan; it is a real road.

This morning, let’s ask the Lord together to retune the dial of our inner receiver to him.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: God Speaking in the Last Days, Men Moved by the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Today we have two key passages, one from 2 Peter and one from Hebrews. To understand them, we first need to stand in the situation of the time.

2 Peter was written by the apostle Peter. From the tone of the letter, these are his last words, written before his martyrdom. He says, “knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.” (2 Peter 1:14) The letter is generally dated to the mid-to-late AD 60s and was written to believers scattered in many places. The church at that time faced a serious problem: false teachers were arising, interpreting God’s word to suit themselves and using grace as an excuse for licence.

In chapter 1 Peter speaks of the Transfiguration, which he saw with his own eyes; he says they “were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Peter 1:16). But straight after that he says something unexpected: “We have the more sure word of prophecy” (2 Peter 1:19). Notice that Peter does not say, “My experience is more reliable than Scripture.” What he says is this — Scripture is more certain than my experience.

This is the foundation of today’s lesson. An apostle who had seen Jesus’ glory with his own eyes and heard the voice from heaven with his own ears turns round and hands the highest authority to the word God inspired. Brothers and sisters, if even Peter did that, how can we place one dream or one feeling of ours above the Bible?

Then Peter explains why: “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:21) The Greek word for “moved” here is pherō, meaning “to be carried along, to be borne.” In Acts 27:15 the same word describes a ship in a storm being “driven along” by the wind. It is a vivid picture: the prophet is like a ship and the Holy Spirit is the wind. The wind sets the course; the ship’s only task is to spread its sails. God’s word is reliable not because the one speaking is so clever, but because the one carrying him along is the Holy Spirit.

As for Hebrews, Scripture doesn’t name its author. It was written to Hebrew believers who were being persecuted, who were wavering, and who wanted to retreat into the old system of Judaism; it is generally dated before the destruction of the temple in AD 70. The book opens with a stunning declaration: “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)

“At many times and in various ways” is, in Greek, two adverbs: polymerōs (in many portions, piece by piece) and polytropōs (in many manners, through many different channels). This is exactly the theme of today’s lesson: the “amount” of God’s speaking has built up portion by portion, and the “ways” of God’s speaking are many and varied. He spoke through the Law, through the prophets, through history, through the altar, through visions and dreams, through the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire.

But Hebrews goes on to its summit: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son. All the ways at last flow together into one Person — Jesus Christ. He is God’s most complete, most clear and most final Word.

So we can sum up the background like this: the ways God speaks are many, but the centre of God’s speaking is one. His channels are many; his focus is One alone. Revelation could not put it more plainly: “for the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy.” (Revelation 19:10)

Brothers and sisters, every voice that truly comes from God will bring you back to Jesus, to let Jesus be King and to let Jesus receive all the glory. Anything that takes you somewhere else — however moving, however overwhelming — calls for you to stop and discern.

sections.heading: 1. God Speaks Through Prophecy: He Entrusts His Heart to People
sections.html:
Scripture says, “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:21)
