What is the essence of prophecy? As soon as many people hear the word “prophecy,” they think of fortune-telling, of predicting what will happen tomorrow. But the emphasis of prophecy in the Bible is not predicting the future; it is conveying God’s heart.

The Hebrew word for “prophet” is nabi, whose root has to do with “proclaiming, announcing.” The Greek prophētēs is made up of pro (before, on behalf of) and phēmi (to speak), meaning “one who speaks on behalf of another.” A prophet is not a futurologist; a prophet is God’s spokesman. What made Moses a prophet was not that he could tell fortunes, but that God says, “Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.” (Amos 3:7)

So the heart of prophecy is this — God entrusts his heart to people.

What an astonishing thing that is. The God who created the universe is willing to tell what is on his heart to people who grow weak, who fail, who run away. It is like a father crouching down to tell his child the family’s plans — not because the child is able to carry them, but because the father wants the child to have a share in them.

In the Old Testament God spoke chiefly through prophets. From Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Isaiah and Jeremiah down to Malachi, God chose a small group of people and put his words in their mouths.

But in the New Testament something even more stunning happened. On the day of Pentecost Peter stood up and quoted Joel: “‘It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams.” (Acts 2:17)

Notice the shift: from “a small group of people” to “all flesh.” From God’s prophets to all God’s children.

God does not use only special people; God is willing to use everyone who belongs to him.

That is what Paul says in 1 Corinthians: “But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3) Brothers and sisters, look closely at those three words — edification, exhortation, consolation. That is the function of New Testament prophecy. God wants to use your mouth to lift up someone who has lost heart, and your word to bring back someone who has lost their way.

I know of a very common kind of scene. Early one morning, as she reads the Bible, a sister finds a friend she hasn’t contacted for years coming to mind, so she sends a short message: “I prayed for you this morning. God hasn’t forgotten you.” The friend replies that only the night before she had been about to give up on everything. That is the essence of prophecy — God entrusts his heart to people, and people pass God’s heart on to people.

But precisely because the door has been opened so wide, discernment becomes all the more important.

Not every voice is God’s voice. Some people use the words “God told me” as a shield, packaging their own ideas, their own emotions, even their own ambitions, as the will of God. That is why Paul laid down rules: “Let the prophets speak, two or three, and let the others discern.” (1 Corinthians 14:29) And again: “Don’t quench the Spirit. Don’t despise prophecies. Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21)

Notice Paul’s balance: don’t quench, but don’t believe blindly either; don’t despise, but don’t swallow everything whole either. These two sayings are like a pair of chopsticks: lose one, and you can’t pick anything up.

So the key to prophecy is not the “speaking” but two things: does it come from the Holy Spirit, and does it agree with Scripture?

Psychology gives us a sobering reminder here. In 1960 the British psychologist Peter Wason found, in his famous “2-4-6 experiment,” that once people have a hypothesis in mind, they unconsciously look only for evidence that supports it and ignore the evidence against it. The phenomenon later became known as “confirmation bias.” In other words, when I already want something in my heart, it is very easy for me to “hear” God agreeing with me — in the Bible, in a sermon, in something someone says.

That isn’t God speaking. That’s me speaking — just using God’s voice.

The 321 vision puts it with great precision here: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred easily speak their own minds; only the selfless can become an outlet for God.

What is selflessness? Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) A truly selfless person is still before speaking; he is in no hurry to prove what he has heard, and he cares far more about whether God’s heart has been passed on accurately.

Brothers and sisters, the cleaner the pipe, the clearer the water. Our “self” is the rust on the inside of the pipe. May the Lord cleanse our pipes today, so that we become an outlet for God’s heart and not a loudspeaker for our own ideas.

sections.heading: 2. God Speaks Through Visions and Dreams: He Opens Our Spiritual Eyes
sections.html:
The Bible is full of visions and dreams.

At Troas, where Paul’s way forward had been blocked again and again, “A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, ‘Come over into Macedonia and help us.’” (Acts 16:9) That one vision carried the gospel from Asia into Europe and rewrote the direction of the whole of Western civilisation.

Jacob, on the run, fell asleep with a stone for a pillow, and “He dreamed and saw a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven. Behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.” (Genesis 28:12) When he woke he said something deeply moving: “Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn’t know it.” (Genesis 28:16)

After the wise men from the east had offered their gifts, “Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country another way.” (Matthew 2:12) A single dream saved the life of the holy Child.

All these accounts tell us the same thing: God speaks to people in “pictures.”

Sometimes it is in prayer, sometimes in sleep, sometimes even in a state wholly taken over by the Holy Spirit. Acts 10 records that while Peter was praying on the roof in Joppa, “he fell into a trance. He saw heaven opened” (Acts 10:10–11), and with a great sheet and all kinds of living creatures God overturned his deep-rooted mindset about the Gentiles. Ezekiel 8 records that as the prophet sat in his house with the elders sitting before him, “the Spirit lifted me up between earth and the sky, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 8:3), showing him the abominations hidden in the temple.

The purpose of these experiences was never mystery for its own sake, but to lead people into God’s heart.

We could put it this way: a vision is like a video from God; a dream is like a message from God.

A video is moving and whole; it lets you take in a whole situation at a glance. A message is short and precise, and it often arrives at the most critical moment. But whether video or message, the point is never how overwhelming the picture is; the point is what God wants you to understand.

There is a very real danger here. Human nature loves excitement; it loves the “special.” An ordinary morning’s Bible reading won’t get anyone excited, but one strange dream can keep someone talking for three years. And so some people start chasing experiences, and hang the thermometer of their spiritual life on the number of visions they’ve had.

Science gives us a helpful reminder. In 1953 Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman of the University of Chicago discovered rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Later sleep research tells us that adults go through roughly four to six sleep cycles a night, each lasting about ninety minutes, and that most dreams happen during REM sleep. In other words, everyone dreams every night; most of the time we have simply forgotten by the time we wake.

This scientific fact reminds us of two things. First, dreaming is a normal physiological mechanism God built into us when he made us, so not every dream has spiritual significance; most dreams are just the afterimages of the day. Second, precisely because dreaming is so ordinary, the fact that God chooses to speak to people through such an ordinary channel actually shows his humility and tenderness — he stoops down to us and slips his heart in at the very moments when we are least on guard and least able to analyse with our brains.

So how do we discern?

The Bible itself gives us the standard. Jeremiah records God rebuking the false prophets: “The prophet who has a dream, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the straw to the wheat?” (Jeremiah 23:28) God does not reject dreams; he simply ranks dreams and his word: the dream is straw, the word is wheat. Straw is not evil; you just can’t make a meal of it.

So please remember: every vision and every dream must be brought back to the Bible to be tested; every picture must point to Jesus.

sections.heading: What the 321 Vision Says Here: Don’t Pursue Experiences — Pursue God’s Heart.
sections.html:
This is exactly the change of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. Pursuing experiences is earthly and temporary, because experiences pass and feelings cool; pursuing God’s heart is heavenly and eternal, because God’s will endures for ever.

Brothers and sisters, visions are for seeing God, not for being seen by people. If you have never had a vision or a dream from God, you have not one bit less than anyone else; if you often have visions and dreams, you are not one bit more spiritual than anyone else. True spirituality is this: whatever God says, I obey.

sections.heading: 3. God Speaks Through Angels and Circumstances: He Rules Over All Things
sections.html:
The Bible tells us that God has two other ways of speaking: one comes from heaven, and the other from the paths you and I walk every day.

First, angels.

An angel brought the news to Mary: “The angel said to her, ‘Don’t be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and give birth to a son, and shall name him “Jesus.”’” (Luke 1:30–31)

An angel made the announcement to the shepherds: “The angel said to them, ‘Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people. For there is born to you today, in David’s city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.’” (Luke 2:10–11)

An angel led Peter out of prison: “And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side, and woke him up, saying, ‘Stand up quickly!’ His chains fell off his hands.” (Acts 12:7)

This shows us that God can send angels to deliver his word. In both Hebrew and Greek the word for “angel” itself means “messenger, one who is sent” (Hebrew malak, Greek angelos). Angels are not objects of worship; angels are couriers carrying a message. Hebrews puts it very plainly: “Aren’t they all serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14)

Notice two important boundaries in this verse. First, angels are “serving spirits”: they serve God and they do service for us, so the one we worship is always God, never angels. Second, the angels’ work is to be “sent out”: they don’t act on their own initiative; they faithfully deliver the word of the One who sent them.

Next, circumstances.

God also speaks through circumstances. Abraham took Isaac up Mount Moriah; the knife was already raised, and “Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and saw that behind him was a ram caught in the thicket by his horns. Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering instead of his son.” (Genesis 22:13) That ram was God speaking. So Abraham named the place “Yahweh Will Provide” (Genesis 22:14).

Lot lived in Sodom and couldn’t bear to leave. “But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand, his wife’s hand, and his two daughters’ hands, Yahweh being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city.” (Genesis 19:16) Those hands that took hold of him were God speaking.

Brothers and sisters, sometimes the things that happen to you are God speaking.

A door that closes, an interview that fails, a sudden illness, a phone call from someone you haven’t heard from in ages, a stranger’s chance remark — God rules over all things, and he can speak through all things. Paul says, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28)

C. S. Lewis is generally credited with writing these words in The Problem of Pain: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains; pain is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world. What makes the saying so profound is that it names a fact: it isn’t that God’s volume is too low; it’s that our ears are too hard.

But here we must be especially careful.

Not every circumstance is God’s guidance. Things going smoothly does not necessarily mean God has given permission, and obstacles do not necessarily mean God has forbidden something. When Jonah fled towards Tarshish there happened to be a ship in the harbour, and he happened to be able to afford the fare — everything went smoothly. But that wasn’t God’s guidance; it was the road he had chosen for himself (Jonah 1:3). When Paul was thrown into prison in Philippi, nothing went smoothly — yet it was God’s plan to bring the jailer and his household to salvation (Acts 16).

So circumstances need to be brought back to the Holy Spirit and the truth to be discerned. Circumstances are God’s megaphone, not God’s standard; the Bible alone is the standard.

Psychology also reminds us that human beings are born pattern-spotters. The brain looks for regularities in noise, a tendency psychology calls illusory correlation, first proposed and demonstrated experimentally in 1967 by the American psychologist Loren Chapman: people link two events that are in fact unrelated into cause and effect in their memory. So when we already want to do something, every green light on the way gets read as God’s permission.

sections.heading: What the 321 Vision Says Here: God Rules Over Circumstances, but Don’t Let Circumstances Carry You Along; Let the Holy Spirit Lead You in Reading Them.
sections.html:
This too is the practice of the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Circumstances are not a fourth foundation; circumstances are material that needs to be interpreted. Who interprets them? The Holy Spirit. With what? The Bible. And once interpreted, to whom do they point? To Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When circumstances become your lord, you start to worry; when Jesus is King, you can rejoice in any circumstance.

sections.heading: 4. How to Discern God’s Voice: Three Important Principles
sections.html:
When it comes to discernment, many people go to one of two extremes.

One extreme is not believing at all that God still speaks today. People like this shut God up inside a closed book; faith becomes a body of knowledge, and prayer becomes a monologue. The other extreme is treating every voice as God’s voice. A thought in the heart, a picture in a dream, a word on the street — everything is “God told me,” until in the end their lives are pulled this way and that by all kinds of voices, and the more they listen, the more confused they become.

God’s heart is neither of these extremes. God’s heart is this — truly to hear, and rightly to discern.

Paul says, “for God is not a God of confusion, but of peace.” (1 Corinthians 14:33) God’s voice will not send you spinning in circles. He will light you up little by little with the light of early morning, not dazzle you with a flash of lightning.

The Bible gives us three very practical confirmations.

(1) The confirmation of Scripture: God’s voice will never contradict the Bible

The first test is the test of truth.

“For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12)

Notice that last phrase: able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. That is exactly what we need most. Our greatest difficulty is not telling God’s voice apart from the devil’s; it is telling God’s voice apart from our own. And God’s word is like a supremely sharp blade that can divide soul from spirit — divide “what I want” from “what God wants.”

The prophet Isaiah puts it even more directly: “Turn to the law and to the covenant! If they don’t speak according to this word, surely there is no morning for them.” (Isaiah 8:20)

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the bedrock of discernment. Every prompting must be brought back to the truth to be tested. If it conflicts with the Bible, it is certainly not God. No need to pray about it for three more days, no need to ask three more people — it is certainly not God.

Someone may say, “But my feeling is so strong.” A strong feeling does not mean it comes from God. Fear can make a feeling strong; desire can make a feeling strong; long-held grievance can make a feeling strong. When the devil tempted Jesus, he quoted the Psalms too (Matthew 4:6). Scripture can be quoted, and it can also be twisted, so we must not look at one verse alone; we must interpret Scripture by Scripture and look at the consistent witness of the whole Bible.

Here is a very practical checklist, all drawn from the Bible: Does this voice lift up Jesus (Revelation 19:10)? Does it bring edification, exhortation and consolation (1 Corinthians 14:3)? Does it bear the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23)? Does it make me more humble, more obedient, more loving?

Jesus said, “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak.” (John 16:13) The Holy Spirit and the Bible always agree, because the Bible was inspired by the Holy Spirit in the first place. The Holy Spirit will not overturn the book he himself wrote.

This is the second of the 321 Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard. A standard is not a reference; a standard is a measuring rod. When the measuring rod and my feelings disagree, it is the feelings that must be adjusted, not the rod.

(2) The confirmation of the body: if God is speaking to the church, he won’t let only one person know

The second test is the test of community.

Paul says, “At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.” (2 Corinthians 13:1) The saying is originally a principle of the Law, quoted from Deuteronomy 19:15, and Paul applies it to the church’s judgements. From the very beginning God set up a safety mechanism: important matters are not decided by one person alone.

The church at Antioch is the finest example: “As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.’” (Acts 13:2) Notice that when the Holy Spirit spoke, it was a group of people serving and fasting together. The call that sent Paul out was not announced by Paul himself; the whole church received it together, laid hands on them together and sent them off together.

The Council of Jerusalem was the same. Faced with the problem of the Gentile believers, the apostles and elders gathered to debate, to listen and to search the Scriptures, and finally said, “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things.” (Acts 15:28) “The Holy Spirit, and to us” — what a beautiful phrase. The Holy Spirit’s guidance is confirmed within a united community.

So please remember: what truly comes from God brings unity, not division.

When a “word you’ve received” makes you start to look down on the church, drift away from your spiritual companions and feel that only you understand God, that voice is already wrong in itself. Satan’s work has always been first to separate the sheep from the flock, and then to devour them one by one.

But the confirmation of the body also takes wisdom. There are two misuses to avoid here.

The first misuse is “making up the numbers.” Some people go round asking everyone until someone says “Amen.” That isn’t confirmation; that’s looking for allies.

The second misuse is “group pressure.” In 1951 the American psychologist Solomon Asch carried out his famous line-judgement experiment: when everyone else in the room deliberately gave an obviously wrong answer, about a third of the participants’ answers in the critical rounds went along with the majority and got it wrong too. The experiment reminds us that the group is not necessarily the truth; a group that has lost the standard of truth can go wrong together.

So the precondition for the confirmation of the body is this — the people in question must be people living in the truth. This is exactly what 321 calls the 235 relationships: become a “2” with someone selfless, a spiritual companion; nurture one another in the “3” relationships of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and stand together as spiritual comrades in the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team. When you have people like that around you, your discernment is no longer a lone battle.

Brothers and sisters, people matter more than tasks. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Someone without relationships has no confirmation; someone without confirmation easily goes astray.

(3) The confirmation of time: what God says will surely come to pass

The third test is the test of time.

“So is my word that goes out of my mouth: it will not return to me void, but it will accomplish that which I please, and it will prosper in the thing I sent it to do.” (Isaiah 55:11)

What God says will surely come to pass. That is God’s nature, and it is his faithfulness. So time will prove everything.

Moses gave Israel this standard in the Law long ago: “When a prophet speaks in Yahweh’s name, if the thing doesn’t follow, nor happen, that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken. The prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You shall not be afraid of him.” (Deuteronomy 18:22)

Brothers and sisters, time is the most honest of sieves.

But the confirmation of time calls for two attitudes.

The first is waiting. God’s promises often have a “gestation period.” Joseph had his two dreams at seventeen and stood before Pharaoh only at thirty — with thirteen years of pit, slavery and prison in between (Genesis 37:2; 41:46). The books of Samuel tell us that after David was anointed, years of life as a fugitive passed before he took the throne. God’s word had not failed; it was simply still on its way. So don’t hurry to dismiss something just because you haven’t seen it yet; and don’t take matters into your own hands to make it happen just because the wait has been long.

The second is humility. If what you received doesn’t come to pass, you need to adjust humbly. This is the hurdle many people find hardest to get over. Once someone has publicly announced “God told me,” it is very hard to admit they heard wrong. So some begin to revise what they said, to explain it away, to blame others for not having enough faith.

sections.heading: What the 321 Vision Says Here, and It Cuts to the Heart: The Humble Will Correct Themselves; the Proud Will Dig In.
sections.html:
Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — wanting to take God’s place. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When I say, “I definitely didn’t hear wrong,” I put myself in God’s place; when I say, “Lord, perhaps I heard wrong — please teach me again,” I return to man’s originally intended position.

Scripture says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) Someone willing to admit they heard wrong will hear more accurately next time; someone who refuses ever to admit a mistake will drift further off the more they listen. For pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Brothers and sisters, hearing wrong is not the frightening thing; refusing to correct it is. These three confirmations — the confirmation of Scripture, the confirmation of the body, the confirmation of time — are like a tripod: take away one leg and it falls. With all three legs in place, our hearts can stand firm, neither closed nor confused.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Only Selfless Ears Can Hear God’s Voice
sections.html:
When we set this lesson back into the whole picture of 321, we see it more clearly still.

First, the Three Foundations are precisely the three coordinates of discernment. Jesus is my role model — so every voice must point to Jesus, and anything that does not lift up Jesus calls for us to stop. The Bible is my standard — so every prompting must pass the test of truth. The Holy Spirit is my guide — so we don’t rely on our own cleverness to guess, but on the Holy Spirit to receive. When the Three Foundations are steady, the ears are steady.

Second, the Two Core Values are precisely the direction we take after we have heard. Let Jesus be King — God speaks to me not to satisfy my curiosity but so that he may take the throne in every corner of my life. Let Jesus receive all the glory — so when God speaks a word through me that builds someone up, the glory goes to him, not to me. Someone who pockets the glory for himself will soon stop hearing.

Third, the Goal is to establish God’s system. God has never spoken in order to create stars, but in order to build up the body. He entrusts his heart to people so that people will be connected to one another, confirm one another and walk together in his will, fulfilling what the Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

Fourth, the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Self-centred ears mostly hear themselves; only selfless ears can hear God. Selflessness is not wiping yourself out, not becoming someone with no thoughts of your own; selflessness is “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). When “I” stop hogging the microphone, God’s voice naturally becomes clear.

Fifth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. What this lesson must change first is our mindset — so God really does speak; so God speaks in all kinds of ways; so after hearing, we must discern. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Many people want to change their ministry directly but refuse to change their mindset first, and so however large their ministry grows, inside they are still the old self.

Sixth, a change of perspective. From man’s perspective to God’s: I no longer ask, “What’s in this for me?” I ask, “Lord, what do you want to say?” From the earthly to the heavenly: I no longer see only the difficulty in front of me; I see the One on the throne. From the temporary to the eternal: I am no longer swept away by passing emotions; I care about the will that lasts for ever. From the worldly to the godly: I no longer measure God’s guidance by the world’s idea of success.

Seventh, the 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. When I live out the selfless “0”, the ninefold fruit of the Spirit grows between me and that person: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, this is in fact the best discernment tool of all. Something truly received from God will make me more loving, more patient and gentler towards my “2”; if a “word I’ve received” makes me harsher, more judgemental or more impatient with people, then I need to be careful.

Eighth, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. First let the Holy Spirit guide (Spirit), then come to understanding through the Bible (Understanding), then live out the life of Jesus (Life), then let Jesus be King in our service (Service), and at last give all the glory to God (God). Hearing God’s voice is only the starting point of this road; walking the whole road is the purpose of God’s speaking.

Brothers and sisters, rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart, and you rejoice; rely on the brain, and you worry. God has never wanted us to become spiritual detectives who take everything apart to analyse it; he wants us to be his children, lying quietly at his feet and saying, like Samuel, “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10)

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared three practices for us. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into effect one by one.

Practice 1: Build the habit of discernment; don’t rush to conclusions

When you have a prompting, a dream or something you believe you’ve received, don’t rush to decide that it’s God. First bring it before God in prayer and test it against the Bible, and slowly cultivate spiritual sensitivity.

Information: today you have already received the information — God speaks in all kinds of ways, but everything must be brought back to the Bible to be tested.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn this information into light within you, so that you really see: “I often take my own voice for God’s voice.”

Conviction: acknowledge from your heart that the Bible’s authority is higher than my feelings. This step is a surrender of the will, not an agreement of the brain.

Implementation: from today, keep a “listening notebook.” Record promptings, dreams, verses and confirmations in separate columns, with dates. Don’t reach a conclusion straight away; leave it for seven days. During those seven days do only two things: pray, and study the Bible.

Evaluation: after seven days, look back. Does this word lift up Jesus? Does it agree with Scripture? Does it bring peace or panic? Does it bear the fruit of the Spirit?

Correction: if you find it was your own idea, write honestly in your notebook, “This one was mine.” That single line will help you hear more accurately next time.

Repetition: set a regular time each week to review your notebook. Discernment is not a gift; it is a habit formed by training. Hebrews says that mature people are those “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14). In the original, “exercised” carries the sense of an athlete’s long training.

Multiplication: teach your method to a brother or sister and do the seven days alongside them. Only what you have taught becomes truly yours.

Practice 2: Learn to confirm God’s leading in community

Bring the important things you believe you’ve received to your spiritual companions or to the church for fellowship, and let the body discern together, so that you don’t slip into mere personal subjectivity but walk on the road of unity.

Information: God has established the witness of two or three as the standard of confirmation (2 Corinthians 13:1).

Revelation: let the Holy Spirit shine his light on you — have you been fighting on your own all along? Do you only go to people who will agree with you?

Conviction: admit that I need the body. Admit that on my own I have blind spots. This is the first step of humility.

Implementation: find your “2” — a selfless spiritual companion who loves the Lord and is willing to tell the truth. This week, bring to them one matter you are hesitating over — not to get their agreement, but to pray and test it together.

Evaluation: after you have talked it through, notice your own reaction. When they offered a different view, were you grateful or defensive? A defensive reaction is very often a sign that “self” is still there.

Correction: if you find you were only looking for approval, confess it to God and put the decision back into God’s hands.

Repetition: make this kind of fellowship a regular rhythm, at least once a month. Let the 235 relationships be truly established in your life.

Multiplication: once you have experienced the blessing of the body’s confirmation, go and be a confirmer for someone else. Be a spiritual companion who is willing to listen, willing to pray and willing to tell the truth.

Practice 3: Turn what you receive into obedient action

Don’t stop at “discerning”; go on into “doing.” Once you are sure it comes from God, step out boldly and let God’s word be fulfilled in your life.

Information: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you what is actually holding you back from obeying — is it fear? Face? Something you can’t bear to let go?

Conviction: say to the Lord from your heart: whatever you say, I am willing to obey.

Implementation: this week choose just one act of obedience — the smallest, most concrete one, one you can complete within seven days. Make that phone call, say that sorry, give that gift, begin those fifteen minutes a day of drawing near to God. Obedience never starts with the big things.

Evaluation: once you have done it, write down what God did and what changed in your heart.

Correction: if you find yourself putting it off, face honestly the fear behind the delay and hand it to the Lord.

Repetition: let “hear it, then do it” become your reflex. Every act of obedience deepens your familiarity with God’s voice.

Multiplication: tell the story of your obedience to someone who needs courage. Your testimony will become their strength.

Brothers and sisters, please remember: hearing is grace, discerning is responsibility, obeying is fruit. God will not entrust more of his words to someone who refuses to act on them.

A Gentle Reminder

God speaks in many ways, but there is only one truth.

God’s voice is neither confused nor contradictory.

God’s voice brings life, peace and unity.

So don’t limit God — don’t say, “God wouldn’t do that today”; and don’t jump to conclusions either — don’t say, “This is definitely God.” Between the two runs a narrow road, and the name of that road is humility.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Jesus Is Always the Focal Point
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

God speaks in endlessly varied ways, but his heart has only one aim — to bring you back into his will.

Elijah waited for God at the mouth of the cave on Mount Horeb. Scripture records that a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke the rocks in pieces before him, but Yahweh was not in the wind; after the wind an earthquake, but Yahweh was not in the earthquake; after the earthquake a fire, but Yahweh was not in the fire; and after the fire, a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–12). Brothers and sisters, of course God has the power to use wind, earthquake and fire, but that day he chose to use a still small voice. Because what he wanted was not to overwhelm, but for you to draw near.

So don’t chase special methods, and don’t exalt spiritual experiences. Jesus is always the focal point.

When you are selfless and humble and rely on the heart, you will discover something wonderful: God is speaking to you everywhere. He speaks in the Bible you open, in your early-morning prayers, in something your child says, at the door you thought was a dead end. Your life will be full of guidance and light.

Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) The sheep can hear because they know the shepherd; the sheep can keep up because they trust the shepherd.

This morning, let’s learn one thing, and only this one thing:

Lord, whatever way you choose, I am willing to listen, and willing to obey.

Let Jesus be King over our ears, let Jesus be King over our decisions, let Jesus be King over our obedience. May all the glory be his.

keyVerses: “knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:20–21)

“God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, let us stand together and declare to the Lord:

Lord Jesus, I believe you are a God who speaks. You are still speaking to me today. I will listen with my heart rather than analyse with my brain. Holy Spirit, guide me to discern, so that I neither stray nor fall into confusion. I will be someone who hears clearly, discerns rightly and walks accurately. Whatever you say, I am willing to obey. In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare it. Amen!
practices: Build the habit of discernment; don’t rush to conclusions
Learn to confirm God’s leading in community
Turn what you receive into obedient action
prayer: Lord Jesus, I believe you are a God who speaks.
In the past you spoke to the fathers at many times and in various ways; in these last days you have spoken to us by your Son; and today you are still speaking to me.

Forgive me for so often analysing with my brain instead of listening with my heart; forgive me for chasing special experiences while overlooking your ordinary voice; forgive me for taking my own ideas for your will.

Holy Spirit, guide me to discern, so that I neither stray nor fall into confusion. Lord, place the Bible in my heart as my standard, place spiritual companions beside me as confirmation, and keep time in your hands as proof.
I want to be someone who hears clearly, discerns rightly and walks accurately.
Lord, I give you my ears, my heart and my plans. Whatever you say, I am willing to obey.
Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Think back over the past year. In what ways has God spoken to you (the Bible, a sermon, a prompting in prayer, a dream, circumstances, or something a brother or sister said)? How did you discern it at the time? Reflect on “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27), and share whether you “heard” — or whether you “followed.”

Of the three tests — the confirmation of Scripture, the confirmation of the body and the confirmation of time — which do you most often neglect? Reflect on “Don’t quench the Spirit. Don’t despise prophecies. Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21), discuss together how to keep the balance between “not quenching” and “testing all things,” and pray for one another.
l127.title: Hear Clearly, Discern Truly, Walk Surely
l127.subtitle: The Ways God Speaks to People (Part 2)
l127.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: The Signal Kept Coming, but the Receiver Was Switched Off
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let’s begin with something that really happened in history.

Late on the night of 14 April 1912, the surface of the North Atlantic was uncannily calm. Less than twenty nautical miles from the Titanic lay a cargo ship, the Californian. That evening the Californian’s wireless operator, Cyril Evans, sent out ice warnings to the ships around him again and again. When he broke in on the Titanic’s channel one last time to tell them, “We are stopped and surrounded by ice,” the Titanic’s operator, busy sending private telegrams for first-class passengers, snapped back: “Shut up, I am busy.”

Not long afterwards, Evans switched off his set and went to bed.

At 11:40 p.m. the Titanic struck the iceberg. For the next two hours and more, the Titanic’s wireless sent out distress calls frantically — CQD, SOS — over and over again. The signals crossed the dark night and reached the Californian’s aerial. But on that ship, no one was wearing the headphones. The British inquiry into the disaster later left behind a heartbreaking conclusion: that ship was close enough — close enough that, had anyone been listening, many lives could have been saved.

Brothers and sisters, the real tragedy of that night was not that the signal was never sent. It was that the receiver had been switched off.

And that is exactly the spiritual lesson we are going to face together today.

This world is full of voices. The voices of people, the voices of our circumstances, the voices of our emotions, the voices of our own thoughts — and the voices online that never stop, day or night, an endless feed you can scroll forever and never reach the end of. But among all these voices, the one that matters most is the voice of God.

The question is this: when God speaks, are we sure to hear him?

The Bible gives us a very sobering answer. Isaiah 6:9 records what Yahweh said to the prophet: “He said, ‘Go, and tell this people, “You hear indeed, but don’t understand. You see indeed, but don’t perceive.”’”

This is a spiritual crisis: some people have ears and yet cannot hear; some have eyes and yet cannot see.

Why?

Because hearing God’s voice has never been an outward ability. It is a condition of the inner life.

Proverbs 20:12 says, “The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, Yahweh has made even both of them.”

To be able to hear is grace; to be able to understand is blessing. God made our ears, and he made our hearts too. But the key is this: are you ready to listen by relying on the heart?

Today the Lord Jesus himself is going to lead us into one of the parables he told. In this parable there is the same sower, the same handful of seed, the same morning — and yet four completely different outcomes. The difference is not in the seed, and not in the sower. It is in the soil.

Brothers and sisters, that soil is your heart.

This morning, may we not simply listen to one more message, but let the Lord’s plough turn over the ground in our hearts that needs turning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Teacher Seated in a Boat, a Field by the Sea
sections.html: To truly understand this parable, we first need to stand where Jesus stood that day and look at the scene in front of him.

sections.heading: 1. Author and Audience
sections.html:
Church history consistently identifies the author of Matthew’s Gospel as the apostle Matthew — Levi, the tax collector whom the Lord called (Matthew 9:9). It is generally dated to the AD 60s, and no later than around AD 70, when Jerusalem was destroyed. Matthew wrote first and foremost for Christians of Jewish background. That is why the whole book quotes the Old Testament so heavily and keeps repeating, “This was to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet.” His aim was to prove that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the King of the Kingdom of Heaven.

Matthew’s Gospel has a very clear structure: the whole book is built around five great discourses of Jesus. The first is the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7); the second is the teaching on sending out the Twelve (chapter 10); the third is the one we are reading today, the parables of the Kingdom (chapter 13); the fourth is the teaching on life in the church (chapter 18); and the fifth is the discourse on the end times (chapters 24–25).

sections.heading: 2. Historical Setting: The Turning Point of the Parables
sections.html:
Matthew 13 does not appear out of nowhere. It follows straight on from chapter 12. Chapter 12 records the Pharisees accusing Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons — a public, formal and hostile rejection. From that moment on, Jesus’ way of teaching changed: he began to speak in parables.

The disciples found this strange and came to ask him why. Jesus answered, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is not given to them” (Matthew 13:11). Then he quoted Isaiah 6:9–10, saying, “for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again; and I would heal them” (Matthew 13:15).

Brothers and sisters, please notice: a parable is a double-edged sword. To those willing to listen, a parable is revelation — it lays the mysteries of the Kingdom open before them, vivid and alive. To those unwilling to listen, a parable is a veil — they hear it and move on, as if it were just a story about a farmer.

The same words: some hear the Kingdom of Heaven in them, others hear only a story. Where is the difference? In the heart.

sections.heading: 3. Geographical Setting: A Pulpit in a Boat
sections.html:
Matthew 13:1–2 says, “On that day Jesus went out of the house, and sat by the seaside. Great multitudes gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat, and sat, and all the multitude stood on the beach.”

This is the north-western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Along that stretch there is a natural, half-moon-shaped little bay, which later came to be called the “Cove of the Sower”. Researchers in acoustics have taken measurements there and found that when someone speaks from the surface of the water, the sound reflects off the water and the slope of the hillside, so that several thousand people on the shore can hear clearly. The Lord Jesus chose the best amplifier there was — he wanted people to hear.

And as he looked up at the hillside above the shore, he may well have seen a farmer out in the field sowing seed. Pointing to the scene before him, he said, “Behold, a farmer went out to sow” (Matthew 13:3).

sections.heading: 4. Farming Background: Sow First, Plough Afterwards
sections.html:
This point is vital, or else we’ll think this farmer rather foolish — how could he throw seed onto the path, onto the rocks, into the thorns?

In first-century Palestine, the farmer’s method was “sow first, plough afterwards”. With a bag of seed on his back, he scattered it evenly across the whole field, and only then brought the ox to draw the plough and turn the seed into the soil. So as he sowed, seed naturally fell on the little path that cut across the field, on the places where the thin soil lay over a bed of limestone, and in the corners where last year’s thorn roots were still buried in the ground.

The farmer showed no favouritism. The sower sowed fairly and generously.

Brothers and sisters, this is a perfect picture of the gospel. God is never stingy with his word. His word comes to the rich and to the poor, to the old and to the young, to those who have believed in the Lord for thirty years and to those opening the Bible for the very first time today.

Luke 8:11 says it plainly: “Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.”

The seed is equally good; the sower is equally generous; and yet there are four outcomes. There is only one reason: the soil is different.

So on the surface this parable is “the parable of the sower”, but at its core it is “the parable of the hearer”. What it asks us is not “Did you listen?” but what Jesus said in Mark 4:24: “He said to them, ‘Take heed what you hear.’” In Luke 8:18 the Lord puts it even more directly: “Be careful therefore how you hear.”

Not “what you hear”, but “how you hear”.

Now let’s walk through it, one patch of soil at a time.

sections.heading: 1. The Roadside Heart: Unwilling to Listen, Unable to Hear
sections.html:
1. The Text: The Seed That Was Snatched Away

Jesus said, “When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside” (Matthew 13:19).

Notice the three actions in this verse: hearing, not understanding, being snatched away.

2. Light from the Original: What “Understand” Means

The word “understand” is the Greek syniēmi, which literally means “to put together”, “to bring scattered pieces together into one”. It describes not the receiving of information but the connecting of insight — God’s word lining up with my life, being joined to it, the current switched on.

In other words, a person can take in every word of a message through his ears and write it all down in neat notes, yet never once syniēmi — because those words have never been wired into his life.

And the word for “roadside”, hodos, simply means “road” or “way”: the footpath along the edge of the field, worn down by people walking.

3. Why Is the Roadside Hard?

No path is born hard. A path is trodden into being.

That strip of earth at the edge of the field was originally the very same soil as the field itself. But because countless feet walked over it time after time, year after year, it was packed down and trampled hard, until it became a path that not even a seed could get into.

Brothers and sisters, our hearts are trampled hard in just the same way. Trampled hard by what?

By habit — we’ve heard the same verses so many times that we no longer feel anything. By prejudice — “I already know that,” and so God can’t get a new word in. By hurt — someone once wounded us, so we laid a coat of tarmac over our hearts, and from then on no one could get in, not even God. By busyness — too many footsteps, too fast, too crowded, and the soil never gets a chance to loosen.

The Bible uses a very weighty expression to describe a heart like this: “stiff-necked”.

Exodus 32:9: “Yahweh said to Moses, ‘I have seen these people, and behold, they are a stiff-necked people.’”

The Hebrew is qāshēh ’ōrep, literally “hard of neck”. It is a farmer’s expression. A farmer yokes his ox to plough the field; a light pull on the reins, and the ox should turn. But there is a kind of ox whose neck is rigid: however you pull, it simply will not turn. What a farmer dreads most is not a lazy ox but a stiff-necked one — because it will not be led.

To be stiff-necked is to insist on our own ideas and refuse to submit to God.

4. Pride: The Greatest Obstacle to Hearing God

The prophet Jeremiah could not have put it more clearly: “Hear, and give ear. Don’t be proud, for Yahweh has spoken” (Jeremiah 13:15).

Look at the order of this verse: first “hear”, then “give ear”, and then, straight away — “don’t be proud”.

Why, while speaking about hearing the word, does he suddenly turn to pride? Because in God’s eyes they are really one and the same thing. The proud cannot hear.

The Hebrew root for “pride”, gā’āh, originally means “to rise up, to swell” — like floodwaters rising, like a person propping himself up higher. Someone who has raised himself up cannot hear the voice that comes from above, because he feels he is already up there.

James 4:6 says, “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’”

Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that God doesn’t speak to the proud; it’s that God himself resists them. How serious that is.

5. A Picture: Seed on Concrete

God’s word is like seed; a proud heart is like a concrete floor.

However good the seed, however plump, however full of life, if it’s scattered on concrete it can only lie on the surface, baking in the sun. Nothing is wrong with the seed; there’s simply no crack in the ground.

And what happens to seed lying on concrete? The sparrows come and peck it up in one bite.

Jesus said, “The evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart.” The easiest work Satan ever does is his work in a hardened heart. He doesn’t need to argue, doesn’t need to attack, doesn’t need to tempt — he only needs to wait. Wait until the meeting ends, until the person is driving home, scrolling on the phone — and within thirty minutes that seed is gone.

6. Psychology Bears Witness: Our Brains Are Built to “Not Hear” Selectively

In 1953 the British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry published his famous study of the “cocktail party effect” in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America. He had subjects hear different messages in each ear at the same time while attending to only one of them. He found that, of the ignored ear, subjects could not even say what language the message had been in. The sound had plainly entered their ears, but it had never entered their awareness.

In 1999 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris of Harvard published the even more famous “invisible gorilla” experiment in the journal Perception. Subjects were asked to count the number of passes in a basketball game, and about half of them completely failed to see a person in a gorilla suit walk right through the middle of the scene, beat their chest and leave. This is called “inattentional blindness”.

Then there is the theory of “cognitive dissonance”, put forward by Leon Festinger in 1957: when new information clashes with a position we already hold, people often don’t revise the position — they reject the information, because changing position hurts too much.

Brothers and sisters, science tells us something entirely in keeping with the Bible: when people “can’t hear”, it is often not because their ears are broken, but because their hearts are already occupied with another focus, another position, another insistence.

That isn’t an excuse. It’s a warning.

7. A 321 Insight: Pride Holds On to Self; Humility Opens Up the Self

Pride is holding on to “self”; humility is opening up the self.

This is precisely the very heart of the 321 vision: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem.

What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. When I say to God’s word, “I don’t agree,” I have in fact taken the judge’s seat and put God in the dock. That is leaving our originally intended position.

What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Brothers and sisters, only selflessness can hear God. For the heart of a self-centred person is already filled with self; there’s no room left for God’s word.

The Lord Jesus himself is our role model. Philippians 2:8 says, “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” The One with the most authority in the universe chose the lowest place. This is what “Jesus is my role model” means.

8. One Thing You Can Do Today

If you find that your heart has been trodden into a path, what should you do?

Hosea 10:12 gives the answer: “Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.”

“Break up your fallow ground” — the sense of the original is “break open hard ground that has long lain unworked”. The plough hurts. But if you won’t let the plough go in, the seed will never go in either.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, are you willing to say to the Lord: “Lord, I won’t insist on my own ideas. Please break open the hard ground in my heart”?

sections.heading: 2. The Shallow Heart: Unwilling to Act, Unable to Understand
sections.html:
1. The Text: The Fastest to Grow, the Fastest to Wither

Jesus said, “What was sown on the rocky places, this is he who hears the word, and immediately with joy receives it; yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he stumbles” (Matthew 13:20–21).

Notice the two contrasts: “immediately with joy receives it” set against “immediately he stumbles”.

The same person, the same heart. As fast as it sprouts, so fast it withers.

2. Original Language and Geography: Rocky Ground Isn’t Ground Full of Rocks

The “rocky places” here, Greek petrōdē, does not mean a field strewn with loose stones. It means a whole shelf of limestone bedrock with only a thin layer of soil over it. Ground like this is everywhere in the hills of Galilee.

This kind of ground has one peculiarity: the thin soil is quickly warmed by the sun, quickly heated, so seed sprouts there faster and more vigorously than anywhere else. From the outside, this is the most beautiful patch in the whole field.

But when the roots push downwards, they hit bedrock and can go no further. So the roots can only spread sideways, tangling shallowly.

Once the sun comes up and the moisture evaporates, it is the first thing in the whole field to wither.

Brothers and sisters, the most dangerous thing in the spiritual life is often not coldness, but “warming up fast with no root”.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Roots Go Down as We Do the Word

“Root” is the Greek rhiza. The Bible uses it again and again to describe the depth of a life.

Colossians 2:6–7 says, “As therefore you received Christ Jesus, the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.”

Notice the order: “walk in him” comes first, “rooted and built up” comes after. Roots aren’t grown by sitting and listening; they’re grown by walking.

Jeremiah 17:8 describes the one who trusts in Yahweh: “For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.”

The same heat, the same drought. Where there are roots, the leaves stay green; where there are none, it withers at once. The difference isn’t the weather. It’s the roots.

The Lord Jesus himself used the picture of a house: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock” (Matthew 7:24–25).

Hearing and doing is a foundation; hearing and not doing is empty talk.

James puts it even more bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). He goes on to describe such a person: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was” (James 1:23–24).

He studies himself in the mirror very carefully, then turns round and forgets what he looks like. Brothers and sisters, does that picture feel a little familiar?

4. A Picture: Rain and Roots

Hearing the word is like rain; obeying it is like putting down roots.

When a good rain falls on ground with no roots, the water just runs off, carrying away the topsoil and leaving the ground thinner than before. When a good rain falls beside a tree with roots, every drop goes downwards — into the roots, into the growth rings, and becomes next year’s fruit.

Without roots, no amount of water helps; in fact, the more water there is, the thinner the soil becomes.

This also explains something: why do some brothers and sisters hear sermons for thirty years, and yet their lives seem to stay exactly where they were? It isn’t that they haven’t heard enough. It’s that they haven’t done enough.

5. Evidence from Science and Psychology: Knowing Is a Long Way from Doing

First, the forgetting curve. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus experimented on memory with himself as the subject. He found that if what we learn is not reviewed, forgetting is sharpest in the earliest stretch of time, and after one day often only about a third remains. Hearing the word is just the same: moved to tears on Sunday morning, and by Monday lunchtime you can’t remember what the sermon was about. Unless — you put it into practice.

Second, the gap between intention and action. In a meta-analytic review published in 2002, the psychologist Paschal Sheeran showed that people’s “behavioural intentions” account, on average, for only about 28 per cent of the variation in their actual behaviour. In other words, between someone sincerely “intending” to do something and actually doing it, there is still a long distance. Being moved is not the same as being changed.

Third, neuroplasticity. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed the famous Hebb’s rule, which later generations often summarise in one line: “Neurons that fire together, wire together.” Repeated behaviour strengthens neural pathways, so that they run more and more smoothly. It’s the same in the spiritual life: obey once, and it is easier to obey a second time; hear once, and it is easier to hear a second time.

Brothers and sisters, this confirms an old saying: we don’t become clear first and then obey; we obey first and then become clear.

6. A Word of Warning

In “The Cost of Discipleship” the twentieth-century German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a well-known warning: cheap grace is the deadly enemy of the church. What he called “cheap grace” is wanting grace without following, wanting forgiveness without repentance, wanting to hear the word without doing it.

And 1 Samuel 15:22 said the same thing three thousand years ago: “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.’”

7. A 321 Insight: Those Who Rely on the Heart Obey; Those Who Rely on the Brain Only Analyse

sections.heading: The 321 vision puts it well: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and find joy, rely on the brain and find worry.
sections.html:
When people who rely on the brain hear God’s word, their first reaction is: “Is this reasonable?” “Can it be done?” “What will others think?” By the time the analysis is over, the moment has passed and the stirring has faded.

When people who rely on the heart hear God’s word, their first reaction is: “Lord, I’m willing.”

Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The fruit of a whole life flows out of the heart, not out of the brain.

The 321 vision speaks of a “fivefold change”: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. And for a mindset to become life, the bridge in between is called “Implementation”.

If we hear but do not put it into practice, the fivefold change stalls at the first stage and never gets any further.

Obey once, and you see a little more clearly. Brothers and sisters, that is a law of the spiritual world.

sections.heading: 3. The Thorny Heart: Crowded Out, Unable to Hear Clearly
sections.html:
1. The Text: It Grew Up, but Bore Nothing

Jesus said, “What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful” (Matthew 13:22).

This kind of soil is actually good soil. It has depth, it has nutrients; the seed really did sprout, really did grow up.

The problem is this: it doesn’t grow only God’s word. At the same time, it grows thorns.

2. Light from the Original: “Choke” Means Strangle

The word “choke” is the Greek sympnigō, made up of “together with” plus “to squeeze tight, to suffocate”. The same word is used in Luke 8:33 to describe the herd of pigs rushing down the steep bank and being “drowned”.

This is a violent word. The thorns don’t defeat God’s word; they strangle it. They don’t need to cut it down or pull it up. They only need to wind themselves around it day after day, stealing its sunlight, stealing its water, stealing its nourishment — and the wheat withers all by itself.

Mark’s Gospel lists the thorns more fully: “and the cares of this age, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful” (Mark 4:19).

Cares, riches, desires — three thorns.

3. Where Thorns Come From: Nobody Plants Them; They Grow on Their Own

In Genesis 3:18 God said to Adam, “It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.”

Brothers and sisters, please notice something: thorns are a product of the fall — and nobody needs to plant thorns.

Wheat has to be sown, watered and tended; thorns only need you to leave them alone, and they grow fast and strong.

This is why the spiritual life needs to be intentional. You don’t have to try to become worldly. Just do nothing at all, and the world will grow over your whole heart by itself.

The Lord Jesus said, “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

The thorny heart is not a heart that doesn’t love God. It’s a heart in which too many things matter as much as God — or even more than God.

4. The Classic Example: The Rich Young Ruler

In Matthew 19 a young man ran up to Jesus and asked a good question: “What good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”

He had zeal, he had morals, he had wealth, he had a future. Mark’s Gospel even records that Jesus, “looking at him loved him”.

Then the Lord spoke: “Jesus said to him, ‘If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’” (Matthew 19:21).

He heard it. He heard the voice of God clearly and unmistakably.

And the result?

“But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions” (Matthew 19:22).

Brothers and sisters, this is one of the most heartbreaking verses in all the Gospels. It wasn’t that he couldn’t hear. It was that he couldn’t let go.

Hearing God’s voice comes at a cost. It isn’t entertainment; it isn’t a spiritual tonic to make us feel good. It is meant to change the direction of our lives.

So sometimes, when we “can’t hear clearly”, it’s really because deep down we already sense what he is going to say — and we aren’t yet ready to pay that price.

5. Psychology and Data: The Truth about Worry, the Limits of Money

First, worry. In 2020 Lucas LaFreniere and Michelle Newman of Penn State University published a study in the journal Behavior Therapy. They asked people with generalised anxiety disorder to write down each worry they had every day, and then tracked what actually happened. They found that about 91.4 per cent of the things the participants worried about never came to pass.

We give a great deal of our life’s soil, sunlight and nourishment to feeding a patch of thorns, 91 per cent of which never bear anything at all.

The Lord Jesus said it long ago: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient” (Matthew 6:34).

Second, money. In 2010 the Nobel laureate in economics Daniel Kahneman and the economist Angus Deaton published a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Analysing some 450,000 survey responses in the United States, they found that higher income does improve day-to-day emotional well-being, but that beyond a certain level the improvement levels off. Later studies have differed over this “turning point” and revised it, but on one thing they agree: the happiness money can buy has a ceiling.

The peace God gives has no ceiling.

Third, distraction. In 2017 Adrian Ward and three colleagues published an intriguing experiment in the Journal of the Association for Consumer Research: simply having your own phone on the desk — even face down, even switched off — lowered subjects’ performance on cognitive tests. The researchers called it “brain drain”.

Brothers and sisters, that phone didn’t even ring. It was just “there”. Thorns are like that too. They don’t need to say a word; they only need to occupy a seat in your heart, and they can choke God’s word.

6. A Picture: The Pruning Hand

In John 15:2 the Lord says, “Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.”

Vineyard workers know one thing better than anyone: an unpruned vine grows a beautiful canopy of leaves but produces only a few bunches of grapes, because all its strength has gone into “growing leaves”.

Pruning hurts, because what gets cut away is often not a bad thing but a “good thing” — it simply stands in the way of the “better thing”.

God prunes us not because he doesn’t care what we lose, but because he cares too much to lose us — he cannot bear to see us busy all our lives and then come before the Lord empty-handed.

7. A 321 Insight: It Isn’t That God Isn’t Speaking; It’s That We Won’t Let Go

The 321 vision says that the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions.

The thorny heart turns that order upside down: tasks first, then possessions, and only then does God get his turn.

The 321 vision also says our perspective must shift — from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly.

The rich young ruler used an earthly abacus and a short-term view. The conclusion he reached was “too expensive”. Had he done the sums once with an eternal view, he would have discovered that this was the one deal in his whole life that could never lose.

Only selflessness can keep us from being choked by the world. For selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Only when we put down what fills our two hands can we catch the fullness God wants to give.

sections.heading: 4. The Good-Soil Heart: Those Who Truly Hear
sections.html:
1. The Text: Thirty, Sixty, a Hundredfold

Jesus said, “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty” (Matthew 13:23).

Luke’s account adds two very important words: “Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance” (Luke 8:15).

“Hold it tightly” and “perseverance”. Good soil doesn’t appear overnight.

2. True “Hearing” Has Three Levels

What does it mean to truly hear?

It isn’t hearing with the ears, and it isn’t being emotionally moved. It has three levels:

First, hearing (akouō) — the message comes in.

Second, understanding (syniēmi) — the message is wired into life.

Third, obeying and bearing fruit (karpophoreō) — life produces fruit.

Many people reach the first level; fewer reach the second; only the third is what the Lord is after.

The Lord Jesus said to his disciples, “But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear” (Matthew 13:16).

Brothers and sisters, being able to hear is a blessing. But that blessing is only truly cashed in at the third level.

3. What a Hundredfold Really Means

Under the farming conditions of first-century Palestine, an ordinary harvest was about seven to ten times what was sown. Thirtyfold was already a good year; sixtyfold, a bumper crop; a hundredfold was a figure farmers of that age wouldn’t have dared dream of.

It appears once in the Bible: “Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him” (Genesis 26:12) — and that year was a year of famine.

Here the Lord Jesus is telling us that a heart of good soil will bear fruit beyond human common sense. Because that isn’t agriculture; that’s a miracle.

Notice too that the Lord didn’t demand that every patch of good soil yield a hundredfold. Thirtyfold is good soil too; sixtyfold is good soil too. God doesn’t measure you by someone else’s multiple; he measures you by your own soil. As long as you are good soil, you will surely bear fruit.

4. Good Soil Isn’t Born; It’s Cultivated

This is the most hope-filled line in the whole parable.

Brothers and sisters, if the four soils were fixed from birth, this parable would be a verdict, not good news. But thank God — the roadside can be ploughed open, the stones can be prised out, the thorns can be burned away.

That is why the prophet cries out: “For Yahweh says to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, ‘Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns’” (Jeremiah 4:3).

Good soil is soil that has been turned over, soil cleared of stones, soil rid of thorns. Behind every patch of good soil is the sweat of a farmer.

And that farmer is the Lord himself.

5. A Role Model: The Boy Samuel

In 1 Samuel 3, in an age when “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions,” God called a child. Once, twice, three times he ran the wrong way, until the old priest Eli taught him how to answer.

So that night Scripture recorded a timeless sentence: “Then Samuel said, ‘Speak; for your servant hears’” (1 Samuel 3:10).

Notice the structure of that sentence. It isn’t “Lord, you listen, for your servant is speaking”; it is “Speak; for your servant hears.”

How often our prayers are the former — we talk and talk, and when we’ve finished, we leave, without leaving a single minute for God.

Brothers and sisters, a good-soil heart is a heart that knows how to be still. When Elijah met God at Horeb, Scripture says, “After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12).

God’s voice is often small. Not because God is speaking quietly, but because he wants us to draw near.

6. Science Bears Witness: What Can’t Be Seen Is What Matters

The Natural Resources Conservation Service of the US Department of Agriculture points out that one small teaspoon of healthy soil may contain more microorganisms than there are people on earth. The fertility of soil doesn’t lie in how lovely its surface looks, but in the ecosystem underneath that you can’t see at all.

Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life is the same. God doesn’t look at our surface; he looks at the world beneath that no one else sees — your prayers when you are alone, the obedience nobody knows about, your faithfulness in small things.

That is “good soil”.

In “The Problem of Pain” C. S. Lewis wrote a much-quoted passage: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains; pain is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world.

God is always speaking. It’s just that sometimes he has to turn the volume up to the level at which we’re willing to listen.

7. A 321 Insight: Hearing God Is Not an Ability but a Condition of Life

The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27).

Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “My sheep are very good listeners.” He said, “My sheep hear my voice.” Sheep can hear the shepherd not because their ears are especially good, but because they are sheep — they belong to this shepherd, and they follow this shepherd every day.

This is the core of the 321 vision: hearing God is not a technique. It is an identity, a condition of life.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Jesus is my role model: he said, “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge” (see John 5:30). Even the Son of God, while on earth, was one who “heard first, then acted”.

The Bible is my standard: every voice must be brought before Scripture and checked against it. Hebrews 4:12 says, “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

The Holy Spirit is my guide: Isaiah 30:21 promises, “and when you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’”

When the heart is right, the voice becomes clear.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Four Soils, One Way Forward
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, let’s look at these four soils once more, in the light of 321.

sections.heading: 1. The Four Soils Are Really Four Spiritual Conditions
sections.html:
The roadside heart is a self-centred heart — holding on to its own ideas, with pride blocking out God’s voice.

The shallow heart is a heart that “relies on the brain and not the heart” — moved but not obedient, the fivefold change stuck at the level of mindset.

The thorny heart is a “worldly, temporary” heart — its priorities upside down, tasks bigger than relationships, possessions bigger than God.

The good-soil heart is a selfless heart — laying down self and letting Jesus be King.

sections.heading: 2. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal
sections.html:
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. When these three are firmly in place, our ears have a reference pitch to tune by.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Anyone who truly hears God will end up here in the end — not “God, please listen to my plan,” but “Lord, you be King.”

The Goal: establish God’s system. When God speaks, it is never merely to comfort one person’s feelings; it is to build his Kingdom on earth.

sections.heading: 3. Humility Overcomes Pride; Selflessness Overcomes Satan
sections.html:
In this parable the evil one appears only once — on the hard ground by the roadside.

What does that tell us? The place where Satan most easily gets his way is a proud heart. He hardly has to lift a finger: as long as that person keeps holding on to “self”, he can carry the seed off in his beak.

Conversely, humility is the most powerful weapon in spiritual warfare. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. The moment we say to God, “I’m willing to be adjusted by you,” Satan loses his foothold.

sections.heading: 4. The Fivefold Change: From Mindset to Ministry
sections.html:
A change of mindset: I no longer ask, “Why doesn’t God speak to me?” I begin to ask, “What kind of soil is my heart?”

A change of life: the hard ground is ploughed open, the stones are prised out, the thorns are cleared away.

A change of daily living: I begin to put what I hear into practice straight away, even if it’s only one small step.

A change of relationships: a soft, selfless heart will change my relationships with my spouse, my children and my co-workers.

A change of ministry: thirty, sixty, a hundredfold — the fruit isn’t borne for ourselves; it’s borne for others.
