The wrong cycle goes like this: look at the world, and you think about the world; think about the world, and you live out the world; live out the world, and you want to look at the world all the more. And so each turn carries you further from God.

The right cycle goes like this: look at Jesus, and you think on the truth; think on the truth, and you live out Christ; live out Christ, and you long all the more to look at Jesus. And so each turn makes you more like Jesus.

Paul turned this cycle into a command: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) Notice the order: first we are transformed by the renewing of our mind, and only then can we prove God’s will. To prove it means to discern what God is saying. If you are not renewed, you won’t be able to discern it.

He also says, “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2) And he gives a list: “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)

Brothers and sisters, this list is really a “spiritual viewing guide”. What will you watch and listen to this morning? Run it through these eight descriptions, and it will become clear.

Brain science also confirms how real this cycle is. Ann Graybiel, a neuroscientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has spent many years studying the basal ganglia and has shown that habits are stored by the brain as “loops”: a cue triggers a chain of behaviour, the behaviour brings a reward, and the reward strengthens the loop. Once formed, it runs with almost no willpower. That’s why your finger opens that app without your ever deciding to; and it’s also why, once morning devotion becomes a habit, you don’t have to struggle — when the time comes, your heart simply turns towards God.

The management writer Jim Collins, in Good to Great, uses the image of a “flywheel” for the same thing: a huge flywheel takes enormous effort to push through its first turn, and the second turn is still hard work, but once you push past a certain point, its own momentum carries it round.

The spiritual life is a flywheel like that. For the first few days of getting up early to read the Bible, it will feel like pushing a boulder; keep pushing long enough, and the wheel will start pushing you.

So 321 gives us a clear standard so that we know how to choose:

Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. These are the Three Foundations.

Let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. These are the Two Core Values.

Establish God’s system. This is the Goal.

When you use this standard to choose what you’ll look at, listen to and think about each day, you will begin to “see rightly” and “hear rightly”, and your life will be changed.

And 321 calls this road the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. First let the Holy Spirit guide, then let Scripture open our understanding, then live out the life of Jesus, then in service let Jesus reign as King, and finally let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: which way is your flywheel turning today?

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Fivefold Change from Mindset to Ministry
sections.html:
Let’s place today’s message within the overall framework of 321.

First, the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal. We don’t hear God’s voice to satisfy our curiosity; we hear it so that Jesus may reign as King. The Three Foundations answer the question “Whom do I listen to?”: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values answer “Why do I listen?”: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal answers “Having heard, what do I do?”: establish God’s system.

Second, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The four key points of today’s lesson are exactly the first two links of this chain. What you see and hear every day forms your mindset; when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships are healed; and when relationships are healed, ministry at last has a foundation.

Third, life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people are desperate to hear God’s voice because they want to know which ministry to take up, whether to change jobs, whether to get married. But what God cares about more is you as a person. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is clear too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If your relationship with God is clear, everything else will gradually become clear as well.

Fourth, a shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. A change in what we see and hear is, at bottom, a change of perspective. If you keep looking at earthly things, your heart will only respond to earthly voices.

Fifth, the 920 practice. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out the selfless “0” in every relationship, we bear the nine fruits of the Spirit — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice this: the most honest test of whether you have truly heard God lies not in your feelings, but in whether one more fruit is growing in your relationship with the “2” beside you.

Sixth, 235 relationships. We become a “2” with a selfless person, each being the other’s spiritual companion; we build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and from there we become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Those who hear God don’t walk alone; God’s voice is very often confirmed through a spiritual companion.

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice: Turning Light into Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s deepen them using the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Deliberately adjust what you see and hear each day.

Review the information you take in every day. Cut back on excessive worldly, negative or chaotic content, and add more Bible reading, worship and spiritual teaching, so that God’s voice becomes the main current of your life.

Information: today you have heard Proverbs 4:20–23. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you what your heart is being fed on. Conviction: admit that “what I see and hear really is shaping me”. Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, give the first ten minutes after you open your eyes to God, and don’t touch your phone. Evaluation: every Sunday evening, honestly note how many days this week you managed it. Correction: if you can’t manage it, move your phone charger out of the bedroom. Repetition: keep it up for forty days and let it become a flywheel. Multiplication: share this practice with your “2” and invite them to do it with you.

Practice 2: Practise guarding your heart every day.

Through prayer, hand your emotions, anxieties and burdens over to God, and ask the Lord to cleanse your heart, so that it stays soft and simple — a place that can receive God’s voice.

Information and Revelation: meditate on Proverbs 4:23, and let the Holy Spirit point out the thorns that are choking you. Conviction: believe that the heart matters more than circumstances. Implementation: every evening, spend three minutes in a “clean-heart prayer”, handing over the day’s emotions, hurts and anxieties one by one; then be still for a minute and say only, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” Evaluation and Correction: notice which anxiety keeps coming back most often — that is the breach that needs special entrusting to God. Repetition: do it every day, until it becomes like breathing. Multiplication: lead the brothers and sisters in your small group in praying this prayer together.

Practice 3: Choose humility and lay down your own ideas.

When God’s word clashes with your own ideas, learn to say, “Lord, I am willing to lay myself down and choose to obey you.” Every time you lay yourself down, you will hear God more clearly.

Information and Revelation: see what it is that your heart clings to most stubbornly. Conviction: admit that insisting is not the same as being right. Implementation: at least once this week, in an argument where you are sure you’re in the right, choose to stop talking first, listen first, apologise first. Evaluation: after that, did the relationship grow closer or more distant? Correction: change “I want to win” into “I want to love”. Repetition: let humility become your first reaction, not your last resort. Multiplication: when your family see that you no longer insist on your own way, you are already passing humility on.

sections.heading: 9. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Hearing God is not a technique; it is a life.

If the heart is chaotic, the voice is chaotic; if the heart is simple, the voice is clear.

To guard your heart is to guard your spiritual hearing.

sections.heading: 11. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, do you want to hear God?

The answer is not to go looking for a method, but to return to one place — your heart.

When your heart is guarded, when your eyes are adjusted, when your ears are cleansed, when you are willing to be humble, you will discover one thing: God has been speaking all along, and you have finally heard him.

The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) Notice that this is the instinct of sheep, not the privilege of super-saints. If you belong to him, you can hear him.

The servant in Isaiah also left us words perfectly suited to morning devotion: “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4) Every morning God is awakening us. The only question is to whom we lend our ears once we’re awake.

So from today, make a choice: adjust what you see and hear, and align your heart with God.

Turn off some of the noise — not because all those voices are bad, but because there is a more beautiful voice that deserves your full attention.

May we not only hear God’s voice but also let Jesus reign as King in our hearts; may the wellspring of our whole life flow from a heart that God guards, giving all the glory to Jesus.

keyVerses: My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings. Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and health to their whole body. Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life. (Proverbs 4:20–23)

For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.” (Isaiah 57:15)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I am willing to give my heart to you.
Cleanse my heart, and adjust everything I see and hear.
Let me no longer be filled with the world, but filled with your word.
I choose to be humble and selfless, and to let you reign as King within me.
I will be someone who sees you, hears you and lives you out.
In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare it. Amen!
practices: Deliberately adjust what you see and hear each day
Practise guarding your heart every day
Choose humility and lay down your own ideas
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. You have never stopped speaking; it is our hearts that are too noisy, too full, too hard.

Lord, this morning we come before you; search our hearts, we pray. Where they are swamped by emotion, calm them; where they are blocked by hurt, heal them; where they are choked by anxiety, clear it away; where they are occupied by self, tear it down.

Give us a new heart; take away the heart of stone and give us a heart of flesh. Cleanse our eyes, so that we turn them away from worthless things; cleanse our ears, so that morning by morning we may hear as those who are taught.
Lord Jesus, we are willing to lay down our own ideas and let you be King. May the Holy Spirit guide us, so that all we see, hear, think and do today is pleasing to you.
May we become people who hear you and who live you out. May all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) This week, what has most often filled your heart — emotions, hurts, anxieties, or self? How specifically do you plan to hand it over to God?

“I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit.” (Isaiah 57:15) Share a time when, after you laid down your own ideas and chose to obey God, you heard him more clearly. What change did that bring?
l130.title: How to Hear God’s Voice
l130.subtitle: Keep Your Heart; Adjust Your Seeing and Listening
l130.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: Where Is Life’s Real Battlefield?
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, let’s grow quiet together and ask ourselves a question that is seldom asked and yet shapes an entire life —

Where is the real battlefield of a human life?

We often assume the battlefield is out there. Some say, my battlefield is the workplace, because the competition there is fierce; some say, my battlefield is the family, because that’s where the friction is worst; some say, my battlefield is my body, because illness has me in its grip; and some say, my battlefield is money, because the pressure is crushing.

These are all real hardships. But brothers and sisters, if we are a little more honest we’ll notice something: in the same workplace, one person withers while another rejoices; in the same hospital ward, one person despairs while another praises; the very same remark leaves one person wounded for three years and makes another laugh it off. The circumstances are the same, yet the outcomes are completely different. Why?

Because the real battlefield is not in our circumstances, nor in other people; it is in a place where we spend every day and yet seldom put in order — our thoughts.

The seventeenth-century French mathematician, physicist and philosopher Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) wrote a line in his Pensées that is still quoted today: “Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed.” Human dignity lies not in physical strength or length of days but in the capacity to think. Yet for that very reason, both our fall and our victory begin in our thoughts.

Scripture puts it very plainly: “bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5b). The verb “bringing into captivity” tells us this is territory that has been seized and must be taken back. When God asks us to take our thoughts captive, it means this: the mind is contested territory.

Scripture also says, “For as he thinks about the cost, so he is.” (Proverbs 23:7a) As you think, so you are. Not how you talk, not what you pretend, but how you think when nobody is watching.

So if we want our lives to change, the order is not to change our behaviour first, but to change our thinking first.

This is the first light that 321 shines: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living; change your daily living and you change your relationships; change your relationships and you change your ministry. The whole fivefold change begins with the first link — the mindset. If the mindset doesn’t change, any change in behaviour is just pruning on the outside, and before long it grows back; but once the mindset changes, life is renewed from the roots, and the whole tree is different.

Today we are going to learn a lesson that bears on our whole life: how to have “right thinking”.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Paul’s Warfare and Two Scenes from David’s Life
sections.html:
To understand “right thinking”, we first need to understand the background of our theme passages.

Second Corinthians was written by the apostle Paul around AD 55–57, during his third missionary journey, while he was in the region of Macedonia, to the church in Corinth. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia and an important trading port in the eastern Roman Empire — populous, culturally mixed, alive with competing ideas, and also notorious for its moral corruption. At that time a group who styled themselves “super-apostles” had entered the Corinthian church and were attacking Paul, saying that “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10). Their weapons were words, debate, human wisdom and worldly prestige.

In chapters 10 to 13 Paul defends his apostleship. But notice: he does not strike back with his opponents’ weapons. He says, “For though we walk in the flesh, we don’t wage war according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:3). He admits he is a limited man living in a body of flesh; but he does not fight with the methods of the flesh.

Here Paul uses a cluster of very forceful military terms. “Strongholds” is the Greek ochyrōma, meaning a fortress or citadel — in the ancient Near East and the Greek world, a fortress built on a hilltop could hold out against a great army for years. “Imaginations” is the Greek logismos, which originally means “reasoning, calculation, argument” — a self-contained system of logic in the human heart. “Thought” is the Greek noēma, an intention, the product of thinking. “Bringing into captivity” is the Greek aichmalōtizō, literally “to take as a prisoner of war” — the picture of enemy soldiers being captured on the battlefield and marched back to camp.

Put these words together, and Paul paints an extremely clear picture: in the human mind stand fortress after fortress built of “reasoning”, and inside them hides “every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God”; the power of the gospel tears down those fortresses and, one by one, captures every fleeing thought inside and brings it to the feet of Christ, to obey him.

This is what spiritual warfare really looks like. It’s not some smoke-filled dramatic scene; it is the first thought that comes to you when you open your eyes in the morning, the first sentence that rises in your heart when you are misunderstood, the video that plays automatically in your head when you are alone.

The other half of our theme passage comes from Proverbs. Proverbs 23 belongs to the major section “the words of the wise” (Proverbs 22:17–24:22). The original setting of 23:6–8 is a warning not to greedily eat the food of a “stingy” man, because his mouth says “Eat and drink!” but his heart is not with you. Solomon puts his finger right on it: “For as he thinks about the cost, so he is.” (Proverbs 23:7a) The Hebrew word for “thinks” here is sha’ar, which carries the sense of “estimating, calculating”. As a person calculates inside, so he is — and no outward courtesy can change the truth within.

In its original context this verse is about a mean host; but the principle it reveals runs through the whole Bible and agrees completely with Proverbs 4:23: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) What is inside a person determines what is real about that person.

The two scenes the lesson sets side by side both come from 2 Samuel. In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Samuel were originally a single book, belonging to the “Former Prophets”. Second Samuel 7 is set around 1000 BC: David is already king, has captured Jerusalem, has brought the ark into the City of David, and is living in the cedar palace that Hiram king of Tyre built for him. Chapter 11 comes not long afterwards, during Israel’s war with the Ammonites. The same man, the same throne, the same heart — and yet, because of two different ways of “thinking”, he walked two completely different roads.

Brothers and sisters, these two scenes are the most powerful teaching material in today’s lesson. Now let’s go step by step into the four key points.

sections.heading: 1. The Mind Is a Battlefield: Not Neutral Ground, but a War Zone
sections.html:
Scripture says, “For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God.” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5a)

Notice what this sentence takes for granted: there are “strongholds” in the mind.

Strongholds don’t appear out of nowhere. A fortress is built brick by brick, raised up over years. In our minds, too, stand fortresses we have grown so used to that we don’t even notice them. The lesson lists four kinds:

First, wrong mindsets. For example: “That’s just the way I am; I can’t change.” “God loves other people, but he doesn’t love someone like me.” “As long as I work hard enough, I can keep everything under control.”

Second, self-centred thinking. In everything, the first question is “What’s in it for me?”, “What will people think of me?”, “Am I losing out?”

Third, logic that is not after God’s heart. This is the strongest kind of fortress, because it “makes sense”. It says, “An eye for an eye — that’s only fair.” “You have to look after yourself first before you can look after others.” “He wronged me first, so of course I can give him the cold shoulder.” It sounds perfectly reasonable, yet it runs directly against the cross.

Fourth, the world’s value system. It measures achievement by money, worth by appearance, and meaning by applause.

What do these fortresses keep us from? The lesson is precise: they keep us from knowing God, from obeying God, from hearing God. That is exactly what Paul’s original says — “every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God”. Note the key word: “high thing”. The Greek hypsōma means something towering. These fortresses block our knowledge of God not because they are low but because they are high; not because they are obvious sins, but because they are the “I” within us that lifts itself up and speaks in God’s place.

So the mind is never a neutral patch of empty ground. It is the place where God and the enemy are at war.

To put it in a picture: the mind is like a castle. A castle is never “unoccupied”. If it is not filled with truth, it will certainly be occupied by something else; if it is occupied by error, it is controlled by the enemy; if it is filled with truth, it is ruled by God. The Lord Jesus told a sobering parable: an unclean spirit leaves a man and wanders through waterless places; when it returns and finds the house “swept, and put in order”, it brings along seven other spirits more evil than itself to live there, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first (Matthew 12:43–45). A house swept clean but left empty isn’t safe — it’s dangerous. The mind is the same: an empty mind is not neutral; it is up for rent.

Psychology has offered fairly consistent confirmation of this truth. In the 1960s the American psychiatrist Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania founded cognitive therapy. In his clinical work he found that people’s emotional distress often comes not directly from events but from certain spontaneous, unexamined “automatic thoughts”; and beneath those automatic thoughts lie deeper, more hidden “core beliefs”. Core beliefs are like the foundation, and automatic thoughts are like walls built on that foundation. If someone deals only with the emotions and not with the beliefs, it’s like knocking down the walls without touching the foundation — the walls soon go back up.

Brothers and sisters, can you hear it? Beck’s “core beliefs” and Paul’s “strongholds” describe the same phenomenon. The difference is this: psychology can help people identify the fortresses, but it has no weapon to tear them down; the gospel does. “For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God.” (2 Corinthians 10:4) Psychology is a very good servant but a very bad master. We use it as an aid; we don’t let it sit on the throne as our standard. The Bible is our standard.

The 321 insight here is very clear: self-centred thinking has self at the centre; selfless thinking has Christ at the centre.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. When the serpent said to Eve, “you will be like God”, that sentence was aimed squarely at the mind. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Every stronghold in the mind has the same word carved into its foundation: “I”. And the way to tear the strongholds down is not to try twice as hard with “I’m going to change” — that is still “I”; it is to let Christ come in and reign as King. Selflessness is not erasing yourself into nothingness; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20b)

This morning we can ask ourselves one honest question: over the castle of my mind, whose flag is flying right now?

sections.heading: 2. Thoughts Determine Outcomes: One Thought Brings Blessing, One Thought Brings Ruin
sections.html:
Scripture gives us a deeply shocking contrast — and it’s the same man: David.

The same man, two ways of thinking, two endings.

The first scene is recorded in 2 Samuel 11. “At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel … But David stayed at Jerusalem. At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at.” (2 Samuel 11:1–2)

Notice how the text sets the scene: when it was time to go to war, he didn’t go; when his place was the battlefield, he was in bed; he got up only in the evening and strolled on the roof. This is not a man so busy he lost control; this is a man so idle he let down his guard. And then — he “saw”. Seeing in itself was not yet sin, but next a wrong “thought” took shape in his heart. James describes the process with pinpoint accuracy: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14–15)

One wrong thought led to adultery; when the adultery could not be covered up, it led to murder; and after the murder came a breach in his household that never closed. The prophet Nathan spoke to him in God’s name: “Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house.” (2 Samuel 12:10a) The later affair of Amnon, the rebellion of Absalom, the blood shed in his family — all fulfilled those words. One thought, and the damage ran on for three generations.

The second scene is recorded in 2 Samuel 7. At that time the nation was secure and there was peace on every side. “When the king lived in his house, and Yahweh had given him rest from all his enemies all around, the king said to Nathan the prophet, ‘See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but God’s ark dwells within curtains.’” (2 Samuel 7:1–2)

Again these were days of peace, again a time with no war to fight. But this time what David was thinking about was not his own comfort but God’s dwelling place; not how well he himself was housed, but where God’s ark was. That one right “thought” brought God’s pleasure, brought blessing, brought the promise of a kingdom: “Your house and your kingdom will be made sure forever before you. Your throne will be established forever.” (2 Samuel 7:16) That promise ultimately points to the Son of David — our Lord Jesus Christ.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The turning points of life lie not in our actions but in “where our thinking begins”.

To put it in a picture: thoughts are seeds; behaviour is fruit. No one plants thistles and harvests grapes; no one sows wheat and reaps darnel. The Lord Jesus said, “Therefore by their fruits you will know them.” (Matthew 7:20) Right seed, right result; wrong seed, wrong result. And the most dangerous thing about a seed is that it is small — so small you don’t think it’s anything at all. The thought that flashed through David’s mind on that rooftop was smaller than a mustard seed. But the very nature of a seed is to grow.

There is a well-known model in psychology that illustrates exactly this order. In the mid-1950s the American psychologist Albert Ellis developed rational emotive therapy, at the heart of which is the “ABC model”: A is the activating event, B is the person’s belief about and interpretation of the event, and C is the resulting emotional and behavioural consequence. Ellis pointed out that most people assume A directly causes C, but in fact there is always a B in between. When the same thing happens to two people and the outcomes are worlds apart, the difference lies in B.

That is exactly the 321 insight: it isn’t events that make you fail; it’s how you think that makes you fail.

And that is why where our focus lies becomes so vitally important. 321 reminds us again and again: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. On the rooftop David’s focus was his own eyes and desires, and the result was ruin; in the palace David’s focus was God’s ark and God’s glory, and the result was a promise. Peter, out on the water, kept his focus on Jesus and walked on the sea; the moment his focus shifted to the wind and waves, he began to sink (Matthew 14:29–30).

Brothers and sisters, what kind of seed are you and I sowing in our hearts today?

sections.heading: 3. What You Think About in Idle Moments Sets Your Direction
sections.html:
Next comes a question that few people ask, and yet it is absolutely crucial:

When you have “nothing to do”, what do you think about?

Brothers and sisters, this question reveals the truth about us better than “What do you serve in at church?” Because when you’re busy, you are occupied by tasks; only when you’re idle does your true nature show. When you’re busy, your thoughts run on rails; when you’re idle, your thoughts automatically slide down the road they know best. And that road is the real direction of your life.

David sinned in a time of idleness — staying in the city when it was time to go to war, getting up only in the evening and strolling on the roof. David was also blessed in a time of peace — in days with no war to fight, his thoughts turned to God’s ark. The same idleness, different thoughts, different lives.

This is exactly what the lesson says: what you think about in idle moments is the direction of your life.

Here there is a scientific finding worth noting. In 2001 the neuroscientist Marcus Raichle and his colleagues at Washington University in St. Louis published a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences describing the brain’s “default mode network”. They found something counter-intuitive: when people stop performing a task and appear to be doing nothing at all, the brain doesn’t go quiet; instead, a particular set of brain regions becomes more active. In other words, the human brain has no such thing as “standby”. You think you are daydreaming, but inside, you are running at full speed.

In 2010 Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert of Harvard University published a study in the journal Science. Using smartphones to sample at random moments, they tracked the daily experience of 2,250 participants. They found that when people are awake, for about 47 per cent of the time their minds are not on what they are doing; and that when their minds wander, people are generally less happy than when they are focused on the present. The title of their paper was “A Wandering Mind Is an Unhappy Mind”.

Brothers and sisters, for nearly half our waking hours, our hearts are drifting. Added together, those drifting hours make up a large part of our lives. Where have they gone?

The lesson points to the most real picture of our day: the moment we have a spare minute, we scroll our phones; the moment we have a spare minute, we look at the world. The result is that our thoughts are filled with the world, and our hearts slowly drift away from God. It’s not because we’ve committed some great evil, but because we have handed over the softest, most malleable part of our time for others to shape.

One important thing needs saying here: God is not against rest. God himself instituted the Sabbath, and the Lord Jesus said to his disciples, “You come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” (Mark 6:31b) The problem has never been “having free time”; the problem is “who we hand our thoughts over to when we have free time”. Rest is handing that space over to God; emptiness is handing it over to the world. In both cases we stop — but one leads into God’s presence, and the other into the enemy’s ambush.

A saying commonly attributed to the Reformer Martin Luther puts it vividly: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair. Thoughts will come, and that is not your sin; but if you let them build a nest, lay eggs and hatch a whole brood, that becomes a stronghold.

Here 321 has a very precious reminder: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you find worry, rely on the heart and you find joy. The wellspring of life flows from the heart (Proverbs 4:23). In our idle moments, if we rely on the brain and ourselves, we go over other people’s motives again and again, calculate our own gains and losses, rehearse disasters that haven’t happened yet — and that is called “worry”; if we rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, we converse with the Lord in the quiet and let God’s word rise to the surface — and that is called “joy”.

The prophet Isaiah left us a beautiful promise: “You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.” (Isaiah 26:3) “Steadfast” in Hebrew carries the sense of “a mind that is upheld, supported”. A mind upheld by God does not drift aimlessly in its idle moments.

So, brothers and sisters, let’s bring this question before the Lord: where is my free time taking me?

sections.heading: 4. Right Thinking: Letting Our Thoughts Be Filled with God’s Word
sections.html:
The first three points have all been about the problem; the fourth is about the way out.

Scripture says, “But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” (Psalm 1:2) Blessed is that man!

Right thinking is not random thinking, not idle daydreaming, and still less forcing yourself to “stop thinking”. Right thinking is “meditating on God’s word”.

Psalm 1 is the prologue to the whole Psalter, like a doorway through which everyone who would enter the Psalms must pass. It divides all humanity into two paths: one is “the counsel of the wicked”, the other is “Yahweh’s law”. Notice that the dividing point between the two paths is not, at first, behaviour but “counsel” and “meditation” — the logic that runs inside a person’s heart.

The word “meditates” here is the Hebrew hagah, and it’s a wonderfully vivid word. In Isaiah 31:4 it describes a lion growling over its prey; in Isaiah 38:14 it describes the moaning of a dove. In other words, biblical “meditation” isn’t zoning out, isn’t emptying your head and sitting there; it is like a lion that has seized its prey and won’t let go, like a dove murmuring over and over — holding a word in your mouth and chewing on it again and again in your heart, chewing on it aloud.

This exposes the bottleneck in many people’s devotional lives. The lesson is very honest: many people read the Bible and they pray, but the problem is — they don’t “meditate”. They read and forget; they pray and that’s the end of it. The verse goes in through the eyes and out through the eyes, without staying in the heart for even a minute.

But God’s desire is that his word should remain in you and guide your thoughts. The Lord Jesus said, “If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.” (John 15:7) The psalmist said, “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” (Psalm 119:11) And God’s command to Joshua was even more direct: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.” (Joshua 1:8)

What becomes of such a person? “He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.” (Psalm 1:3)

Notice how precise this picture is: the tree is not watered; it is “planted” by the streams. Watering is occasional and passive; being planted by the streams is long-term, with the roots driven deep. When a drought year comes to a tree planted by the streams, the leaves of other trees wither but it stays green, because its water source is not the clouds in the sky but the stream beneath the ground. Brothers and sisters, that isn’t good luck; it’s right thinking — it’s because the roots go down into God’s word.

Paul also says, “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)

There is a beautiful insight from the original in this verse. “Think about” is the Greek logizomai, meaning “to calculate, to consider carefully, to reckon into the account”. And the “imaginations” in our theme passage that must be thrown down is the Greek logismos — the two words share the same root. What does that tell us? That the capacity for thinking God has given us is in itself a neutral tool: it can be used to build fortresses against God, or to build a temple for worshipping God. The same capacity of logos, turned downwards, becomes a stronghold; turned upwards, it becomes an altar.

So our thoughts can be “chosen”. Paul uses the imperative: “think about these things.” He doesn’t say, “I hope these things will come to mind naturally”; he says: think on them. It is an act of the will, and it can be practised.

Brain science bears this out too. The learning principle proposed in 1949 by the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb is often summed up in a single line: neurons that fire together wire together. The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons (the estimate of Azevedo and colleagues, a research team at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, 2009), and the connections between them grow stronger with repeated use and weaker with long disuse. This is “neuroplasticity”. In other words, every time you choose to meditate on God’s word, you widen one road in your brain; every time you let yourself dwell on things you shouldn’t, you are widening another. The road you travel most becomes, in the end, your motorway.

Scripture said this three thousand years before science, and said it more deeply: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “Be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is, in the original, a continuous passive — it is not you remaking yourself, but you letting God continually renew you.

The twentieth-century preacher A. W. Tozer (1897–1963) wrote at the opening of The Knowledge of the Holy: “What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us.” What you think about God shapes everything about you.

Here the 321 insight reaches its peak: what you think on is what you become; think on Christ, and you live out Christ.

Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5) And again, “But we have Christ’s mind.” (1 Corinthians 2:16b) Brothers and sisters, this is not some far-off ideal; it is an inheritance already given. The only question is whether, every morning, we plug this mind in.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: From a Change of Mindset to the Establishing of a System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we set this lesson back within the whole panorama of 321, it becomes even clearer.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Every key point in this lesson is fastened to these three foundations. Who is the role model for our thinking? The Lord Jesus. When he was tempted in the wilderness, all three times he answered, “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10) — that was a battle fought purely in the realm of thought, and the Lord won it with Scripture. What is the standard for our thinking? The Bible — not feelings, not public opinion, not my experience. Who is the guide for our thinking? The Holy Spirit. “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth.” (John 16:13a)

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Paul says we are to bring every thought captive “to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5b). “Obedience” means letting Jesus reign as King in my thoughts. Brothers and sisters, we often let Jesus be King of the church, King of the meeting, King of Sunday, yet we don’t let him be King of that thought inside us. True surrender is handing that thought over in the place where no one else can see.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Where does a system begin? Not with an organisation, but with thoughts renewed one by one. When a group of people whose thoughts are ruled by Christ gather together, they naturally become God’s system; when a group of people whose thoughts are still ruled by the world gather together, even if they hang up a church sign, what actually operates is still the Babylonian system.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. And where does pride live? It lives in those “high things exalted against the knowledge of God” within our thoughts. That is why 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. At the level of our thinking, this means: I no longer act as king of my own thoughts; I give up the throne.

Remember too: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Many marriages and many co-worker relationships break down not starting with a sentence but starting with a thought — “He just looks down on me.” Once that thought arises, defences go up, the tone of voice changes, the other person’s pride is provoked too, and both sides lose. If, the moment the thought first arises, we take it captive and hand it over to Christ, the ending is completely different.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This lesson stands at the first link. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living; change your daily living and you change your relationships; change your relationships and you change your ministry. So it is life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. When a person’s thoughts are renewed, first their relationship with God is restored; next they are able to forgive themselves; then the way they look at others changes; and finally even their motives for what they do are cleansed.

A shift of perspective is the most practical exercise in this lesson: from man’s perspective to God’s, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) On the rooftop David took a human, earthly, temporary, worldly perspective; in the palace, when he thought of the ark, David took God’s, heavenly, eternal, godly perspective. The same heart; change the perspective, and you change the life.

Then there is the 920 practice. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23a) Brothers and sisters, think about it: which of these nine fruits does not first happen in our thoughts? Patience is first holding back that sentence in your heart; gentleness is first laying down, in your heart, the urge to win; peace is first stopping, in your heart, that argument nobody else can see. If our thoughts are not renewed, the nine fruits cannot grow; once our thoughts are renewed, the fruit grows naturally, because it is borne by the Spirit, not squeezed out by our own effort.

The Path of Serving is the same road: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). The order cannot be reversed. Many people skip “Spirit” and “Understanding” and go straight into “Service”, and after a few years of serving they dry up, because their thinking has never been reshaped by God’s word.

sections.heading: 6. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html: The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s deepen them one by one using the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they don’t just stay as things we know, but truly become life.

sections.heading: 1. Practise Noticing What You Are Thinking
sections.html:
Each day, take a few minutes to be still and ask yourself, “What have I been thinking about most lately?” Write down the thoughts that are negative, self-centred, anxious or untrue, and begin consciously to identify them.

Information: first grasp one fact — thoughts can be noticed. I am not the same as my thoughts; I can stand to one side and watch them. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light. David’s prayer is the best model: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24) Conviction: admit that there really are strongholds within me, and stop defending and rationalising them. Implementation: get a small notebook, and for seven days in a row write down each evening three thoughts that kept coming back that day. Evaluation: after a week, look back and find the pattern — you’ll be surprised to discover that almost all of them come from the same one or two fortresses. Correction: for each fortress, find a verse that targets it. Repetition: it isn’t enough to write for seven days; let it become a lifelong habit. Multiplication: take this practice to your “2”, and remind one another.

sections.heading: 2. Replace Wrong Thinking with God’s Word
sections.html:
When you discover wrong thinking, don’t suppress it and don’t indulge it; replace it with Scripture.

Pay special attention to these two phrases in the lesson: don’t suppress, don’t indulge. Suppressing is pushing a thought down, and it will pop up somewhere else; indulging is letting it spread, and it will build itself into a fortress. Scripture’s way is a third way — replacement. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he didn’t debate with Satan, nor did he pretend not to hear; he said, “It is written …” (Matthew 4:4b)

Information: know that “replacing” beats “suppressing”. Revelation: see that God’s word itself has power — “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword.” (Hebrews 4:12a) Conviction: believe that declaring the truth is not self-hypnosis but handing sovereignty back to God. Implementation: for the three wrong thoughts that come to you most often, prepare one verse each. For example, when fear comes, declare: “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.” (Psalm 23:4a) When feelings of inferiority come, declare: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” (Psalm 139:14a) When bitterness comes, declare: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:32) Evaluation: record the moments when you succeeded in replacing a thought and the moments when you were swept away. Correction: adjust your verses, and find one that fits your situation more closely. Repetition: keep going until the declaration becomes a reflex. Multiplication: share your list of verses with a companion.

sections.heading: 3. Build a Habit of Meditating on God’s Word
sections.html:
Each day, choose one verse to ponder over and over, repeat quietly and pray through, letting it enter your thinking system and shape your choices and actions.

Information: understand what hagah means — meditation is chewing over and over, not reading once and moving on. Revelation: ask God to make that verse “open up”, turning from words on a page into light. Conviction: believe that one verse digested is worth more than ten chapters skimmed. Implementation: here is a very simple method — copy out one verse in the morning, recite it once as you leave home, think on it once at midday, and pray it once before bed. Four times, under five minutes in all. Evaluation: in the evening, ask yourself whether the verse rose to the surface at some moment today. Correction: if it didn’t surface all day, perhaps the passage is too long; switch to a shorter one. Repetition: you can meditate on the same verse for a whole week; there’s no need to change it every day. Multiplication: in your small group, lead everyone in using the same verse, and after a week share with one another how God has used it.

A Gentle Reminder

The lesson closes by giving us three reminders, every one of them worth writing on the tablet of our hearts:

First, thoughts are not automatic; they can be renewed. You are not destined to think this way for the rest of your life.

Second, if you don’t deal with your thoughts, your thoughts will control you. If you don’t manage them, they’ll manage you.

Third, right thinking brings a right life.

So pay attention to “what you are thinking”.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Let Our Thoughts Fully Obey Christ
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, let’s return to the question we began with: where is life’s real battlefield?

The answer is now very clear. Where your life is lost is not in your abilities but in your “thinking”.

Wrong thinking, wrong life; right thinking, right life.

Many brothers and sisters weep before the Lord: Lord, change my circumstances; Lord, change my husband; Lord, change my children; Lord, change my boss. God hears all these prayers; but today God wants first to do something more fundamental — he wants to renew your thinking; he wants to rebuild what is inside you.

Because if your circumstances change but your thinking doesn’t, you’ll repeat the old pain in the new circumstances; but if your thinking changes, even if your circumstances don’t, you can live a completely different life in the very same place. Paul and Silas were in the prison at Philippi, their feet in the stocks, their backs covered in wounds, and yet at midnight they were “praying and singing hymns to God” (Acts 16:25b). The prison didn’t change; their thinking had changed, and so the prison became a temple of worship, the ground shook violently, and the chains came loose.

When your thoughts are ruled by Christ, you will find —

Your choices change. Because you no longer act on your first impulse; you first ask, is this in line with the Lord’s heart?

Your life changes. Because your roots are no longer sunk in other people’s opinions, but planted by the streams of water.

The course of your life changes too. Because the wellspring of life flows from the heart; when the heart is right, what flows from it is right.

Brothers and sisters, this road isn’t about gritting our teeth and forcing our way through. If we rely on ourselves, we have only swapped in a more refined version of the self-centred life. This road is letting Jesus be King — letting him reign as King in our thoughts. He was the first to hand his will over completely to the Father: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39b) He won that battle of the mind in the Garden of Gethsemane, and so he was able to win salvation for all humanity at Golgotha.

So from today, let’s make a decision together:

My thoughts no longer belong to me; they fully obey Christ.

Not once today, but once every morning; not by my willpower, but by his Holy Spirit. I will bring every thought before him, let him be King, and let him receive all the glory.

As we are renewed like this, one by one, our families will change, our small groups will change, our fellowship will change; God’s system will be established on earth, and the longing of the Lord’s Prayer will be fulfilled — “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

keyVerses: “For though we walk in the flesh, we don’t wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:3–5)
“For as he thinks about the cost, so he is.” (Proverbs 23:7a)
practices: Each day, take a few minutes to be still and ask yourself, “What have I been thinking about most lately?” Write down the untrue thoughts and identify them.
When you discover wrong thinking, don’t suppress it and don’t indulge it; replace it with Scripture.
Each day, choose one verse to ponder, repeat quietly and pray through, building a habit of meditating on God’s word.
prayer: Lord Jesus, I am willing to give my thoughts to you.
Tear down every false stronghold within me, remove every thought that is not of you, and demolish every high thing that exalts itself and keeps me from knowing you.

Lord, I confess that I often rely on the brain and on myself rather than on the heart and the Holy Spirit; I confess that I have often given my free time to the world and not to you. Have mercy on me and forgive me.
Today I will take back my thoughts and bring every thought into obedience to Christ.

I will think on the truth, and I will live out the truth. Let your word remain in me and guide my thoughts, so that I may be like a tree planted by the streams of water, producing its fruit in its season, whose leaf does not wither.
Make my life more and more like yours. May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For as he thinks about the cost, so he is.” (Proverbs 23:7a) Share honestly: over the past week, when you had “nothing to do”, what did you think about most? In which direction are those thoughts taking you?

“Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8b) Each person, choose the one wrong thought that most often holds you back, find a verse that can replace it, declare it to one another in your small group, and agree to remind each other this week.
l131.title: Thinking Rightly
l131.subtitle: The Battlefield of the Mind Decides the Direction of Your Life
l131.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: Your First Reaction Betrays Your Thinking
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, let us grow quiet together and first ask ourselves a very simple, yet very honest, question —

When circumstances turn against you and things don’t go the way you hoped, what is your first reaction?

Is it worry? Is it fear? Does your mind immediately start playing the worst possible outcome on a loop?

The test results aren’t even back, and in your heart you’ve already passed a death sentence on yourself; your child is half an hour late home, and your mind has already run an entire disaster film; your manager glances at you one second too long, and you spend the whole afternoon wondering whether he’s about to let you go; you haven’t finished reading the text from the bank, and your heart has already sunk to the bottom. Brothers and sisters, we often say, “People are knocked down by their circumstances.” In fact, they aren’t. Very often, before circumstances have lifted a finger, our thoughts have already knocked us down.

This is the most honest picture of the human condition — our thinking is led around by our circumstances. Whatever the circumstances say, we think; when the circumstances turn dark, our thinking turns dark with them; when the circumstances fall into chaos, our thinking falls into chaos too. We are like a little boat without an anchor: wherever the wind blows, there the boat drifts.

But God’s intention is nothing like that. God’s intention is this: not that your circumstances should decide your thinking, but that truth should lead your thinking.

Scripture says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). The Chinese Union Version, with many ancient manuscripts, reads “the word of Christ”. This verse is a chain of life: the word of Christ enters our ears and becomes “hearing”; that hearing enters our thinking, is digested and believed, and becomes “faith”. In other words, faith is not a feeling that appears out of nowhere; faith is the fruit that grows out of “right thinking”. How you think determines how much faith you have; how much faith you have determines how much of God’s work you experience.

So the 321 insight is very clear: it is not events that change you; it is how you think that decides whether you overcome.

In the last lesson we saw that our thinking is contested territory, that the real battlefield of life lies in the mind. In this lesson we go a step further and look at four keys: what right thinking is, how to cut off the wrong voices, how to step beyond past experience, and how the thinking of faith brings forth a victorious life.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Chain from “Hearing” to “Faith”
sections.html:
To understand “right thinking”, we first need to understand the background of today’s two key passages.

Romans was written by the apostle Paul, probably between AD 56 and 57, very likely in Corinth. At that time he was preparing to take the offering from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, and then to go on west to Spain (Romans 15:24–26). The church in Rome that received the letter was not one Paul had planted himself; its members included Jewish believers and a great many Gentile believers, and the tension between the two groups was considerable. So in this letter Paul sets out the gospel of “justification by faith” from chapter 1 to chapter 8, and from chapter 9 to chapter 11 he deals specifically with one heavy question: why is it that Israel, God’s chosen people, stumbled before the gospel?

Paul’s answer is not that they lacked zeal, but that their thinking was pointed in the wrong direction. He says, “For I testify about them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans 10:2). The zeal was there, but it was built on a wrong mindset — “seeking to establish their own righteousness” (Romans 10:3) instead of submitting to God’s righteousness. Brothers and sisters, please notice: what was lost here was not, at heart, behaviour. It was mindset.

So in chapter 10, verses 13–17, Paul draws out a complete chain: “For, ‘Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.’ How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:13–15a). Then he draws his conclusion: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

Read backwards, the chain is clearer still: the word of Christ → hearing → faith → calling on him → salvation. The link in the middle is precisely our subject today — what you take in through hearing, and what you think about, determines the weight of your faith.

The word “faith” in the original is pistis, that is, “faith”; the word “hearing” is akoē, meaning “the message heard”. So the sentence could also be rendered literally: faith comes from the message heard, and the message heard comes through the word of Christ. Whatever your thinking feeds on, that is the shape your faith will grow into.

The other key passage comes from 1 John. In his old age the apostle John lived in Ephesus, and he wrote this letter somewhere between AD 85 and 95 to the churches around Asia Minor. False teachers had already appeared, denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh (1 John 4:2–3), and shaking the foundations of believers. In that setting John wrote, “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4).

Notice the tense of the verb in this verse. In the original, “has overcome the world” is in a completed tense — not “will overcome”, but “has already overcome”. Victory is not a battle still waiting to be fought; victory is an accomplished fact, waiting for us to draw on it by faith. And faith, as Romans says, comes from right hearing and right thinking.

Put the two passages together, and you have today’s main line: rightly hearing God’s word → thinking rightly → faith arising → living out victory.

sections.heading: 1. Right Thinking: Return to 321 — Let Truth Overcome the Facts
sections.html:
Many people assume that “right thinking” simply means positive thinking. Today slogans like these are everywhere: be optimistic, motivate yourself, believe in yourself, attract good things. Brothers and sisters, these words sound warm, but they are not the “right thinking” the Bible speaks of.

Right thinking is not “optimism”; right thinking is “God-centredness”.

Where is the difference? Optimism focuses on myself — I believe I can. Right thinking focuses on God — I believe God can. Optimism is cheering yourself on in the dark; right thinking is lifting your head in the dark and seeing that God is still seated as King. Optimism is held up by emotion, and when the emotion collapses, everything collapses; right thinking stands on the word of God, and however bad the circumstances become, the word does not move.

So where does right thinking begin? It begins by returning to 321:

Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide; let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; in order to establish God’s system.

When your thinking is anchored by these Three Foundations, Two Core Values and one Goal, your whole inner set of coordinates changes. When something happens, the first question you ask is no longer “What am I going to do?” but “What would Jesus do?”; no longer “What will other people say?” but “What does the Bible say?”; no longer “How do I feel?” but “Where is the Holy Spirit leading me?”

When you think this way, you will discover a vitally important principle: truth is always greater than the facts.

What are the facts? The facts are the situation your eyes can see right now. What is truth? Truth is what God has said, the word that never changes. Facts pass away; truth does not pass away. Facts are temporary; truth is eternal.

Circumstances often say three things to us: impossible, too late, no hope. But God’s word answers with three things: possible, not too late, God can do a new thing.

There are two people in the Bible who lived out this principle beautifully.

The first is the centurion of Capernaum. His servant was paralysed and suffering terribly. Jesus said he would go to his house, but the centurion replied, “Lord, I’m not worthy for you to come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matthew 8:8). This centurion was a Roman officer who lived every day within a “chain of command”. His reasoning went like this: if I, a minor officer, give an order and the soldiers go and do it, then when the Lord of all things speaks a word, how could the sickness not leave? He was looking not at his servant’s condition but at the authority of Jesus’ word. When Jesus heard it, he marvelled and said, “Most certainly I tell you, I haven’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel” (Matthew 8:10b).

The second is the woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. She pushed her way through the crowd and touched the fringe of Jesus’ garment. Scripture records what was in her mind: “for she said within herself, ‘If I just touch his garment, I will be made well’” (Matthew 9:21). Notice this phrase — Scripture deliberately points out that she “said within herself”. Her healing did not begin with her hand; it began with her thinking. She settled the matter in her mind first, and only then reached out to touch.

Brothers and sisters, their thinking determined their experience.

Notice that both of them were in very unfavourable situations. The centurion was a Gentile and an officer of the occupying army; by Jewish custom, a rabbi who entered his house would become unclean. The woman with the bleeding was unclean under the regulations of Leviticus 15; in everyone’s eyes, reaching out to touch someone was breaking the rules. Their “facts” were not pretty. But they did not look at the facts; they looked at whether the Lord’s word had power. Truth is greater than the facts — not by denying the facts, but by refusing to let the facts have the final word.

Psychology bears this out as well. In the 1960s Aaron T. Beck, a psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania, developed “cognitive therapy”. He found that what drags people into depression is often not the event itself, but the “automatic thoughts” that flash by between the event and the emotion, so fast that people do not even notice them. At almost the same time, the psychologist Albert Ellis put forward his well-known ABC model: A is the Activating event, C is the Consequence; but what determines C is not A, but B in the middle — the Belief.

Psychology has seen that “B” exists; the Bible tells us what that “B” ought to contain. God’s children do not simply swap negative thoughts for positive ones; they exchange human thoughts for the word of God. “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

A 321 insight: think on God’s word and faith is born; think on your circumstances and fear is born. This is exactly the change of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. Four shifts, one direction: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

sections.heading: 2. Don’t Dwell on the Enemy’s Words: Cut Off the Wrong Source
sections.html:
How did humanity’s first fall happen?

In the Garden of Eden, Eve’s sin did not begin with an action. It began with — a thought.

Scripture records it in remarkable detail. The serpent spoke first: “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1b). Then it went on: “You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:4–5). And then Scripture says, “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6a).

Look closely at the route: first she “listened” to the serpent’s words, then she “looked” at the fruit, then she began to “think” — thinking that this fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes, able to make one wise — and only then did she reach out and “do”.

Listen wrongly and you look wrongly; look wrongly and you think wrongly; think wrongly and you act wrongly. Change the thinking and the action changes; change the action and the ending changes.

Brothers and sisters, notice one thing: the serpent did not force the fruit into Eve’s mouth. Satan has no power to compel anyone to sin. His only skill is to “speak” — to drop a sentence into your thinking. The Lord Jesus said, “He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies” (John 8:44b). Satan’s weapon is the lie; his battlefield is the mind.

So what is the safest way? Don’t let the wrong voices in.

Many people think, “It won’t hurt to listen for a moment,” “It makes no difference if I take a look,” “I’m only finding out about it.” But the truth is this: once something enters your thinking, it begins to affect your life. You cannot drop a drop of ink into clear water and then say, “It was only one drop.” The water is already different.

In a study in 1960, the psychologist Peter Wason identified what is now called “confirmation bias”: once people have accepted a certain hypothesis, they unconsciously gather evidence that supports it and ignore the evidence against it. This reveals something frightening — once a lie has moved into your thinking, your mind will start finding reasons for it, building it a house and paying its rent. That is why “debating with Satan” is always a losing battle: the moment you open your mouth to argue, you are already standing on his question.

A series of studies from 1991 onwards by the Yale psychologist Susan Nolen-Hoeksema showed that “rumination” — chewing over negative events again and again — markedly deepens and prolongs depressed moods. People often think that if they go over something a few more times, they will think it through; in reality, going over it a few more times only digs the rut deeper. Brothers and sisters, some thoughts cannot be “thought through”; they can only be “cut off”.

The Lord Jesus gives us the best role model. When he was tempted in the wilderness, he did not discuss things with Satan, did not analyse, did not explain. He said only, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth’” (Matthew 4:4b). Three temptations, three times “It is written”. This is what “the Bible is my standard” means — not debating, only declaring.

The apostle James says, “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). The order matters: first submit to God, then resist the devil. A person who will not submit to God has no power to resist the devil; when a person who submits to God stands up, the devil runs.

The Reformer Martin Luther is commonly said to have put it like this: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair. A thought flying past is not your sin; letting it stay, feeding it and living alongside it is what becomes your snare.

A 321 insight: do not debate with Satan, and do not let the lie in. For our thinking is not a toy; it is a battlefield. And that is why “selflessness overcomes Satan” — every attack of Satan is designed to stir up our “self”: my face, my rights, my grievances, my fears. When the “self” is exalted, the lie has a foothold; when we return to selflessness and let Jesus be King, the enemy’s words can no longer stick to us.

sections.heading: 3. Don’t Be Limited by the Past: God Is Doing a New Thing
sections.html:
The third key is to walk out of the “past”.

Scripture says, “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert” (Isaiah 43:18–19).

The background of these words matters. Isaiah 40–66 is God’s word of comfort to a people who would go into exile and would also return. Just before this, God has reminded them of his mighty power at the Exodus — how he made a way through the Red Sea (Isaiah 43:16–17); and immediately afterwards he says: don’t remember the former things. God is not asking them to forget his works; he is asking them not to lock him into the way he acted “that one time before”. Last time it was a way through the sea; this time it is a way through the wilderness. Last time he parted the Red Sea; this time he brings rivers to the desert. The method is different; God is the same.

Yet many people’s thinking is tied up by the “past”.

They failed once, so they conclude they will certainly fail this time too; they were hurt once, so they conclude that no one can be trusted; they prayed once and were not healed, so they conclude that God probably won’t do anything more for them. And so two sentences quietly move into the heart: this time nothing will change; God probably won’t act.

Brothers and sisters, those two sentences do not come from God; they come from experience. And experience is always smaller than God.

This is exactly where Martha and Mary landed. Lazarus fell ill, and the sisters sent word to Jesus, yet Jesus stayed where he was for two more days. By the time Jesus reached Bethany, Lazarus had already been in the tomb for four days. Martha came out to meet him and said, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died” (John 11:21). Later, when Mary saw Jesus, she fell at his feet, and what she said was exactly the same: “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died” (John 11:32b).

Where did the two sisters’ faith stop? It stopped at “if you would have been here”. They believed Jesus could heal the sick — because they had seen it; but they did not believe Jesus could raise the dead — because they had never seen it. Their thinking had a line drawn across it by experience.

But Jesus rubbed that line out. He said, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” (John 11:25–26). And at the tomb he said to Martha again, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?” (John 11:40).

Listen carefully to the order here: not “see, then believe”, but “believe, and then you will see”. Man’s order is that seeing is believing; God’s order is that believing is the evidence. “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7).

God is never limited by his own past methods either. Take the healing of leprosy. In the Old Testament, Elisha sent a messenger to Naaman, saying, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall come again to you, and you shall be clean” (2 Kings 5:10). In the New Testament, the Lord Jesus stretched out his hand and touched a man with leprosy, saying, “I want to. Be made clean” (Matthew 8:3b). Another time he said to ten men with leprosy, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went, they were cleansed (Luke 17:14). Washing seven times, a touch of the hand, cleansed along the road — the methods were all different, yet the God who healed was one and the same.

God himself could not say it more clearly: “‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts’” (Isaiah 55:8–9).

Psychology offers a painful piece of corroborating evidence for this truth. In 1967 Martin Seligman and Steven Maier conducted their well-known experiments on “learned helplessness” at the University of Pennsylvania: when animals repeatedly experienced pain they could not control, later, even when the door of escape was open, they no longer tried; they simply lay down and endured it. People are the same. If experiences of failure are not renewed by truth, they become an invisible door — the door is actually open, yet the person no longer walks out.

The good news is that the brain God made is not set in concrete either. Neuroscience today widely recognises “neuroplasticity”: the brain’s neural connections change with repeated thoughts and experiences, and they keep changing throughout life. The principle the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed in 1949 was later often summed up in one sentence: neurons that fire together wire together. Whatever you think about repeatedly, that road grows wider and wider. The old pathways of thought were worn in over decades; a new pathway can begin to be walked from today.

Abraham is a role model of exactly this. “Without being weakened in faith, he didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb. Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God” (Romans 4:19–20). Here the Chinese Union Version, following other ancient manuscripts, reads that he did “consider” his own body as good as dead. Notice, then: he did not deny the facts — he truly took account of a body as good as dead; but above the facts, he looked to the greater promise.

So a person limited by the past has in fact shrunk God down to the size of his own memory. That is not humility; it is actually a hidden pride — I have used my limited experience to draw a boundary around the infinite God. Return to your originally intended position, brothers and sisters: let man be man and let God be God. Man’s position is to believe; God’s position is to act.

A 321 insight: don’t define God by the past, and don’t limit God by experience. God is the God who is forever doing new things. “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). He who sits on the throne is still saying today, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5b).
