sections.heading: 4. The Thinking of Faith: Bringing Forth a Victorious Life
sections.html:
The fourth key is to carry right thinking all the way into a victorious daily life.

Scripture says, “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4).

The key to victory is faith. So where does faith come from? It comes from our thinking. “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

Put these two verses together and you have one complete lifeline: God’s word → hearing → thinking → faith → victory.

When you think on God’s word, three things happen: your faith is built up, your life is lifted, your circumstances are turned around. When you think on negative words, three things also happen: your faith is weakened, your emotions are crushed, your life is trapped. The same twenty-four hours, the same head on your shoulders — whatever you feed it is what grows.

Here is a picture: your thinking is like a steering wheel, and your life is like a car. Set the direction right and the road is right; set the direction wrong and, however hard you press the accelerator, you only go wrong faster. Many people are not lacking in effort; they are working hard with the steering wheel turned the wrong way. That is also why God’s order is to change the mindset first and then the behaviour — if the steering wheel hasn’t turned, no amount of acceleration will help.

But brothers and sisters, please be sure to remember this: faith is not a feeling; faith is choosing to believe God’s word.

Feelings change; the word does not. Feelings rise and fall with sleep, blood sugar, the weather and the look on other people’s faces; but God’s word is “settled in heaven forever” (see Psalm 119:89). If we build our faith on feelings, it is like building a house on the waves. The Bible defines faith like this: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Neither “assurance” nor “proof” is the language of emotion; they are the language of law and property — a title deed for something not yet seen, yet already held in your hand.

This is exactly where the Israelites lost at Kadesh Barnea. Twelve spies saw the same land of Canaan and the same sons of Anak, but they brought back two kinds of thinking. Ten of the spies said, “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33b). But Caleb said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30b). The difference was not in the intelligence they gathered but in their thinking; not in how tall the giants were but in what they saw themselves as in their own hearts. In the end, the generation that said “grasshoppers” fell dead in the wilderness, while Caleb, who said “well able to overcome”, was still going up to take the hill country at eighty-five.

In 1998 the psychologist Barbara Fredrickson put forward her “broaden-and-build theory”, showing that positive emotions broaden the range of a person’s thinking and action in the moment, while negative emotions narrow attention. This is a glimmer of light within common grace; but the thinking of faith goes deeper than positive emotion — positive emotion looks inward for resources, while the thinking of faith draws upward on God’s resources. “Above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16).

The concentration-camp survivor and psychologist Viktor Frankl wrote a stunning sentence in Man’s Search for Meaning: everything can be taken from a man but one thing, the last of the human freedoms — the freedom to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances. Even in the darkest place, a person still has one authority that cannot be taken away: the choice of how to think. Brothers and sisters, how much more is this true for God’s children: not only can we choose how to think, we also have God’s word to think on, and the Holy Spirit within us guiding our thinking.

So how, concretely, do we practise the thinking of faith? Paul gives us a list: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). Eight qualities, like eight thresholds. Before any thought comes in, ask it first: Are you true? Are you honourable? Are you pure? Whatever cannot get over the threshold, show it the door. This is something every brother and sister can begin doing today.

A 321 insight: faith is not a feeling; it is choosing to believe God’s word. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you find joy, rely on the brain and you find worry. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: It Begins with a Change of Mindset
sections.html:
Let us set today’s four key points back into the full picture of 321.

First, the Three Foundations are the three pillars of “right thinking”. Jesus is my role model — however he thought in the wilderness, that is how I think. The Bible is my standard — it isn’t right because I feel it is right; it counts only because God has said it. The Holy Spirit is my guide — the Counsellor who lives within me reminds me whenever my thinking drifts.

Second, the Two Core Values are the direction of “right thinking”. Let Jesus be King: only one can sit on the throne of my thinking — not my circumstances, not other people’s verdicts, not my emotions, but Jesus. Let Jesus receive all the glory: when I choose to believe God’s word and experience God’s work, the glory goes not to my optimism, not to my willpower, but entirely to him.

Third, the Goal is where “right thinking” belongs. Only a person whose thinking has been renewed by truth can be of one heart with others and establish God’s system together.

Fourth, the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Think about it: almost all our negative thoughts revolve around a “self” — my face, my losses, my grievances, my sense of security, my future. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; when I insist on thinking my own way, I am really trying to make God’s decisions for him. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. So only the selfless can truly rest: I hand the facts over to God, and I am responsible only for believing the truth. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Fifth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This lesson moves the very first link. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — the order cannot be reversed.

Sixth, the change of perspective. From man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The facts are earthly and temporary; truth is heavenly and eternal.

Seventh, the 920 practice. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. When we think on God’s word and live out a selfless (0) life, the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23a) — flow naturally in our relationships. You will find that once your thinking changes, the words that come out of your mouth are different; once your words are different, the atmosphere at home is different.

Eighth, the 235 relationships. Fighting your own thoughts alone is very hard. Find a selfless spiritual companion to be your “2”, reminding each other and praying for each other; be shepherded, and shepherd others, within the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally, in the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, fight this battle of the mind together. One person thinking alone easily goes round in circles; when two or three think God’s word through together, they become an alliance for victory.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let us use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to carry them through thoroughly.

Practice 1: When problems come, go back to God’s word first

When you face difficulty, don’t start by analysing the circumstances; start by asking: “What does God’s word say?” Let truth be the starting point of your thinking.

Information: today, copy three verses onto a card — Romans 10:17, 1 John 5:4 and Isaiah 43:19. Information is the entrance; words you have not stored up cannot be drawn on in an emergency.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine on them, so that one of the verses suddenly “lights up” and becomes his word to you personally.

Conviction: settle it in your heart — not “let’s try and see”, but “this is how it is”.

Implementation: from tomorrow morning, whenever anything goes wrong, pause for three seconds and ask, “What does God’s word say?” Only then speak, only then act.

Practice 2: Deliberately reject negative and lying thoughts

When a negative thought appears, immediately replace it with a declaration of God’s word, such as “God reigns” or “God can make a way”, and stop the wrong thought from developing any further.

Evaluation: every evening, take three minutes to look back — which thought did I let settle in today? Did it come from God, or from the enemy?

Correction: not suppression, but replacement. An empty house will be occupied again; only when God’s word moves in does the lie have nowhere to live. “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11).

Practice 3: Practise thinking with faith every day

Choose one of God’s promises, think on it and declare it again and again, so that your system of thinking is renewed by faith and transformation begins from within.

Repetition: one verse, one week — morning, noon and night, read it once, think on it once, declare it once. Neural pathways are worn in by repetition, and so are spiritual pathways.

Multiplication: share what you have experienced with your “2”. When you speak the truth out, it takes root more deeply in you; when you help someone begin to think rightly, you have taken part in establishing God’s system.

A Gentle Reminder

If our thinking is not led by truth, it will be carried off by circumstances.

If you don’t deal with your thoughts, your thoughts will bind you.

God’s word is the one standard for your thinking.

So pay attention to “what you are thinking”.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Change Your Thinking, Change Your Life
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, the key to life lies not in circumstances but in thinking.

Think wrongly and you fall into trouble; think rightly and you enter into victory.

Today God is inviting you: change your thinking, change your way of seeing, change your life.

When you begin to think God’s way, you will discover — there is a way in the wilderness, there are rivers in the desert, there is resurrection in the midst of death. The wilderness is still the wilderness, but now there is a road through it; the desert is still the desert, but now there are rivers in it; the tomb is still the tomb, but in front of it stands the Lord who said, “I am the resurrection and the life.”

All this change is not merely so that life will go a little more smoothly for us; it is so that Jesus may reign as King in our thinking, and so that Jesus may receive all the glory in our lives.

So from today, let us make a decision: I will no longer think by feelings; I will think by the truth.

keyVerses: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17)
“For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith.” (1 John 5:4)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I choose to believe your word.
Whatever my circumstances, I will not dwell on the negative, and I will not accept the enemy’s lies.
I will think on the truth, on your promises and on your power.
Let my thinking be filled with faith.
By faith I will overcome the world.
In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare it. Amen!
practices: When problems come, go back to God’s word first
Deliberately reject negative and lying thoughts
Practise thinking with faith every day
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
You know how easily our thinking is led around by our circumstances. Forgive us, Lord: so often we worry before we have prayed, and draw conclusions before we have searched your word.

Lord, renew our hearts and minds with your truth. Help us no longer to think by our feelings but by your word; no longer to be limited by the past, but to believe that you are still doing new things today. Give us strength, so that when the enemy’s lies come, we do not argue and do not accept them, but simply declare your word.
Holy Spirit, guide our thinking every day; let Jesus reign as King on the throne of our minds, and let all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: What recent situation has led your thinking around by the circumstances? Set beside “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17), which verse of God’s word could you put in its place as a new starting point for your thinking?

Recall a disappointment of the “if you would have been here” kind. As you read, “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing” (Isaiah 43:18–19a), in what matter are you willing to believe afresh that God can work in an entirely new way?
l132.title: Let Truth Lead Our Thinking
l132.subtitle: Thinking Rightly (Part 2): Circumstances Don’t Decide Whether You Overcome — How You Think Does
l132.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Nothing Happens “Suddenly”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

First, picture a scene in your mind. In a delivery room, a mother holds her newborn baby, and the nurse beside her smiles and says, “Congratulations — your baby was born today.” That is quite true; the child really was born today. But we all know this child’s life certainly did not begin today. He has been forming in his mother’s womb for two hundred and eighty days. What we see today is simply the unseen process at last coming into view.

Brothers and sisters, life is like that too.

We often see it in the news: someone who has always been gentle suddenly does something unbelievable; a co-worker who has served for years suddenly falls; a family that looked happy suddenly breaks apart. People shake their heads and say, “How could he suddenly turn into this?”

But brothers and sisters, I must tell you very honestly: nothing happens “suddenly”. Whatever is born today was conceived yesterday. Whatever can be seen on the outside has long been growing to maturity on the inside.

Many people think the problem in life is “what I did wrong”. But God wants us to see a deeper layer: we don’t do wrong first; we think wrong first. It isn’t our behaviour that goes wrong first; it is our thinking that has gone wrong.

Scripture says, “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:15).

This verse uncovers a vitally important spiritual principle: life begins with “thinking”; and thinking is a process of “gestation”.

Whatever you are thinking inside is what you will one day live out. Whatever you feed in your heart today, you will harvest in your life tomorrow.

That is why changing a life does not start with changing behaviour; it starts with changing how we “think”. Behaviour is the fruit; thinking is the root. If you only prune the fruit, next year the same fruit will grow again; if you deal with the root, the whole tree will be different.

In the 321 vision we see this even more clearly. The path of the old self is: think about myself, and so conceive sin, which in the end brings death. The path of the new self is: think about Jesus, and so conceive life, which in the end brings victory. The same heart, the same person — the only difference is what you let move in, and what you let grow inside you.

The seventeenth-century French thinker Blaise Pascal said in his Pensées that man is only a reed, the feeblest thing in nature, but he is a thinking reed. All our dignity lies in thought. Scripture goes a step further: our destiny, too, lies in our thinking.

So today we are going to enter together into a crucial practice: managing our thinking is managing the very source of our life.

Please hold three questions in your heart, and carry them with you to the end of today’s message: What am I carrying inside me right now? How long have I been feeding this thought? If it were born, would it be sin, or would it be Christ?

Brothers and sisters, may the Holy Spirit shine on our thinking today — not to make us condemn ourselves, but to bring us back to the source and let us start again.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: James and “Two Kinds of Birth”
sections.html: To truly grasp the power of this passage, we first need to get to know the book itself.

sections.heading: 1. Author, Date and Recipients
sections.html:
Evangelical scholars generally agree that the author of James is James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. In Galatians 1:19 Paul mentions “James, the Lord’s brother”; and Acts 15:13 records that at the Jerusalem Council it was this same James who gave the closing address. At first he did not believe in the Lord Jesus (John 7:5 records, “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him”), until the risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7); only then did he become a pillar of the church in Jerusalem.

The letter was written roughly between AD 45 and 49, which may make it one of the earliest books of the New Testament. As for its recipients, James 1:1 says it plainly: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion: Greetings.” This refers to the Jewish Christians scattered everywhere by the persecution that followed Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1).

They were a suffering people. They had left their homes, lost their property, lived as poor people in strange cities, been oppressed by the rich and rejected by their own countrymen. In such a situation, the easiest thing for anyone to do is this — to complain in their heart. To complain about their circumstances, about other people, about God. And what James sets out to deal with is exactly that inner world, quietly taking shape in the midst of trouble.

sections.heading: 2. Genre and Context
sections.html:
The genre of James is very distinctive. It is close to the wisdom literature of the Old Testament, every sentence a gem like the Proverbs; and at the same time it echoes the Lord Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount at every turn. This younger brother, who once sat at the same table with Jesus in their home in Nazareth, now engraves his elder brother’s words, one by one, into his own letter.

Our key passage falls within a crucial argument. James 1:2–4 says that trials produce endurance; James 1:12 says, “Blessed is a person who endures temptation, for when he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life.” Reading this far, someone is bound to ask: if trials are given by God, then when I am tempted and fall, can I blame God for that too?

James immediately blocks that escape route. James 1:13 says, “Let no man say when he is tempted, ‘I am tempted by God,’ for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.”

Here there is an important point from the original language. The Greek word peirasmos can be translated either “trial” or “temptation”. One word, two outcomes: God permits circumstances to test us, in order to make us complete; Satan and our own lust use the very same circumstances to tempt us, in order to destroy us. The difference is not in the circumstances but in the “thinking” inside.

So James is absolutely categorical: the source of the problem is not God, not circumstances, not other people, but “his own lust”.

sections.heading: 3. Two Pictures in the Original
sections.html:
James 1:14–15 uses two very vivid sets of pictures, which unfortunately are hard to see in the Chinese.

The first is a picture of fishing and hunting. “Drawn away” in the original is exelkō, which originally means luring prey out of the hole where it is hiding; “enticed” is deleazō, a word whose root is “bait”, meaning to lure a fish onto the hook with tasty bait. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that Satan never shows you the hook? He only shows you the bait. In the Garden of Eden he did not say, “Come and rebel against God.” What he said was, “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5).

The second is a picture of pregnancy and birth. “Conceived” in the original is syllambanō, the very word used of a woman conceiving; “bears” in “bears sin” is tiktō, which means to give birth; and “produces death” uses apokyeō, meaning to deliver a child. James is describing a family tree of three generations under one roof: lust is the grandmother, sin is the mother, death is the grandchild. One generation gives birth to the next, with no break in between.

Even more striking: James uses the very same word, apokyeō, again just five verses later. James 1:18 says, “Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The theme of this whole passage is “two kinds of birth”.

On one side, lust conceives and gives birth to sin, and gives birth to death. On the other side, God, by the word of truth, gives birth to us and brings forth first fruits.

Two kinds of gestation, two delivery rooms, two kinds of life. And what decides which delivery room you are in is not your circumstances, not your background, but what you let into your thinking every day.

This brings us to today’s first teaching.

sections.heading: 3. Teaching One: Thinking Is Not Neutral — It Is “Pregnant”
sections.html:
1. The text: the moment of conception has already begun

“But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14–15)

James uses a very striking metaphor — conception.

Our thinking is like a womb; a thought is like a seed. Whatever is planted in it is what will grow.

Brothers and sisters, there is one thing to pay special attention to here: there is no such thing as being “a little bit pregnant”. A woman cannot say, “I’m only slightly pregnant.” Either she has conceived or she hasn’t. In the same way, when a thought enters you, you either hand it back or you take it in; and once you have taken it in, the gestation has already begun.

What you constantly think about inside will not disappear by itself. It will only grow, accumulate, mature, and finally be born.

Many people say, “I’m only thinking about it; I haven’t actually done anything.” But God says: you are already pregnant.

Just as a mother’s pregnancy does not begin on the day the child is born but from the moment of conception — from that moment on, whatever the mother eats, the child absorbs; wherever the mother’s blood flows, there the child grows.

So we must understand one thing: thinking is not “no big deal”; thinking is “something happening right now”.

2. Scripture interpreting Scripture: the Lord Jesus moves the starting point of sin earlier

In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus puts it even more directly:

“but I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.” (Matthew 5:28)

Brothers and sisters, notice the Lord’s word — “already”. Nothing has yet been done on the outside, but on the inside it is already complete.

The law looks at what has been carried out; God looks at the motive. Human courts begin their judgement with behaviour; God’s court begins with the thought.

The Lord Jesus also said, “For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19).

Look at the order: evil thoughts come first. Murder is not the first to come out; evil thoughts are. Evil thoughts are the firstborn, and all the rest are their brothers.

Let us trace it back further, to humanity’s first fall. Genesis 3:6 says, “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.”

Count the order of the verbs here: saw, delighted, desired, took, ate, gave. The first three are all on the inside; only the last three are on the outside. Before Eve’s hand ever reached out, her heart had already reached out.

The apostle John sums up this order with great precision: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16).

And the corruption of that whole generation before the Flood, Scripture sums up in a single sentence: “Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil” (Genesis 6:5).

When God looked at that generation, he looked first not at their violence but at their thinking. For the thinking is the factory; the behaviour is only the product.

Proverbs says it more briefly still; the Chinese Union Version renders Proverbs 23:7, “For as he thinks in his heart, so is he.”

3. Key word: lust is not merely a “bad thought”

The Greek word for “lust” is epithymia, which literally means “a strong desire”. The word itself is neutral: in Luke 22:15, when the Lord Jesus says, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer,” the word for “earnestly desired” is the verb form of this same word.

In other words, God made us with the capacity to desire, and that in itself is good. The problem is not “having desires”, but that the object and the centre of our desire have turned towards ourselves.

When desire is centred on the self, it becomes lust; when desire is centred on God, it becomes a holy pursuit.

This is exactly what 321 says: the root of the problem is not “desire” but “the self-centred life”. The old self is self-centred, so even its most beautiful desires go astray; the new self is selfless, so even the most ordinary days can glorify God.

4. An example from daily life: the one that gets fed

Brothers and sisters, thoughts have one characteristic: the ones that aren’t fed starve to death; the ones that are fed grow.

Have you ever had this experience? Someone says something without meaning anything by it, and it has already passed. But that night you can’t sleep, so you take those words out and turn them over and over, thinking about them again and again. The next day, when you see that person, there is a wall in your heart. On the third day you begin telling others what’s wrong with him. By the seventh day you are already convinced that this is just the kind of person he is.

Tell me: during those seven days, what did that person do? He did nothing at all. It was you who fed a thought for seven days, and raised it from a seed into a tree.

5. Supporting evidence from science and psychology

In the 1960s Aaron T. Beck, a psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania in the United States, developed cognitive therapy. In his clinical work he found that patients with depression did not first feel low and then have negative thoughts; rather, first came a chain of “automatic thoughts” they were not even aware of, and the emotions followed. So his method of treatment was not to tell patients “don’t be sad”, but to help them catch the thought that flashed by and lay it out to be examined.

Brothers and sisters, this is the clinical version of James 1:15: first comes the thinking, then comes the fruit.

Another piece of supporting evidence comes from brain science. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed what is known as “Hebb’s rule”: if two neurons are repeatedly active at the same time, the connection between them grows stronger. Later generations have often condensed this rule into one sentence — neurons that fire together wire together.

In other words, every repeated thought is building a road in your brain. Think it once and you have walked across a lawn; think it a hundred times and you have trodden a footpath; think it a thousand times and it has become a tarmac road. No wonder some people say, “I can’t control myself” — it isn’t that they can’t control themselves; it is that the road has already been built.

In 2000, a team at University College London led by Eleanor Maguire published research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that London taxi drivers, because they had memorised complex streets for years, had noticeably more grey matter in the posterior hippocampus than a control group — and the longer they had been driving, the greater the difference.

Brothers and sisters, this is the wonder of God’s creation: what you think about day after day changes your brain. That is a warning, and it is also a promise. The warning is that wrong thinking will build a broad road inside you; the promise is that thinking on the truth can just as surely build a new road.

6. A 321 insight: thinking is the first stop of the “fivefold change”

321 says the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Notice that the first stop is mindset, not ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Many people have the order reversed: rush into ministry first, then patch up relationships, and the mindset never moves at all. The result is a lot of activity on the outside, but no change on the inside.

Brothers and sisters, 321 does not tell us to do less; it tells us to put the order right — life first, then relationships, then ministry. And the starting point of life is mindset; it is our “thinking”.

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

The word “transformed” in “transformed by the renewing of your mind” is metamorphoō in the original — the same change as a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. What God wants is not a polishing of behaviour but a change of nature; and the entrance to that change is your mind.

sections.heading: 4. Teaching Two: Wrong Thinking Naturally Gives Birth to Wrong Behaviour
sections.html:
1. A real tragedy: Herodias

There is a story in the Bible that plays out the process of “thoughts in gestation” to the full: the killing of John the Baptist.

It began very simply, with a single sentence.

“For John said to Herod, ‘It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.’” (Mark 6:18)

Herod Antipas had married Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, something expressly forbidden by Jewish law (Leviticus 18:16). John the Baptist said what ought to be said, and that one sentence fell into someone’s heart.

What Scripture records next is very important:

“Herodias set herself against him, and desired to kill him, but she couldn’t.” (Mark 6:19)

The Greek behind “set herself against him” (the Chinese Union Version: “held a grudge against him”) is enechō, which literally means “to hold something tightly inside, gripping it and never letting go”. Used here, it is precisely a picture of “conception” — she took that sentence inside herself and then held on to it day and night.

Notice what the text says: “desired to kill him, but she couldn’t.”

Brothers and sisters, this phrase “but she couldn’t” is crucial. It was not that she did not want to; it was that she could not yet. Her actions were held back, but her thinking was not. So through those days of “couldn’t”, she kept thinking, and thinking, and thinking.

And what was the result? The thought began to gestate, the hatred began to build, and when the opportunity came, the action followed naturally.

2. The due date arrives: a birthday banquet

Mark 6:21–28 records that the opportunity finally came. On Herod’s birthday a banquet was held; Herodias’ daughter came in and danced, and pleased Herod and his guests.

The king swore to her, “Whatever you shall ask of me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom” (Mark 6:23).

There is a detail here we must read carefully. It was Herod, not Herodias, who offered “half of my kingdom”. The daughter went out and asked her mother, “What shall I ask?” Herodias’ answer was only a few words: the head of John the Baptist.

Brothers and sisters, do you see the terrible arithmetic?

Before her lay half a kingdom. She could have asked for cities, for gold and silver, for position, for a lifetime of wealth and honour. But she wanted none of it; she wanted only one head.

Why? Because once something carried for too long reaches its due date, reason has nothing more to say. She was not acting on impulse in that moment; in that moment she was giving birth. The child had long been fully formed; when the time came, it was naturally born.

So the text continues: “The king was exceedingly sorry, but for the sake of his oaths, and of his dinner guests, he didn’t wish to refuse her” (Mark 6:26).

One person’s thinking finally took away another person’s life, and bound a king’s conscience as well.

3. Scripture interpreting Scripture: “gestation periods” in the Bible

This is not an isolated case. Again and again the Bible lets us see the gestation period of a thought.

Cain. “Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell” (Genesis 4:5). God himself came to reason with him: “If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it” (Genesis 4:7). The picture behind “crouches at the door” is of a wild beast crouching at the doorway, waiting to pounce. God said: you must rule over it. But Cain did not rule over it; he fed it. In the very next verse there is blood in the field.

Absalom. After his sister Tamar was violated, Scripture says, “Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad; for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar” (2 Samuel 13:22). Neither good nor bad — on the surface, all was calm. Then the next verse says: “After two full years” (2 Samuel 13:23). Two years later, Amnon died at a feast.

Brothers and sisters, two years. Those were not two years of forgetting; they were two years of gestation.

David. “At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at” (2 Samuel 11:2). Next came the enquiry, and then the sending for her. Looking, thinking, enquiring, sending for her — at every step he could have stopped, but at no step did he stop. In the end adultery gave birth to murder, and murder gave birth to the sword in his own household. The family tree of James 1:15 played out in full in David’s life.

So we must learn one thing: don’t deal only with “the wrong thing done”; go back to the source and deal with “the wrong thought thought”.

4. Confirmation from psychology: rumination

In 1991 Susan Nolen-Hoeksema, a psychologist at Yale University in the United States, put forward her “response styles theory”, studying a thinking habit she called “rumination”: going over one’s negative emotions and their causes again and again, without taking any action.

Her research showed that people in the habit of rumination have a markedly higher risk of later becoming depressed; rumination does not help people think things through — on the contrary, it amplifies hostility.

Brothers and sisters, “rumination” is a remarkably apt word. A cow brings up the grass it has swallowed and chews it all over again. That is exactly what Herodias did: she chewed over that one sentence more times than anyone could count.

And what the psychologists did not say, the Bible does: rumination does not only harm the emotions; rumination conceives.

Martin Luther is commonly thought to have said something like this: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair. The source of the saying is hard to confirm, but the line it draws is thoroughly biblical: a thought flying past is not your sin; letting it build a nest is your choice.

5. A 321 insight: both sides lose, or both sides win

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

The story of Herodias and Herod is a textbook case of “both sides lose”.

One of them, to protect her own face and her marriage, killed God’s prophet; the other, to protect his own face before his dinner guests, went against his own conscience. They both won that banquet, and both lost themselves.

History adds a footnote. The Jewish historian Josephus records in his Antiquities of the Jews that Herod Antipas was later deposed by a ruling of the Roman emperor Gaius (Caligula) and banished to the region of Gaul, and that Herodias went with him. The position they had schemed so hard to keep, they did not keep in the end.

And 321 wants us to see a deeper layer still: Herodias’ problem was not only hatred; it was “the self-centred life”. Her centre was herself — her own marriage, her own reputation, her own position. Anyone who threatened that “self” had to be removed.

But Paul speaks of another way: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The self-centred life lets lust conceive within; the selfless life lets Christ be formed within.

Paul says to the church in Galatia, “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

“Formed” in the original is morphoō, referring to formation in one’s very nature, not outward dressing-up. Paul says he is “again in travail” for them — he puts himself in the place of a midwife and a mother, so that Christ may be formed in them.

Brothers and sisters, please keep these words in your heart: at this moment, either sin is taking shape in you, or Christ is taking shape in you. There is no third possibility, and no middle ground.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Three: What You See and Hear Decides What You Carry Within
sections.html:
1. Thoughts don’t appear out of nowhere

We have already seen that thoughts conceive and thoughts give birth. So now we must ask an even more crucial question — where do thoughts come from?

Brothers and sisters, thoughts don’t appear out of nowhere. Thoughts have a source. And that source is what you “see” and what you “hear”.

Wrong seeing brings wrong thinking; wrong hearing brings wrong intentions. Right seeing brings right thinking; right hearing brings life-giving intentions.

That is why the Lord Jesus particularly emphasises the eyes, and Proverbs particularly emphasises the ears.

2. The Lord Jesus on the eyes: one lamp decides the whole house

“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

Notice the Lord’s metaphor: the eye is a lamp. A lamp is not the thing you look at; a lamp is the thing that decides what you are able to see. Whatever your eyes look at, that is the kind of light your whole self lives in.

And even more worth noticing is the context of these words. Just before, the Lord Jesus says, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Just after, he says, “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

In other words, the eye is not an isolated organ. The eye is the door of the heart, the indicator of loyalty. Wherever your eyes rest for a long time, your heart is already there.

Job understood this, so he said, “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1).

Notice that he does not say, “I try hard not to think about it.” He says, “I made a covenant with my eyes.” He was dealing with the entrance, not the exit.

David also says, “I will set no vile thing before my eyes” (Psalm 101:3).

“Set no vile thing before my eyes” — this is an active decision. It is about where the screens in your home are placed, what time you put your phone down, which page you open when you are alone late at night.

3. Proverbs on the ears: putting the words into your heart

“My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings. Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and health to their whole body. Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:20–23)

Brothers and sisters, look at the order in this passage: attend, turn your ear, let them not depart from your eyes, keep them in your heart, keep your heart. From the ear, to the eyes, to the heart; from the entrance outside to the source within.

The Hebrew word for “keep” is natsar, meaning to guard or watch over, used of keeping watch over a city or guarding a vineyard. In other words, your heart is a city, and you must post sentries at the city gate.

Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

Faith comes by hearing. What about fear, then? Doubt? Bitterness? They also come by hearing. Whatever voice you let speak in your ear every day will sooner or later become the voice in your heart.

4. Scripture interpreting Scripture: twelve spies, one land, two ways of seeing

Numbers 13 records that Moses sent twelve spies to explore the land of Canaan. Forty days later they returned, bringing back the same grapes, the same terrain, the same city walls, the same inhabitants. Yet they brought back two completely different reports.

Ten of the spies said, “There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33).

Notice what is so terrible about this sentence: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers.” Who said they were grasshoppers? Not God, not the enemy — they came to see themselves that way by looking at themselves. Then they projected their own view onto the enemy — “and so we were in their sight.” In fact, the sons of Anak had never said any such thing.

But Caleb said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30).

The same land, the same giants. Where was the difference? The difference was this: the ten spies looked at the giants and then looked back at God; Caleb looked at God and then looked back at the giants.

Brothers and sisters, the order in which you look decides the content of your thinking; the content of your thinking decides the road you walk. That night the whole congregation of Israel raised a loud cry and wept, and forty days of spying out the land bought them forty years in the wilderness.

5. Supporting evidence from science: what you see shapes you

When God made us, he placed an extraordinarily precise receiving system in us. Each human optic nerve has about a million nerve fibres, carrying the outside world inward day and night without ceasing, encoding every day, shaping you every day.

In 1961 the Stanford University psychologist Albert Bandura published his famous “Bobo doll experiment”: one group of children watched an adult attack an inflatable doll, while another group watched an adult play quietly. Afterwards, the children who had seen the aggressive behaviour imitated those actions markedly more in their own play. From this he developed social learning theory — people do not have to experience something themselves; simply seeing it is enough for them to learn.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the Bible said long ago: whatever you look at, you will become like.

And Paul turns this principle around and applies it in the most glorious direction: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

“Are transformed into the same image” — here “transformed” is again metamorphoō in the original, the same word as “transformed by the renewing of your mind” in Romans 12:2.

Brothers and sisters, what great grace this is: fix your eyes on the Lord, and you will become like the Lord. You don’t have to remake yourself through gritted teeth; you only have to put your eyes in the right place every day.

So the writer of Hebrews issues the call: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2).

6. A 321 insight: the Three Foundations are the three entrances

Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations of 321 line up exactly with our three entrances.

Jesus is my role model — this is the direction of the eyes. I don’t look at myself, at other people or at my circumstances; I look at Jesus. Jesus is the focal point.

The Bible is my standard — this is the content of the ears. It isn’t right because I feel it is right; it counts only because God has said it. In this way, the voice in my heart is corrected by the truth.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — this is the renewal of the heart. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you find worry, rely on the heart and you find joy.

When you choose this way, the life of Christ begins to form within you.

So listen carefully to today’s main point: the key to victory is not struggling with all your might not to sin, but, at the source, not letting sin conceive.

Those who try to stop it at the exit grow more and more weary; those who stand guard at the entrance find the going lighter and lighter.

If you are constantly looking at the negative, constantly comparing, constantly feeding lust and hatred, you are nurturing the old self. If you are constantly looking at Jesus, constantly reading God’s word, constantly thinking on grace and truth, you are nurturing the new self.

Our perspective must change: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

Paul says it categorically: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Letting Christ Be Formed in Us
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us set today’s message within the whole picture of 321.

1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, so the direction of my thinking is corrected; the Bible is my standard, so the content of my thinking is renewed; the Holy Spirit is my guide, so the power behind my thinking is exchanged.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — including in my thinking; let Jesus receive all the glory — including in my most hidden thoughts.

Brothers and sisters, a person’s true king is the one who reigns when he is alone, in the places in his heart that no one else sees. If Jesus reigns only in my mouth and not in my thinking, that is not yet truly letting him reign.

The Goal: establish God’s system. And God’s system begins with renewed thinking. For any system is nothing more than the accumulated mindsets of many people. The essence of the Babylonian system is self-centred thinking magnified into a whole world; God’s system is selfless thinking built by God into a family.

2. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The old self is self-centred: it thinks about itself, conceives sin, and brings death.

The new self is selfless: it thinks about Jesus, conceives life, and brings victory.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. In our thinking, pride says: I will judge personally, I will condemn personally, I will take revenge personally — I move God’s seat over and sit in it myself.

What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. In our thinking, humility says: I hand this person over to God, I hand this matter over to God, and I return to where I ought to stand.

Brothers and sisters, Herodias would not return to her originally intended position, so she had to remove the man who pointed out what that position was. And this is the most frightening thing about pride: pride cannot bear to be exposed to the light; pride must protect its own ideas.

James says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Proverbs says, “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

3. Life first, then relationships, then ministry

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s lesson stands at the first stop. But if we get this stop right, the other four will move along with it.

The priority of relationships is the same: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions.

Only a person whose thinking has been renewed has the power to restore relationships. For most broken relationships are not snapped by a single event; they are worn through by a string of thoughts that were never dealt with.

4. The 920 practice

321 says: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; we are to practise living out a selfless (0) life, bearing the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit towards them.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: who is the person who most easily takes over your thoughts?

The one whose name makes your heart sink, the one you have already judged a hundred times in your heart — that person is exactly the “2” God has given you.

And the first of the nine fruits is love. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.”

Notice the last one: self-control. In the original it is egkrateia, meaning “ruling from within”. Brothers and sisters, self-control is not only keeping your mouth and your hands in check; self-control is first of all keeping your thinking in check.

5. The 235 relationships

321 says: to become a “2” with a selfless person is to be spiritual companions; to build a “3” is to be spiritual parents and spiritual children; to become a “5” is to be a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Why does the renewal of our thinking need a “2”? Because what our thoughts thrive on most is being alone too long with no one knowing.

James 5:16 says, “Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed.”

A thought kept hidden will grow; a thought spoken aloud will shrink. When you say honestly before your “2”, “I’ve been thinking about this for days — please pray for me,” at that moment the gestation is interrupted.

Brothers and sisters, don’t fight your own thoughts alone. God never designed us to fight on our own.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Manage Your Thinking, Stop the Wrong Gestation
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices. We are going to follow them, and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take each practice deeper.

Practice 1: Thought awareness — catch the first thought

Every day, notice the thoughts that come up most often. When negative thoughts, lustful thoughts or judgemental thoughts appear, notice them at once. Ask yourself one question: “Did this thought come from God?”

Brothers and sisters, awareness is not condemnation; awareness is standing guard. You are not picking faults with yourself; you are checking identities at the city gate.

David’s prayer can become our daily prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

A suggestion: get a small notebook, and for seven days in a row write down the three thoughts that recur most each day. You will be surprised to find that they are almost the same three.

Practice 2: Thought exchange — replace lies with truth

When a wrong thought appears, don’t suppress it, and don’t let it run free either; replace it with God’s word.

Why not suppress it? In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner conducted a famous experiment: he asked participants “not to think of a white bear” for five minutes. The result: the harder people tried not to think of it, the more often the white bear appeared; and after the experiment there was a rebound, with people thinking of it even more often than at the start. He called this the “ironic process”.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a vitally important reminder: you cannot empty your mind by saying “don’t think about it”. An empty house will be occupied; an occupied house can only be taken over by a better master.

So Paul says, “throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5).

Notice the phrase “bringing into captivity” (the Chinese Union Version: “taking back”). Taking back is not emptying; taking back is a change of master.

Paul also says, “whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8).

In practice: prepare three to five “pocket verses” of your own, written on cards or on your phone’s home screen. The moment that thought comes, read them aloud at once and declare them.

For example, the declaration in the lesson: I am not ruled by sin; I belong to the Lord. Its basis is Romans 6:14: “For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace.”

Practice 3: Cleansing what you see and hear — change your input

Deliberately cut down on negative information, sexual stimulation and content that breeds comparison; deliberately increase Bible reading, worship and spiritual teaching. Change the input, and you change the source of your thinking.

Brothers and sisters, this practice is the most practical, and also the one fewest people are willing to do.

Here is a simple check: open your phone’s screen time for the past seven days and take a look. Where you spend the most time is the kind of life you are feeding. This is not law; it is a health check.

A suggestion: set a boundary for the evening — after a certain time, the phone stays in the living room; set an order for the morning — when you open your eyes, look at God’s word first, and only then at your messages.

The psalmist says, “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). Notice: first the hiding, then the not sinning. The hiding is the daily groundwork; the not sinning is the result in the moment of testing.

Practice 4: Walking with the Holy Spirit — let the Lord govern your thinking

Pray every day: “Lord, govern my thinking; let me think what pleases you.”

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain and you find worry; rely on the heart and you find joy.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t turn the renewal of your thinking into hard labour of willpower. Using willpower to quit a thought is like holding a ball under water with your hand — the moment you let go, it bounces back up.

Romans 8:6 says, “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.”

The word “mind” in the original is phronēma, referring to the inclination of one’s thinking, what the heart is bound to. So this verse is really saying: wherever your thinking leans, that is the kind of result you will receive.

In practice: every morning, speak aloud and hand over the day’s thinking; whenever your thoughts are stirred up, stop and be still for thirty seconds and say, “Holy Spirit, please take control.”

Practice 5: Choosing selflessness — don’t let yourself be king

When “what I want” rises to the surface, stop, and ask instead: “If Jesus were me, how would Jesus think?” Then choose obedience rather than indulgence.

Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). The passage that follows is the great hymn of the Lord Jesus emptying himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbling himself in obedience to the point of death.

Brothers and sisters, “have this mind which was in Christ Jesus” is not a slogan; it is an exchange of places — handing the throne of your thinking out of your own hands.

Going deeper with the eight stages

Information: today you heard the truth that “thinking is a process of gestation”. That is information.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn this information into revelation for you — so that over one specific thought you suddenly see: so I have been carrying this for this long.

Conviction: not merely feeling that it makes sense, but truly yielding in your heart, willing to admit: I have been feeding it all along.

Implementation: starting today, do the smallest thing first. Not all five practices at once — just one to begin with.

Evaluation: after a week, ask yourself: have those three recurring thoughts changed? Which days did I hold my ground? Which days did I lose it? Before I lost it, what had I been watching, what had I been listening to?

Correction: not self-blame, but adjustment. Rearrange the time of day, the entrance, the situation that tripped you up.

Repetition: Hebb’s rule reminds us that a new road has to be walked many times before it takes shape. Don’t give up because you have failed three times; a tarmac road is trodden out one step at a time.

Multiplication: when you have experienced change, pass it on to your “2”. Bring someone along to do these seven days of practice with you. You will find that when you are leading someone else, you stand at your steadiest.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder: Only Humility Can Stop the Wrong Gestation
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, before we come to the close, allow me to add a small reminder.

Thinking is not a small thing; thinking is the starting point. Don’t wait until the behaviour comes out and then regret it; deal with the thought just as it first appears. For the sooner you deal with it, the easier it is. A seed can be pulled up with two fingers; a tree needs a saw; a forest takes a lifetime.

What is growing inside you right now is not an accident; it is the result of what you allow every day.

And whether the wrong gestation can be stopped depends, in the end, on one thing — humility.

The humble let God shine his light on their thinking; the proud protect their own ideas.

When the humble hear a word of warning, they say, “Lord, is it really so? Search me.” When the proud hear a word of warning, they say, “You don’t understand my situation.”

Herodias heard one true sentence spoken by God’s prophet. She did not let that sentence shine light on her; she chose to remove the man who spoke it. Brothers and sisters, we must be careful: when we find ourselves wanting again and again to get rid of the person who warns us, of that voice, of that passage of Scripture, we are already walking the same road.

So please remember: only humility can stop the wrong gestation; only selflessness can let Christ be formed within.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call: Begin with Your Thinking, Return to Him
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

Life is not lost in our behaviour; it is lost in our thinking.

Thinking is where everything begins; thinking is the gestation of life.

Today God is not asking you to try harder. God is inviting you: begin with your thinking, and return to him.

Notice the difference: if it depends on trying harder, the pressure is on you, and the more you do the wearier you become; if it is returning to him, sovereignty goes back into his hands, and all you need to do is come home every day.

Jesus said, “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free” (John 8:32).

Freedom does not mean there will be no more temptation; freedom means that when temptation comes, you are no longer someone who has no choice but to follow it.

When you choose to see rightly, hear rightly and think rightly, you will live out a right life, a right way of living, a victorious life.

May we all become people like this: no longer carrying sin within, carrying only Christ.

Live out the selfless life; let Jesus live in us, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to give you a specific call.

First, admit honestly in your heart: there is a thought I have been feeding for a long time. Don’t gloss over it; name it.

Second, hand it over. Hand it over now; don’t wait until you feel ready.

Third, put a verse in its place. Choose one today, and carry it with you through the day.

Fourth, find a “2”. Before today is over, tell a spiritual companion: I am going to practise in my thinking; please pray for me, and please ask me about it in a month.

Brothers and sisters, Paul says, “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

You are not patching up an old self; you are letting a new self grow. May Christ be formed in you today, may he reign as King in your thinking, and may all the glory be his.

keyVerses: But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death. (James 1:14–15)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, let us open our mouths together and declare in the name of the Lord Jesus:
My thinking will be renewed by God, and my heart will be filled with truth.
I will not let lust conceive within me; I will let Christ be formed in me.
I reject every wrong thought; I choose to think on God’s word.
I choose to look to Jesus, listen to Jesus and follow Jesus.
I do not live in the cycle of the old self; I live in the life of the new self.
I will surely be an overcomer. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen!
practices: Thought awareness — catch the first thought
Thought exchange — replace lies with truth
Cleansing what you see and hear — change your input
Walking with the Holy Spirit — let the Lord govern your thinking
Choosing selflessness — don’t let yourself be king
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we grow quiet before you.
Lord, you search us and you know us. You see not only our actions but our thoughts; you hear not only our words but what our hearts have left unspoken.

Lord, we confess that there are thoughts within us that we have been feeding for a long time. There is bitterness, there is comparison, there is fear, there is lust, there is judgement. We once thought it was only thinking and did no harm; today you have shown us that it is a pregnancy under way.
Lord, forgive us. Wash our hearts and minds clean with your precious blood.

Help us, from today, to look at what we ought to look at, to listen to what we ought to listen to, and to think what pleases you. Be the gatekeeper of our eyes, the watchman of our ears and the King of our minds.
Holy Spirit, take control of our thinking yourself. When wrong thoughts come, remind us at once; when we are weak and lose our ground, lift us up, and do not let us lie down in self-reproach.
Lord Jesus, be formed in us. It is no longer we who live, but you who live in us. Reign as King in our thinking, and receive all the glory.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: James 1:14–15 says, “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” Please be quiet for a minute and think honestly: over this past month, what thought has recurred most often within me? How long have I been feeding it? If it grows to full size, what will it give birth to?

Matthew 6:22 says, “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” Please share specifically: among the things I “see” and “hear” each day, which entrance most needs adjusting? This week, what clear change will I make that others can check on? Please name the time, the place and the method, and ask the group to follow up with me in a month.
l133.title: Thinking Is a Process of Conceiving
l133.subtitle: Managing Your Thoughts Is Managing the Source of Life
l133.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Thought That Sits on the Edge of Your Bed at 3 a.m.
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we come to today’s lesson, let me first walk with you into a night that many of us know all too well.

It is three o’clock in the morning. You didn’t want to wake up, but you’re awake. The house is still, the family is asleep, and there’s no hint of daylight at the window. You lie there. Nothing has happened yet, and yet a thought is already sitting on the edge of the bed, waiting for you.

Maybe it’s something a colleague said during the day. You smiled it off at the time, but now it replays, line by line. Maybe it’s someone you have already forgiven three times. You thought that page was long turned, but now that hot, sour feeling rises in your chest again. Maybe it’s an image you shouldn’t have looked at twice. At the time you just scrolled past it, but now it floats back up on its own, sharp and clear.

You tell yourself: stop thinking about it, stop thinking about it, go to sleep. But the harder you tell yourself not to think about it, the clearer the thought becomes. You roll over, and it rolls over with you; you shut your eyes, and there it is, behind your closed eyelids.

Brothers and sisters, if you have ever had a night like that, then today’s lesson is something God has prepared especially for you.

In our last lesson we saw together a very deep truth: thinking is a process of conception. Whatever you are thinking inside will give birth to something. A thought doesn’t stay a thought; a thought grows. Desire doesn’t stay desire; desire conceives. Scripture puts it very plainly: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14–15)

Once they grasped this truth, many brothers and sisters immediately asked a second question: “Pastor, I know that thoughts conceive. But I didn’t invite the thought — it came by itself. So what am I supposed to do?”

What a good question. If faith stops at “knowing”, people only end up blaming themselves more. Faith has to move on to “knowing what to do” before people can be set free.

So today God wants to take us a step further: the point is not only that “thoughts conceive”; the point is “how we manage the process of conception”.

The question has never been “Will we think?” As long as we’re alive, we will think. The question is this — how do we deal with the thoughts that have already appeared in our hearts?

Brothers and sisters, please remember this sentence; it is the key to the whole lesson today: some thoughts are not ones we actively choose, but we can choose — whether to let them stay, and whether to let them grow.

Whether a thought comes is not entirely up to you; whether it moves in is entirely up to you.

There is a saying, usually attributed to the Reformer Martin Luther, that puts it beautifully: “You cannot keep the birds from flying over your head, but you can keep them from building a nest in your hair.” A bird flying over takes a second; a bird building a nest takes a whole season. The flying over is called temptation; the nesting is called sin. God hasn’t asked you to chase every bird out of the sky. He asks you not to build them a nest on your head.

So how do we do it? Today Scripture gives us three very clear directions, the three teachings of this lesson. First, “I made a covenant with my eyes” (Job 31:1) — manage the entrance at the source. Second, all bitterness and wrath — “let [them] be put away from you” (Ephesians 4:31) — end the conception early. Third, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2) — overcome by replacing, not merely by refusing.

Put these three passages side by side and a beautiful order appears: one at the entrance, one in the process, one at the root. Job deals with “what hasn’t come in yet”; Ephesians deals with “what has already come in”; Romans deals with “the whole system”.

So, brothers and sisters, today we need to see one thing: God doesn’t merely want you not to sin; God wants to renew the whole system of your thinking.

Not sinning is defence; renewing the system is rebuilding. God doesn’t just want to give you stronger willpower; he wants to give you a new mind. This is exactly the starting point of the fivefold change 321 speaks of — change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Everything begins with the mindset; everything begins with our thoughts.

This morning, may the Holy Spirit himself come — not merely to prune the branches and leaves of our thinking, but to renew its roots.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Battlefields
sections.html:
To truly understand today’s message, let’s first stand at the historical scene of these three passages and hear the situations in which they were first spoken.

The first is Job 31:1.

The author of Job is unknown. It is generally thought to be one of the oldest books in the Bible, and its story is most likely set in the patriarchal period, around the time of Abraham. Job was a man of “the land of Uz”, and “this man was the greatest of all the children of the east” (Job 1:3).

Job 31 is the close of Job’s final defence. From chapter 29 to chapter 31, before God and before his three friends, he sets out his conduct item by item, like a “checklist of conscience”: how he treated his servants, how he cared for orphans and widows, his heart towards money, his heart towards his enemies.

What deserves our attention is the very first item on that list. It isn’t conduct, it isn’t money, it isn’t speech — it’s the eyes. “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1)

“Covenant” in Hebrew is berit, one of the most solemn words in the Old Testament: God made a covenant with Noah, with Abraham, and with Israel at Mount Sinai. A covenant is not a passing thought or a momentary feeling. It is a formal commitment, with witnesses, with terms, with a cost, one you can be held to account for.

Brothers and sisters, Job didn’t say, “I’ll try not to look.” He said, “I made a covenant with my eyes.” This isn’t a resolution; it’s a covenant.

The second is Ephesians 4:31.

Ephesians was written by the apostle Paul, generally dated between AD 60 and 62. It is one of the “prison letters” Paul wrote during his first imprisonment in Rome, addressed to the churches of Ephesus and the surrounding province of Asia.

Ephesus was a great city of the Roman province of Asia, home to the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The city was not only idolatrous; it was steeped in sorcery. Acts records that when Paul preached in Ephesus, “Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.” (Acts 19:19)

In other words, the believers in the Ephesian church had been rescued out of an extremely polluted world of thought. That is why Paul says, “you no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind” (Ephesians 4:17).

Then Paul gives a vitally important structure: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:22–24)

Look closely at these three verbs: put away, be renewed, put on. The middle one, “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”, is precisely the renewal of our thinking. And from 4:25 onwards Paul works this principle out point by point: don’t lie, speak the truth; don’t steal any more, but work honestly with your own hands; let no corrupt speech come out of your mouth, only what builds others up. Only then does he arrive at today’s verse (Ephesians 4:31).

So remember: Ephesians 4:31 is not an isolated moral command. It is one link in the whole “put off — put on” structure. And it is followed immediately by verse 32: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:32)

Where there is “putting away”, there must also be “putting on”. That is exactly what sets up today’s third teaching.

The third is Romans 12:2.

Romans is the most complete of Paul’s letters, generally dated around AD 56–57, very likely written from Corinth in Greece. Chapters 1 to 11 set out the truth of the gospel; from chapter 12 on he sets out the life of the gospel. Romans 12:1–2 is the hinge of that door:

“Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:1–2)

Here two Greek verbs form a beautiful contrast.

“Be conformed” is syschēmatizō, from the root schēma, meaning outward form, appearance, fashion. Think of a biscuit pressed out of a mould: its shape follows the mould.

“Be transformed” is metamorphoō, from the root morphē, meaning the essential form within. We know this word already — the biological term “metamorphosis” comes from it. When a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, nobody paints the caterpillar a new colour; it is remade entirely from the inside.

What’s more, both verbs are present-tense imperatives in the original. They aren’t one-off actions but continual ones: keep refusing to be pressed into the world’s mould; keep letting yourself be renewed and transformed.

“Mind” in the original is nous, the faculty of thought, understanding and judgement — in other words, the inner system by which a person “sees things”.

Brothers and sisters, put these three passages together and you see a complete picture:

Job guards the entrance — he doesn’t let the wrong seed in.

Paul in Ephesians deals with the process — what has already come in must be removed, not merely held down.

Paul in Romans renews the system — the whole mind remade by God, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.

These three steps are today’s three teachings.

sections.heading: 3. Teaching One: What We See and Hear Sets the Odds of a Thought Being Conceived
sections.html:
The lesson says something very precise: the conception of a thought is not random; it has “odds”.

The more you see, the more likely conception becomes; the more you hear, the more easily it enters your thinking.

Brothers and sisters, read that slowly, twice. It turns something we always assumed was “beyond our control” into something we “can manage”. We often think thoughts are random, like the weather — something we can only endure. They aren’t. What springs up in your heart is closely tied to what you have been feeding it over the past few months.

The lesson uses the simplest picture of all: it’s like a field. Whatever seed you sow most of, that’s what grows most.

This is the very principle Scripture repeats again and again: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.” (Galatians 6:7–8)

Notice what Paul says first: “Don’t be deceived.” Why? Because sowing time is when we most easily deceive ourselves. A tiny seed drops into the ground, nothing on the surface changes, and we tell ourselves: “It’s only a quick look. Listening for a bit won’t hurt.” But harvest season will surely come. The soil doesn’t debate fairness with you; it simply, faithfully grows whatever you planted.

So the lesson puts it bluntly: if someone constantly takes in what is negative, complaining, comparing or lustful, wrong thoughts will naturally be conceived within them. If someone constantly takes in God’s word, his grace and Jesus, thoughts of life will naturally be conceived within them.

The Lord Jesus himself taught the same. He said: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

The Lord Jesus also said: “Take heed what you hear.” (Mark 4:24) Luke records it another way: “Be careful therefore how you hear.” (Luke 8:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord Jesus didn’t say, “Be careful what you say.” He said, “Be careful how you hear.” Because hearing is the entrance; speaking is only the exit. Problems at the exit are always caused at the entrance.

Science makes this even clearer. The human optic nerve is made up of more than a million nerve fibres — the widest information channel into the brain. Your eye is not a window; it’s a conveyor belt, every second carrying things into your heart. And neuroscience has a famous principle, from the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb’s 1949 book “The Organization of Behavior”: neurons that fire together wire together. The more often you think two things together, the thicker, faster and more automatic that pathway in the brain becomes.
