So a person who constantly watches angry content finds anger rising without any reason at all — because he himself has worn that road into a motorway.

Brothers and sisters, which road are you paving in your heart every day?

That is why Job said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1)

Look at two details.

First, Job didn’t wait until he had sinned to deal with it; he set a boundary at the source. The Lord Jesus said: “but I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.” (Matthew 5:28) Job had already grasped the same spiritual principle: the battlefield isn’t the behaviour; the battlefield is the eyes.

Second, the word Job uses is “covenant”. Not “I’ll be careful”, not “I’ll do my best”, but a commitment with witnesses, a cost and accountability. Brothers and sisters, between us and our eyes there is usually only a “suggestion”, never a “covenant”. That’s why we keep losing ground, time after time.

David made the same covenant: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes” (Psalm 101:3). And he prayed: “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.” (Psalm 119:37)

Psychology bears witness in the same direction. The process model of emotion regulation proposed in 1998 by the Stanford psychologist James Gross divides strategies for regulating emotion into two broad types: “antecedent-focused” and “response-focused”. Antecedent-focused strategies — choosing not to enter a situation, for example, or turning your attention elsewhere — happen before the emotion is fully formed; they work well and cost little. Response-focused strategies — forcing an emotion down once it has already surged — work poorly, cost a great deal, and drain a large amount of mental resources.

In other words, what scientific research has discovered is exactly what the Bible said three thousand years ago: dealing with things at the entrance is far, far easier than dealing with them at the exit.

Let me give you a picture. A waterworks doesn’t put most of its effort into your kitchen tap; it puts it into the intake. Brothers and sisters, your eyes and ears are the water intake of your life.

I have to be very honest: the challenge of this generation is far greater than in Job’s day. For Job to “look lustfully” he still had to lift his head and walk to the door. We lie in bed, flick a finger, and the filth of the whole world plays automatically — and it learns your preferences, getting more accurate the more you feed it.

So, brothers and sisters, the most urgent question today is not “Why do I have thoughts like this?” but —

What am I letting into my heart today?

This brings us to the 321 insight.

The selfless manage the entrance; the self-centred leave the entrance wide open, and in the end are ruled by sin.

Why? Because at the heart of the self-centred life is this: “I have the right to decide what I watch and what I listen to.” That sounds like freedom, but it is actually the greatest bondage. When you insist on that “right”, you hand yourself over to the hand that feeds you; and in the end, it isn’t you who decides what you think — it’s a system you don’t even know.

Selflessness doesn’t mean gouging out your eyes; selflessness means handing the sovereignty over your eyes back to God. The selfless person says: my eyes are not my own, my ears are not my own; they are the Lord’s. This is what it means to let Jesus be King — and his reign begins with reigning over my eyes.

321 says: the Bible is my standard. A standard isn’t a feeling; it’s a measuring rule. When I’m unsure whether I should watch something, the question isn’t “Does this count as sin?” but “Will this make God’s word clearer in my heart?”

321 also says: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Brothers and sisters, very often, before we tap, the Holy Spirit has already gently held us back once. That moment isn’t a struggle; it’s guidance. The first step to victory is often not a hard-fought battle but obeying that gentle nudge.

So the first step to victory is not struggle but choice.

sections.heading: 4. Teaching Two: When a Wrong Thought Appears, End the Conception Early
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if we’re honest we all know one thing: even when we guard the entrance, things still get in.

Some come from what other people say, some float up from memory, and some are flaming arrows fired straight in by Satan. So when a wrong thought has already got in, what do we do?

The lesson points out that many people handle it in one of two wrong ways.

The first wrong way: letting it run. We think, “What harm can a bit of thinking do? Let it be.”

The second wrong way: suppressing it. We frantically tell ourselves not to think about it, grit our teeth, and push back with willpower.

Brothers and sisters, one of these is too loose and the other too tight, but the outcome is the same — failure.

First, the danger of letting it run. Scripture says: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14–15) This verse uses the language of childbirth: conceiving, bearing, growing to full size. A thought that lingers in your heart doesn’t stay the way it is. It grows.

Before the first murder in human history, God warned Cain: “If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.” (Genesis 4:7) Picture it: sin crouching at the door like a wild beast. It hasn’t come in yet; it’s waiting for you to open the door. God didn’t say, “You must put up with it.” He said, “You are to rule over it.”

Now, the futility of suppression. This is one of the lesson’s most precious reminders: dealing with a thought is not a matter of fighting it non-stop. Because the more you fight it, the more you are actually thinking about it.

Psychology has a famous experiment on this. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They asked participants to do something that sounds simple: for the next five minutes, don’t think of a white bear. The result? Those told “don’t think of a white bear” thought of white bears more often than those who weren’t told; and once the restriction was lifted, their white-bear thoughts even rebounded. Wegner called this the “rebound effect” of thought suppression.

Brothers and sisters, this research isn’t teaching us a new truth; it simply bears witness to Scripture: fighting with willpower is itself a form of constant attention. You can’t shine a searchlight on something and then order yourself not to look at the beam.

So God gives us a deeper, more precise principle: “deal with it”, don’t just “put up with it”.

What does Scripture say? “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.” (Ephesians 4:31)

The word for “put away” in Greek is airō, meaning “to lift up, take away, remove, carry off”; it is used of carrying things away and lifting off a burden. When John the Baptist saw Jesus he said: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29) The “takes away” there is the same word.

So God doesn’t say “hold it down”; God says “put it away”.

When you hold it down, the thing is still in the house — it’s just been stuffed into a cupboard. When you put it away, you carry it out of the door. Holding it down takes constant effort; putting it away deals with it once and for all.

So in practice, how do we “put it away”? Scripture’s answer isn’t gritting our teeth; it’s three actions: confess it in the light, lay it at the foot of the cross, and put on what God gives. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9) And Ephesians 4:32 follows straight on: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:32)

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? The way to put away bitterness isn’t to stop thinking about the person who hurt you; it’s to forgive them. Forgiveness isn’t suppression; forgiveness is dealing with it. Forgiveness formally transfers that debt from your hands into God’s.

Next, the lesson gives us a vital principle of timing: if a wrong thought isn’t dealt with, it will grow, take shape and give birth to action. So the sooner you deal with it, the better.

The lesson uses a wonderful picture: it’s like a flame. At first it’s easy to put out; once it’s blazing, there’s a price to pay.

Firefighters often say the first few minutes of a fire are critical. In the first minute a small extinguisher can save a whole building; the same extinguisher at the tenth minute can only help you get out faster. The fire hasn’t got worse; it has just got bigger.

It’s like tooth decay. At first it’s a small dark spot, and the dentist can fill it in five minutes. If you put it off — “It doesn’t even hurt” — by the time it does hurt, you need a root canal and a crown, and if you keep putting it off, the tooth has to come out.

So here is a spiritual principle; hold on to it firmly:

The earlier you deal with a thought, the smaller the cost; the later you deal with it, the greater the cost.

Scripture says: “lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1). Notice the words “so easily entangles”. Sin doesn’t bind you with one iron chain all at once; it wraps you thread by thread. The first thread you can snap with a tug; by the hundredth thread, you can’t move.

Brothers and sisters, that very second, the moment a thought first pops up, is the moment you have the most power. If you turn to the Lord then, the cost is almost nothing.

Here again we come to the 321 insight.

First, humility overcomes pride. What is pride in dealing with our thoughts? It’s “I can hold this down myself.” The proud won’t admit there is anything inside them that needs to be put away; they want to tough it out alone, because admitting it means losing face. The humble, the moment they notice something wrong, go straight to God and say: Lord, there is bitterness in me; please take it away. Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5) So you see, those who deal with things early are always the humble.

Second, rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Relying on the brain and ourselves is a one-man tug of war with Satan on the other end of the rope: the harder you pull, the harder he pulls. Relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit is turning around, taking refuge, putting your hand in the Lord’s. Scripture says: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7) Look carefully at the order: first submit to God, then resist the devil. Get the order backwards, and you’re fighting a battle without the Lord.

Third, the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, and finally with others. When a wrong thought appears, the first thing isn’t to phone someone and have it out, nor to give yourself a good scolding, but to come back before God. Once your relationship with God is set right, your relationship with yourself becomes settled; once you’re settled with yourself, there’s a way forward with others. Reverse the order and usually pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

Brothers and sisters, when the flame first catches, don’t look anywhere else. Turning to the Lord is that bucket of water.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Three: True Victory Comes by “Replacing”, Not by “Refusing”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, now we come to the most crucial part of today’s lesson, and the most important strategy in spiritual warfare.

The lesson says: don’t just refuse wrong thoughts; “replace” them with right ones.

Why? The lesson gives a very precise reason: a person can only focus on one thought at a time. When you are thinking about what is “right”, you naturally won’t be thinking about what is “wrong”.

Psychology has been studying this for more than half a century. In 1958 the British psychologist Donald Broadbent proposed his famous filter theory of attention: at every moment our senses receive a flood of information, but the channel through which it enters awareness and is processed in depth is very narrow. Later research kept revising the details, but one conclusion has never been overturned — attention is a limited resource; you cannot give two things your full focus at the same time.

More interesting still, after the white-bear experiment Wegner also found that instead of telling people “don’t think about it”, giving them something specific and different to think about works markedly better. He called this method “focused distraction”.

Brothers and sisters, do you see? Psychology went the long way round and finally arrived where Scripture had been standing all along.

What does Scripture say? “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

The lesson has a beautiful line, and I’d like you to write it down: renewal is not emptying; renewal is replacing.

Brothers and sisters, this matters enormously. Because emptying alone is dangerous.

The Lord Jesus told a parable that should make us tremble: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order. Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first.” (Matthew 12:43–45)

Notice those three descriptions: empty, swept, put in order. The house wasn’t dirty; it had even been done up. It had just one problem — it was empty. It had no master.

Brothers and sisters, so many people’s repentance stops at “swept clean”. They give up a habit, delete a few apps, cut off a few relationships — and then what? The inside sits empty. And three months later, what comes back is more, and worse, than what left.

So renewal isn’t emptying the heart; renewal is having a new Master move in.

The lesson gives an example close to all of us: when there is “resentment” inside you, don’t keep thinking, “I mustn’t hate.” Because you’re still thinking about “hate”. The right way is to turn to thinking about “God’s love”, to meditate on “how God has accepted me”. As love grows more and more, hate naturally loses its place.

This is just what Paul writes at the end of the same chapter: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” (Romans 12:21)

Notice: it isn’t “overcome evil with nothing”; it’s “overcome evil with good”. Evil isn’t driven out by a vacuum; evil is crowded out by good.

Paul gives us a very concrete replacement list: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)

“Think about” in the original is logizomai, meaning “to reckon, to weigh up, to keep turning something over in your mind”. Paul didn’t say, “Don’t think about bad things.” He said, “Think about these things.” He gives us a list of what to think about, not a list of what we mustn’t.

Colossians puts it even more directly: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) First set your mind on things above, and only then not on things on the earth. The order is the strategy.

Let me give you a few pictures.

The first is darkness. There’s something fascinating in physics: darkness is not a thing. There are photons, but there are no “dark-ons”. Darkness has no mass, no speed, no particles; darkness is simply the absence of light. So you can never sweep darkness out of a room. You can’t sweep it with a broom or carry it out in a bucket. You can do only one thing — switch on the light.

This is exactly what the lesson says: when the light comes, darkness leaves of its own accord.

Scripture says: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.” (John 1:5) And again: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” (1 John 1:5) Brothers and sisters, you don’t need to negotiate with the darkness; you only need to let the light in.

The second picture is a glass of muddy water. How do you make muddy water clear? Do you pick out the mud grain by grain, or do you put the glass under the tap and let clean water keep flowing in and spilling over? God’s word is that living water.

At the opening of Book One of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a line that has been repeated for sixteen hundred years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” There is a place in the human heart that only God can fill. If you don’t let God move in, something else will.

This is spiritual victory: not by willpower, but by the replacement of one life with another.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this distinction. Willpower is me trying to out-muscle sin; the replacement of life is Christ living in me.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Paul used the same strategy against the desires of the flesh: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) He didn’t say, “Hold down your lusts with all your might, and then you’ll be able to walk by the Spirit.” He said the reverse — walk by the Spirit, and the lusts naturally fall behind. No one can walk in two directions at once.

Here the 321 insight comes into view.

The lesson says: rely on the heart and the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and life is renewed naturally; rely on the brain and fight in your own strength, and you are far more likely to get stuck in a loop.

Those who rely on the brain and themselves have their focus on “that sin”; those who rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit have their focus on Jesus. 321 says it very clearly: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. And now we add one more: not that sin either.

Because if you stare at sin, sin grows bigger; if you fix your eyes on Jesus, Jesus fills you.

321 also says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. We empty ourselves not in order to stay empty, but in order to be filled by God. This is the spiritual principle behind renewal and replacement. The old self is self-centred, so it keeps clinging to its own ideas, its own rights, its own wounds; the new self is selfless, so it is willing to let the thoughts of Christ replace its own.

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5)

This is why 321 puts “Jesus is my role model” first among the Three Foundations. Victorious thinking isn’t a set of techniques; it’s a Person — the mind of Christ, living in you.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: God’s System Begins with Our Thoughts
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, put today’s three teachings back into the framework of 321 and you’ll see a complete picture.

The Three Foundations correspond exactly to today’s three teachings.

Jesus is my role model. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he didn’t debate with Satan, nor did he grit his teeth and suppress it. Three times he said, “It is written…” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10) He replaced the enemy’s words with God’s words. That is the role model for “replacing”.

The Bible is my standard. The standard isn’t whether I feel something is all right; the standard is what God’s word says. The psalmist says: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” (Psalm 119:11) Notice that hiding it in the heart is done before sinning, not after.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. “Walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) The renewal of our thinking isn’t a self-improvement project; it’s the work the Holy Spirit does within.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, the truest battlefield for letting Jesus be King isn’t the pulpit; it’s that thought no one else sees. A person can let Jesus reign as King at church, and at three in the morning let bitterness reign. True kingship sits on the throne of our thoughts. And when others see the change in us, we get the chance to say: it isn’t that I’ve become better; it’s Jesus living in me. That is letting Jesus receive all the glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

Where does a system begin? A system begins with mindset. A family’s system is how the whole family thinks; a church’s system is how everyone in it thinks. So when God sets out to establish his system, he will surely begin by renewing our minds. Today’s lesson isn’t a psychology class; it is God preparing, for the last days, a people whose thinking has been renewed.

The fivefold change is in today’s message too.

Change of mindset — I understand now: whether a thought comes is not up to me; whether it moves in is up to me.

Change of life — I no longer rely on suppressing things myself; I let Christ live in me.

Change of daily living — my phone, my eyes and my ears begin to have a new order.

Change of relationships — bitterness is put away, forgiveness comes in, and relationships come alive.

Change of ministry — only someone whose thinking is clean can become a blessing to others.

The shift in perspective is in today’s message too.

From man’s perspective to God’s: man says, “What harm can a bit of thinking do?” God says, “the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin.”

From the earthly to the heavenly: man says, “Everyone’s watching it.” God says, “Set your mind on the things that are above.”

From the temporary to the eternal: the pleasure of that one look lasts a few seconds; its consequences may last for years.

From the worldly to the godly: the world feeds you “You deserve it”; God says, “whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are pure… think about these things.”

Next, the 920 practice.

920 says: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, see how perfectly today’s message fits 920. What is to be put away? Bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry and slander. What is to be put on? Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Exchange them one for one: bitterness for love, wrath for kindness, anger for patience, outcry for peace, slander for goodness. That is replacing, not refusing.

And best of all — you cannot “strive” to bear fruit. Fruit grows out of life; it isn’t squeezed out by willpower. “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Finally, 235 relationships.

Renewing our thinking is a road that’s hard to walk alone. 235 says: become a “2” with a selfless person — a spiritual companion; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, if you have a spiritual companion you can honestly tell, “This week I failed twice in this area,” then the moment those words are spoken, the darkness has already lost half its power. Scripture says: “But all things, when they are reproved, are revealed by the light, for everything that reveals is light.” (Ephesians 5:13) The battle of the mind is fought in secret, and the light very often shines in through a spiritual companion.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Renewing and Replacing Our Thoughts
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices. Let’s take them one at a time and deepen each with the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: managing the entrance — choosing what I see and hear today.

Every day, choose deliberately: less contact with negative, lustful and comparing content; more contact with God’s word, worship and testimonies. Begin by lowering the odds of wrong thoughts at the source.

What does that look like in practice? Set yourself three boundaries, and write them down. For example: when you wake in the morning, read one verse of God’s word before you turn on your phone; after a certain time at night, the phone doesn’t come into the bedroom; unfollow the two or three accounts that always leave your heart feeling sour and dark.

Practising the eight stages: Information is hearing today that “what we see and hear sets the odds of conception”; Revelation is the Holy Spirit showing you what you are actually being fed; Conviction is admitting before God that this is true, without defending yourself; Implementation is unfollowing those two accounts today.

Practice two: noticing in the moment — recognising wrong thoughts.

When bitterness, irritation, lust or judgement appears, notice it at once and don’t let it develop any further. Ask yourself: “Is this from God?”

Brothers and sisters, form a habit: the moment you notice your heart “heating up” or “going dark”, immediately call out in your heart, “Lord!” No long prayer — just that one word. That is the bucket of water when the flame first catches.

Practising the eight stages: Evaluation means spending three minutes each evening looking back — at what moment today was I too slow to notice? Where was I? Who was I with? What had I just been looking at? Evaluation isn’t condemning yourself; it’s tracing the enemy’s line of attack. David’s prayer is the best evaluation of all: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Practice three: replacing thoughts — exchanging error for truth.

Don’t fight the wrong thought; turn directly to the right one. For example: with resentment, turn to meditating on God’s love; with anxiety, turn to declaring that God reigns. Fill your thoughts with truth.

I suggest you prepare a “replacement list” and put it somewhere you’ll see it: when bitter, read Ephesians 4:32; when anxious, read Philippians 4:6–7; when tempted by lust, read Philippians 4:8; when you feel worthless, read Romans 8:31–39.

Practising the eight stages: Correction. The first time, you may find you can’t even get to your replacement list in time, because the thought comes too fast. That’s all right — correct it. Shorten the verse to a single line, short enough to say in three seconds. Correction isn’t failure; correction is the road to maturity.

Practice four: meditating on Scripture — letting God’s word take the lead.

Each day choose one verse to ponder and declare again and again, letting God’s word be “conceived” in your thoughts so that life grows out of it naturally.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most beautiful contrast of the day. In our last lesson we saw: desire conceives and gives birth to sin. Today we see: God’s word conceives too, and gives birth to life. Your heart will always conceive something; the only question is — whom do you let move in?

Scripture says: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.” (Joshua 1:8)

The word “meditate” in Hebrew is hagah, which originally means to murmur, to mutter under your breath, like the cooing of a dove. It isn’t reading something quickly; it’s turning it over and over in your mouth and keeping it in your heart.

Practising the eight stages: Repetition. One verse read for seven days has more power than seven verses read for one day each. Repetition is the only road by which truth sinks from the head down into the heart.

Practice five: selfless surrender — letting Jesus hold sovereignty over my thoughts.

When “what I want” rises up, stop and ask: “If Jesus were me, how would he think?” Then choose to obey, rather than let things run.

Brothers and sisters, this practice is the root of the other four. Who is managing the entrance? Who does the replacing? In the end it all comes back to one question — who is sitting on the throne of my thoughts?

Practising the eight stages: Multiplication. Once you have walked this road for a while, go and find someone and pass on what you’ve learned. Find a spiritual companion too, and ask each other: “This week, what has been conceiving in your heart?” Multiplication is the most solid step of all — because whatever you teach others, you will live out first yourself.

“for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5)

“Bringing into captivity” is the language of war. Brothers and sisters, your mind is territory God has bought back. Rise up and take it back.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, at the very end the lesson gives us four short but powerful reminders. Let me read them to you one at a time.

First, thoughts are not the surface of the problem; thoughts are the root of the problem.

We often spend a lifetime pruning branches and leaves: I said the wrong thing, so I apologise; I did something badly, so I put it right. But if the root isn’t touched, the same branches will grow back next year. The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies.” (Matthew 15:19) Evil thoughts come first; everything else follows.

Second, don’t wait until the behaviour shows before you repent; turn the moment the thought appears.

The Greek word for repentance is metanoia, which literally means “a change of mind”. True repentance has never started with behaviour; it starts with thought. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Third, don’t strain to drive out the darkness; let the light in. When the light comes in, darkness leaves of its own accord.

Fourth, the humble are willing to let God adjust their thinking; the proud insist on their own ideas.

Brothers and sisters, this is the line that cuts deepest today. Why won’t a person change their thinking? Not because they don’t understand, but because that idea is “mine”. What the self-centred life clings to is often not money or power, but “my opinion”; letting go of an opinion is harder than letting go of money. That is why the lesson says: humility brings renewal; selflessness brings freedom.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. This law holds just as true inside our own heads: the prouder you are of your own ideas, the more tightly they bind you; the humbler you are before God, the freer you become.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, today we have seen together that your thoughts are not beyond your control; your thoughts are something you can choose.

You can’t decide whether a thought will come, but you can decide whether it stays.

What God has given us today is a road to victory. It isn’t the road of suppressing or fighting; it is the road of renewing and replacing.

When you let God’s word in, when you let Jesus fill your thoughts, you’ll find two wonderful things happening at once: sin no longer has room, and life grows naturally.

Brothers and sisters, notice that word “naturally”. Holiness isn’t squeezed out; it grows. An apple tree doesn’t have to grit its teeth to produce apples; it only needs to be joined to its roots and to have sunlight and water. “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” (John 15:5)

So this morning I want to give you three calls.

First, the call at the entrance. Today, like Job, make a covenant with your eyes. Don’t just make a resolution; make a covenant before God.

Second, the call to act early. That bitterness you’ve been holding on to for three years, that thought you assumed would one day disappear by itself — bring it to the Lord today and say: Lord, please take it away.

Third, the call to replace. Today, choose one verse of God’s word and let it live in your heart for a whole week. Stop shouting at the darkness — go and switch on the light.

May we walk this road all our lives: conceiving no sin, conceiving only Christ.

Let us live out the selfless life and let Jesus live in us; let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: Job 31:1
“I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1)
Ephesians 4:31–32

“Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice. And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:31–32)
Romans 12:2
“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare:
My thoughts will be renewed by God; my mind will be transformed by the truth.
I reject every wrong thought; I will not let sin conceive within me.
I will fill my thoughts with God’s word; I will let God’s love replace all bitterness.
Jesus reigns as King within me; the Holy Spirit guides my thoughts.
I live in the new self; I live in victory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Manage the entrance: choose what I see and hear today
Notice in the moment: recognise wrong thoughts
Replace my thoughts: exchange error for truth
Meditate on Scripture: let God’s word take the lead
Surrender selflessly: let Jesus hold sovereignty over my thoughts
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that this morning you have not only reminded us to be careful with our thoughts, but have clearly shown us the road to victory.

Lord, we confess that we often leave the entrance wide open, and then often try to suppress things in our own strength; struggling and failing, struggling and failing, until we are worn out. Today we are willing to take a different road.
Help me to make a covenant with my eyes, and a covenant with my ears. Shine your light on me, and let me see what I am actually being fed.
Lord, the bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry and slander already inside me, and all malice — I will no longer hold them down. I lay them one by one at the foot of your cross; please take them away.
Replace my hatred with your love, my anxiety with your peace, the enemy’s voice with your word. Lord, please come in, for when the light comes, darkness leaves of its own accord.
Jesus, reign as King on the throne of my thoughts. All my life, may I conceive no sin, but conceive only Christ.
May all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: Job said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1) In your life right now, which entrance most needs a “covenant”? Your phone, your eyes, your ears, or a particular conversation? What specific boundary are you willing to set today?

Paul said: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) Share one wrong thought that keeps coming back to you most often, and together find a verse that can “replace” it, to meditate on every day this week.
l134.title: Conceive Only Christ
l134.subtitle: Thinking Is a Process of Conceiving (Part 2)
l134.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: A Single Thought Is Rewriting Your Future
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

This morning, before you had even opened your eyes, before you had got out of bed, a first thought had already surfaced in your heart.

What was that thought?

Was it “Here we go again,” or “This is the day that Yahweh has made”? Was it “I can’t keep going,” or “Lord, walk with me today”?

Brothers and sisters, don’t underestimate that one thought.

We often assume that what decides a life is the big events — changing jobs, moving house, getting married, falling ill, retiring. Not really. What decides a life are the thoughts that no one sees and no one hears. Big events don’t happen every day, but thoughts happen every minute. The real direction of a life is not settled once and for all by a handful of big events; it is pushed along, day after day, by tens of thousands of small thoughts.

So the theme of this lesson comes down to a few words: the power of thought.

Thinking is no small thing. Thinking is a spiritual tool of tremendous power.

How you think decides how you live. How you think also decides whether God can work in you.

Many brothers and sisters set great store by prayer, and rightly so; but we tend to neglect our thinking. We imagine that as long as the ten minutes on our knees are spiritual, it doesn’t matter what we think about for the other fourteen hours. But that is not what God’s word says. In Ephesians 3:20 Paul writes: “Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us” (Ephesians 3:20).

Notice the two verbs set side by side in that verse: “ask” and “think”.

God works not only through what you ask; God also works through what you think. Prayer is speaking out the words in your heart; thinking is the words your heart keeps speaking all the time. We pray for twenty minutes a day, yet we think a thousand times a day. If our thinking is wasteland, prayer is like scattering good seed on rocky ground; if our thinking has been renewed by the truth, prayer is like sowing seed in good soil.

The French thinker Blaise Pascal wrote in his “Pensées” that man is only a reed, the feeblest thing in nature, but he is a thinking reed. Man’s dignity lies not in physical strength but in thought; and the Bible tells us something deeper still: man’s spiritual battle is not fought with physical strength either, but in his thoughts.

In the 321 vision this becomes even clearer:

Selfless people, whose thinking is aligned with God, experience God accomplishing his work; self-centred people, whose thinking drifts away from God, hinder what God would do.

The same almighty God, the same precious promise, can come to two people and produce completely different results. The difference does not lie with God; the difference lies in how we think.

Today we will see two things together: thinking can accomplish God’s will; thinking can also wreck a life.

The lesson gives us three teachings. First, thinking carries a promise from “receiving” through to “fulfilment”. Second, right thinking brings miracles; wrong thinking brings destruction. Third, God is at work within you, and you cooperate with him by the way you think.

May the Holy Spirit shine on our thoughts and intentions this morning, so that we don’t just hear a lesson but take on a new way of thinking; and not just a new way of thinking, but a new life.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A Prisoner Praying for Other People’s Minds
sections.html:
To understand Ephesians 3:20 rightly, we first need to know who said these words and in what circumstances.

The author of Ephesians is the apostle Paul. He says at the very opening of the letter: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 1:1). At the opening of chapter 3 he says: “For this cause I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles” (Ephesians 3:1). And in 4:1 he says it once more: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you …” (Ephesians 4:1).

Brothers and sisters, hold this picture in your heart: the man who wrote “to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think” was not standing in a pulpit or sitting in a church office at the time — he was locked up in prison. In the view of most evangelical scholars, this is one of the “prison letters”, written during Paul’s first house arrest in Rome, around AD 60 to 62, belonging to the same group as Philippians, Colossians and Philemon.

A man whose freedom had been taken away wrote one of the most expansive sentences in the whole Bible. His body was chained; his thinking was not. His surroundings were a prison; his thinking was in heaven. Acts 28 tells us that for those two years he went on “preaching God’s Kingdom … with all boldness” (Acts 28:31).

This is the lesson’s first living illustration: a person can be locked in a very small place and yet live inside a very large thought; or a person can live in a free world and yet be imprisoned all his life by his own narrow thinking.

The letter was sent to the church in Ephesus. Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, and the home of the temple of the goddess Artemis — a temple the ancients counted among the Seven Wonders of the World. Acts 19 lets us feel the spiritual atmosphere of that city: those who practised magic brought their books and burned them, and their value came to “fifty thousand pieces of silver” (Acts 19:19); the silversmith Demetrius stirred up a crowd who shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” (Acts 19:28). The believers in Ephesus did not live in a greenhouse. Day after day they were surrounded by a whole system of thought given over to idol worship, sorcery and the worship of power.

Paul knew that to help such people stand firm, it was not enough to give them rules; their minds had to be renewed. So the whole of Ephesians deals with the question of thinking. He prays that they would have “the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know …” (Ephesians 1:18); he says, “that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23); he tells them to “take the helmet of salvation” (Ephesians 6:17) — and what does a helmet protect? The head, of course; the mind.

Now look at the surrounding context. Ephesians 3:14–19 is Paul’s second prayer: “For this cause, I bow my knees to the Father … that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth, and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God” (Ephesians 3:14, 16–19).

Only after the peak of that prayer comes the doxology of verse 20. So verse 20 is not a stand-alone motivational slogan; it follows straight on from “that you may be strengthened with power … in the inner person”. God’s mighty power does not first go to work in your circumstances; it is first “the power that works in us”.

There is a key word in the original here. “Works” is the Greek ἐνεργέω (energeō), the root of the English word “energy”, meaning to exert power, to produce an effect, to be at work. The same word appears in Philippians 2:13: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

Brothers and sisters, these two verses are two sides of the same thing. Ephesians says: God’s mighty power is at work in us; Philippians says: God is at work in us, giving us both the will and the doing. God’s power is not waiting far away up in heaven; it has already been set in motion inside you.

The phrase “exceedingly abundantly” is more wonderful still. The Greek is ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ (hyperekperissou), made up of “beyond” and “overflowing abundance”; literally, “beyond the very limit, more than could ever be more”. It is as if Paul felt that one “beyond” wasn’t enough, so he piled another on top. He wants to tell us: God’s provision is always bigger than your imagination.

And “think” is the Greek νοέω (noeō), meaning to grasp with the mind, to ponder; its noun is νοῦς (nous), the mind, the understanding. When Romans 12:2 speaks of being “transformed by the renewing of your mind”, that “mind” is precisely nous.

Put these words together and the meaning is very clear: God’s power, which goes beyond every limit, is at work in the depths of your mind; what he means to accomplish goes far beyond all that you ask or think.

So here is the question: if God’s power is already at work in me, why is my life still stuck where it was?

That brings us to the lesson’s first teaching.

sections.heading: 3. Teaching One: Thinking Carries a Promise from “Receiving” to “Fulfilment”
sections.html:
The lesson begins by pointing out a distinction that is often overlooked.

The Lord Jesus said: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you” (Matthew 7:7).

That verse is about “receiving”. God is a God who delights to give: you ask, and he gives.

But Ephesians 3:20 uses a different word — “accomplish”. God “is able to do exceedingly abundantly …”, to bring all things to completion.

Brothers and sisters, remember this distinction: receiving is not the same as fulfilment.

The lesson uses a beautiful illustration. A woman prays for a child; God answers, and she conceives. Let me ask you: at the moment she conceived, had she “received”? Yes, she had. But had the child been “brought to fulfilment”? Not yet. Between receiving and fulfilment lie ten months — a whole process of carrying and nurturing that life.

Spiritual things work the same way.

When you pray and God gives you a promise, a prompting, a clear word, at that moment you have already “received”. The seed is already inside you. But what is the key from there on?

It is how you think.

The lesson puts it very plainly: while you wait, if you doubt, if you give up, if you look only at your circumstances, it is like a miscarriage — what you had already received is lost along the way. But if you keep meditating on God’s promise, thinking with faith, letting the promise grow slowly within you, you will move step by step towards fulfilment.

The Bible knows this picture of conception well. James 1:14–15 says: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:14–15).

Do you see it? Negative thoughts conceive, grow, and give birth to death. And by the same token, thoughts of faith also conceive, grow, and give birth to life. Whichever one you feed in your heart day by day is the one that grows.

Abraham is the finest role model of this.

“Without being weakened in faith, he didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb. Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform.” (Romans 4:19–21)

Notice two phrases in this passage. The first concerns his body, already as good as dead — the Chinese Union Version reads, “though he considered his own body as good as dead”. Abraham was not someone who ran away from reality. He knew perfectly well that he was a hundred and Sarah ninety; humanly speaking, the matter was finished. The second: “looking to the promise of God … being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform.”

Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that Abraham had no pressure from his circumstances; it’s that under the pressure of his circumstances he chose to “think with faith”.

The phrase “being fully assured” is the Greek πληροφορέω (plērophoreō), meaning “filled to overflowing, utterly convinced”. His mind did not sway back and forth, half believing and half doubting; it was completely taken up with God’s promise.

How did he manage it? Genesis tells us that God brought him outside and said: “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them … So your offspring will be” (Genesis 15:5). From that night on, every time Abraham looked up at a sky full of stars, it was another “promise meditation”. God gave him not just a sentence but a picture he could see every day. God placed the promise into his thinking and let his thinking carry that promise, day after day, for twenty-five years.

Here we see the power of sustained thinking. Modern brain science offers us a good piece of supporting evidence. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb, in his book “The Organization of Behavior”, put forward a famous principle that later came to be summed up as “neurons that fire together wire together”. In other words: what you think about over and over wires itself in the brain into a road that becomes smoother the more it is travelled. In 2000 a team led by Eleanor Maguire at University College London published a study in the “Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences” showing that London taxi drivers, after years of memorising and rehearsing complex routes in their heads, had a larger volume of grey matter in the rear of the hippocampus than a control group — and the longer they had been driving, the more marked the difference.

Brothers and sisters, what science observes is simply the principle God built into creation: whatever you think about day after day, that is the kind of person you become, day by day. Thinking paves roads inside you. If you dwell on doubt every day, doubt gets paved into a motorway; if you dwell on the promise every day, faith gets paved into a motorway too.

That is why God said to Joshua: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success” (Joshua 1:8). The Hebrew word for “meditate” (הָגָה, hagah) originally means to murmur over and over in a low voice, to chew, like a cow chewing the cud. Meditation is not emptying the mind; meditation is chewing on God’s word again and again until it becomes your flesh and blood.

A 321 Insight is very clear here:

Thinking with the heart — meditating on God’s promise in faith — carries the promise to term and accomplishes God’s will. Thinking with the brain — only analysing, only looking at circumstances, only calculating the odds — shakes us with doubt and cuts the promise short.

As we often say: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life (Proverbs 4:23).

So, brothers and sisters, this morning ask yourself one honest question:

Is my thinking right now carrying God’s promise to term, or bringing God’s promise to an end?

sections.heading: 4. Teaching Two: Right Thinking Brings Miracles; Wrong Thinking Brings Destruction
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, on this matter the Bible gives us two extremely sharp contrasts.

One is the woman with the bleeding; the other is Judas Iscariot. One received a miracle because of a single thought; the other went to destruction because of a single thought.

The Woman with the Bleeding: One Thought Touched the Power of God

Matthew 9 records: “Behold, a woman who had a discharge of blood for twelve years came behind him, and touched the fringe of his garment; for she said within herself, ‘If I just touch his garment, I will be made well’ ” (Matthew 9:20–21).

First, look at her situation. Mark says she “had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse” (Mark 5:26).

Twelve years. Under the regulations of Leviticus 15:25 and following, a woman with such a discharge was ritually unclean, and whatever she touched or sat on counted as unclean too. So in those twelve years she lost not only her health but her relationships — she could not go into the temple, could not mix normally with others. She lived among people and yet was cut off from them.

Thinking according to her circumstances, what would she think? “It’s no use.” “Not even the doctors could cure me.” “The money’s all gone.” “I’m not even worthy to come near him.”

Yet the Bible makes a point of recording the one sentence in her heart: “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well.”

There is a precious detail in the original here. The verb “said” in “she said within herself” is in the Greek imperfect tense (ἔλεγεν), which expresses a continuous, repeated action. This was not a thought that flashed through her mind on the spur of the moment; it was what she said to herself again and again, all the way as she pushed through the crowd.

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the order:

First she “thought”, then she “acted”, and finally she “received”.

The thought came first. Had that sentence not first been in her heart, her hand would never have reached out; and had her hand not reached out, her illness would never have been healed.

And the result? “But Jesus, turning around and seeing her, said, ‘Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well.’ And the woman was made well from that hour” (Matthew 9:22).

The Lord did not say, “Your hand has made you well,” nor “My garment has made you well.” The Lord said, “Your faith has made you well.” And her faith began with that one sustained, right “thought” in her heart.

Brothers and sisters, the miracle did not begin at her fingertips; the miracle began in her thinking.

That day there were so many people crowding around Jesus that the disciples even said, “You see the multitude pressing against you” (Mark 5:31). How many people bumped against Jesus’ body, yet only one touched Jesus’ power! Where was the difference? The difference was that only one person came to touch him carrying a thought of faith.

It is the same today. So many people come to the meetings, so many read through the scriptures, so many sit through the sermon; but those who truly receive are the ones who say to themselves in their hearts, “God’s word will surely be fulfilled in me today.”

Judas: One Thought Ruined a Whole Life

Now look at the other side. John 13:2 says: “During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him” (John 13:2).

The Greek verb behind “put into the heart” is βάλλω (ballō), meaning “to throw, to cast in”. The devil “threw” a thought into Judas’s heart.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to something very important: a thought being thrown in is not, in itself, sin.

The Lord Jesus himself had thoughts thrown at him by the devil. During the forty days in the wilderness, Satan said to him time after time: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (Matthew 4:3). But every time, the Lord answered: “It is written …” (Matthew 4:4). The Lord did not hold a conversation with that thought; he pushed it back with the word of God.

The question is not whether a thought comes. The question is how you respond to it.

Judas did not deal with it. Far from refusing it, he welcomed it, fed it and gave in to it. John 12:6 tells us that this thought had in fact been living in his heart for a long time: “Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it” (John 12:6). The thought of greed was allowed in again and again, until in the end it knew its way around.

And so we see a terrible downward slope: thought → action → outcome.

John 13:27 says: “After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). Luke also records: “Satan entered into Judas, who was also called Iscariot, who was counted with the twelve” (Luke 22:3).

At first it was “put into the heart”; later it was “entered into him”. At first a guest was knocking at the door; later the master was sitting in the living room.

And the end? “Then Judas, who betrayed him, when he saw that Jesus was condemned, felt remorse, and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, ‘I have sinned in that I betrayed innocent blood.’ … He threw down the pieces of silver in the sanctuary, and departed. He went away and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:3–5).

Betrayal, remorse, self-destruction.

There is a heartbreaking contrast here. Judas was not the only one who fell that night; Peter fell too, denying the Lord three times. Why did one come back and the other not?

Paul says in 2 Corinthians 7:10: “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

After Peter fell, he “went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75), and he brought himself back to the Lord. After Judas fell, he threw the silver down in the temple but did not give himself back to the Lord. Both felt remorse; but one turned towards God in his thinking and the other turned towards himself, and the result was the difference between life and death.

So the lesson states a shattering truth:

One thought can bring a miracle; one thought can also bring destruction.

The Battlefield of the Mind: Taking Our Thoughts Captive

So what are we to do?

Paul gives us very concrete orders for battle: “For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

The word “bringing into captivity” is the Greek αἰχμαλωτίζω (aichmalōtizō), which originally means “to take prisoner, to capture in war”.

Brothers and sisters, this is military language. What Paul means is: don’t let your thoughts take you prisoner — you take your thoughts prisoner. Don’t let your thinking lead you around by the nose; seize your thoughts, bring them before Christ, and make them kneel.

Psychology offers a helpful piece of supporting evidence here. In the 1960s Aaron T. Beck, a psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania, developed cognitive therapy. He found that many people trapped in depression had hearts full of what he called “automatic thoughts” — thoughts that come uninvited, recur again and again, and are never examined by the person who has them. The core of Beck’s therapy is simple: catch the thought, write it down, check whether it is true, and replace it with a thought that fits the facts better.

Brothers and sisters, when people test their thoughts against “the facts”, it already helps a great many; what God gives us is to test our thoughts against “the truth”, and that is a higher level altogether. Facts change; the truth never changes.

That is why Proverbs says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The Hebrew word “keep” (נָצַר, natsar) means to watch over, to guard, and is used of the watchmen on a city wall. Your heart is a city, and your thoughts are the people coming and going at the city gate. The watchman cannot stop people walking up to the gate, but the watchman can decide who is allowed into the city.

A saying commonly attributed to the Reformer Martin Luther puts it vividly: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair.

A 321 Insight:

Selfless people refuse wrong thoughts and submit to God’s thoughts; self-centred people accept wrong thoughts and head towards self-destruction.

C. S. Lewis writes in “Mere Christianity” that pride leads to every other vice: it is the complete anti-God state of mind. And the first place pride breaks out is never the mouth; it is the mind. Self-centred people can’t bear to let go of their own ideas, because their own name is written on them. Selfless people are willing to hand over their own ideas, because what they want is not “I was right” but to “let Jesus be King”.

The humble let God govern their thinking; the proud insist on their own ideas.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Three: God Works Within You, and You Cooperate by the Way You Think
sections.html:
Philippians 2:12–13 says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

This is a remarkable passage. The first half says “you work it out”; the second half says “it is God who works”. So who is actually doing the work?

The answer is: both are. God works first, and we respond; God works within, and we work it out.

Notice that both “to will” and “to work” are things God works in us. “To will” (θέλειν) belongs to the realm of thoughts and intentions; “to work” (ἐνεργεῖν) belongs to the realm of action. God’s work does not begin with your hands; it begins with your “wanting to”.

So, brothers and sisters, when a thought suddenly rises in your heart — perhaps to reach out to someone, perhaps to forgive someone who has wronged you, perhaps to take a step and do something by faith — very often that is not something you came up with yourself. It is God already at work within you.

God has already placed the intention inside you. But God does not force you; he invites you to take part.

How do you take part? By responding to God with the way you think.

Faced with a prompting God has placed in our hearts, we have two paths.

The first path is doubt and retreat. “Is that even possible?” “I can’t.” “Let’s leave it till later.”

The Bible has plenty of examples. At the burning bush Moses said: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” (Exodus 3:11). And again: “O Lord, I am not eloquent … for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10). At the winepress Gideon heard the angel call him a “mighty man of valor”, yet he answered: “O Lord, how shall I save Israel? Behold, my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house” (Judges 6:15).

The classic case is the ten spies at Kadesh. They came back and reported: “There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33).

Brothers and sisters, notice that sentence — “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers.”

Nobody had measured their height. They had shrunk themselves in their own hearts first. They were not defeated by giants; they were defeated by their own thinking. Their tragedy was not that “the giants were too big” but that “God was too small in their thinking”. As a result that whole generation fell in the wilderness and could not enter Canaan for forty years.

The second path is meditation and response. “Since God has said it, he will surely do it.” “Lord, I am willing.”

Mary is the most beautiful role model. The angel announced to her something utterly beyond reason, and she asked an honest question: “How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?” (Luke 1:34). After the angel answered, she said: “Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

Her question was not unbelief, because once she had asked it, she submitted. She handed her thinking over to God’s word. From that moment the plan of salvation began to be fulfilled in her.

That is why James reminds us: “But let him ask in faith, without any doubting, for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven by the wind and tossed. For that man shouldn’t think that he will receive anything from the Lord. He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways” (James 1:6–8).

“Doubt” (διακρίνω) originally means “to divide, to argue back and forth inside oneself”; “double-minded” (δίψυχος) literally means “two-souled”. A person whose heart is split in two — half trusting God, half trusting circumstances — is like a wave of the sea, tossed whichever way the wind blows.

Brothers and sisters, this does not mean God is stingy and unwilling to give. It means that while one of our hands reaches out, the other pulls back, and so we can’t catch hold of what is given.

So: thinking affects receiving; thinking also affects fulfilment.

It is not that God lacks power; it is whether our thinking is working together with God.

There is a scientific observation worth considering here too. In 2007 Alia Crum and Ellen Langer of Harvard University published a study in the journal “Psychological Science”. They divided eighty-four hotel room attendants into two groups and told only one group that the work they did every day already met the level of exercise recommended by health authorities. Four weeks later, the group that had been told showed measurable improvements in weight, blood pressure and body fat — though their work and daily routine had not changed.

What changed was not the work; what changed was the mindset. And once the mindset changed, the body actually followed.

Brothers and sisters, if a single human idea can affect the body to that degree, how much more when God’s word enters our thinking!

In 1977 the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward the theory of “self-efficacy”, showing that whether a person believes he can do something really does affect whether he is willing to try, how long he keeps going, and whether he gives up when he meets setbacks. But on the spiritual level, we do not believe in ourselves; we believe in God at work within us. Paul says: “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13). Not “I am very capable”, but “he gives the strength”.

A 321 Insight here runs like this:

God’s power has long been at work within you — that is “receiving”. You respond with thoughts of faith — that is “working together”. And so God does exceedingly abundantly, bringing all things to completion — that is “fulfilment”.

The stretch of road between receiving and fulfilment has a name: “how you think”.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Let Jesus Be King in Your Thinking
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us gather up the three teachings and set them within the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations give us the measuring line for our thinking. Jesus is my role model — in the wilderness he answered every thought Satan threw at him with “It is written”. The Bible is my standard — it isn’t that whatever I feel is right is right; what God says is what is right. The Holy Spirit is my guide — Paul says: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6). Behind “mind” in the original is φρονέω (phroneō), meaning precisely “to set one’s mind on, to be preoccupied with”. Wherever your thinking clings, your life goes.

The Two Core Values tell us whom our thinking belongs to. Let Jesus be King — not only King of the church, King of Sunday, but King of that first thought of yours at dawn, King of the thought that wakes you in the middle of the night. Let Jesus receive all the glory — so our thinking is not about proving ourselves right or getting the better of anyone, but about bringing him glory. Straight after Ephesians 3:20 comes verse 21: “to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations forever and ever. Amen” (Ephesians 3:21). God does far beyond all we ask or think for one purpose only — that he may receive the glory.

The Goal gives our thinking its direction: establish God’s system. A mind governed by the truth will establish a home governed by God, a team governed by God, a church governed by God.

Now look at the old self and the new self.

For the self-centred, the centre of thinking is “me”: my face, my feelings, my analysis, my plans, my grievances. So the phrases that come up most often in their hearts are “I feel”, “I don’t want to” and “Why should I?” The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem — and pride’s deepest lair is in our thinking. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; at the level of thinking, pride is “my view should replace God’s view”.

For the selfless, the centre of thinking is Christ. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Selflessness does not mean having no thoughts or switching the mind off; selflessness means emptying out a mind that was crammed with “me” and letting Christ fill it. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. For Paul says: “But we have Christ’s mind” (1 Corinthians 2:16).

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Judas’s failure did not happen in a day; it was fed one thought at a time. The bleeding woman’s victory did not happen in a day either; it was spoken to herself one sentence at a time.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Nowhere is this clearer than in relationships. When what you’re thinking is “Why would he treat me like this?”, your words come out with thorns, the other person sends thorns back, and both sides lose. When what you’re thinking is “Lord, please change me first”, your words come out gently, the other person’s heart softens, and both sides win. A breach in a relationship almost always begins with a thought that was never dealt with.

The fivefold change is the fullest explanation of this lesson: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

Notice that the first step is not behaviour; it is mindset. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships. How many people try to go straight to step five — serving twice as hard, being twice as busy — without ever dealing with step one, their thinking, and after years of service, inside they are just the same as before! This lesson is performing the first operation on you: a change of mindset.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s message is the entrance to that order — your relationship with God begins with how you think about God; your relationship with yourself begins with how you think about yourself (the ten spies thought wrongly about themselves); your relationship with others begins with how you think about them.

The shift of perspective is in this lesson too: from man’s perspective to God’s — “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers” is man’s perspective, “Yahweh is with you” is God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly — “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2); from the temporary to the eternal — thirty pieces of silver were temporary, yet Judas traded eternity for them; from the worldly to the godly — the thought-system of Ephesus belonged to the world, and Paul wanted them to “be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23).

The 920 practice is especially practical when it comes to thinking. Every person connected with us is our “2”; practising a selfless (0) life, we bear the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, fruit grows from the inside; it isn’t stuck on from outside. If in your heart you dwell on that person’s faults every day, however gentle you try to look on the outside, you won’t last three days; if in your heart you first bless them, first see them through God’s eyes, patience and kindness will flow out naturally. To bear the nine fruits, first change the way you think.

235 relationships also need right thinking to hold them together. Becoming a “2”, a spiritual companion, to a selfless person means having someone who dares to tell you the truth when your thinking goes crooked; building the “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children, passes right mindsets down from generation to generation; becoming the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, means establishing God’s system together.

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit guides my thinking, the Bible corrects my thinking, the life of Jesus takes shape in my thinking, and so my service lets Jesus be King, and all the glory goes to him.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Five Practices to Set Faith-Filled Thinking in Motion
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practical exercises. Let’s look at them one by one, and use “the eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deeper.

Practice 1: Promise Meditation — Let God’s Word Work in Your Heart

Each day choose one of God’s promises and turn it over and over in your mind. Don’t just read past it; “think” it, and let the promise grow slowly within you.

The psalmist says: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). “Hidden” doesn’t mean put on a bookshelf; it means stored away in the depths of the heart.

How do you actually do it? Choose just one verse — don’t be greedy for more. Copy it onto paper or into your phone, read it three times in the morning, think about it once at midday, and say it again before you sleep. As you read, put the stress on different words, and you’ll find several rays of light within the same verse.

Practice 2: Faith Visualisation — See the Future with Faith

Take the promise God has given you and see in your heart what it looks like fulfilled; let your thinking step into God’s plan ahead of time.

We need to be especially clear here: this is not “using the power of imagination to create reality”. That is man-centred thinking, not biblical faith. Biblical faith says: because God has already spoken, I see in my heart ahead of time what he has said. Hebrews says: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1).

This is exactly how God led Abraham into “faith visualisation”. He told him to go out and count the stars, and said, “So your offspring will be” (Genesis 15:5). From then on, every night sky rehearsed God’s promise once more in his heart.

You can do the same. For the family member who doesn’t yet believe, see in your heart the day they raise their hand to give their life to Christ; for the relationship that is still frozen, see in your heart the picture of the two of you reconciled. Then pray over that picture.

Practice 3: Refusing Doubt — Don’t Let Negative Thoughts Linger

When doubt shows up, don’t hold a conversation with it; turn at once to God’s promise, and replace doubt with faith.

Those few words, “don’t hold a conversation with it”, are very precious. Eve’s failure began when she started discussing things with the serpent: “Has God really said …” (Genesis 3:1). The moment she started discussing, she had lost. The Lord Jesus, by contrast, never debated with Satan; he only said, “It is written …” (Matthew 4:4).

The practical method is “one sentence for another”: for the negative thought that comes to you most often, prepare a verse in advance as its “answering line”. When the thought says, “I can’t,” you say: “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13). When the thought says, “There’s no hope,” you say: “With God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26). No explaining, no debating — just swap it straight out.

Practice 4: Walking with the Spirit — Stay Alert to the Thoughts God Places in Your Heart

When you feel a prompting in your heart, stop and think: “Is this from God?” Then obey, and keep thinking on it.

How do you discern? The Three Foundations are the best filter. Is it in line with Scripture (the Bible is my standard)? Is it like something Jesus would do (Jesus is my role model)? Is there peace inside (the Holy Spirit is my guide)? Isaiah says: “You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you” (Isaiah 26:3).

A very practical suggestion: keep a “promptings notebook”. As soon as you sense a prompting, write it down first; look back a week later, and you will gradually learn to tell which voice comes from God.

Practice 5: Selfless Obedience — Let Jesus Lead My Thinking

When “I don’t want to” shows up, ask yourself one question: “If Jesus were me, how would he think?” Then choose to obey God rather than give in to yourself.

This is the most central practice of all. Behind every “I don’t want to” stands an “I”. “I don’t want to forgive.” “I don’t want to back down first.” “I don’t want to give any more.” Those feelings are all real; the question is whether that “I” should be king.

In the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus gave us the supreme role model: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). He did not pretend it wasn’t hard; he told the truth. But he placed “what I desire” beneath “what you desire”.

That is selflessness. Selflessness is not having no feelings; it is having feelings and still letting Jesus be King.

Using the Eight Stages to Turn Practice into Life

Stage one, Information. Today’s lesson is the information: the power of thought, the difference between receiving and fulfilment, how a thought can bring a miracle or destruction.

Stage two, Revelation. If information stays in the head, it is only knowledge. Ask the Holy Spirit to drive one sentence of it into your heart, so that suddenly you see: “So what has been holding me back all these years was not my circumstances but my thinking.” At that moment, information becomes revelation.

Stage three, Conviction. Acknowledge that God’s view is more reliable than mine. This stage is the surrender of the will: Lord, I will no longer insist on my own ideas; I want yours.

Stage four, Implementation. Pick one of the five practices first, and start today. Don’t try all five at once — you won’t keep it up. Pick one, and do it for seven days.
