When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23) At the very moment when the Lord Jesus was most able to defend himself, he chose not to, because there was no “self” in him to protect.

The Bible is my standard — the words I speak must be tested by the word of God. Whatever God’s word says, I say; where God’s word is silent, I don’t speak carelessly.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — before speaking, first ask the Holy Spirit. Isaiah says, “The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4) Notice: first comes the “taught ear”, and only then the “tongue of those who are taught”. Only an ear awakened morning by morning produces a mouth that can sustain the weary.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive the glory

Let Jesus be King — the most practical testing ground of his kingship is your mouth. A person can say, “Lord, I give you everything,” and yet refuse to swallow the cutting remark already on the tip of his tongue. Brothers and sisters, if Jesus cannot be King of my tongue, he is not yet King of my life.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — Paul says every knee will bow, “and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:11) The highest use of the mouth is to give glory to God. If our words only pull the focus back onto ourselves, we are stealing God’s glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system

God’s system is made up of a community of people who have life in their mouths. In this system, what passes between people is not gossip, not complaint, not comparison, but truth, grace and building up.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The self-centred mouth: complaining, judging, boasting, arguing, self-pity.

The selfless mouth: thanksgiving, blessing, confession, encouragement, declaring God’s faithfulness.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. In speech, pride says, “I will pass judgement on God’s behalf”; humility says, “I hand the right of judgement back to God.”

And remember: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Nowhere is this clearer than in speech. One defiant word draws an even harsher one back, and both people are hurt; but one gentle word can soften the whole room. Solomon said it long ago: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1)

A shift in perspective

Before our mouths speak, let us make four shifts:

From the human perspective to God’s perspective — don’t ask, “What do I want to say?” Ask, “What does God want me to say?”

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly perspective — don’t ask, “How can I say this so I don’t lose out?” Ask, “How can I say this so heaven’s will is done?”

From the temporary perspective to the eternal perspective — a remark that feels good for a moment may wound someone for a lifetime.

From the worldly perspective to the godly perspective — we don’t win people with clever talk; we gain them with truth.

The Lord Jesus said, “I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matthew 12:36–37) This passage reminds us that words carry eternal weight.

The 920 practice and 235 relationships

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. Living the selfless (0) life, we will bear in these relationships the nine fruit of the Holy Spirit — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice this: at least eight of these nine fruit are seen in the way we speak. Love is spoken; joy is spoken; peace is brought by the mouth; patience and gentleness show most plainly in “speaking when we should and keeping silent when we shouldn’t”; and self-control is hardest, and most real, on the tongue. So the first battlefield of the 920 practice is our mouth.

235 relationships: becoming a “2” with a selfless person — spiritual companions must be able both to speak the truth and to hear it; establishing a “3” — the words of spiritual parents to their spiritual children are seeds of life; becoming a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades is a company of people who open their mouths for the Lord.

You can tell the spiritual temperature of a small group by listening to thirty minutes of its conversation.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves

When we speak relying on the brain and ourselves, we calculate, we defend, we want to win; when we speak relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit, we are simple, we are at peace, we bless.

Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. The wellspring of life flows from the heart (Proverbs 4:23).

So this is also how we walk the Path of Serving: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Our mouths must walk this whole road.

sections.heading: 7. Practice for Daily Living: Building a Life of Right Speaking
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word isn’t hard; doing it is. The five practices below are the road this lesson asks us to walk together. Please don’t treat them as five rules; treat them as five doors, and walk through them one by one.

Practice 1: Awareness of speech — notice what you say each day

Every day, observe what you say: is it complaint, or faith? Is it judgement, or building up?

How to do it: set two reminders on your phone, one at midday and one before bed. Ask yourself three questions: What was the most powerful thing I said today? What was the thing I most regret saying today? If Jesus were sitting beside me, which sentence would I want to take back?

Why does awareness matter? Because most hurtful words are forgotten by us the moment we say them, while the one who was hurt remembers them for a long time. The psalmist prays, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” (Psalm 141:3) In the original, “keep” carries the sense of “guarding a city gate”. If no one guards the city gate, anything can come and go.

Brothers and sisters, from today on, post a guard at your mouth.

Practice 2: Transforming your words — turn the negative into the positive

When you want to say something negative, deliberately turn it into words of faith.

For example: “It’s hard” → “With the Lord I can.”

A few more examples:

“I can’t do it” → “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

“There’s nothing more we can do” → “With God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26b).

“He’ll never change” → “God can change him, and I am praying for him.”

“This family is hopeless” → “As for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Joshua 24:15b).

Please note, this is not self-hypnosis or the power of suggestion. Suggestion repeats to yourself a sentence you don’t even believe; a declaration of faith repeats to yourself what God has already said. The first relies on yourself; the second relies on God’s faithfulness.

A pastor once reminded his congregation: don’t tell God how big your problem is; tell your problem how big your God is. That is the essence of transforming your words.

Practice 3: Declaring Scripture — fill your mouth with God’s word

Every day, open your mouth and declare God’s promises, so that your mouth comes into line with God and your faith is built up.

How to do it: choose one verse for this week, and read it aloud three times when you get up in the morning. Reading aloud matters — Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10:17a). Your own ears need to hear your own mouth speaking God’s word.

Suggested verses to declare this week:

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21)

“Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, Yahweh, my rock, and my redeemer.” (Psalm 19:14)

When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, three times he struck back at the enemy with “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). Brothers and sisters, God’s word spoken aloud is the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17).

Practice 4: Building others up — speak more encouragement and blessing

Every day, speak words that build up to at least one person: encouragement, affirmation, blessing.

How to do it: pick someone today and be specific. Don’t say, “You’re great.” Say, “Yesterday you kept on being patient over that matter — I saw it, and it wasn’t easy.” Vague praise is like sweets; specific affirmation is like bread.

“A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” (Proverbs 25:11)

“Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” (Proverbs 16:24)

Brothers and sisters, “health to the bones” — Solomon knew that words can reach right into our bones. Modern medicine also tells us that when people live for long periods surrounded by belittling language, their stress hormones stay elevated, affecting sleep and immunity. God said it long ago: a gentle tongue is a tree of life (Proverbs 15:4a).

Practice 5: Selfless surrender — let Jesus govern my mouth

Pause for one second before you speak and ask yourself, “If Jesus were me, how would he say it?” Then choose to say what pleases God.

That one second is the cross. In that one second, the “self” has to die once more.

James’ reminder is the most practical of all: “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19b). Swift to hear, slow to speak — people today do exactly the opposite: swift to speak, slow to hear, and very swift to anger.

Brothers and sisters, in that one second, if you let Jesus be King, your words will be different.

Deepening these five practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset

321 practice is not about gritting your teeth by willpower; it is about having your mindset changed. There are eight stages of changing our mindset; let us take today’s lesson through all of them:

Stage 1, Information: I now know — the tongue is a fire, and also a rudder; out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; words are seeds.

Stage 2, Revelation: the Holy Spirit lets me see myself. Ask the Lord to shine his light: What is the negative thing I say most often? What is the “self” behind it? Is it fear? Is it wanting? Is it resentment?

Stage 3, Conviction: I don’t just agree; I truly believe. I believe my words carry weight; I believe what I say today will become tomorrow’s fruit.

Stage 4, Implementation: start today. Of the five practices, pick one and do it for seven days. Don’t do all five at once — that usually means none of them gets done.

Stage 5, Evaluation: spend three minutes before bed each night facing things honestly. Where did I hold the line today? Where did I give way? At the moment I gave way, what was going on in my heart?

Stage 6, Correction: confess to God, and where necessary apologise to people. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9) One sincere apology often carries more power than a hundred fine speeches.

Stage 7, Repetition: once doesn’t count, twice doesn’t count. Neuroscience tells us that changing behaviour takes repeated practice before stable pathways are formed. Spiritual practice is the same — only repetition takes us from “I am holding back” to “this is simply who I am”.

Stage 8, Multiplication: pass on what you have received. Find someone, share with them how your “speaking” has changed this week, and invite them to practise with you. This is the “3” — spiritual parents bringing forth spiritual children.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Never underestimate a single sentence, because one sentence can change a whole life.

Words are seeds — sown today, reaped tomorrow.

Words are fire — they can cook a meal, and they can burn down a house.

Words are power — you use this power every day, and you are either building up or tearing down.

Brothers and sisters, please remember:

The humble let God govern their mouths; the proud say whatever they please.

Humility brings forth words of life.

Selflessness lets Jesus speak through you.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

“Speaking” is no small thing; “speaking” is the outlet of your life.

Whatever is inside you is what will come out.

What God invites us to today is not merely a change of behaviour, but letting him govern our mouths.

Do you remember Isaiah in the temple? He saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and he cried out, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!” (Isaiah 6:5)

Brothers and sisters, notice: his first reaction on seeing God was not “my hands are unclean” or “my feet are unclean”, but “I am a man of unclean lips”.

And then what did God do? “Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar. He touched my mouth with it, and said, ‘Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.’” (Isaiah 6:6–7)

God cleansed his lips. Only then, in the very next verse, did Isaiah hear the Lord say, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And he said, “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8)

First the mouth is cleansed, then the person is sent. Brothers and sisters, this morning, are you willing to bring your mouth to the altar?

When you begin to speak God’s words, words of faith, words that build up, you will see lives changed, relationships established and revival set in motion.

May we all become people like this: mouths full of life, words that bring forth revival.

Living the selfless life, letting Jesus live in us, letting Jesus be King, letting Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” (James 3:5)
“For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34b)
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare:
My mouth will be governed by God, and my words will bring forth life.
I reject all negativity and judgement; I choose to speak faith and truth.
God’s word fills my heart, and God’s word fills my mouth.
I will build people up with my words; I will glorify God with my words.
What I speak will bring forth the fruit of life; what I speak will become a blessing.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Awareness of speech — notice what you say each day
Transforming your words — turn the negative into the positive
Declaring Scripture — fill your mouth with God’s word
Building others up — speak more encouragement and blessing
Selfless surrender — let Jesus govern my mouth
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

Thank you that this morning you have shone your light on us through your word. You have shown us that our mouths are not just organs of speech; they are the outlet of our lives, the place where what is within us is revealed.

Lord, we confess that we have often hurt people with our mouths, grumbled against you with our mouths, argued for ourselves with our mouths, and sown seeds of unbelief with our mouths. Please forgive us. As you cleansed Isaiah’s lips, cleanse our lips with the fire of the altar.

Lord, we give our mouths to you. Be King of our tongues. When we want to complain, remind us of your faithfulness; when we want to judge, remind us of your mercy; when we want to stay silent rather than bear witness to you, put within us the fire that says, “We can’t help telling.”
Fill our hearts with your word, so that our mouths naturally pour out your word. Make us people who, at home, at work and in our small groups, speak what is good for building others up.
May the words of our mouths and the meditation of our hearts be acceptable in your sight. May every word we speak in our whole lives become a seed of life, bearing fruit that glorifies you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34b) Looking back over this week, what have you said most often? What does that reveal your heart is currently full of? Which part of your “inside” are you willing to ask God to change first?

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21) Share specifically one practice you plan to take up this week (awareness, transforming, declaring, building up, selfless surrender), and say to whom you will speak a word that builds up. Group members can pray for one another and check in with each other next week.
l137.title: Speaking Rightly
l137.subtitle: Let Jesus Rule My Mouth; Let My Words Bring Life
l137.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: Four Hundred Million Words in a Lifetime — What Will You Leave Behind?
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to do some arithmetic.

In July 2007 the journal Science published a fascinating study. A group of researchers — Matthias Mehl, Simine Vazire, Nairán Ramírez-Esparza, Richard Slatcher and James Pennebaker — used a portable electronic recording device to track and record what three hundred and ninety-six university students said in the course of their daily lives. They found that, men and women alike, a person speaks on average about sixteen thousand words a day.

What does sixteen thousand words look like? It is roughly one chapter of a master’s thesis. A chapter a day, three hundred and sixty-five chapters a year. If we live to seventy, we will speak more than four hundred million words in a lifetime.

Brothers and sisters, what will those four hundred million words leave behind?

A sister once told me with tears in her eyes, “Pastor, my husband said something to me twenty years ago, and I still remember it today.” I asked her, “What did he say?” She said, “He said — ‘If I’d known, I’d never have married you.’” Twenty years have gone by. They have moved house, the children have grown up, she has changed jobs three times — and that sentence is still there. A handful of words; twenty years.

A brother also told me, “The thing I will never forget is what my mother said to me the day I failed my entrance exam. She said, ‘Son, God still has a better plan for you.’” That one sentence has walked with him for thirty years.

Both were just one sentence. One pushes a person off a cliff; the other pulls a person back from the edge. How precisely Solomon put it:

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21)

In the last lesson we saw how important “speaking” is. Since speaking matters so much, today we will go a step further and ask two questions: what is right speaking? And what is wrong speaking?

Brothers and sisters, the truth is that most people don’t lack the desire to say the right thing. In our hearts we all want to say the right thing. The problem lies in two things: first, we don’t know what actually counts as right; second, we don’t know when we ought to speak. So we speak by feeling, by habit, by the emotion of the moment — and only afterwards do we regret it.

Thank the Lord, Jesus gives us the clearest of role models. He said, “For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” (John 12:49)

Notice the difference here. Jesus did not “speak whenever he felt like it”; Jesus spoke “only when the Father wanted him to speak”.

In the 321 vision, this is precisely the watershed between the self-centred life and selflessness. The self-centred life means I decide for myself what I am going to say; selflessness means letting God decide what I am going to say. Today’s lesson has only one aim: that our mouths would no longer belong to ourselves, but would become God’s outlet.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Son of God Who Did Not Speak from Himself
1. Author, Date and Audience
sections.html:
The early church was unanimous that the author of John’s Gospel was John the son of Zebedee, the “disciple whom Jesus loved”. He bears witness himself at the end of the book: “This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true.” (John 21:24)

The book is generally thought to have been written between AD 85 and 95, and tradition places its writing in Ephesus in Asia Minor. By then most of the first generation of apostles had been martyred; the church was facing persecution from the Jewish synagogue as well as the infiltration of early Gnostic ideas. John’s purpose in writing is crystal clear:

“But these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

sections.heading: 2. The Historical and Cultural Setting
sections.html:
In the Jewish rabbinic system of the first century, a disciple’s greatest duty was to “pass on” his teacher’s words accurately, adding nothing and taking nothing away. The rabbis would often say, “Rabbi So-and-so said in the name of Rabbi So-and-so.” Yet within that culture Jesus stood up and said: what I speak is what the Father has said to me. He was not passing on the words of some rabbi; he was passing on the words of God the Father.

At the same time, the Graeco-Roman world this book addressed was a world that idolised eloquence. Orators (rhetors) won status by their words; sophists earned money and fame by debate. Whoever could speak held the power. In just such an age, John recorded the most astonishing confession of the Son of God: “I spoke not from myself.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see the tension here? John’s Gospel opens with the proclamation: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” (John 1:1) Jesus himself is “the Word”, the God who speaks. Yet when this “Word” became flesh and dwelt among us, the first lesson he learned on earth was this — not to speak from himself.

If even the Word does not speak from himself, what right do we have to speak from ourselves?

sections.heading: 3. The Surrounding Context
sections.html:
John chapter 12 is a major turning point in the whole book. Scholars commonly call chapters 1–12 “the Book of Signs” and chapters 13–21 “the Book of Glory”. John 12:37 says, “But though he had done so many signs before them, yet they didn’t believe in him.” And the second half of verse 36 says, “Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them.”

In other words, his public ministry had come to an end. At just such a moment, verse 44 records: “Jesus cried out and said, ‘Whoever believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me.’” This is the last public proclamation of Jesus’ public ministry. A person’s parting words are often the words he values most.

And what Jesus left last was not a debate, not a miracle, but a testimony about “speaking”: everything I speak is what the Father wants me to speak.

Brothers and sisters, this is the role model we are learning from today.

Teaching 1: Right speaking is not from ourselves, but from God

sections.heading: 1. Jesus’ Principle: Not from Himself, Only from the Father
sections.html:
“I know that his commandment is eternal life. The things therefore which I speak, even as the Father has said to me, so I speak.” (John 12:50)

In the original, verse 49 uses two different verbs. The “say” in “what I should say” is the Greek εἶπον (eipon, from λέγω legō), which focuses on “the content of what is said”; the “speak” in “what I should speak” is the Greek λαλέω (laleō), which focuses on “the act and manner of speaking”.

In other words, the commandment the Father gave Jesus governed not only “what content he said” but also “how he spoke, when he spoke and to whom he spoke”. Both content and manner were in the Father’s hands.

And the word “commandment”, in Greek ἐντολή (entolē), means a specific instruction issued by a king or a father. Jesus did not speak out of some vague feeling; he spoke according to a clear commission.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, we find a whole string of the same confession in John’s Gospel:

“The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” (John 5:19)

“I do nothing of myself, but as my Father taught me, I say these things.” (John 8:28)

“The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself; but the Father who lives in me does his works.” (John 14:10)

Three times, “not of myself”. This was the central thread of Jesus’ thirty-three and a half years of life on earth. It was not that he lacked the power to act of himself; he was willing not to act of himself. That is selflessness.

sections.heading: 2. We Often Do the Opposite: Speaking by Emotion, Feeling and Habit
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, yet we so often do the opposite. We speak by emotion — the moment we feel upset, the words are out. We speak by feeling — we feel we ought to say something, so we say it. We speak by habit — we have always spoken this way, so we keep on speaking this way.

And the result? Once the words are out, they bring hurt.

I once saw a scene at the site of a car accident. Two cars had collided, and when the drivers got out, the first thing they said was not “Are you hurt?” but “Can’t you drive?” The second sentence turned into an exchange of insults; the third turned into shoving. Standing to one side, I thought: the cost of this accident is two bumpers, but the cost of these few sentences may be two people’s peace for the whole day — maybe even the whole year.

The 321 vision puts it very plainly: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. This isn’t just a slogan; it is a law proven again and again every day — on the road, in the office, at the dinner table.

The Bible said it long ago: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1)

sections.heading: 3. Why Do We Say the Wrong Thing? Because We Are Too Quick
sections.html:
James puts his finger right on the root of the disease:

“So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” (James 1:19–20)

“Swift” is the Greek ταχύς (tachys), meaning “quick, rapid”; “slow” is βραδύς (bradys), meaning “sluggish, unhurried”. James is not telling us not to speak; he is adjusting our speed: quick to listen, slow to speak.

There is an interesting point of comparison here. When God made human beings, he gave us two ears and one mouth. The Greek philosopher Zeno of Citium is generally credited with saying that we have two ears and one mouth so that we may listen more and speak less. The very design of creation is itself a lesson.

Psychology also provides a footnote to this verse. In 1995 the psychologist Daniel Goleman, in his book “Emotional Intelligence”, used the term “amygdala hijack” to describe a phenomenon: when a person is strongly provoked, the amygdala — the part of the brain responsible for emotional alarm — seizes control in a split second, and before the person has time to think rationally, the words have already burst out.

In 2007 Matthew Lieberman’s team at the University of California, Los Angeles published a study in Psychological Science entitled “Putting Feelings into Words”. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, they found that when subjects “named” their emotions, activity in the amygdala decreased, while activity in the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex increased. Put simply: when a person is willing to stop and first identify his own emotions, the alarm bell of impulse grows quieter.

Brothers and sisters, this is what “slow to speak” looks like in scientific terms. Many problems arise not because things are difficult, but because the words come out too fast.

sections.heading: 4. A Spiritual Discipline: Pause First, Listen First, Then Speak
sections.html:
So right speaking involves three actions: pause first, listen first, then speak.

Pause first. The psalmist cries out, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” (Psalm 141:3) “Keep” is a military term — like a guard at a city gate, checking each one before letting them through.

Listen first. The boy Samuel was called three times in the night, and in the end he learned how to respond: “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10) Brothers and sisters, notice the order of these words. He did not say, “Servant, speak; Lord, listen.” He said, “Speak; for your servant hears.” Our problem is very often that we say it the wrong way round.

Then speak. Isaiah describes how the Servant’s mouth was formed: “The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4) First comes the taught ear, then the taught tongue. Listen first every morning, and then you will be able to speak through the day.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t this exactly what 321 Morning Devotion is about? When we give our ears to God first thing in the morning, our words for the day have a source.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight and Practice
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. The wellspring of life flows from the heart.

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

When we rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit guides us, we say what God wants said; when we rely on the brain and react on our own, we say what we will regret.

So every time we are about to open our mouths, we can ask ourselves one question — and this question is one of the most practical disciplines of 321:

If Jesus were me, would he speak now? And how would he say it?

Brothers and sisters, to ask this question is to hand the throne back to Jesus. To ask this question is to let Jesus be King.

Teaching 2: Right speaking means speaking more of God’s words and less of our own

sections.heading: 1. When It Is Inside, It Comes Out Naturally
sections.html:
Because Peter and John had healed the lame man at the Beautiful Gate, they were arrested and brought before the council for trial. The council strictly forbade them to speak any more in the name of Jesus. Peter and John’s reply became one of the most courageous sentences in the history of the church:

“For we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.” (Acts 4:20)

The original uses a double negative here: οὐ δυνάμεθα... μὴ λαλεῖν, literally “we are not able not to speak”. That wasn’t bravado; it was a pressure from within. When it is inside, nothing can hold it back.

This reminds me of Jeremiah. Mocked for proclaiming God’s word, he once said in frustration that he would no longer mention Yahweh. But he said:

“If I say, I will not make mention of him, or speak any more in his name, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones. I am weary with holding it in. I can’t.” (Jeremiah 20:9)

Brothers and sisters, is that fire burning in you?

sections.heading: 2. Three Fruits of Speaking It Out
sections.html:
The lesson reminds us of a very practical discipline: speak more of “what God has said to you”. When God moves you, shines his light on you, reminds you of something, don’t just keep it in your heart — speak it out.

Why speak it out? There are three results.

First, speaking it out deepens it. Cognitive psychology has a phenomenon that has been confirmed again and again, called the “production effect”. A study by Colin MacLeod and colleagues at the University of Waterloo in Canada, published in 2010 in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, showed that from the same list of words, the words read aloud were remembered more firmly and for longer than those read silently. As early as 1885, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus experimented on himself and plotted the famous “forgetting curve”, showing that what we have learned, if not rehearsed, is largely lost within a short time.

Brothers and sisters, it is the same with God’s word. A prompting kept only in your heart fades in three days; a prompting spoken out is still there three years later.

Second, speaking it out makes it certain. Paul says, “For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.” (Romans 10:10) Believing in the heart is the root; confessing with the mouth is the fruit. Once the mouth confesses, faith moves from vague to clear, from private to public.

Third, speaking it out leads to living it out. Moses instructed the Israelites:

“These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.” (Deuteronomy 6:6–7)

Sitting, walking, lying down, rising up — that is the whole of a day. If God’s word is to become our daily living, it must first become our conversation.

sections.heading: 3. An Outlet for Living Water: the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
sections.html:
I often use an example from geography to illustrate this.

The Jordan River flows down from the north, first into the Sea of Galilee, then out again from its southern end, all the way down to the Dead Sea. The Sea of Galilee has both an inflow and an outflow, so it is a lake of living water. More than twenty kinds of fish live in it; there are fishing villages along its shores; it was there that Jesus called his disciples and worked miracles.

Yet the water of that same Jordan, once it flows into the Dead Sea, never flows out again. The Dead Sea has no outlet; it loses water only by evaporation. Over time its salt concentration has reached around thirty per cent, roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater. No fish live there, no water plants, and so it is called the “Dead Sea”.

Brothers and sisters, the same water — with an outlet it lives; without an outlet it dies.

When God’s word comes into us, if it only comes in and never goes out, in time it turns salty, bitter, dead. When God’s word comes in and flows out again, we become a lake of living water. Jesus said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.” (John 7:38)

sections.heading: 4. This Is Not Putting on a Spiritual Show, but Helping Ourselves Live in the Truth
sections.html:
Some brothers and sisters worry: if I often talk about God’s word, will people think I’m showing off how spiritual I am?

Jesus did indeed warn us: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1)

So the key is motive, not volume. In “Life Together” (1939), Dietrich Bonhoeffer placed “the ministry of holding one’s tongue” first among the ways believers serve one another — only when we have learned to keep our mouths shut rather than judge a brother are we fit to open them to build him up. First the ministry of silence, then the ministry of words.

In other words: speaking more doesn’t make you spiritual; speaking rightly does. We share God’s word not to prove that we have it, but to help ourselves live in the truth; as others are built up, you yourself are built up all the more.

Conversely, if God’s word is inside you but you don’t speak it, and instead you keep voicing your own opinions, your own analysis, your own complaints, your life will stagnate. For whatever we speak, we deepen.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight and Practice
sections.html:
The fivefold change in the 321 vision is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Brothers and sisters, notice where “speaking” sits within this fivefold change. God’s word first enters our mindset; then, by being “spoken out”, it seeps into our life, takes root in our daily living, flows through our relationships, and finally becomes ministry. “Speaking” is the bridge from mindset to life.

The selfless: speak God’s words, and so live out God’s words.

The self-centred: speak their own words, and so live inside themselves.

The 321 vision says: the Bible is my standard. If the standard stays only on the bookshelf, it cannot govern my tongue; the standard must be in my mouth before it can hold my tongue in check.

So there is one thing we must practise: letting God’s word become the main content of our mouths.

Teaching 3: Right speaking means always giving thanks and praise, and never grumbling

sections.heading: 1. Always Giving Thanks, Always Praising — a Choice, Not a Mood
sections.html:
The Bible clearly teaches us two things.

The first is always giving thanks: “giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God, even the Father” (Ephesians 5:20). “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18)

The second is always praising: “I will bless Yahweh at all times. His praise will always be in my mouth.” (Psalm 34:1) “Through him, then, let’s offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name.” (Hebrews 13:15)

The Greek for “give thanks” is εὐχαριστέω (eucharisteō), made up of εὖ (good, well) and χάρις (grace); its literal sense is “speaking well because of grace”. Etymologically, then, thanksgiving was always a kind of “speaking”.

The Hebrew for “praise”, הָלַל (halal), is the root of “Hallelujah”; its basic meaning is to shine, to boast, to extol aloud. Praise is not a soft, murmured mood; it is an offering with a voice, with action, with a cost.

Please pay special attention to two phrases in Hebrews 13:15: “a sacrifice of praise” and “the fruit of lips”. A sacrifice implies a cost; fruit implies there was first a seed. Giving thanks when things go well is easy; giving thanks when things go badly is faith.

Brothers and sisters, this is not a mood; it is a choice.

sections.heading: 2. A Negative Example: Israel Shut Off the Promise with Their Mouths
sections.html:
Numbers 13 and 14 is one of the most grievous passages in the whole Bible.

Twelve spies came back from exploring the land of Canaan, and ten of them brought back an evil report. They said, “There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.” (Numbers 13:33)

Notice: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers” — that is their self-image; “and so we were in their sight” — that is something they imagined and attributed to their enemies. The enemy had not yet said a word, and they had already said it all on the enemy’s behalf.

Then the whole congregation joined in grumbling: “All the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, ‘We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt, or that we had died in this wilderness!’” (Numbers 14:2)

The Hebrew for “murmur” is לוּן (lun), whose basic meaning is “to lodge overnight, to stay”, and by extension “to mutter over and over, all night long”. What makes grumbling so dreadful is not how loud it is, but that it moves in and refuses to leave.

And then came God’s answer. Listen carefully to this passage:

“How long shall I bear with this evil congregation that complain against me? I have heard the complaints of the children of Israel, which they complain against me. Tell them, ‘As I live, says Yahweh, surely as you have spoken in my ears, so I will do to you.’” (Numbers 14:27–28)

“Surely as you have spoken in my ears, so I will do to you.” They said, “We wish we had died in this wilderness,” and God, taking them at their word, let them fall dead in the wilderness. Their own mouths pronounced their sentence.

Brothers and sisters, the problem was not their circumstances. The wilderness hadn’t changed, the land of Canaan hadn’t changed, God’s promise hadn’t changed. What had changed was their “speaking”. With their mouths they shut off the blessing; with their mouths they refused the promise.

Yet from the same land and among the same group of spies, Caleb said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30) And God’s verdict on him was: “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and has followed me fully, him I will bring into the land into which he went.” (Numbers 14:24)

The same land, two ways of speaking, two endings.

sections.heading: 3. A Positive Example: Paul and Silas Singing Hymns in Prison
sections.html:
Now look at the other side. Philippi was a leading city of that district of Macedonia and a Roman colony (Acts 16:12) — a settlement of retired Roman soldiers, proud of its Roman citizenship. There Paul and Silas cast a spirit out of a slave girl, and with it went her owners’ hope of profit. They were dragged before the magistrates, their clothes were torn off, they were beaten with many rods, thrown into the inner prison, and their feet were fastened in the stocks (Acts 16:22–24).

Wounds on their backs, stocks on their feet, the time midnight, the place the inner prison. What would a person say in such a situation? Most likely groaning, complaining, “God, why?”

But the Bible says:

“But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.” (Acts 16:25–26)

Notice the order. First came prayer and praise, then the great earthquake. First came the fruit of lips, then the prison doors flung open.

And the result was not only their own release. The jailer fell down trembling and asked what he must do to be saved, and Paul answered, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” (Acts 16:31) That night the jailer’s whole household was baptised, and the church in Philippi was born.

Brothers and sisters, the same kind of hardship, different “speaking”, and completely different outcomes. The Israelites grumbled in the wilderness and talked themselves out of the Promised Land; Paul and Silas praised God in prison and talked that prison into a delivery room for the church.

sections.heading: 4. Why Thanksgiving Has Power
sections.html:
Someone asks: giving thanks can’t change the facts, so why give thanks?

True, thanksgiving often doesn’t change the facts — but it changes the person looking at the facts.

Psychology offers some supporting evidence. In 2003 Robert Emmons of the University of California, Davis, and Michael McCullough of the University of Miami published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They divided the participants into groups: one group wrote down each week five things they were grateful for, another five things that had annoyed them, and another neutral events. After a few weeks, the “gratitude group” rated their lives more positively overall, reported fewer physical complaints, and were more willing to help others.

In addition, Roy Baumeister and others, in their 2001 review paper “Bad Is Stronger Than Good”, pointed out that in human psychology the impact of negative events and negative remarks is generally stronger than that of positive events of equal weight. This is why one hurtful sentence takes many kind sentences to make up for. The marriage researcher John Gottman, through long-term laboratory observation, also found that in stable marriages the proportion of positive interactions is markedly higher than that of negative ones.

Brothers and sisters, please hear this clearly: these studies are not our reason for believing in thanksgiving — the Bible is. God’s word says, “In everything give thanks,” so we give thanks. Science merely catches up from behind and takes a photograph of what God’s word has said.

And the reason the Bible gives is higher than any study:

“Whoever offers the sacrifice of thanksgiving glorifies me, and prepares his way so that I will show God’s salvation to him.” (Psalm 50:23)

Giving thanks glorifies God. This is the second of the Two Core Values in 321 — let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight and Practice
The 321 vision reminds us of a crucial shift: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.
sections.html:
The Israelites’ focus was on the sons of Anak, so they saw themselves as grasshoppers. Paul’s focus was on Jesus, so even in the inner prison he could still sing hymns.

This is the shift in perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective; from the earthly perspective to the heavenly perspective; from the temporary perspective to the eternal perspective; from the worldly perspective to the godly perspective.

Later, writing from prison to the church in Philippi, Paul said, “Do all things without complaining and arguing” (Philippians 2:14). He had every right to say so, because he had practised it himself in that very city’s prison.

The selfless: give thanks in all things, and experience God at work.

The self-centred: always complain, and lose God’s blessing.

So the key is not what happens, but how you speak about it.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Let Jesus Be King of My Mouth
1. The Three Foundations Are Three Gatekeepers
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations of 321 correspond exactly to today’s three teachings.

Jesus is my role model. He said, “I spoke not from myself,” so I too will not speak from myself. That is Teaching 1.

The Bible is my standard. His word becomes the main content of my mouth, so I speak more of God’s words. That is Teaching 2.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. He prompts me to speak when I should speak and to stop when I should stop, and he enables me to sing thanksgiving even in trouble. That is Teaching 3.

In other words, the Three Foundations are three gatekeepers standing in front of our lips. Before a word leaves the mouth, first consult the role model, then the standard, then the guide. Only words that pass all three checkpoints are right speaking.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values Are the Two Purposes of Speaking
sections.html:
Let Jesus be King. Kingship means that my mouth belongs to a sovereign. My tongue is no longer my private property; it is the King’s instrument. James says:

“For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.” (James 3:2)

“Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.” (James 3:4)

The tongue is the rudder. Whoever holds the helm decides the course of the ship. To let Jesus be King is to hand the helm over to him.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. This is the ultimate purpose of speaking. I open my mouth not to win, not to prove I am right, but so that he may be glorified. Psalm 50:23 says that whoever offers the sacrifice of thanksgiving glorifies God.

sections.heading: 3. The Goal: Establishing God’s System with Our Words
sections.html:
What is a fellowship, a family, a church built with? With words.

Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29) The original word for “building up” is a builder’s term, meaning “putting up a house”.

Brothers and sisters, every single day we are either building a house with our mouths or pulling one down with our mouths. God’s system is not established by organisation; it is established one upbuilding word at a time.

sections.heading: 4. The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless
sections.html:
The self-centred life means: I say whatever I want to say; my mouth is my own. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; in speech, pride says: I will do the defining, I will do the judging, I must have the last word.

Selflessness means: my mouth no longer belongs to me. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God; in speech, humility says: I don’t need to have the last word, because God has it.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. This plays out every day — in conversations between husband and wife, between parent and child, between co-workers.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says:

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20)

When my mouth is no longer mine, Christ can speak through my mouth. One small tongue is connected to the infinite.

sections.heading: 5. The Priority of Relationships and the Fivefold Change
sections.html:
321 says: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Applied to “speaking”, this order gives us today’s three actions: pause first (with ourselves), listen first (with God), then speak (with others), and only last deal with the matter at hand (with things). When we fail, it is usually because we have turned the order upside down — dealing with the matter first, then opening our mouths to people, and thinking of God only at the very end.

321 also says: the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Brothers and sisters, so often, in order to get the “task” right, we wound the “person” with our words. The task gets done; the people scatter. That is not victory.

sections.heading: 6. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships
sections.html:
The 920 practice says: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living the selfless (0) life and bearing the nine (9) fruit of the Holy Spirit.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Count them: love has to be spoken; joy has to be spoken; peace has to be spoken; patience means not rushing to speak; kindness means speaking gently; goodness means speaking words that build up; faithfulness means keeping your word once you’ve given it; gentleness means not crushing people with words; self-control means stopping when it is time to stop. All nine fruit grow on the lips.

Doesn’t Hebrews 13:15 speak of “the fruit of lips”? Brothers and sisters, a great deal of the fruit of the Spirit grows on our tongues.

235 relationships say: become a “2”, a spiritual companion, with a selfless person; establish a “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. And all of this is built beginning with “speaking”. If spiritual companions won’t speak the truth to each other, they are not companions at all; if spiritual parents won’t speak words that build up, they will never bring forth spiritual children; if a team of comrades speaks words that tear one another down, it will fall apart before the battle has even begun.

sections.heading: 7. The Path of Serving
sections.html:
321 says the Path of Serving is: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide: listen first. Understanding — the Bible is my standard: receive the word. Life — Jesus is my role model: the word becomes life. Service — let Jesus be King: speak with your life. God — let Jesus receive all the glory: let your words give the glory to him.

Brothers and sisters, one right word walks this whole road from beginning to end.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Building Spiritual Habits of Right Speaking
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five very practical disciplines. Let’s look at them one at a time.

Practice 1: The one-second pause — stop before you speak

Every time you are about to speak, pause for one second and ask yourself, “Is this what God wants me to say?”

One second is very short, but in that second the amygdala and the Holy Spirit are fighting over the microphone. That second decides whether the next sentence will be a blessing or a curse.

How to do it: put a small mark on your phone case, your desk, your steering wheel; whenever you see it, remember “pause one second”.

Practice 2: Sharing God’s word — speak more of what God has said to you

Each day, find one opportunity to share one of three things: a verse, a prompting, or a testimony.

No need for a long speech; two or three sentences are enough. It can be in your family group chat, at fellowship, over lunch. Remember the “production effect” — only what is spoken out is remembered; only what is spoken out is lived out.

Practice 3: Thanksgiving and praise — build positive speaking habits

Every day, deliberately speak out three things you are thankful for and three sentences of praise to God.

Please note the words “speak out”. Not thinking it in your heart, but opening your mouth and saying it. You can say them when you get up, before meals, or at bedtime together with your family.

Practice 4: Turning the negative around — stop grumbling

When you feel like grumbling, immediately turn that complaint into a prayer or a thanksgiving, replacing emotion with faith.

The method is simple: change “How could this happen?” into “Lord, what do you want to teach me in this?”; change “How could he do that?” into “Lord, please bless him, and change me too.”

Remember Numbers 14:28: God said, “Surely as you have spoken in my ears, so I will do to you.” Our words come back to us.

Practice 5: Selfless surrender — let Jesus govern my mouth

In conflict or when emotions run high, ask yourself, “If Jesus were me, how would he say it?” Then choose to submit to God.

This question is not asking us to pretend; it is asking us to change places — from the self-centred life to selflessness, from my throne to his throne.

Deepening these five practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset

The eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let us use these eight stages to turn the five practices above into real life.

Stage 1, Information. Today’s lesson is the information. You now know: right speaking means not speaking from yourself, speaking more of God’s words, and always giving thanks and praise.

Stage 2, Revelation. If information stays in the head, it is only knowledge. Ask the Holy Spirit for a specific light: this week, where does my mouth most often go wrong? Is it speaking too quickly? Speaking too much of my own words? Or grumbling? Write it down.

Stage 3, Conviction. Truly believe that “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21) — believe it so much that you are willing to confess a single sentence as sin, and to apologise for a single sentence. Without conviction, practice is mere form.

Stage 4, Implementation. Pick one of the five practices and do it today. Don’t do all five at once, or you won’t keep it up. I suggest starting with “three things to be thankful for”, because it is the easiest place to begin.

Stage 5, Evaluation. Each night before bed, take two minutes to look back: was there anything I said today that Jesus would not have said? Was there anything God wanted me to say that I didn’t?

Stage 6, Correction. When you find you have said something wrong, put it right the same day. A simple “I’m sorry, what I said just now was wrong” often carries more power than ten sermons.

Stage 7, Repetition. Behavioural science agrees: habits are formed by repetition, not by a single moment of inspiration. Keep it up for twenty-one days, for forty days, until it becomes muscle memory.

Stage 8, Multiplication. Once you have had a taste of the sweetness, go and find your “2” — your spouse, your children, a colleague, your spiritual companion — and invite them to do it with you. When two practise together, the success rate is far higher than for one alone. This is 920; this is 235.

Brothers and sisters, the eight stages are not eight assignments; they are one road. Walk it all the way round, and your mouth will have a new master.

A Gentle Reminder

Don’t be in a hurry to speak; first learn to listen to God. Don’t speak out of habit; learn to discern before you speak.

Saying the right thing matters more than saying a lot. Solomon says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.” (Proverbs 10:19)

The humble let God govern their mouths; the proud are used to speaking for themselves.

Humility brings right speaking. Selflessness lets Jesus speak through you.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: A Mouth Full of God’s Voice
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, “speaking” is a spiritual key. How you speak determines how you live.

Jesus said, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) The mouth is the outlet of the heart. We cannot harbour bitterness and speak blessing at the same time; nor can we be full of Christ and have a mouth full of complaints.

So today God extends an invitation to us: no longer to speak from ourselves, but to let him speak.

When you begin to speak God’s words, words of thanksgiving, words of faith, you will see three things happen: lives are changed, circumstances are turned around, and miracles begin to happen.

In the wilderness the Israelites spent forty years proving what wrong speaking brings; in Philippi, Paul and Silas took one midnight to prove what right speaking brings. Today, which will you choose?

May we all become people like this: mouths full of God’s voice, words that bring forth God’s works.

Living the selfless life, letting Jesus live in us. Letting Jesus be King, letting Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” (John 12:49)
“I know that his commandment is eternal life. The things therefore which I speak, even as the Father has said to me, so I speak.” (John 12:50)
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19)
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare:
My mouth will no longer speak from itself; my mouth will be governed by God.
I will say what God wants me to say, and I reject all wrong words.
God’s word is in me, and it will flow out of my mouth.
I will always give thanks; I will always praise.
My words will bring forth life; my words will bring forth blessing.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: The one-second pause — stop before you speak
Sharing God’s word — speak more of what God has said to you
Thanksgiving and praise — build positive speaking habits
Turning the negative around — stop grumbling
Selfless surrender — let Jesus govern my mouth
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
You are God made flesh; you had the authority to say anything at all, yet you willingly said, “I spoke not from myself.” Lord, your humility puts us to shame, and it also sets us free.

Lord, please forgive us. We have hurt people with our mouths; we have spoken out of our emotions; we have grumbled before you. We have swallowed back the promptings you placed in our hearts, while voicing our own opinions loud and long. Lord, cleanse our lips, as you cleansed Isaiah’s lips with the burning coal.

Lord, give us the ear of those who are taught, and give us the tongue of those who are taught. Holy Spirit, in the very second we are about to open our mouths, remind us: pause, and listen to you first.

Put your word in our mouths, and let it become what we talk about every day. Help us give thanks when things go well and praise you when things go hard; let our homes, our fellowships and our churches be built up by our mouths, not torn down.
Lord, we hand you this small rudder, our tongue. Take the helm, and steer us along the course you want us to sail.
May the words of our mouths and the meditation of our hearts be acceptable in your sight. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: Jesus said, “For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” (John 12:49) Looking back over the past week, was there something you said “from yourself” that you regretted afterwards? If you could do it again, what would you say? Please share specifically.

Question 2: God said to the Israelites, “Surely as you have spoken in my ears, so I will do to you.” (Numbers 14:28) Yet Paul and Silas, at midnight in the inner prison, were “praying and singing hymns to God” (Acts 16:25). What difficulty are you facing right now? In front of your small group, put that difficulty into a sentence of thanksgiving, and ask the group to pray for your “mouth”.
l138.title: Right Speaking and Wrong Speaking
l138.subtitle: Let My Mouth Be God’s Outlet
l138.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: Once Words Are Spoken, They Are Not Over
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

In our last lesson we learned together to “speak the right words.” This morning God wants to help us in a more specific, more personal way, by asking two very practical questions —

What words “should not be spoken”? What words “should be spoken”?

Brothers and sisters, we need to be honest about something: much of the time, it isn’t that we don’t know we should “speak good words.” We’ve heard that since we were children. The real difficulty lies in two other things — first, we don’t know which words are actually “wrong”; second, we don’t know how to tell.

A sister once said through her tears, “I thought I was simply concerned for that brother. That’s why I told two other people about what was going on in his family. I didn’t mean any harm.” Yet three weeks later that brother left the small group and never came back. She hadn’t lied. Every sentence she said was true. Her motive was even kind. But those words still killed a relationship.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the difficulty we face today: it isn’t only “false words” that wound — many “true words” wound too; it isn’t only “malice” that is sin — much that is “thoughtless” must also be accounted for.

Jesus spoke of this with great seriousness:

“I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matthew 12:36–37)

Notice one word: “every.” Not “more or less,” not “the important parts” — every word.

So the mindset the Bible gives us is this: once words are spoken, they are not over. Words must be accounted for.

In our generation, speech has never been so cheap. In the past, passing on a message meant walking for miles; today, one press of a finger, and within a second a sentence can reach the other side of the earth — and stay in the cloud for ever. The cost of broadcasting has fallen almost to nothing, but the weight of our words before God has not lessened one bit.

In the 321 vision we see a clear dividing line:

Self-centred people speak carelessly — because their centre is themselves. They speak to express themselves, to prove themselves, to protect themselves, and the result is loss.

Selfless people speak before God — because their centre is Jesus. Before they speak, they first look up; as they speak, they speak in reverence; and the result is life.

Brothers and sisters, in this lesson today we are going to do one thing: examine our words by God’s standard.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Words Jesus Spoke in a Dispute, a Letter Paul Wrote amid Chaos
sections.html:
To receive today’s message accurately, we first need to understand where our two key passages come from.

The first is Matthew 12:36–37.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, the tax collector sitting at the tax booth when the Lord called him (Matthew 9:9). This Gospel is generally thought to have been written around AD 60, mainly for Jewish readers. Throughout, it quotes the Old Testament again and again to prove that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the son of David, the King of kings.

The context of these two verses matters a great deal. Jesus had just healed a man who was demon-possessed, blind and mute, and all the crowds were amazed and said, “Can this be the son of David?” (Matthew 12:23) But when the Pharisees heard it, they said that Jesus drove out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. What a grave thing to say — they called the work of the Holy Spirit the work of a demon. It was in this setting that Jesus gave a teaching about “words”:

“You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks. The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things.” (Matthew 12:34–35)

Brothers and sisters, see the order here: the heart comes first, the mouth comes after. The mouth is the outlet of the heart; words are the water pipe of our life. What flows out of a pipe isn’t decided by the pipe — it’s decided by the source. That is why Jesus goes on to say that every idle word must be accounted for. He isn’t talking about rhetoric. He is talking about life.

The Greek word for “idle” is ἀργός (argos), formed from the negative prefix a plus ergon, “work.” Literally it means “not working,” “idle,” “bearing no fruit.” The same word is used in Matthew 20:3 for the labourers “standing idle in the marketplace.” So the idle words Jesus speaks of are not necessarily foul words, not necessarily lies, but “words that are not at work” — words that spin in neutral, words that produce nothing, words that contribute nothing at all to the kingdom of God.

And that is precisely why idle words are so dangerous: they look the most innocent.

The second passage is 1 Corinthians 14:3.

First Corinthians was written by the apostle Paul around AD 55, during his third missionary journey, while he was in Ephesus, to the church in Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:8). Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia and one of the most prosperous ports in Greece — a city of constant comings and goings, a jumble of ideas, morally corrupt. The Corinthian church was rich in gifts yet riddled with problems: factions, quarrels, lawsuits, incest, food offered to idols, disorderly meetings.

In chapters 12 to 14, Paul deals specifically with spiritual gifts. At the centre of these three chapters stands the great love chapter, chapter 13. Paul’s logic is clear: the value of a gift lies not in how conspicuous it is, but in whether it has love and whether it builds people up. So when he reaches chapter 14, he sets speaking in tongues beside prophesying, and says:

“But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3)

Brothers and sisters, notice Paul’s standard. He doesn’t ask: Was that beautifully said? Was it profound? Did it win applause? He asks only three things: Did it build up? Did it comfort? Did it encourage?

One is a warning Jesus gave in the middle of a dispute; the other is a standard Paul wrote in the middle of chaos. One tells us what we should not say; the other tells us what we should say. Put together, these two passages become the two doors of today’s lesson.

Teaching 1. Wrong Speech: Words We Should Not Say

Brothers and sisters, the Bible is deeply loving and also deeply honest. It doesn’t only show us the direction; it plainly points out where the landmines are. Today we will look at three kinds of words we should not say.

First, Idle Words: Seemingly Harmless, Actually the Most Costly

Idle words are words without meaning, without upbuilding, without value.

They aren’t lies, they aren’t curses, they aren’t slander. They are simply … useless. They are like an engine revving in neutral: the fuel still burns, the noise still roars, the temperature still climbs — and the car does not move forward a single inch.

First, a number. In 2007 Matthias Mehl of the University of Arizona and his colleagues published a study in the journal Science. Using recording devices, they actually captured university students’ everyday conversations, and found that, men and women alike, people speak on average around sixteen thousand words a day.

Brothers and sisters, what does sixteen thousand words look like? Roughly one chapter of a master’s thesis. Every day, we “publish” a chapter with our mouths. Over a year, that is nearly six million words. The question is: of those six million words, how many are “words at work”? How many are words God can use to build people up?

Now another study. In 2019 Megan Robbins and Alexander Karan of the University of California, Riverside, published research in the journal Social Psychological and Personality Science. Analysing near round-the-clock recordings of more than four hundred participants, they found that adults spend on average about fifty-two minutes a day talking about people who are not present. The researchers noted that most of this was in fact neutral exchange of information, while clearly negative content made up a little over a tenth.

This study is revealing because it shows two things at once: first, talking about others is an extremely common human behaviour — we do it more often than we think; second, precisely because it is so common and so natural, we hardly notice we are doing it.

Fifty-two minutes a day. That is more than three hundred hours a year. Brothers and sisters, if someone told us, “This year you are going to spend three hundred hours on something that neither builds anyone up nor glorifies God,” we would be shocked. Yet that is exactly how we live.

Idle words bring three losses.

The first: they waste life. Moses prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” (Psalm 90:12) Time is the fairest resource God has given us, and the one we can least recover. Money spent can be earned again; time once gone cannot be recalled by a single second. The most frightening thing about idle words is not how bad they are, but that what they steal can never be given back.

The second: they create problems. Once words leave our lips, they no longer belong to us. They are repeated, edited, embellished. What you said at six out of ten has become ten out of ten by the time it reaches the third person, and by the fifth it is unrecognisable. There is a vivid picture for this: idle talk is like flinging a pillowful of feathers into the wind — by the time you regret it, you can never gather them back.

The third: they damage relationships. James puts it even more strongly: “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest! And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.” (James 3:5b–6)

That image rings even truer today. According to the U.S. National Park Service, about 85 per cent of wildland fires in the United States are caused by people. Most are not arson, but campfires left smouldering, cigarette ends tossed aside, sparks no one noticed. One cigarette end burns down a forest. Brothers and sisters, our idle words are often that cigarette end — we drop it without any malice, but the wind blows, and the whole mountainside goes up in flames.

A 321 Insight: idle talk is the self-centred life’s most comfortable resting posture. We are at our most relaxed in idle talk, because in that moment we don’t have to take responsibility, we don’t have to be examined, we don’t have to pay a price. But precisely because we are relaxed, the old self’s tone of voice quietly slips out. Selfless people are not those who keep their mouths shut, but those who have handed their mouths to Jesus, so that every word is at work.

Second, Judgemental Words: Judging Others by Our Own Standard

“Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged. For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.” (Matthew 7:1–2)

The Greek word for “judge” is κρίνω (krinō). Its root meaning is “to separate, to distinguish,” and by extension “to pass judgement, to condemn.” Jesus does not forbid us to discern right from wrong — in the same chapter he says, “Therefore by their fruits you will know them.” (Matthew 7:20) What he forbids is our taking the judge’s seat.

Brothers and sisters, what is the essence of judging? Its essence is this: judging others by our own standard.

And inside it hides a problem we find very hard to admit — judging is in fact a form of pride. When I judge someone, I do three things: I assume my standard is right; I assume what I see is the whole picture; I assume I am qualified to sit in that seat.

But what is the truth?

Truth one: we cannot see completely. We see behaviour, not motive; we see this moment, not the thirty years he has walked through; we see the outcome, not how many times he has already resisted, how many nights he has struggled. God says, “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7b)

Truth two: we have problems of our own. Jesus used an image almost tinged with humour:

“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye;’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.” (Matthew 7:3–5)

The “speck” is a splinter of wood; the “beam” is the main timber of a house. A man with a roof beam sticking out of his eye wants to pick a splinter out of someone else’s. The picture is so absurd it’s funny — and yet, brothers and sisters, that man is so often us.

Psychology confirms this. Social psychology has a repeatedly verified phenomenon called the “fundamental attribution error,” a concept formally put forward by the American psychologist Lee Ross in 1977: when we explain other people’s failures, we tend to attribute them to their “character”; when we explain our own, we tend to attribute them to the “situation.” Someone else is late because he’s irresponsible; I’m late because of the traffic today. Someone else loses his temper because he lacks self-discipline; I lose mine because I’m under so much pressure.

Brothers and sisters, this is why judging is always strict with others and lenient with ourselves. Not because we are especially wicked, but because our “self” sits in the middle and blocks our view.

The Bible reminds us of something even more fundamental: that office simply isn’t ours.

“Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.” (Romans 14:4)

“Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. … Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?” (James 4:11–12)

At bottom, judging is “leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take God’s place” — and that is the very definition of pride. One saint in church history understood this deeply. According to his biographer Possidius in his Life of Augustine, Augustine of Hippo (AD 354–430) had two lines inscribed on his own dining table, to this effect: whoever loves to wound the good name of the absent is not welcome at this table. Once, when some of his own fellow bishops began to talk about others at the meal, he rebuked them sternly on the spot. A giant of theology used a dining table to guard the purity of fellowship.

The Reformer Martin Luther (1483–1546), explaining the eighth commandment, “You shall not give false testimony,” in his Small Catechism (1529), said that we must not only refrain from slandering our neighbour with lies, but rather defend him, speak well of him, and put the best construction on everything. Brothers and sisters, that one phrase — “put the best construction on everything” — is the antidote to judging.

A 321 Insight: judging is the self-centred life’s most hidden throne. Sitting on it, I feel a little higher, a little more right, a little cleaner. Selfless people step down from that seat, hand judgement back to God, and keep mercy for their brothers and sisters. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Third, Words Unlike Christ: Lies, Slander, Malice, Bitterness, Empty Chatter

The Bible lists this third kind of forbidden speech very specifically. Paul says:

“but now you also put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and shameful speaking out of your mouth. Don’t lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his doings,” (Colossians 3:8–9)

“Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.” (Ephesians 4:31)

Let’s look at them one by one.

Lies. What makes lies so terrible is not only that they twist the facts, but that they twist our relationship with God. Jesus said the devil “is a liar, and the father of lies” (John 8:44b). When we lie, we are speaking the enemy’s mother tongue.

Slander. The original word is βλασφημία (blasphēmia). Used of God, it is translated “blasphemy”; used of people, it is translated “slander.” The very same word! Brothers and sisters, hear this warning: to slander a person made in the image of God is, in God’s eyes, of a piece with blasphemy.

Malice and bitterness. The original word for “bitterness” is πικρία (pikria), meaning “a bitter taste.” The most frightening thing about bitterness is that it embitters us first. We mix a cup of poison meaning to throw it at someone else, and most often we are the ones who end up drinking it.
