Hebrews warns: “looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and many be defiled by it,” (Hebrews 12:15) Bitterness has a root, and once the root goes down, our words carry poison.

Empty chatter. The original word is κενοφωνία (kenophōnia), formed from kenos, “empty,” plus phōnē, “sound” — literally, “empty noise.” Paul warned Timothy twice: “Timothy, guard that which is committed to you, turning away from the empty chatter and oppositions of what is falsely called knowledge,” (1 Timothy 6:20) “But shun empty chatter, for it will go further in ungodliness,” (2 Timothy 2:16)

Notice Paul’s wording: “it will go further in ungodliness.” Empty chatter doesn’t stay where it is; it moves downhill. A little empty talk today, a little colder tomorrow, a little further away the day after.

These five kinds of words share three features: they don’t build people up, they don’t glorify God, and they are not like Jesus.

So the principle is perfectly clear — any word that is not like Jesus should not be spoken.

Brothers and sisters, how did our Lord speak? “All testified about him, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth” (Luke 4:22a). The officers sent to arrest him came back empty-handed and reported, “No man ever spoke like this man!” (John 7:46b) And when he was falsely accused, insulted and crucified, Peter says: “who didn’t sin, ‘neither was deceit found in his mouth.’ When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:22–23)

When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. Brothers and sisters, this is the hardest test of all. We may manage not to lie and not to slander, but in the moment we are wronged, the words practically burst out by themselves.

A 321 Insight: self-centred people let the old self do the talking — that’s just my personality, he started it, I’m only telling the truth. Selfless people refuse the old self’s tone of voice — because it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

So from today on, there is one question we need to ask ourselves often. Just one is enough:

Does this sound like Jesus?

Teaching 2. Right Speech: Words We Should Say

Brothers and sisters, God never simply tells us “don’t.” When he closes one door, he always opens another for us. He tells us not to speak idle words because he wants us to speak living words; he tells us not to judge because he wants us to bless.

So what should we say? Paul gives a very clear direction:

“But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3)

Three standards — and each of them is something we do.

Standard 1: Building Up — Helping People Be Established

The Greek word for “edification” is οἰκοδομή (oikodomē), compounded from oikos, “house,” and the root for “build” — literally, “house-building.”

That’s a telling picture. Building a house is slow; it goes up one brick at a time. Demolishing a house is fast; one machine can do it in half a day. Brothers and sisters, our words are the same: words that build people up must be spoken a hundred times before you see the result; words that tear people down need only be spoken once.

Psychology has solid research on this imbalance. In 2001 the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a well-known paper in the Review of General Psychology, titled simply “Bad Is Stronger Than Good.” Reviewing a large body of research, they showed that in human psychological experience, negative events generally have a stronger impact than positive events of equal intensity.

In other words, one wounding word takes several upbuilding words to repair.

The marriage research that John Gottman and Robert Levenson of the University of Washington began publishing in 1992 likewise showed that what predicts whether a marriage will be stable is not whether there is conflict, but the ratio of positive to negative interactions; among couples in stable relationships, that ratio leans clearly towards the positive.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t asking us to go and calculate ratios. It’s asking us to understand one thing: relationships are built by words, brick by brick, and they are also torn down by words, blow by blow.

That is why Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29)

Those words “as the need may be” are precious. Words that build people up are not rehearsed lines; they are spoken on the spot, according to the situation and the need of the moment. And to be able to speak “as the need may be,” there has to be something stored up inside us all along — only what fills the heart can come out of the mouth.

Standard 2: Comforting — Bringing Encouragement and Healing

The two words the Chinese Union Version renders “comfort” and “exhortation” are, in the original, παράκλησις (paraklēsis) and παραμυθία (paramythia).

παράκλησις is formed from para, “beside,” and kaleō, “to call” — meaning “to call alongside”: going over, standing beside someone, giving them a hand up. The name of the Holy Spirit, the “Counsellor,” παράκλητος (paraklētos), comes from exactly the same root. Brothers and sisters, what a high standard this is: when we comfort people, we are doing what the Holy Spirit does.

παραμυθία carries the sense of “speaking softly at someone’s side,” used especially when a person is grieving. It isn’t reasoning with them; it’s keeping them company. It isn’t solving the problem; it’s not leaving them alone.

The Bible defines comfort very practically: “who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.” (2 Corinthians 1:4)

Notice this “chain of comfort”: God comforts us, and we comfort others. So the wounds we have received, if placed in God’s hands, become someone else’s medicine.

Here is a saying worth keeping in our hearts: “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” (Proverbs 16:24) The bones are the deepest part of the body. Words can reach that deep.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: is there such a sentence in our own lives? Perhaps twenty years ago, at our most desperate moment, someone said, “It’s all right. I’m here with you.” That sentence is still holding us up today. God wants us to be the ones who say that sentence to others.

Standard 3: Encouraging — Helping People Walk the Right Path

Exhortation is bringing someone who has strayed back onto the right path.

Exhortation is not rebuke, and it is not flattery. Rebuke cares only about truth and not about the person; flattery cares only about the person and not about truth. Exhortation wants both: it won’t give up the truth, and it won’t give up this person.

“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Galatians 6:1)

The original word for “restore,” καταρτίζω (katartizō), is used in Matthew 4:21 of James and John “mending their nets,” and in medical usage it also meant “setting a dislocated bone.” Brothers and sisters, this is the heart of exhortation: bone-setting. Setting a bone hurts, but the aim is restoration, not punishment. And the one setting the bone needs hands that are steady, gentle and skilled.

That is why Paul says “in a spirit of gentleness,” and also “looking to yourself.” Whoever exhorts others must first be standing firm themselves.

These three standards can become the “filter” for our mouths. Before a word goes out, let it pass three checkpoints:

Does what I’m about to say build anyone up?

Does it comfort anyone?

Does it point in the right direction?

But Take Note: Right Words Are Not the Same as Pleasant Words

Brothers and sisters, there is a pit here that is very easy to fall into.

Some people hear “build up, comfort, encourage” and think that Christian speech means: from now on, say only nice things, only what makes people happy, and never anything hard to hear.

No. Right words must be true.

Jesus said, “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.” (Matthew 5:37)

In Jesus’ day the Jews had developed an elaborate set of rules for oaths: swearing by the temple didn’t count, but swearing by the gold of the temple did; swearing by the altar didn’t count, but swearing by the gift on the altar did (Matthew 23:16–18). On the surface it was piety; in reality it was a way of keeping a back door open in what one said — leaving room to go back on one’s word.

Jesus cut through all of it at a stroke. He said: you don’t need to swear at all, because if a person’s word is true, “Yes” is enough.

Brothers and sisters, there is a deep spiritual principle here: when a person has to work hard to guarantee what he says, it is often precisely because his words carry no weight of their own.

So the Bible binds truth and love together: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,” (Ephesians 4:15)

The original, ἀληθεύοντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ (alētheuontes en agapē), literally means “being truthful in love.” Truth and love have never been two options; they are two sides of the same thing.

We can remember it like this: truth is the foundation; love is the manner.

Truth without love is a stone — throw it, and it will injure someone. Love without truth is sugar water — drink it, and it will only leave people weaker. And our Lord Jesus Christ, “The Word became flesh, and lived among us … full of grace and truth” (John 1:14) — in him grace and truth are both full, and both at once.

A 321 Insight: self-centred people can only ever choose one, truth or love — either they say false nice things to protect the relationship, or they hurt people to stand their own ground. Selfless people don’t have to choose, because their centre is not themselves: they don’t need false niceness to buy others’ acceptance, and they don’t need to be right to prove their own worth. They can speak the truth, and speak it with love.

Teaching 3. The Highest Purpose of Speech: Building Relationships, Drawing People to God

Brothers and sisters, let’s take one more step forward.

When we speak, it isn’t only that the content must be right; more importantly — the purpose must be right.

A person can speak truth that is one hundred per cent correct and still push people further from God. Job’s three friends are the best example. Much of what they said sounds very pious and very theological, yet in the end God said to one of them, “My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.” (Job 42:7b)

Right doctrine, wrongly used, is still wrong.

So what is the right purpose? Jesus gave us the greatest standard of all:

“Jesus said to him, ‘ “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” ’” (Matthew 22:37–39)

Love God, love people. All our speaking should head in these two directions.

So before we speak each time, we can ask two questions:

Will this help someone come closer to God?

Will this help a relationship be built up?

Not Only What We Say, but How We Say It

Brothers and sisters, we must admit something: some words, though “true,” still knock people down. Why? Because besides content, three other things determine the effect of what we say.

First, the wrong timing. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” (Proverbs 25:11) The Hebrew behind “fitly” carries the sense of “in its season, as its wheel turns” — the same sentence spoken too early is pressure, spoken too late is hindsight, and only spoken at the right moment is it a golden apple. As Ecclesiastes says so well, “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;” (Ecclesiastes 3:7b)

Second, the wrong tone. “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1) The same words — “How could you forget again?” — said in different tones, can be a reminder or a humiliation. God cares about our tone, because our tone gives away our heart.

Third, the wrong motive. This is the deepest layer. Sometimes we say something that on the surface is for the other person’s good, but underneath we want him to know we were right; on the surface it is concern, underneath it is curiosity; on the surface it is a reminder, underneath it is revenge. People may not hear it, but God does — and in fact, the listener can usually sense it too.

So the conclusion is clear: it’s not only “what we say,” but also “how we say it.”

And sometimes the best choice is not to speak at all.

“In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.” (Proverbs 10:19)

“Even a fool, when he keeps silent, is counted wise. When he shuts his lips, he is thought to be discerning.” (Proverbs 17:28)

Brothers and sisters, better not to speak than to speak wrongly. A word left unspoken, we remain its master for ever; once it is spoken, we become its servant.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945), in Life Together (1939), devotes an entire section to the discipline of the tongue. His point, in essence, is this: in Christian fellowship, what most protects one another is often the discipline of not speaking about a brother behind his back; when a person stops talking about his brother, he truly begins to learn to pray for him.

Brothers and sisters, this is worth remembering for a lifetime: only when we stop talking about others do we start interceding for them.

Speech That Truly Belongs to God

So what is speech that truly belongs to God? It’s simple — look at the fruit:

It makes people love Jesus more.

It makes people love one another more.

If, at the end of a conversation, the other person wants to draw nearer to God, wants to be reconciled with their brothers and sisters — that was speech that belongs to God. If, at the end of a conversation, the other person is colder towards God and more guarded towards people — then however correct our content was, we need to re-examine it before God.

A 321 Insight: self-centred people speak for themselves — to prove they are right, to be seen, to make themselves comfortable — and the result is that pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. Selfless people speak for love — to build people up, to glorify God — and the result is that humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

This is exactly the 321 order of “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” When our life is right, our words are right; when our words are right, relationships are built; when relationships are built, ministry has a foundation. We often do it backwards — rushing to get the task done, and wrecking people along the way. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From a Self-Centred Mouth to a Selfless Mouth
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message back on the foundation of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

When it comes to speaking, these Three Foundations become three lines of defence.

Jesus is my role model: so the question I ask is not “What do other people say?” but “What would Jesus say?” When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back; he spoke gracious words to sinners; he spoke hard words to hypocritical religious leaders; and when it was time to be silent, he answered not a single word (Matthew 27:14). His mouth is my pattern.

The Bible is my standard: so my standard for speaking is not my feelings, not my personality, not my culture, but the word of God. Building up, comforting, encouraging — the Bible set this, not I.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: so before I open my mouth, I must first be still and let the Holy Spirit tell me what to say, when to say it and in what tone. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll find joy, rely on the brain and you’ll find worry.

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

To let Jesus reign as King, the first place we must surrender is often our mouth. For the mouth is the last fortress of the “self.” A person can offer up money, time and talent, and still cling tightly to the sovereignty of his speech: I’ll say what I like, I have a right to say it, I’m only telling the truth. Brothers and sisters, if Jesus is King, then he has the authority to decide what I say today and what I don’t.

To let Jesus receive all the glory means this: my words are not so that people will see how eloquent I am, how insightful, how spiritual, but so that people will see Jesus.

The Goal — establish God’s system.

God’s system is built with words. In the beginning, when God created the heavens and the earth, he did it by speaking: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:3) And the system of Babylon is also built with words — with lies, with slander, with judgement, with empty chatter. Brothers and sisters, every day we are building a house with our mouths; the only question is: whose house are we building?

Now look at the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s lesson starts precisely at the first link. Our mindset changes from “speaking is my right” to “speaking is a stewardship God has entrusted to me”; once the mindset changes, our life gains reverence; once our life changes, our everyday conversations are different; once our daily living changes, our family and colleagues can feel it; once our relationships change, our witness has power.

A shift of perspective is in this too. From man’s perspective, a word is over once it is said; from God’s perspective, every word must be accounted for. From an earthly perspective, speaking is socialising; from heaven’s perspective, speaking is service. From a temporary perspective, this is just a chat; from an eternal perspective, it echoes in eternity.

Finally, let’s bring it down to the 920 practice.

The 920 practice is this: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life; and what is produced is the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, notice something beautiful: almost every one of the nine fruits of the Spirit is borne in our mouths.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23a)

Love gives our words warmth; joy makes our words carry hope; peace keeps us from saying words that stir up strife; patience keeps our mouths shut when we are misunderstood; kindness softens our tone; goodness keeps our motives pure; faithfulness makes us do what we say; gentleness keeps us from wounding people when we exhort them; and self-control — this one is the most direct of all: it bridles the tongue.

That is exactly what James says: “Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.” (James 3:2b) The original word for “bridle,” χαλιναγωγέω (chalinagōgeō), means “to guide with a bit.” A horse weighing a ton can be steered with one small bit; a person’s whole life is likewise carried along by one small tongue.

Brothers and sisters, every “2” we face each day — husband or wife, children, parents, colleagues, neighbours, the brothers and sisters in our small group — is a lesson God gives us for practising selflessness. And the front line of that practice is on our lips.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Building the Ability to Discern and to Speak
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices. Let’s combine them with the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that these five practices really take hold.

Practice 1. The Three-Question Filter: Check Before You Speak

Every time before you speak, ask three questions: Does this build people up? Is this true? Does this carry love?

Information: Copy 1 Corinthians 14:3, together with Ephesians 4:15 and 4:29, onto a card and stick it on the back of your phone or in front of your desk.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to let us see with our own eyes the harm one of our sentences once caused. Not condemnation — revelation. When revelation comes, the principle becomes true knowing.

Conviction: Admit before God: my mouth needs to be governed by God.

Implementation: Starting today, for thirty days, stop at least one sentence a day that fails the three questions.

Evaluation: Every evening, be still for three minutes and recall which sentence today should not have been said.

Correction: Apologise to the person we hurt — no explaining, no defending, just owning it.

Repetition: If you can’t manage it one day, try again the next, until it becomes a reflex.

Multiplication: Teach these three questions to our children, our small group, our co-workers.

Practice 2. Stopping the Mouth: Learning Not to Say the Wrong Thing

When the urge to gossip or to judge rises in your heart, choose “not to say it,” and let your mouth be still.

This is the simplest practice, and also the hardest. The prefrontal cortex is the region of the brain responsible for restraining impulses, and long-term brain-imaging research from the U.S. National Institute of Mental Health shows that this region does not fully mature until around the age of twenty-five. In other words, “holding back from speaking” is physiologically hard work in the first place — no wonder it takes practice, and no wonder it takes the Holy Spirit.

David’s prayer can become our prayer every morning: “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” (Psalm 141:3) The Hebrew paints a vivid picture here: “the door of my lips.” David is asking God to post a guard at the door of his lips. Brothers and sisters, our mouths need a doorkeeper.

In practice: when the urge comes, count to three silently in your heart, and at the same time say, “Lord, I hand this sentence to you.”

Practice 3. Blessing Instead: Replacing Bad Words with Good Ones

When you want to criticise, speak a blessing instead; when you want to blame, speak encouragement instead.

The principle behind this practice is that old habits can’t be removed by “deleting” them; they can only be crowded out by “replacing” them. An empty seat will always be taken back by the old thing.

“not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.” (1 Peter 3:9)

In practice: every day, for the one person who makes us most uncomfortable, say one sincere good word — whether to their face or before God. Keep it up for thirty days. Brothers and sisters, we will discover something wonderful: the one who changes most is not the other person, but ourselves.

Practice 4. Relationships First: Let Love Be the Starting Point of Our Words

In a conflict, don’t rush to prove you’re right; choose first to protect the relationship.

This is the most practical exercise of the 321 conviction that “people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.” When we argue, there is actually a pair of scales in our hearts: on one side, “I am right”; on the other, “this person.” Self-centred people choose the former; selfless people choose the latter.

In practice: in your next conflict, begin with this sentence: “I’d like to hear you out first.” Then genuinely close your mouth and listen to the end.

“So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;” (James 1:19)

God gave us two ears and one mouth — a ratio of two to one.

Practice 5. Selfless Obedience: Let Jesus Decide What I Say

Before speaking, ask: if Jesus were in my place, would he say it? How would he say it? Then obey the Holy Spirit’s guidance.

This is the highest of the five practices, because it is no longer a technique but a surrender of sovereignty.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20a)

Brothers and sisters, if it is no longer I who live, then it is no longer I who speak.

In practice: early every morning, place the people you will meet today, the meetings you will attend, the messages you will reply to, one by one into the Lord’s hands, and pray: “Lord, today my mouth is yours. Give me the tongue of those who are taught.”

For Isaiah gives us a beautiful promise, one prepared especially for the early morning:

“The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4)

He awakens morning by morning. Brothers and sisters, this is what our morning devotion is about: first let the ear be taught, and then the mouth will be taught.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, before we finish, there are a few words I want to lay gently on our hearts.

Not everything that “can be said” should be said; not everything that is “true” is fitting to say.

Speaking is not only a right; speaking is a responsibility.

One sentence can heal a person; one sentence can also harm a person. “There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.” (Proverbs 12:18) The same tongue — one is a sword, the other is medicine.

Humble people restrain their mouths; proud people say whatever they please.

Why? Because proud people think their opinions are so important that they simply must say them; humble people know their limits, so they listen first, think next and speak last.

Humility brings wise words; selflessness lets love flow out.

On the day the prophet Isaiah saw God, the first thing he discovered was not other people’s problems, but his own mouth: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!” (Isaiah 6:5) Then God did something: “Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar. He touched my mouth with it, and said, ‘Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.’” (Isaiah 6:6–7)

Brothers and sisters, only lips that have been cleansed can say, “Here I am. Send me!”

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

“Speaking” is a spiritual discipline to be learned.

What we should say and what we should not say — all of it needs learning, all of it needs practice, all of it needs the Holy Spirit.

Today God has given us a very clear direction: refuse wrong words, speak right words.

Brothers and sisters, when we begin to practise like this, what will happen?

Our life will change — because the mouth is the outlet of the heart, and the process of governing our mouth is really God repairing our heart.

Our relationships will change — because relationships are built with words, and once our words change, relationships begin to be rebuilt.

Our surroundings will change — because “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21) The Hebrew puts it even more directly: death and life are “in the hand of the tongue.”

For words are an authority God has given us.

God created the world with words, and God has also placed words in our hands. This is no small thing; it is a very weighty trust.

So may we all become people like this:

Truth in our mouths, love in our hearts, and lives that bring blessing.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, let us hand over our mouths.

Not to self-discipline, not to technique, but to the Lord who sits on the throne.

Live out the selfless life, let Jesus live in us, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matthew 12:36–37)
“But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3)
declarations: Let us declare together — in the name of the Lord Jesus we declare:
My mouth will be cleansed by God; my words will bring forth life.
I reject all idle words and judgement; I reject every word that does not please God.
I will speak words that build up; I will speak words that comfort; I will speak words that encourage.
My words will be true; my words will carry love.
I will build relationships with my words; I will glorify God with my words.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: The three-question filter: check before you speak
Stopping the mouth: learn not to say the wrong thing
Blessing instead: replace bad words with good ones
Relationships first: let love be where your words begin
Selfless obedience: let Jesus decide what I say
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

This morning you have shone your word on the state of our mouths. Lord, we confess: we have said many things we should not have said. We have spoken idle words and wasted the time you gave us; we have judged our brothers and sisters and sat in a seat that does not belong to us; we have spoken words unlike Jesus and brought loss to your name. Lord, please forgive us.
As you once cleansed Isaiah, touch our mouths with the live coal from the altar; cleanse our lips, and cleanse our hearts too, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

Lord Jesus, today we hand the sovereignty of our speech to you. From today on, may we look up to you before every time we open our mouths; may all that comes out of our mouths be words that build up, comfort and encourage; may we speak the truth with love, and love people without losing the truth.
Holy Spirit, please be our guide. When we are about to speak idle words, remind us; when we are about to judge, stop us; when someone needs a word, put that word in our mouths.
May the words of our mouths and the thoughts of our hearts be acceptable in your sight. May our mouths become instruments for establishing God’s system.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: Matthew 12:34b says, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” Looking back over the past week, which thing you said do you regret most? What does that sentence reveal was filling your heart at the time? Are you willing to ask the Lord to work in that place?

1 Corinthians 14:3 says, “But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” Who around you most needs a word of building up, comfort or encouragement right now? When and how do you plan to say that word to them this week?
l139.title: Truth on the Lips, Love in the Heart
l139.subtitle: What Should Not Be Said, and What Should
l139.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: One Mouth, Two Outcomes
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to be still for thirty seconds and call two sentences to mind.

The first is a kind word someone once spoke to you — one you still remember to this day. Perhaps it was a primary-school teacher who crouched down beside you and said, “You’re actually very bright — you just haven’t found the way yet.” Perhaps it was your mother, on the day you failed, who simply warmed up the food and said, “You’re home. That’s all that matters.” Perhaps it was an older believer who, when you were at your lowest, laid a hand on your shoulder and said, “I’m praying for you. God hasn’t given up on you.” That sentence may have been only a handful of words, yet it was like a nail driven into the wall of your life, and for decades afterwards you have been able to hang your hope on it.

The second is a wounding word someone once spoke to you — one you still haven’t entirely forgotten. Perhaps it was “How can you be so stupid?” Perhaps it was “This family would be no different with you or without you.” Perhaps it was in church, when a brother said to you in a very “spiritual” tone, “That’s not what I’d call submission.” That sentence may have been only a few words, yet it lodged in you like a thorn, and every time the weather turns grey it still aches.

Brothers and sisters, both of those sentences came out of a human mouth. The same organ, the same vibration of air, the same language — and yet two utterly different outcomes. Proverbs 18:21 says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” This verse uses a very weighty word — “power.” The tongue carries authority. It is not the strongest muscle in the body, but it is the most influential organ. James 3:5 says, “So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!”

In a study published in 2007 in the journal Science, the psychologist Matthias Mehl of the University of Texas and his colleagues used recording devices to capture the everyday conversations of nearly four hundred university students. They found that men and women alike speak on average about sixteen thousand words a day. Brothers and sisters, sixteen thousand words a day comes to nearly six million words a year. Printed as books, that would fill dozens of volumes every year. The question is: of those dozens of volumes, how much is a tree of life, and how much is the deceit that crushes the spirit? How much brings health to people’s bones, and how much breaks their hearts?

We often think of the spiritual disciplines as prayer, Bible reading, gathering together and giving. But there is one discipline we practise every day — sixteen thousand times a day — and yet very few of us practise it seriously: speaking. James 3:2 says, “For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.” So by the Bible’s standard, our words are the most honest thermometer of our spiritual maturity.

Today’s lesson is called “The Art of Speaking.” Please notice: the Bible never teaches us how to “speak beautifully.” What the Bible teaches us is how to let our mouths become an outlet for life. And there is a crucial dividing line here — not a line of technique, but the line of “self.” When the old self is self-centred, words become a tool for protecting ourselves, proving ourselves and venting ourselves. When the new self is selfless, words become a channel for the Holy Spirit, a vessel of grace and a seed of life.

So today we will look at five things together: the motive of our speaking, the relationship behind our speaking, the authority and timing of our speaking, the outcome of our speaking, and learning to bridle the tongue and wait for God’s time. May the Holy Spirit shine his light on each of our mouths this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Seven Passages, One Thread
sections.html: Today’s key passages span the Old and New Testaments. They may look scattered, but they are tied together by a very clear thread. Let’s first get the background of each one straight, so that our interpretation doesn’t go astray.

sections.heading: 1. Proverbs: A “Theology of Speech” in the Wisdom Literature
sections.html:
The principal author of Proverbs is King Solomon. Proverbs 1:1 says, “The proverbs of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel:” Solomon reigned from roughly 970 to 930 BC. 1 Kings 4:32 records, “He spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs numbered one thousand five.” The later part of Proverbs also gathers the words of Agur and of King Lemuel, and Proverbs 25:1 notes, “These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out.” Clearly this book is a treasury of wisdom, preserved by the Holy Spirit and compiled over a long span of years.

Proverbs belongs to the genre of Hebrew wisdom literature. It is not a code of law; it is a set of standards for daily living that grow out of “the fear of Yahweh.” Here is something worth noticing: in the mere thirty-one chapters of Proverbs, there are more than a hundred verses about lips, the tongue and speech. That is an exceptionally high proportion for any book of the Bible. Why? Because in the societies of the ancient Near East there were no recordings, and written contracts were far from common; the most important asset between one person and another was their “word.” Once a word was spoken, a covenant was made; once a word was spoken, a judgement was passed. Solomon was the most eloquent man in all Israel — when the Queen of Sheba heard his words of wisdom, 1 Kings 10:5 says, “there was no more spirit in her” — and yet it is this most eloquent of kings who devoted the most space to warning us: speaking is dangerous.

Proverbs 15:4 says, “A gentle tongue is a tree of life.” That image of the “tree of life” carries us all the way back to the Garden of Eden in Genesis 2:9. Humanity left the tree of life because of one sentence spoken by a serpent; now a tongue renewed by God’s grace can once again hand the fruit of the tree of life to someone else. What a restoration that is!

sections.heading: 2. Matthew 7:6: A Sense of Proportion in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
The author of Matthew’s Gospel is Matthew the tax collector. He wrote chiefly for Jewish readers, and the Gospel is generally dated between AD 50 and 70. Matthew 7:6 sits in the final chapter of the Sermon on the Mount, and its context is crucial. Just before, in 7:1–5, the Lord Jesus says, “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.” Then, right after, in verse 6, he says, “Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs.”

Is that a contradiction? No. The Lord Jesus first blocks our pride — do not judge; then he blocks our sentimentality — do not fail to discern. Not judging deals with “self”; discerning deals with indiscriminateness. Put together, it means this: you have no right to pass judgement on others, but you do have a responsibility to discern the right moment. In Leviticus, “that which is holy” refers to the sacrificial meat offered to God, which only the priests could eat; and in those days pearls were things of very great value. The Lord Jesus is not saying that certain people are dogs and pigs — that is the most common misunderstanding. He is saying that if the most precious truth is thrown into a heart that isn’t yet ready, the result is not that the other person receives it, but that the truth is trampled and the speaker is torn to pieces. Brothers and sisters, this is the skeleton of today’s lesson: truth is a pearl, but pearls are to be handed over, not thrown.

sections.heading: 3. Ephesians 4:15: The Secret of the Body’s Growth
sections.html:
Ephesians is a letter the apostle Paul wrote during his first imprisonment in Rome, generally dated to AD 60–62, addressed to the churches in Ephesus and across the province of Asia Minor. The theme of Ephesians 4 is “unity and growth.” Verses 11–12 say that God gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” Verse 14 says that we should no longer be children, “tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, after the wiles of error.”

Only then comes verse 15: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ.” Here “speaking truth in love” is in Greek alētheuontes en agapē, literally “being truthful in love.” Please notice that the emphasis of the original is not only on “speaking” but on “living out the truth in love.” Truth is not a stone hurled at someone; it is life handed over in the warmth of love. Verse 16 goes on: “from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.” So this is how the church grows: by speaking the truth in love. Words are the body’s circulation.

sections.heading: 4. James 4:6: The Battle Behind Our Words
sections.html:
The author of James is generally held to be James, the Lord Jesus’ brother according to the flesh and the leader of the Jerusalem church. It may have been written as early as AD 45–50, making it one of the earliest books of the New Testament, and it is addressed to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1). The whole of James 3 is about the tongue, and chapter 4 opens by asking, “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?”

In other words, James connects “the problem of the tongue” directly to “the problem of self.” In 4:6 he quotes the Septuagint of Proverbs 3:34: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” The Greek for “resists” is antitassomai, a military term for an army drawing up in battle formation against an enemy. Brothers and sisters, how sobering this is: when we speak with a proud mouth, God doesn’t merely disapprove — God draws up his battle lines against us. Verse 7 follows straight on: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Submission and humility come first; resisting Satan comes after. This is exactly what 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

sections.heading: 5. 1 Corinthians 10:23–24: The Boundary of Freedom Is Love
sections.html:
1 Corinthians is the letter Paul wrote from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, generally dated to around AD 55. Corinth was a prosperous port city, and its church was full of spiritual gifts — and full of strife: factions, lawsuits, food offered to idols, disorder at the Lord’s Supper, confusion over tongues. Chapters 8 to 10 deal with the question of whether food offered to idols may be eaten. Paul’s conclusion is superb: “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.”

The Greek for “lawful” is exestin, meaning “to have the right”; “build up” is oikodomei, whose root means “to build a house.” Paul is saying: having a right doesn’t mean you ought to exercise it; the measure is not whether I am free, but whether the other person has been built up. Brothers and sisters, apply that principle to today’s theme and it becomes: having the right to say something doesn’t mean you ought to say it. Being right doesn’t mean the other person has been built up.

sections.heading: 6. One Thread
sections.html: Set the seven passages side by side and the thread emerges: words are pearls (Matthew 7:6), a honeycomb (Proverbs 16:24), a tree of life (Proverbs 15:4); but they must be handed over in love (Ephesians 4:15), handed over at the right time (Proverbs 15:23), handed over by a humble person (James 4:6), and handed over for the good of others (1 Corinthians 10:23–24). This is “the art of speaking” — not the art of eloquence, but the art of life.

sections.heading: 1. The Motive of Our Speaking: Without Love, Don’t Speak
sections.html:
Ephesians 4:15: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,”

1 Corinthians 13:1: “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal.”

Brothers and sisters, speaking in itself is never the problem; the motive is what matters. The same words — “What you’re doing is wrong” — spoken out of love are healing; spoken out of emotion, they wound. The same verse of Scripture spoken from a heart of grace is living water; spoken from a heart of grievance, it is a stone.

Here is the self-deception we fall into most easily: we think we are “speaking the truth,” when in fact we are “venting our emotions.” Truth becomes the respectable justification for our feelings, and Scripture becomes the ammunition for our attacks. The Lord Jesus put it with piercing clarity in Matthew 12:34: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” The idea in the original is overflow — what the mouth says is simply what the heart holds, spilling over. When a cup gets knocked, what splashes out doesn’t depend on who knocked you; it depends on what was in the cup to begin with.

So the question is never “How could he say that about me?” The question is “What is inside me?” Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The wellspring of life flows not from the mouth but from the heart; the mouth is only the heart’s estuary.

The self-centred life and selflessness: two sources of speech

The core insight of 321 applies perfectly here: when there is “self” inside a person, the purpose of their speaking is to prove themselves right; only when a person enters into selflessness does the purpose of their speaking become a longing for the other person to be built up. The self-centred person wants to win the conversation; the selfless person wants to love in the conversation. When the self-centred person hears a different opinion, their first reaction is to defend; when the selfless person hears a different opinion, their first reaction is to listen.

Paul says in 1 Corinthians 8:1, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” Knowledge inflates people; love builds people. Inflating is blowing yourself up; building is putting the other person up. Brothers and sisters, do we want to be balloons blown up big, or labourers building houses?

Psychology bears witness: contempt is the fatal wound to a relationship

The American psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington has studied marital interaction for more than forty years. In research he published with Robert Levenson in 1992, he found that in stable, happy marriages the ratio of positive to negative interactions is roughly five to one. He also identified the “Four Horsemen” of relationships: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Of these, the most destructive — and the strongest predictor of divorce — is contempt.

What is contempt? Contempt says, “I am above you.” It can hide in a roll of the eyes, in a cold laugh, in a remark like “I told you so.” Brothers and sisters, notice this: the essence of contempt is pride, and the essence of pride is the self-centred life. What psychology has measured, the Bible said long ago: “God resists the proud.”

In addition, the social psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a well-known paper in 2001 in the Review of General Psychology whose very title was “Bad Is Stronger Than Good.” Drawing together a large body of research, they showed that negative events have a far greater psychological impact on people than positive events of equal strength. That explains Gottman’s five to one exactly — because it takes five kind words to make up for the damage of one harsh one. Brothers and sisters, what we often tear down in a minute takes a year to build back up.

Relying on the heart, or relying on the brain?

The lesson leaves us with two sentences to remember: the person who relies on the heart speaks for the other person’s good; the person who relies on the brain speaks for their own comfort. The 321 teaching puts it well: rely on the heart and you will have joy; rely on the brain and you will have worry. Relying on the brain means calculating for ourselves, scheming for ourselves, finding our own justifications; relying on the heart means depending on the Holy Spirit, following the Holy Spirit and being guided by the Holy Spirit.

So if you are still angry inside, still feeling wronged, still nursing a grievance — don’t speak yet. First come before God and deal with that “self.” A saying generally attributed to the American writer Ambrose Bierce goes, “Speak when you are angry and you will make the best speech you will ever regret.” Brothers and sisters, that one deserves a place on the fridge door.

James 1:19 says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;” Look at the order: swift to hear comes first, slow to speak in the middle, slow to anger last. God gave us two ears and one mouth — a ratio of two to one; the discipline of Scripture is to live out that ratio.

Applying the 321 Vision: deal with “self” first, then open your mouth

On the 321 Path of Serving, the order is Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Our speaking should follow that same order. First let the Holy Spirit guide my heart, then let the Bible be my standard, then learn the way of Jesus, and finally let Jesus be King in this conversation and let the glory go to him.

Brothers and sisters, before you open your mouth, ask one question: is this sentence going out to make me feel better, or for his good? Is it to prove that I’m right, or to let Jesus be King? If the answer is the former, close your mouth and go and pray first. Without love, don’t speak.

sections.heading: 2. The Relationship Behind Our Speaking: Without Relationship, Don’t Speak
sections.html:
John 15:15: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.”

Proverbs 27:6: “The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.”

Brothers and sisters, the depth of our words depends on the depth of our relationship. This is a law of spiritual physics; break it, and no matter how much force you put behind your words, they won’t get through.

Jesus is the best role model

The Lord Jesus did not begin by speaking his deepest words. He first called his disciples and walked with them for three years — walking the roads together, eating together, sailing together, sleeping out in the wilderness together. He washed their feet; he turned water into wine at the wedding they attended; he calmed the wind and the waves when they were frightened half to death. The relationship was built, and only then did he gradually open the Father’s heart to them.

Only at the Last Supper did he say, “I have called you friends.” And even then, in John 16:12, he still said, “I still have many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now.” Brothers and sisters, look at that: even the Son of God held words back for the sake of the relationship and of what the hearers could carry! Who are we, then, to think we can pour out everything we see onto someone all at once?

Mark 4:33 also says, “With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it.” “As they were able to hear it” — that is the art of speaking. Not according to what I want to say, but according to what he is able to hear.

Why do words that are correct still wound?

This is why some things that are “correct in content” still sound harsh, cause offence, and can even break a relationship. Truth without relationship becomes pressure; only truth with relationship becomes provision. The same sentence, from an older believer who walked with you through the valley, is support; from someone who has met you three times online, it is commentary.

This is precisely the wisdom of Matthew 7:6: don’t throw your pearls before the pigs. There is nothing wrong with the pearl itself; the problem lies in the act of “throwing,” and in a receiving heart that isn’t yet prepared. Pearls are to be handed over, not thrown. Handing over requires being close enough; handing over requires reaching out your hand; handing over requires the other person being willing to take it.

Psychological safety: confirmation from modern research

In 1999 Amy Edmondson, a professor at Harvard Business School, introduced the concept of “psychological safety” — the belief among team members that they can take interpersonal risks without being humiliated or punished. Beginning in 2012, Google carried out “Project Aristotle,” analysing more than a hundred and eighty teams within the company, and in 2015–2016 it published its conclusion: the most important factor in predicting a high-performing team was not how clever its members were or how senior, but “psychological safety.”

Brothers and sisters, how closely that finding agrees with the Bible. People don’t change when they are corrected; people change when they are loved. Galatians 6:1 says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” The Greek word for “restore” is katartizō; ancient medicine used it for setting a dislocated bone, and fishermen used it for mending nets. How close must a bonesetter come to the patient? How gentle must the net-mender be? That is the attitude we ought to have when we speak to others.

Paul’s example: give life first, then words

In 1 Thessalonians 2:7–8 Paul says, “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” Brothers and sisters, this was the apostle’s secret: what he gave was not only teaching, but his very life. That is why his words carried weight.

Applying the 321 Vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry

321 has a very clear order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice that ministry always comes last. Pointing out someone’s fault, teaching them, correcting them — that is all ministry; and ministry must stand on relationship, and relationship must stand on life.

The lesson puts it beautifully: it isn’t first about “getting the words right” but about “getting the love right.” As deep as the relationship goes, that is how deep you may speak; without relationship, however right your words are, they find no way in. 321 also reminds us of the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. People matter more than things; relationships matter more than possessions. The “thing” you want to correct will never matter more than the person.

This is exactly the training ground of the 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” Within those “2” relationships we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Brothers and sisters, notice that the last one is self-control — the fruit of the Spirit includes the power not to speak.

So when you badly want to say something harsh to someone, first ask yourself: have I made enough deposits in his life? Have I walked alongside him? Have I wept for him? How many times have I prayed for him? If the balance in the relationship account is zero, don’t make a withdrawal yet. Without relationship, don’t speak.

sections.heading: 3. The Authority and Timing of Our Speaking: Without Authority, Without Prayer, Don’t Speak
sections.html:
James 4:6: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’”

Proverbs 15:23: “Joy comes to a man with the reply of his mouth. How good is a word at the right time!”

Brothers and sisters, not every problem you see requires you to open your mouth. Please hear that once more: not every problem you see requires you to open your mouth. Seeing is a burden God gives you; opening your mouth requires God’s sending.

The rush to correct is often pride doing the talking

Sometimes when we rush to correct others, it is actually “pride doing the talking,” not “the Holy Spirit leading.” 321 defines pride very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When I am in a hurry to change someone, I have actually stepped into the Holy Spirit’s place and am trying to do the Holy Spirit’s work with my tongue.

James says, “God resists the proud.” Even God himself does not force anyone to listen. In Genesis 3:9, when the man had sinned and was hiding, God did not shout a rebuke; he asked only one question: “Where are you?” In Luke 15 the father did not chase his younger son to the far country to lecture him; he waited at the door of his house. Brothers and sisters, if even God is willing to wait, why can’t we?

321 says: pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. A correction delivered from on high only ignites the same pride in the other person, and then both people lose.

True authority is the other person’s willingness to let you speak

True authority is not only a matter of position; it is whether the other person is willing to let you speak. This must be said plainly: an office gives you a position; a life gives you weight. Position without weight, and your words only provoke defensiveness; only words that carry weight can get into the heart.

In 2 Samuel 12 the prophet Nathan went to see King David, who had committed adultery and murder. He didn’t walk in and jab a finger in the king’s face; first he told a story about a poor man and his little ewe lamb. Only when David’s heart had been opened and his righteous anger aroused did Nathan speak those four words: “You are the man” (2 Samuel 12:7). Brothers and sisters, Nathan had a prophet’s authority, yet he still took the path of wisdom. And the result? David didn’t kill him; David repented and wrote Psalm 51. That is a word spoken with authority and at the right time.

Before you speak, always pray first

What’s more, our speaking must always pass through prayer first. Not saying what we want to say, but saying what the Holy Spirit wants said. The Lord Jesus says in John 12:49, “For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” Brothers and sisters, even the Lord Jesus did not speak from himself! On what grounds do we speak from ourselves?

In Nehemiah 2:4 the Persian king asked Nehemiah, “What is your request?” And Scripture records, “So I prayed to the God of heaven.” Standing before the king, in those few brief seconds, Nehemiah prayed first and then spoke. That one opening of his mouth rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Brothers and sisters, isn’t your most important conversation worth three seconds of silent prayer first?

Timing: the chemistry of a single sentence

Proverbs 25:11 says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” Notice the word “fitly” — fitting the moment. With the wrong timing, even truth turns into hurt; with the right timing, a single sentence can turn a life around. Ecclesiastes 3:7 says, “a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.” Silence comes before speech.

Sometimes God is already at work in the other person’s heart, and all we need to do is say the right word at the right moment. It’s like a midwife at a birth: the child is made by God, the due date is set by God, and the midwife simply reaches out her hands at the right moment. Job 2:13 records of Job’s three friends: “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.” Those seven days were the best thing they did in the whole book; from chapter 3 onwards, the moment they opened their mouths, the more they said, the more wrong they got.

Neuroscience, too, reminds us how much timing matters. A study by Matthew Lieberman’s team at the University of California, Los Angeles, published in 2007 in the journal Psychological Science, found that when people put their emotions into words, activity in the amygdala goes down and the regulating function of the prefrontal cortex goes up. This shows that at the peak of emotion, the reasoning brain is temporarily “offline.” Brothers and sisters, reasoning with someone whose reason is offline is like typing commands into a computer that’s switched off.

Applying the 321 Vision: the focus is on Jesus

So before you open your mouth, ask yourself: have I prayed? Is this God’s time? 321 reminds us: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. When my focus is on myself, I’m in a hurry to prove myself; when my focus is on others, I’m in a hurry to correct them; when my focus is on my circumstances, I’m in a hurry to fix them. Only when my focus is on Jesus can I wait quietly for him to say, “Now — speak.” Without authority, without prayer, don’t speak.

sections.heading: 4. The Outcome of Our Speaking: Without a Way Forward, Don’t Speak
sections.html:
1 Corinthians 10:23–24: “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.”

Ephesians 4:29: “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.”

Brothers and sisters, the purpose of truth is not to make people “see the problem” but to help them “find the way forward.” If a sentence only leaves someone more self-reproachful, more ashamed and more helpless, yet brings no hope and no direction, then that sentence is not building up — it is tearing down.

God’s pattern: naming the sin and offering salvation at the same time

Look at how God himself speaks. In Genesis 3, as God names the sin of Adam and Eve, in that very passage — verse 15 — he promises the offspring who will crush the serpent’s head. This is the first gospel in the Bible. God shines his light into the darkness and at the same time brings a way out.

In John 8, the woman caught in adultery is thrown down in front of the Lord Jesus. The Lord Jesus doesn’t say, “You have no sin.” What he says is: “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more” (John 8:11). The first half is grace; the second half is truth and direction. Grace is given first, direction afterwards — that is the order of speaking in the kingdom of heaven.

John 1:14 says, “The Word became flesh, and lived among us… full of grace and truth.” Notice the order: grace first, truth after; and both are there in fullness. The lesson puts it superbly: truth plus grace equals life; truth minus grace equals accusation. And accusation is never the work of the Holy Spirit — Revelation 12:10 tells us that the one who accuses our brothers before our God day and night is Satan.

A scientific picture: why honey heals

Proverbs 16:24 says, “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” Scientifically, this picture is remarkably precise. Honey has a very low water content and a very high sugar content, creating a high-osmotic environment in which bacteria struggle to survive; honey is acidic, with a pH of roughly 3.2 to 4.5; and the glucose oxidase that bees secrete slowly releases tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide. Precisely because of these properties, medical-grade manuka honey dressings have been cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration for wound care.

Brothers and sisters, three thousand years ago the Holy Spirit used a picture that laboratories only confirmed in the twenty-first century: kind words are not merely sweet — kind words disinfect, heal and help new flesh to grow. And the verse says “health to the bones” — the bones are the deepest, hardest, innermost part of the body, and the place where blood is made. A good word can reach a person’s deepest place and make new blood for them.

Hope is the name of the way forward

So before you open your mouth each time, ask: will what I’m about to say help this person move forward, or leave them stuck? Words that truly come from God always carry “an outlet of hope.” Romans 8:1 says, “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” That is the gospel; that is the way forward.

In psychology, the American psychologist Barbara Fredrickson proposed the “broaden-and-build theory” in 1998. She showed that positive emotions broaden a person’s immediate range of thought and action and, over time, build up lasting personal psychological resources; negative emotions, by contrast, narrow a person’s attention and responses. This explains why shame leaves people stuck while hope moves them forward: the person who has been shamed has a narrowed field of vision and thinks only of escape or counter-attack; only the person upheld by hope can see their options.

Applying the 321 Vision: a shift of perspective

321 speaks of a shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Man’s perspective sees “he’s wrong”; God’s perspective sees “he’s still on the way.” The earthly perspective wants the problem solved immediately; the heavenly perspective is willing to wait for the work God is completing in him. The temporary perspective just wants to get everything said today; the eternal perspective cares whether this person will still be in God’s house thirty years from now.

Brothers and sisters, do you want to be the one who freezes a person on their worst day, or the one who points them towards the best ending God has for them? Without a way forward, don’t speak.

sections.heading: 5. Learning to Bridle the Tongue: Waiting for God’s Time
sections.html:
Proverbs 15:23: “Joy comes to a man with the reply of his mouth. How good is a word at the right time!”

James 3:2: “For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.”

Brothers and sisters, very often the problem isn’t that we can’t speak, but that we speak too soon. The lesson reminds us of three sentences — please hold them in your heart: speaking when you shouldn’t is hurtful; not speaking when you should is a debt left unpaid; only speaking in God’s time is a blessing.

Knowing how to speak, and how not to

One important mark of spiritual maturity is “knowing how to speak, and knowing how not to.” James 3:2 says something very weighty: the one who does not stumble in word is a perfect person. The original word for “bridle” is chalinagōgeō, formed from the words for “bit” and “lead” — literally, “to steer with a bit.” This word tells us two things. First, the tongue is like a powerful, untamed horse. Second, the untamed horse is not to be killed but to be steered. God doesn’t want us to become mute; God wants our tongues to be steered by the Holy Spirit.

In Psalm 39:1 David says, “I will watch my ways, so that I don’t sin with my tongue. I will keep my mouth with a bridle while the wicked is before me.” And in Psalm 141:3 he prays, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” The original carries the sense of “keeping the door” — asking God to post a doorkeeper on my lips. Brothers and sisters, does your mouth have a doorkeeper?

Proverbs 10:19 says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.” This is a law of probability: the more you talk, the greater the odds of getting something wrong. The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer says in Life Together that the first service a Christian owes his brother is to listen; and he warns that the one who will not listen to his brother will soon no longer be listening to God either.

Bridling the tongue is denying of self

This is the discipline of denying of self — not saying whatever we feel like saying, but letting Jesus reign as King within us. Matthew 16:24 says, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” One of the most concrete battlegrounds of denying ourselves is the sentence that has already reached the tip of your tongue and that you swallow back down.

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” When we are selfless, our mouths no longer speak for ourselves; they become an outlet for the Holy Spirit.

Isaiah 50:4 describes the suffering Servant: “The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” Brothers and sisters, look at the order: first an ear that is taught, then a tongue that is taught; first listening morning by morning, then knowing how to sustain the weary. This is exactly what morning devotion is for — we come every morning to listen, so that every sentence we speak today can hold up someone who is weary.

Applying the 321 Vision: let Jesus be King

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Letting Jesus be King in our speech means handing the decision “Should I say this or not?” entirely back to him. The focus is not on whether I want to speak; the focus is on whether Jesus wants me to speak.

Brothers and sisters, silence sometimes takes more faith than speaking. Because when I am silent, I have to trust that God does not need a sentence from me to accomplish his work. This is the deepest humility — laying down our rights, returning to our originally intended position, letting man be man and letting God be God.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Words Are an Outlet for Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, set today’s five points within the 321 framework and you will see a complete picture.

The Three Foundations determine the groundwork of our speaking. Jesus is my role model — he spoke as people were able to hear; he waited three years for the sake of relationship; he gave grace first and direction afterwards. The Bible is my standard — what I say is not my opinion; it is God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — I don’t speak from my emotions, but by the Holy Spirit’s guidance.

The Two Core Values determine the aim of our speaking. Let Jesus be King: who has the final say in this conversation? Not my face, not my position — him. Let Jesus receive all the glory: when this sentence goes out, is it my insight that gets exalted, or his grace?

The Goal determines the direction of our speaking: establish God’s system. A system is made up of relationships, and relationships are nourished by words. Every sentence you speak today is either building God’s house or tearing it down.

The fivefold change is the very path of this lesson: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. When my mindset shifts from “I must get the words right” to “I must get the love right,” my life changes; when my life changes, the language of my daily living changes; when my language changes, relationships are healed; and when relationships are healed, ministry finally has a foundation. So the order is always: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

The 920 practice is the best training ground for our words. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”: spouse, children, parents, colleagues, small-group members. In every “2” relationship we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit. Today’s assignment is very concrete: in front of the “2” you most easily speak harshly to, bear these two fruits first — gentleness and self-control.

235 relationships are the safest setting for our words. Becoming a “2” with a selfless person — a spiritual companion — means having someone with whom we can speak the truth to each other; building a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — means relationships that can bear the weight of the truth; becoming a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades — means a unit that can fight the battle together with the truth. Brothers and sisters, truth needs a vessel that can carry it; 235 is that vessel.

Finally, there is the shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. When I look at the person in front of me with eternal eyes, I’m willing to wait; when I look at this conflict with heavenly eyes, I don’t need to win. Because humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan; pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Let Your Words Become an Outlet for Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices. Let’s use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into practice one by one.

Practice 1: Pause for three seconds — let your heart grow quiet before you speak

Every time you’re about to speak, pause for three seconds and ask yourself: am I relying on my heart right now, or on my emotions? Am I doing this for the other person, or for myself? Practise letting the Holy Spirit speak first, and then open your mouth.

Information and Revelation: know that “out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34), and ask the Holy Spirit to show you what your heart really holds. Conviction and Implementation: from today on, every time you’re about to respond, count silently to three and say, “Lord, you speak.” Evaluation and Correction: each evening, look back — how many times did I pause today, and how many times didn’t I? On the occasions I didn’t, what was the “self” in me?

Practice 2: Build the habit of “five questions before speaking”

Before every important conversation, ask yourself five questions: One, is this coming from love? Two, is my relationship with him deep enough? Three, do I have the authority to say it? Four, have I prayed? Five, am I offering a way forward? Let these five questions become the spiritual filter for your words.

Repetition and Multiplication: write the five questions on your phone’s wallpaper or on the first page of your notebook, and practise them for forty days straight; then teach your family and your small-group members to ask them too. The final stage of the eight is Multiplication — a mouth that has been healed should multiply into many more healed mouths.

Practice 3: Move from “explaining what’s right” to “offering a way forward”

When you need to point out a problem, prepare three things at the same time: one concrete suggestion, one act of companionship and one prayer of blessing. Let your words not only point out the problem but lead the person towards change.

An example of Implementation: don’t just say, “Your devotions have been really slack lately.” Say instead, “I’ve been finding it hard to be still lately too. Why don’t we send each other a verse every morning at seven? And I’ll pray for you today.” — suggestion, companionship and blessing, three in one.

Practice 4: Practise a life of “speaking less and loving more”

Deliberately cut down on meaningless, emotional, critical and judgemental words, and replace them with more encouragement, affirmation and blessing. Let your mouth become a tree of life.

Evaluation and Correction: remember Gottman’s five to one. Of the things you said to your family today, what was the ratio of positive to negative? If you spoke a harsh word yesterday, then today you need to add five sincere kind words — not flattery, but repair.

Practice 5: Bless someone with one sentence every day

Every day, speak at least one word that builds someone up: encouragement, thanks, affirmation, blessing. Let your words begin to become instruments of healing and building.

Multiplication: three hundred and sixty-five sentences of blessing a year are three hundred and sixty-five seeds of life. Ephesians 4:29 says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.”

A Gentle Reminder

The ability to speak is not the same as spiritual maturity; speaking a lot doesn’t mean speaking rightly; and speaking rightly doesn’t mean speaking at the right time. Truly godly people are not those who are “good with words,” but those who “let God decide when to speak, what to say and how to say it.” The focus is not on whether I want to speak; the focus is on whether Jesus wants me to speak. When you let Jesus be King, your mouth will become an outlet for life.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: One Mouth — What Will You Let It Become?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, words are an outlet for life.

The same mouth can build people up or tear them down; it can bring revival or bring ruin. James 3:9–10 says, “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God. Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.”

The key is not “whether you can speak” but “who is speaking inside you.” When you choose selflessness and let Jesus live in you, your words are no longer merely a human voice but a voice that carries the power of the kingdom of heaven.

This morning I want to issue you a call: place your tongue back into the hands of Jesus. Let him be King of your mouth. Let every time you open it first pass through his permission; let every silence become an act of trust in him.

Let us spend our whole lives learning this heavenly art — letting every sentence become a seed of life. May the fruit of our mouths not be praise for our cleverness, but that Jesus Christ receives all the glory.

keyVerses: Matthew 7:6
“Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you to pieces.”
Proverbs 16:24
“Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.”
Proverbs 15:4
“A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.”
Ephesians 4:15
“but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,”
Proverbs 15:23
“Joy comes to a man with the reply of his mouth. How good is a word at the right time!”
James 4:6
