“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’”
1 Corinthians 10:23–24
“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.”
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare: my mouth no longer speaks for myself, but for the Lord. I do not speak from my emotions, but by the guidance of the Holy Spirit. My words carry love, carry truth and carry a way forward; they become healing, building up and blessing. I am a person of self-control, of wisdom and of anointing; my tongue is a tree of life. All glory to the Lord Jesus. Amen.
practices: Pause for three seconds — let your heart grow quiet before you speak
Build the habit of “five questions before speaking”
Practise a life of “speaking less and loving more”
Bless someone with one sentence every day
prayer: What’s more, our speaking must always pass through prayer first. Not saying what we want to say, but saying what the Holy Spirit wants said. The Lord Jesus says in John 12:49, “For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” Brothers and sisters, even the Lord Jesus did not speak from himself! On what grounds do we speak from ourselves?

In Nehemiah 2:4 the Persian king asked Nehemiah, “What is your request?” And Scripture records, “So I prayed to the God of heaven.” Standing before the king, in those few brief seconds, Nehemiah prayed first and then spoke. That one opening of his mouth rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Brothers and sisters, isn’t your most important conversation worth three seconds of silent prayer first?

Proverbs 25:11 says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” Notice the word “fitly” — fitting the moment. With the wrong timing, even truth turns into hurt; with the right timing, a single sentence can turn a life around. Ecclesiastes 3:7 says, “a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.” Silence comes before speech.

Sometimes God is already at work in the other person’s heart, and all we need to do is say the right word at the right moment. It’s like a midwife at a birth: the child is made by God, the due date is set by God, and the midwife simply reaches out her hands at the right moment. Job 2:13 records of Job’s three friends: “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.” Those seven days were the best thing they did in the whole book; from chapter 3 onwards, the moment they opened their mouths, the more they said, the more wrong they got.

Neuroscience, too, reminds us how much timing matters. A study by Matthew Lieberman’s team at the University of California, Los Angeles, published in 2007 in the journal Psychological Science, found that when people put their emotions into words, activity in the amygdala goes down and the regulating function of the prefrontal cortex goes up. This shows that at the peak of emotion, the reasoning brain is temporarily “offline.” Brothers and sisters, reasoning with someone whose reason is offline is like typing commands into a computer that’s switched off.

So before you open your mouth, ask yourself: have I prayed? Is this God’s time? 321 reminds us: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. When my focus is on myself, I’m in a hurry to prove myself; when my focus is on others, I’m in a hurry to correct them; when my focus is on my circumstances, I’m in a hurry to fix them. Only when my focus is on Jesus can I wait quietly for him to say, “Now — speak.” Without authority, without prayer, don’t speak.
Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
You are the Word; you are the God who spoke, and it was done, who commanded, and it stood firm. This morning we bring our mouths before you.

Lord, forgive us for wrapping our emotions in the packaging of truth; forgive us for rushing to speak when we had no love, no relationship, no authority, no prayer and no way forward to offer. Forgive us for using our tongues to tear down the people you love.

Cleanse our hearts, for out of them is the wellspring of life. Post a doorkeeper on our lips, so that we may be swift to hear and slow to speak. Give us the tongue of those who are taught, so that we may know how to sustain with words those who are weary.
Lord, let our mouths no longer speak for ourselves, but for you. Let our tongues become a tree of life, and our pleasant words a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and health to the bones.
Be King in our words, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Proverbs 15:4: “A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.” Please share: over the past month, has your tongue been more like a “tree of life,” or more like the deceit that “crushes the spirit”? Is there a sentence you regretted the moment you said it? What was the “self” in you at the time?

Ephesians 4:15: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,” Use the lesson’s “five questions before speaking” to examine a relationship that is weighing on you right now: Is it coming from love? Is the relationship deep enough? Do you have the authority? Have you prayed? Are you offering a way forward? This week, which one do you plan to work on first?
l140.title: Let the Mouth Be an Outlet of Life
l140.subtitle: Do Your Words Bring Life, or Do They Wound?
l140.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: Real Flowers and Silk Flowers
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

First, picture a scene in your mind. Two pots of flowers sit on a table. In the one on the left, the petals are evenly coloured, the leaves spotless, the shape perfect, and it never wilts, all year round. In the one on the right, the petals are a little crooked, there are a few small insect bites on the leaves, some flowers open early and some late, and in a few days they will fade.

If you looked only at the outside, which pot would you choose? Most people would choose the one on the left. It’s neater, prettier, and much less trouble.

But the pot on the left is silk flowers. The pot on the right is real.

Silk flowers need no sunlight, no water, no roots. They are always that beautiful, because they have never been alive. Real flowers carry insect bites, they bloom and they fade, because they are alive. Inside them runs an unseen channel of water, from the root all the way to the tip of every petal.

Brothers and sisters, this morning we have to ask a very honest question: is my Christian life more like the silk flowers, or more like the real ones?

Many of us try very hard. We try hard to read the Bible, try hard to come to meetings, try hard to love people, try hard not to lose our temper, try hard to be a good husband, a good wife, a good parent, a good co-worker. Yet late at night, when all is still, there is a weariness in our hearts we can’t put into words. You find that the more you do, the emptier you feel inside; the better you perform, the more false you feel within.

That weariness doesn’t come from not doing well enough. It comes from always “doing” and never “living”.

At the opening of Book One of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a sentence that has been handed down for sixteen hundred years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The restlessness of the human heart can’t be filled with more behaviour. It is stilled only by returning to the Lord who made us.

That is the theme of this lesson: right doing is not something done from the outside; it is something lived out from within.

In Ephesians 4:20–24 Paul gives us a complete order: hearing his word, receiving his teaching, learning his truth — and only then putting off the old self, being renewed in mind and putting on the new self. The change in behaviour comes last, not first.

And in 1 Corinthians 15:10 Paul tells us the source of power behind it all: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”

Brothers and sisters, may God place these two passages inside us this morning. May we no longer be a pretty pot of silk flowers, but a living tree with roots, with channels of water, with life.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Writing and Setting of Ephesians
sections.html:
To understand Ephesians 4:20–24 rightly, we first need to stand where Paul stood as he wrote and take a look.

Ephesians is one of Paul’s “prison letters”. Along with Philippians, Colossians and Philemon, it is generally thought to have been written during Paul’s first imprisonment in Rome, somewhere between AD 60 and 62. Twice in the letter Paul mentions that he is a prisoner: in 4:1 he says, “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you,” and in 6:20 he calls himself “an ambassador in chains”. A man in chains wrote the most expansive, most glorious book in the whole Bible — and that in itself is a testimony: the circumstances outside were locked up, but the life within was not.

The letter was addressed to the church in Ephesus. Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, the most important commercial port and religious centre in Asia Minor. In the city stood the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — vast in scale, thronged with worshippers and thick with incense. The whole city’s economy, festivals and sense of identity were bound up with that temple. Acts 19 records that Paul worked in Ephesus for nearly three years, reasoning daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus, “so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks”. At that time many who practised magic repented and burned their books in public: “They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.”

Notice the setting. The believers in Ephesus didn’t live inside a church culture; they lived in a city of idol worship, show and outward appearance. Every day they stepped out of the door, their eyes saw the statues of the temple and their ears heard the drums of the festivals. In an environment like that, someone who only “looked like a Christian on the outside” wouldn’t last long. Paul knew this, so he didn’t begin by demanding that they change their behaviour; he began by changing the mindset within.

The structure of Ephesians is very clear: three chapters on each side, like the two leaves of a door.

Chapters 1 to 3 are about “doctrine” — who we are in Christ. Before the foundation of the world God chose us and in love predestined us for adoption as sons; once we were dead in trespasses and sins, but now we have been made alive together with Christ; the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile has been broken down, and together we are being built into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit. Chapter 3 ends in a glorious prayer and doxology.

Chapters 4 to 6 are about “daily living” — since we are such people, how we ought to live. The turning point is 4:1: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.”

Look at this order: first grace, then conduct; first identity, then responsibility; first “who you are”, then “what you do”. This is the logic of the whole Bible, and it is exactly what the 321 vision means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry”.

Now look at the more immediate context. In 4:17–19 Paul first describes the condition of the old self: “This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind, being darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts. They, having become callous, gave themselves up to lust, to work all uncleanness with greediness.”

Notice the order of Paul’s diagnosis: first “the futility of their mind”, then “darkened in their understanding”, then “alienated from the life of God”, then “ignorance” and “the hardening of their hearts”, and only at the very end, “gave themselves up to lust, to work all uncleanness with greediness”. The Gentiles’ problem did not begin with behaviour; it began in the mind. Corrupt behaviour is simply the last stop of a darkened mind.

And so in 4:20 comes a tremendous turn: “But you didn’t learn Christ that way.”

The way the original puts it here is remarkable. Paul doesn’t say, “you learned teaching about Christ”; he says, “you learned Christ” — what is learned is a person, not a curriculum. In the Greek world people studied philosophy by learning a system of thought; in Christ we learn a person, a Lord who is true and living. This is what the first of the 321 vision’s foundations means: Jesus is my role model.

The background of 1 Corinthians 15:10 also deserves a word. First Corinthians was written around AD 55, while Paul was in Ephesus (16:8 says, “But I will stay at Ephesus”). Chapter 15 is the fullest chapter on the resurrection in the whole Bible. In verse 9 Paul first admits: “For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.” Verse 10 continues: “But by the grace of God I am what I am.”

A man who once carried letters from the high priest to arrest Christians went on to write more than half of the books of the New Testament. He knew better than anyone: this was not the fruit of self-cultivation; it was the work of grace.

Brothers and sisters, of these two passages, one speaks of “order” and the other of “power”. The order is: seeing and listening come first, doing comes after. The power is: not I, but the grace of God which was with me. These are the two pillars of this lesson.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Right Doing Begins with “Seeing and Listening”
1. What the Scripture Says
sections.html:
Ephesians 4:21–23: “if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind.”

Here Paul sets out a crystal-clear order, four steps in all:

Step one: you heard his word.

Step two: you received his teaching.

Step three: you learned his truth.

Step four: you put off the old self, are renewed in mind, and put on the new self.

Brothers and sisters, see it clearly: the change in behaviour comes fourth. It is not the starting point; it is the result.

Many people, as soon as they come to faith, rush to change their behaviour: I won’t lose my temper any more, I won’t lie any more. These are all good desires, but if we haven’t first gone through the three steps before them, those resolutions won’t survive three months. Because you are only managing the fruit; you haven’t dealt with the root.

The lesson puts it precisely: “A change in behaviour is not the starting point but the result.” And again: “If a person has not first changed his ‘seeing’ and ‘listening’, his ‘doing’ is only imitation, suppression or forcing.”

Imitation, suppression, forcing — those three words say all there is to say about lifeless religious behaviour.

sections.heading: 2. A Light from the Original: Renewed in Mind
sections.html:
Where the Chinese Union Version renders 4:23 as “have your mind made entirely new”, the original reads, “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”. The word for “mind” is the Greek nous, meaning the mind, reason, the way one thinks — that is, the angle from which a person sees things and the standard by which he judges.

Paul uses the same word in Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” The “mind” here is also nous.

Notice that “renewed” in the original is passive voice and present tense — not “go and renew yourself”, but “keep on being renewed”. The one doing the renewing is God; we are the ones being renewed. Our part is to place ourselves where God’s word and the Holy Spirit can renew us.

The Bible never tells us to grit our teeth by willpower. The Bible tells us to change the way we see.

Proverbs 4:23 says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” This sentence is the key to this lesson. What flows out of a whole life does not come from the hands, nor from the mouth; it comes from the heart. Whatever your heart sees, that is where your whole life will go.

The Lord Jesus said the same thing. Luke 6:45: “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.”

Out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks. Put the other way round: what isn’t in the heart can’t be squeezed out of the mouth however hard you try; and even if you squeeze something out, it’s false.

sections.heading: 3. See Wrongly and You Will Do Wrongly: A Famous Psychology Experiment
sections.html:
The lesson sets out a powerful contrast:

See wrongly, and you will hear wrongly; hear wrongly, and you will think wrongly; think wrongly, and you will do wrongly.

Only by seeing rightly will you hear rightly; only by hearing rightly will you think rightly; only by thinking rightly will you do rightly.

This isn’t only a spiritual principle; it is also an observable psychological fact.

In 1999 the American psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris published in the journal Perception an experiment that later became world-famous. Participants were asked to watch a short film of two teams passing basketballs, one team in white shirts and one in black. Their task was to count the passes made by the team in white. Halfway through the film, a person in a gorilla suit walked slowly through the middle of the scene, even stopping to face the camera and thump its chest — nearly nine seconds in all.

The results astonished everyone: under the key conditions, about half the participants never saw the gorilla at all.

Their eyes were open, and the image really did fall on their retinas, yet they “did not see” it. Why? Because their attention was wholly taken up by the task of “counting passes”. The phenomenon later came to be called “inattentional blindness”.

Brothers and sisters, this experiment gives us a deep reminder: what we see depends on what we are paying attention to. It isn’t the eyes that decide what we see; it’s the heart.

Faced with the same event, one person sees a crisis and another sees grace; walking the same road, one person sees thorns and another sees the presence of God. The difference in what they see isn’t a difference in eyesight; it’s a difference of heart.

Take it one step further. In the mid-twentieth century, around 1955, the psychologist Albert Ellis proposed “rational emotive behaviour therapy”, using a simple ABC model to explain it: A is the activating event, B is the belief we hold about the event, and C is the consequence — our emotions and behaviour. Ellis pointed out that most people assume A directly causes C, when in fact what really determines C is B. Later, in the 1960s, Aaron T. Beck developed cognitive therapy and likewise showed that the most effective point of entry for changing a person’s long-standing behaviour is not the behaviour itself but the automatic thoughts and core beliefs behind it.

Notice, though: psychology is only a helper, not the standard. Psychology can tell us about the phenomenon that “mindset shapes behaviour”; only the Bible can tell us “what mindset to change to”. Psychology says to change to “more rational beliefs”; the Bible says to change to “God’s way of seeing”. Between the two lies a world of difference.

For the Bible’s goal is not to make us live more comfortably, but to make us live out the image of God. 4:24 says it plainly: “the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.”

sections.heading: 4. An Example from Daily Life: Yellowed Lenses
sections.html:
There’s a picture that can help us remember this point.

A man wore a pair of glasses whose lenses had turned yellow, and after wearing them for so long he thought the world was simply that colour. He complained that the sky wasn’t blue enough, that the colours in his photos were off, that the curtains at home looked strange. He tried all kinds of ways to fix the problem: new curtains, a new camera, new light bulbs. Until one day he took off his glasses and wiped them clean, and suddenly the world was clean and bright.

Brothers and sisters, how many years have we spent “changing the curtains”, without ever thinking of “cleaning our glasses”?

Ephesians tells us that the gospel doesn’t give you a new set of curtains. The gospel gives you a new pair of glasses — indeed, it gives you a new pair of eyes.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: The Fivefold Change
sections.html:
The 321 vision states it very clearly: the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; only when relationships change can there be healthy ministry.

The order of these five can’t be reversed.

The lesson’s “321 Insight” is exactly this: change the mindset, change the life, change daily living.

Many people start with the fifth — they do ministry first. They look very zealous, but the roots never go down, and after a while they dry up. Many others start with the fourth — they mend relationships first, holding on for a while with technique and patience, only for the relationship to go back to square one. Because the real problem lies in the first: the mindset hasn’t changed.

How is our perspective to change? The 321 vision is very concrete: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one.

2 Corinthians 4:18: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”

Colossians 3:2: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.”

Brothers and sisters, this morning’s first practice is this: before you open your mouth, before you lift a hand, first ask one question — whose eyes am I looking at this through right now?

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Two Kinds of Doing — Lived Out and Acted Out
1. What the Scripture Says
sections.html:
Ephesians 4:24: “and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.”

The phrase “put on” is fascinating. Putting on clothes is an outward action, but when Paul speaks of “putting on the new self”, he doesn’t mean adding a new coat over the old self; first you “put away”, then you “put on”. Verse 22 says, “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man”. Putting off and putting on belong together as one movement, and between them stands verse 23: “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”.

This makes one thing plain: the new self is not an upgraded version of the old self. The new self is another person altogether.

The lesson divides “doing” into two kinds, and very accurately: one kind of doing is “lived out”, the other is “acted out”.

sections.heading: 2. The First Kind of Doing: Lived Out, Like a Tree
sections.html:
The lesson says: “It is like a tree: when the root is healthy, it bears fruit naturally; when the life is right, the behaviour is right.”

The Lord Jesus said in Matthew 7:17–18: “Even so, every good tree produces good fruit; but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit. A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit.”

Notice the Lord’s words: a good tree “can’t” produce bad fruit, a corrupt tree “can’t” produce good fruit. Not “shouldn’t” — “can’t”. Because fruit is the natural expression of life, not the product of outside force. You can’t tie apples onto a willow and turn it into an apple tree; however tightly you tie them, they are only hanging there.

In John 15:4–5 the Lord says it even more directly: “Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me. I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.”

The Lord didn’t say, “Branches must try hard to bear fruit.” He said, “Remain in me.” The branch’s work is not bearing fruit; the branch’s work is staying connected. Fruit is the natural result of that connection.

A tree’s roots usually spread as wide as its crown, or even wider. What we see is the branches, leaves, flowers and fruit above; what we don’t see is the vast root system below. The stronger the wind, the more the roots matter. A tree that looks lush on the surface but has shallow roots falls in the first typhoon.

Brothers and sisters, how much of your time goes into the “branches and leaves”, and how much into the “roots”?

In Mark 4:26–28 the Lord uses another parable to describe the growth of God’s kingdom: “God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how. For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.”

“Though he doesn’t know how” — what a comfort those words are. Part of the growth of life is something we don’t understand and can’t control. Our responsibility is to sow the seed and to remain in the Lord; it is God who makes it grow.

sections.heading: 3. The Second Kind of Doing: Acted Out, Like a Christmas Tree
sections.html:
The lesson’s picture is wonderfully vivid: “It is like a Christmas tree: beautiful on the outside, but without life.”

Let’s look a layer deeper into this picture. What is a Christmas tree? A Christmas tree is a tree that has been cut down. Severed from its roots, it is set up in the living room, hung with baubles, strung with lights and sprayed with artificial snow. For the first few days it looks splendid — better, even, than any tree growing on the mountainside. But day by day its needles drop onto the carpet. All you can do is hang on more decorations to cover the bare patches.

Brothers and sisters, doesn’t that look like our condition at times? More and more hung on the outside, drier and drier on the inside. Our roles in service grow heavier, while our closeness to the Lord grows fainter. We use “more decorations” to cover the fact that we have “no roots”.

The lesson says: “Under pressure, you do it; without pressure, you stop.” That is the most obvious mark of doing that is “acted out”.

The Lord Jesus spoke his sternest words about this condition. Matthew 23:27: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.”

And in 23:26 the Lord points out the right order: “You blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and of the platter, that its outside may become clean also.”

First the inside, then the outside. God’s order has never changed. 1 Samuel 16:7: “for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

In Colossians 2:23 Paul says of those who restrain themselves by rules: “These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body; but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.”

Hear Paul’s conclusion clearly: not of any value. Not of little value — of no value at all.

Galatians 3:3 cuts even deeper: “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?”

So often we come in through the door by grace, and then walk the road by ourselves. That is the root of so many Christians’ exhaustion.

sections.heading: 4. Supporting Evidence from Psychology: Intrinsic Motivation and Burnout
sections.html:
Here a piece of psychological research fits very well.

In 1985 Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan, psychologists at the University of Rochester in the United States, put forward “self-determination theory”. They distinguished two kinds of motivation: intrinsic motivation, which comes from the meaning and satisfaction the activity itself brings; and extrinsic motivation, which comes from rewards, pressure, evaluation or punishment. Their research showed that when a person’s behaviour is driven mainly by outside control, it can be pushed along in the short term but is hard to sustain, and it often comes with a loss of the sense of autonomy.

That is exactly what the lesson says: under pressure, you do it; without pressure, you stop.

Consider another study. In 1981 the American psychologists Christina Maslach and Susan Jackson published their well-known burnout inventory, which divides burnout into three dimensions: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation (becoming cold and detached towards people), and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment.

Brothers and sisters, don’t those three dimensions also show up in some people who have served for a long time? First weariness, then coldness towards people, and finally the feeling of having accomplished nothing at all.

The lesson describes it exactly: “The more you do, the more tired you get; the more you do, the more false you become; the more you do, the less joy you have.”

Psychology can describe this phenomenon, but it can’t solve the problem. The solution isn’t in psychology; it’s in the gospel. For the deepest root of burnout isn’t too heavy a workload; it’s the self-centred life — I am doing it, I am holding it together, I am proving I can.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Selflessness — Letting Jesus Live
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem.

What is the self-centred life? It is “I” standing at the centre. I will do it, I will hold it together, I will prove it, I will get the glory. A person like that works very hard, but his strength comes out of himself, and when it’s used up there is none left.

What is selflessness? The 321 vision puts it beautifully: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the heart of this lesson.

“It is no longer I who live” — that is putting off the old self.

“But Christ lives in me” — that is putting on the new self.

One sentence in the lesson is worth memorising: “What God wants is not ‘doing right’ but ‘living right’.”

The 321 vision also says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Doing that is “acted out” is, at its core, a kind of pride: I want to become that good person by my own effort.

Doing that is “lived out” is, at its core, a kind of humility: I let God be the Lord within me.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. A family where everyone holds on by their own strength to be good people will make demands of one another, find fault with one another and wear one another down; a family where Christ lives within will cover one another, supply one another and strengthen one another.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Right Doing Is the Work of the Holy Spirit
1. What the Scripture Says
sections.html:
1 Corinthians 15:10: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”

Notice that there is something in this verse that looks like a contradiction. Paul says, “I worked more than all of them” — that sounds like great effort; and the very next words are, “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” — which is not himself at all.

So is it effort, or not effort?

The answer is: working very hard at relying, not working very hard at holding it together yourself. Paul’s labour was not the source of his strength; it was the result of grace. Philippians 2:12–13 expresses this relationship most clearly: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.”

On the outside you can see the “working out”; on the inside it is “God who works in you”.

The lesson puts it well: “Change is not ‘I try harder’; change is ‘I let God do it’.”

sections.heading: 2. From a Heart of Stone to a Heart of Flesh: The Old Testament Promised It Long Ago
sections.html:
This is not a teaching that only appears in the New Testament. In Ezekiel 36:26–27, God made this promise among his people in exile: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them.”

Look at the order: first a new heart, then a new spirit, and only then “cause you to walk in my statutes”. God never required his people to obey first and get a new heart afterwards. God changes the heart first, and obedience follows.

In Zechariah 4:6 the angel said to Zerubbabel: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.”

Isaiah 64:6 reminds us of the limits of relying on ourselves: “For we have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteousness is like a polluted garment.”

Brothers and sisters, if our best behaviour does not come from the Holy Spirit, its worth in God’s eyes is limited. This isn’t meant to discourage us; it’s meant to bring us back to the right source.

sections.heading: 3. The Holy Spirit Does Two Things: Illumines and Guides
sections.html:
The lesson says: “Only when the Holy Spirit shines his light on us do we see our own problems; only when the Holy Spirit guides us do we have the strength to live out the truth.”

That is exactly what the Bible teaches.

First, illumination. John 16:8: “When he has come, he will convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment.” Without the Holy Spirit’s light, people can’t see the truth about themselves. We can list a long string of other people’s faults and yet be completely unaware of our own blind spots.

David’s prayer is the prayer of everyone willing to be searched by the light. Psalm 139:23–24: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.”

Second, guidance. Romans 8:13–14: “For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.”

Notice: putting to death the deeds of the body is done “by the Spirit”, not by gritted teeth.

2 Corinthians 3:18 describes the process of this change: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.”

“With unveiled face seeing” — “seeing” once again. “Are transformed into the same image” — this is passive: we are transformed; we don’t transform ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, we see, and then we are changed. That is the Bible’s consistent way.

sections.heading: 4. Confirmation from Science: It Isn’t You Who Makes Your Heart Beat
sections.html:
Here is a very simple yet highly persuasive physiological fact.

An adult’s heart beats roughly seventy times a minute at rest, around a hundred thousand times a day, and from our mother’s womb until the day we leave this world it never stops. Let me ask you: when you got up this morning, did you first remind yourself, “Heart, remember to beat”?

No. Because the basic rhythm of heartbeat and breathing is maintained by the autonomic nervous system and doesn’t need your will to take part. If you really try to control your breathing by will, you can keep it up for a few dozen seconds, not for a whole morning. By contrast, raising your hand, walking, writing — these are voluntary movements of the skeletal muscles; they need the will, and they tire.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a deep spiritual analogy: whatever is sustained by willpower will surely tire; only what flows naturally from life within can last.

Do you want to live your whole Christian life “the way you raise your hand”, or “the way your heart beats”?

In Matthew 11:28–30 the Lord Jesus gives his invitation: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

Notice: the Lord didn’t say, “I will take the yoke away.” He said, “Take my yoke upon you.” A yoke is a harness made for two oxen. To take the Lord’s yoke means to share one yoke with the Lord, walking beside him and keeping in step with him. Whether you’re weary doesn’t depend on whether there is a yoke; it depends on who is pulling beside you.

sections.heading: 5. A Saying and a Testimony: Becoming Little Christs
sections.html:
In Book Four of Mere Christianity, the English writer C. S. Lewis says that the Church exists for nothing else but to draw people into Christ and make them “little Christs”; if the Church is not doing that, all the cathedrals, clergy, missions, sermons, even the Bible itself, are simply a waste of time.

That fits the theme of this lesson exactly. The aim of Christianity is not to manufacture well-behaved people, but to put the life of Christ within people.

1 John 2:6: “he who says he remains in him ought himself also to walk just like he walked.” Notice the order: first “remains in him”, then “walk just like he walked”.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves
sections.html:
The 321 vision has a saying that many people never forget once they’ve heard it: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry.

The lesson says: “Relying on the brain and on ourselves, acting it out — exhausting. Relying on the heart and on the Holy Spirit, living it out — natural.”

This isn’t telling us not to use our minds. God gave us minds so that we could use them to know the truth. It’s a reminder: the mind is a vessel for receiving, not an engine for generating power. The engine is the Holy Spirit.

The Three Foundations of 321 line up perfectly here: Jesus is my role model — it is him I look at; the Bible is my standard — it is his word I listen to; the Holy Spirit is my guide — it is his power I rely on.

The lesson’s last sentence is more powerful still: “The true overcomer is not the one who tries hardest, but the one most willing to let the Lord be King.”

This is exactly the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, if overcoming depended on effort, overcoming would become a contest, with winners and losers. But if overcoming depends on letting the King be King, then everyone willing to step aside can overcome. The door of the gospel stands open to everyone.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: A Map for Living Out from Within
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, put the three key points together and we see a complete map.

The Three Foundations are where we stand. Jesus is my role model — so I no longer imitate others or compare myself with them; I look only at him. The Bible is my standard — so I no longer go by feelings, by experience or by public opinion; I use God’s word to correct my sight. The Holy Spirit is my guide — so I no longer grit my teeth in my own strength; I learn to receive, moment by moment, the strength that comes from above.

The Two Core Values are our direction. Let Jesus be King — wherever the King is, there is his kingdom; if he reigns as King in my heart, then my tongue, my temper, my wallet and my time all come under his rule. Let Jesus receive all the glory — so I don’t need to perform, I don’t need to prove anything, I don’t need to earn a good name before people. I can say honestly: not I, but the grace of God which was with me.

The Goal is our destination: establish God’s system. This system isn’t piled up out of structures and procedures; it is joined together, one life at a time, out of lives that have been “set right within”.

Now see how the core message of 321 runs right through this lesson.

First, the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The “old self” of Ephesians 4:22 is the “me” with self at the centre; the “new self” of 4:24 is the “me” remade in the likeness of God. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. A drop of water held in your palm evaporates; put it into the ocean and it never runs dry.

Second, humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. The most dangerous thing about religious behaviour that is “acted out” isn’t the weariness; it’s pride. When people do well they become self-righteous; when they do badly they feel inferior; and self-righteousness and inferiority actually share one root — both have self at the centre. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When we say, “Lord, I can’t, but you can,” Satan has no foothold left in us.

Third, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Key Point 1 dealt with the first and second: change the mindset and you change the life. Key Point 2 dealt with the second and third: when the life is right, daily living is right. Key Point 3 dealt with the one who drives the whole process — the Holy Spirit.

Fourth, life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. So many people are worn out precisely because they’ve turned the order upside down: busy with tasks first, and thinking of God only last. Once the order is reversed, the whole person falls apart.

Fifth, the shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. Man’s perspective looks at “how I performed today”; God’s perspective looks at “whether Christ has been formed in me”. The earthly perspective looks at “what others say about me”; the heavenly perspective looks at “how the Lord sees me”.

Sixth, the 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. Before them I practise living out the selfless “0”, letting the Holy Spirit bear his ninefold fruit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Galatians 5:22–23 says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Notice that the passage speaks of “the fruit of the Spirit”, not “the performance I produce by effort”. The nine are one cluster, not a choice of one out of nine, because they are the expression of one and the same life.

Seventh, the 235 relationships. Become a “2” with someone who is also pursuing selflessness, supporting and reminding one another; go on to build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and finally become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, building up the body of Christ together. Ephesians 4:11–12 speaks of exactly this: God gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers to equip the saints, so that each does his part in building up the body of Christ.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus is right, everything begins to fall into place.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: From Acting It Out to Living It Out
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices. Following the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — we will deepen them one by one.

Practice 1: Practise “starting from the source” every day

Don’t rush to change your behaviour. First ask yourself two questions: Am I seeing things today with God’s eyes? Have I let the truth come inside me? Read and meditate on the Bible at a set time every day, so that your “seeing and listening” are renewed first.

Information: Write Ephesians 4:20–24 on a card and put it somewhere you are sure to see it every day — your phone’s home screen, the mirror, your desk.

Revelation: As you read, ask the Holy Spirit to open it to you. Don’t only ask, “What does this passage say?” Ask, too, “Lord, which mindset do you want to change in me?”

Conviction: Truly believe that “a change in behaviour is not the starting point but the result.” This step is the hardest, because from childhood we have been trained to earn approval through behaviour.

Implementation: Every morning, for ten minutes, do just one thing — let God’s word come in first, and then let the day begin.

Evaluation: In the evening, take three minutes to look back: at which moment today did I react first and think afterwards?

Correction: Write that moment down, bring it before God, and ask him to renew that mindset.

Repetition: Keep going for forty days in a row. A change of mindset doesn’t come from being moved once; it comes from soaking steadily.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister to do it with you, and share with each other what you see each day. That is the beginning of your “2”.

Practice 2: Discern whether your doing is “lived out” or “acted out”

When you are doing something right, ask yourself: Am I doing this because of pressure, or because life is flowing out? Is there joy inside me, or reluctance? If it is reluctance, go back to God; don’t grit your teeth and push through.

Information: First learn the difference between the two kinds of doing — the tree and the Christmas tree, roots and decorations.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to shine his light on the few things in your life that “look good outside but are forced inside”.

Conviction: Believe that God doesn’t want your performance; God wants the real you. He would rather have an honest weakling than a flawless performer.

Implementation: This week choose one thing and honestly admit before the Lord: “Lord, this is something I’ve been acting out, not living out.”

Evaluation: Ask yourself, why do I do this? For whose eyes am I doing it?

Correction: If it’s for people’s eyes, offer it up afresh; if it’s what the Lord has entrusted to you, ask him first to renew your heart, and then do it.

Repetition: Once a week, take a “motive inventory”.

Multiplication: Ask each other this question with your spiritual companion. Sincere mutual support is the first shape of the 235 relationships.

Practice 3: Stop relying on yourself; learn to rely on the Holy Spirit

When you come to something you can’t do, don’t blame yourself; pray instead: “Lord, I can’t, but you can. Please live it out in me.” Turn “effort” into “reliance”.

Information: Learn Philippians 2:13 by heart: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.”

Revelation: See that your “I can’t” is actually God’s invitation, not God’s condemnation.

Conviction: Accept a fact — where I come to an end is where God begins.

Implementation: Set that prayer as a reminder on your phone, three times a day, fifteen seconds each time.

Evaluation: Note how many times this week you blamed yourself first instead of praying first.

Correction: Replace words of self-blame with words of reliance. Self-blame makes us shrink back; reliance makes us strong.

Repetition: Let “Lord, you come” be your first response, not your last resort.

Multiplication: When others come to you with their troubles, lead them in the same prayer rather than handing them a pile of methods.

Practice 4: Practise a life of “letting Jesus live”

In everything, ask: If Jesus were me, how would Jesus live? Am I the one living right now, or am I letting the Lord live? Learn to give way to the Lord in daily living.

Information: Read Galatians 2:20 until you can recite it.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to let you see him in concrete situations — in a traffic jam, when you’re misunderstood, when your child answers back, when a colleague takes the credit.

Conviction: Believe that “giving way” is not losing but gaining. When I let Jesus be King, I don’t become smaller; I enter the infinite.

Implementation: Today choose the situation where you most easily lose control, and decide in advance: at that moment, I will be still for three seconds first and say, “Lord, you come.”

Evaluation: In the evening think it over: how many times today did I succeed in giving way? And the times I failed — what caused them?

Correction: For the times you failed, don’t condemn yourself; simply entrust it to him again.

Repetition: Practising one situation for a month bears more fruit than practising ten situations for three days each.

Multiplication: Share your experience. What people need most isn’t more teaching; it’s someone who has really lived it out in front of them.

Practice 5: Give yourself time; accept the process of growth

Don’t lose heart because you haven’t changed yet. The change of life is like a seed growing: unseen, but happening; slow, but it will bear fruit. Keep abiding in the truth, and let God do his work.

Information: Remember Mark 4:28: “For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.”

Revelation: See that God’s timetable is different from yours, and his never runs late.

Conviction: Believe Philippians 1:6: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.”

Implementation: Don’t measure yourself by “results in a few days”; measure yourself by “whether the direction is right”.

Evaluation: Look back once every quarter, and you’ll be amazed at how far you’ve already come.

Correction: If you find you’ve stalled, first check whether you’ve gone back to the source of “seeing and listening”.

Repetition: A farmer doesn’t dig up his seeds every day to check on them. He sows, he waters, he waits.

Multiplication: Let your experience of waiting become strength for others not to lose heart.

A Gentle Reminder

Don’t look only at outward behaviour; God looks at the life within.

Don’t rush to get things right; first let the inside be set right.

Don’t strain to change yourself; learn to let Christ live in you.

The focus isn’t “how I do it”; the focus is “whether Jesus is living in me”.

When the inside is right, the outside will naturally be right.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the two pots of flowers we began with.

Silk flowers never wilt, because they have never been alive. Real flowers wilt, because they truly live. What God wants is not a showpiece that never goes wrong, but a life that is truly growing.

The lesson’s conclusion puts it beautifully: right doing is not the result of effort but the overflow of life. While you are still “doing”, you will be weary; when you begin to “live”, you will have joy.

God has not called us to be “people who perform well”; he has called us to become “people through whom Christ is lived out”.

So this morning I want to extend three invitations to every brother and sister.

The first invitation: put down the decorations in your hands. You no longer need more service, better performance or a more perfect image to cover the dryness within. God already knows. He doesn’t want to rebuke you; he wants to renew you.

The second invitation: go back to your roots. Begin again today with “seeing and listening”. Colossians 3:2 says: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” Once the mindset changes, the life changes.

The third invitation: let Jesus be King. Not your consultant, not your backup plan — your King. The King has absolute authority; the King’s word is final. When you place your life in the King’s hands, you will discover something wonderful — you no longer need to strain so hard, because the one really doing the work is him.

Paul says: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” One day, when people praise the change in our lives, may we too be able to say these words honestly and joyfully.

The glory does not go to our efforts; the glory goes to Jesus Christ, who lives within us.

From today on, stop forcing yourself to do, and learn to let the Lord live in you. When Jesus becomes your life, your doing will naturally line up with heaven.

keyVerses: Ephesians 4:20–24

“But you didn’t learn Christ that way, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.”
1 Corinthians 15:10
“But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus, I declare:
I no longer rely on myself to produce right behaviour; I let Christ live himself out in me.
I put off the old self and put on the new self; my mind is being renewed.
I do not live by the strength of the flesh, but by the Holy Spirit.
My life will bear fruit, living out truth, righteousness and holiness.
None of this is I, but the grace of God which is with me.
Amen.
practices: Stop relying on yourself; learn to rely on the Holy Spirit
Practise a life of “letting Jesus live”
Give yourself time; accept the process of growth
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that your word has come to us this morning and shone its light on what is within us.

Lord, we confess that we have spent too much strength on the outside and too seldom come back to the inside. We have covered dryness with busyness and replaced reliance with effort. We have done many right things, yet inside we have grown ever more tired and ever more joyless.
Lord, have mercy on us.

Renew our minds; turn us from man’s eyes to your eyes, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from temporary sight to eternal sight. Help us to put off the old self of our former way of life and put on the new self, created in the likeness of God in righteousness and holiness of truth.
Lord, today we no longer ask for more strength; we ask for you yourself. We no longer say, “I must try harder”; we say, “Lord, I can’t, but you can. Please live it out in me.”
Holy Spirit, shine your light on us so that we see our true condition; guide us so that we have strength to walk in the truth.
May Jesus reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Ephesians 4:22–24: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” Please share: what “way of seeing things” has God been renewing in you lately? How has that renewal affected your words or actions?

Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Please share honestly: what is one thing in your life right now that is “acted out” rather than “lived out”? How will you hand it over to the Lord this week and learn to let him live it?
l141.title: Lived Out from Within
l141.subtitle: Doing Rightly (Part 1): Lived Out from Within, Not Done from Without
l141.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: The Seed in Your Hand That Was Never Sown
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to ask you first to be still for thirty seconds and answer one question: over this past year, of the things God has shone his light on in your heart, how many have you actually gone and done?

Not “how many have you agreed with”, not “how many have moved you”, but “how many have you lived out”.

An old farmer once said something that has stayed with me ever since: “A farmer’s greatest failure in life isn’t a poor harvest; it’s keeping his seed in his pocket until it goes mouldy.” Seed in the pocket can be touched, can be counted, can even be taken out and shown to people. But a seed’s destiny isn’t to be looked at; it’s to be buried in the ground. Only when it falls into the earth does it die; only when it dies does it grow; only when it grows does it bear thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. A seed left in the pocket is only ever a seed.

The greatest trap in the spiritual life is “stopping at knowing”.

Christians of our generation are the least short of “information” of any generation in history. One swipe of the phone and there are countless sermons; open the computer and there are pages of exposition. We know far more than believers did a hundred years ago. But we must honestly ask: are our lives stronger than theirs? Are our families more united than theirs?

That is the question this lesson has to face. In the last lesson we talked about “right doing”, and saw the importance and the direction of doing the word; this lesson takes one step further — from knowing to doing, and from doing to receiving.

Between these three words stand two checkpoints. The first lies between “knowing” and “doing”, where a chasm called “procrastination and self-deception” stretches across the way; the second lies between “doing” and “receiving”, and what it requires is the perseverance of “continuing”. Most people get stuck at the first.

Brothers and sisters, remember the heart of today: knowing is not having; only doing leads to receiving.

God’s word is living and powerful, but his power isn’t released in our notebooks; it’s released in our obedience. That seed you’re holding in your hand — will you sow it this morning?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Scenes
sections.html: Today’s theme passages are three, from three different writers and three different scenes. When we see the backgrounds clearly, we can see the consistent intention of the Holy Spirit throughout the whole Bible.

sections.heading: 1. James 1:22–25: A Family Letter to People Scattered Abroad
sections.html:
Evangelical scholars generally hold that the author of James was James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh (Matthew 13:55 names James among Jesus’ brothers), who later became the leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9). James may well be one of the earliest books of the New Testament to be written, dating from around the AD 40s, and it was addressed “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — that is, to Jewish Christians scattered abroad by persecution.

Notice who James was. He grew up alongside Jesus. John 7:5 says, “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” James at first did not believe; then the risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and only then did he become God’s servant. A man who went from “knowing a great deal about Jesus” to “truly knowing Jesus” is the one best qualified to say, “not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” For he himself had once known the most and yet been furthest away.

The style of James is like the wisdom literature of the Old Testament — every sentence practical, every line piercing. The flow of chapter 1 runs: trials (verses 2–12), temptation (verses 13–18), and then hearing and doing the word (verses 19–27). James doesn’t trade works for salvation; he says works prove salvation.

The “mirror” of verse 23 was, in the first century, a mirror of polished metal, usually bronze or silver — not as clear as today’s glass mirrors. To see clearly you had to lean in, catch the light and stay there. So James draws a weighty contrast: one kind of person takes just a “look” and walks away; the other kind “looks into” it. The Greek for “looks into” is parakuptō, which means to bend down, to stoop and lean close to look carefully; the same word is used in John 20:5, when John ran to the empty tomb and, “stooping and looking in”, saw the linen cloths. James is saying: that is the posture we should take towards the word of God.

sections.heading: 2. John 13:17: A Word Spoken Beside the Washbasin
sections.html:
The scene of this verse is the Last Supper. The Lord Jesus got up from the table, took off his outer garment, tied a towel around his waist, poured water into a basin, and washed his disciples’ feet one by one. When he had finished, he put his clothes back on, sat down and spoke to them, and then came verse 17: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”

Pay attention to the Lord’s wording: “If you know … if you do them … blessed are you.” Knowing is a premise already established; doing is a condition not yet fulfilled; blessing is the result once the condition is met. The Lord did not say, “Blessed are you if you know”; he said, “blessed are you if you do them.” Nowhere in the whole Bible is there a promise that “those who know are blessed”, yet again and again it promises that “those who obey are blessed” (Psalm 1:1–2; Luke 11:28; Revelation 22:14).

What’s more, the context of this sentence is foot-washing. What the Lord wanted his disciples to go and do was not some lofty set of doctrines; it was the posture of bending down to serve others. We often think of “doing the word” as some great, hard undertaking, yet the Lord placed it in a basin of water and a towel.

sections.heading: 3. Matthew 7:24–25: The Seal on the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
Matthew chapters 5 to 7 are the Sermon on the Mount. The Lord Jesus spoke of the blessings, of the true meaning of the law, of prayer, of not worrying, of not judging. When he had finished, he closed with a parable: two men, two houses, two outcomes.

Notice that this is the very last part of the whole sermon. The Lord Jesus didn’t close with a prayer, nor with a blessing; he closed with “doing or not doing”. It’s as if he were saying: I’ve spoken for three chapters, and you’ve listened for three chapters; now everything depends on what you do after you come down the mountain.

Verses 26–27 are the other half: “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell — and great was its fall.” Both men heard; the only difference was one word — “do”.

The terrain of Palestine makes this parable especially real. There are many dry riverbeds there, which the Hebrew calls “dry streams” — wadis. In the dry season the riverbed is a flat stretch of soft sand, the easiest place of all to build; but when the rainy season comes, water pours down from the hills, and within a few hours that stretch of sand becomes a torrent. A house built on it is swept away, foundations, walls and all. The Lord’s hearers had all seen such things.

Brothers and sisters, three passages, three scenes, one message: God’s word counts only when it is lived out.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Only by Moving from Knowing to Doing Do We Receive
sections.html:
“If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)

The greatest trap in the spiritual life is stopping at “knowing”.

There are so many people around us like this — perhaps we ourselves are such people: we know a great many truths, have heard a great many messages, can even preach a great deal, yet our lives haven’t changed. Why? Because the most crucial step is missing — “doing”.

sections.heading: 1. See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do, Receive: A Six-Stage Spiritual Cycle
sections.html:
For a truth to enter our lives, it usually passes through six stages: seeing, listening, thinking, speaking, doing and receiving.

“Seeing” is contact, “listening” is reception, “thinking” is digestion, “speaking” is putting it in order, “doing” is transformation, “receiving” is possession.

The trouble is that the first four stages all give us the illusion that “I’ve already made progress”. We see a moving testimony and our hearts burn; we hear a piercing message and our eyes fill with tears; we meditate on a verse again and again and feel full of light; we tell others about that light and are even praised for it. We can go through all four stages and our lives may not have moved an inch.

Because it is in the fifth stage, “doing”, that truth turns from knowledge into life. Without “doing”, we never reach “receiving”.

It’s like a seed. You may have seen the seed, heard all about the seed, thought about what the seed will grow into, even shown the seed to others — and the seed is still a seed. The Lord Jesus said: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Falling into the ground — that is “doing”.

sections.heading: 2. Knowing Can Deceive: Two Real Studies
sections.html:
Psychology has some well-known findings that can help us see clearly how unreliable “knowing” is.

The first is the forgetting curve. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus carried out a series of memory experiments with himself as the subject, and found that newly learned material, if not reviewed or used, is lost in large amounts within a very short time; after one day, often only about a third is retained. Brothers and sisters, what does that mean? It means that if the message you hear this morning is only “heard”, by this time tomorrow two thirds of it will be gone. The only way to keep hold of the truth isn’t to hear it again; it’s to do it once. Because what we have done stays in our muscles, stays in our relationships, stays in our lives.

The second is “the curse of knowledge”. In 1990 Elizabeth Newton, a psychology researcher at Stanford University, carried out an experiment: one group was asked to tap out with their fingers the rhythm of a song everyone knows well, and another group had to guess which song it was. The tappers predicted that the listeners would guess right about half the time; in fact, out of a hundred and twenty songs only three were guessed correctly — a hit rate of about two and a half per cent. The reason is simple: the tappers had the melody in their heads; the listeners had only the tapping in their ears.

This experiment is a wake-up call for us. When we “know” a truth, we have the whole melody in our heads, and so we think we already possess it. But what others see isn’t the melody in our heads; it’s the sound our hands tap out — that is, what we actually live. And that is how God sees us too.

sections.heading: 3. The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea: Only What Flows In and Out Is Alive
sections.html:
Israel has two famous bodies of water, both fed by the Jordan River, yet with completely opposite fates. In the north, the Sea of Galilee: water flows in from the north and out to the south; it teems with fish, the towns on its shores have flourished, and most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry took place there. In the south, the Dead Sea: water only flows in and never out, its one exit being evaporation, so the salt keeps building up; fish can’t live there and plants can’t grow, and so it is called the “Dead Sea”.

The same living water — one becomes a sea of life, the other a sea of death, and the difference lies in one thing only: whether there is an outlet.

Brothers and sisters, our spiritual lives are the same. God’s word keeps flowing in, but if there is no outlet of “doing”, the truth that comes in settles inside, crystallises and turns salty — until it becomes knowledge for judging others, a standard for criticising sermons, a heart that understands everything and yet moves for nothing.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight: Changing the Mindset Is the Beginning; Living Out the Life Is the Result
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Notice that “mindset” is only the first of the five, not the last. Many people treat a “change of mindset” as the finish line — they celebrate having worked it out, having understood it, and then they stop there. But the fivefold change is a chain, and if any link in the middle breaks, nothing after it will happen. And the link that joins mindset to life is precisely “doing”.

The 321 vision also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. Proverbs 4:23 says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” Relying on the brain, you can know a great deal, yet produce no fruit; what flows out of a whole life comes from the heart, and the heart’s outlet is action.

Brothers and sisters, here is this morning’s first decision: no longer be satisfied with “I understand”. From today, when you finish hearing a message, don’t ask, “What did I learn?” Ask instead, “What am I going to do today?”

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Not Doing the Word Is Spiritual Self-Deception
sections.html:
“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

These are very weighty words. It turns out that a person may think he is growing, yet if there is no “doing”, he is actually “deceiving himself”.

sections.heading: 1. How Weighty the Original Is: “Deluding Your Own Selves”
sections.html:
The Greek for “deluding” is paralogizomai, made up of two parts, “beside” and “to reckon, to reason”; literally it means “to miscalculate the accounts”, “to mislead with plausible but false reasoning”. The same word appears in Colossians 2:4: “Now I say this that no one may delude you with persuasiveness of speech.”

In other words, people who only hear the word and don’t do it aren’t stupid; they know how to keep accounts — they’ve just got the sums wrong. They have entered “heard it” as “received it”, “moved” as “obeyed”, “agreed” as “changed”. In their spiritual passbook the figures look very fine, but in reality it’s a set of falsified books.

And the most dangerous thing is this: no one else is deceiving them; they are deceiving themselves. When others deceive you, someone can still warn you; when you deceive yourself, you have switched off the alarm yourself.

sections.heading: 2. Three Actions in Front of the Mirror
sections.html:
James uses the mirror as a picture, describing three actions of such a person: “for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.” (James 1:24)

He sees — the truth shows up the problem.

He goes away — his body leaves the mirror.

He forgets — his heart leaves the light as well.

Brothers and sisters, aren’t those three actions a portrait of our every Sunday? The meeting is moving, the sermon pierces us, and by the time we reach the car park after church we’re back to how we were; we get home to the same temper, the same coldness, the same hurtful remark.

There’s nothing wrong with the mirror, nothing wrong with the light; the problem is that we’ll only “take a glance” and won’t “bend down”. As we said earlier, “looks into” in verse 25 is parakuptō — to stoop, to bend low and lean in close to look carefully. Truly doing the word means being willing to stay in front of that mirror thirty seconds longer, letting the truth shine on the places in ourselves we’d rather it didn’t.

sections.heading: 3. Knowing Without Doing Ends in Becoming a Pharisee
sections.html:
This is James’s deepest warning, and the Lord Jesus’ sternest rebuke.

Matthew 23:2–3 records the Lord’s words: “The scribes and the Pharisees sat on Moses’ seat. All things therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do, but don’t do their works; for they say, and don’t do.”

“They say, and don’t do” — those few words are the most dreadful end that spiritual knowledge can come to. The Pharisees didn’t know too little; they knew too much and did too little. If knowledge isn’t used to deal with ourselves, it automatically turns to deal with others.

The Lord goes on: “For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them.” (Matthew 23:4) This is the inevitable end of not doing the word: a life that stalls, a spirit that dries up, even a turning to judge others — demanding of others what we don’t demand of ourselves.

Psychology has observed something similar. In 1957 the American psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t match, an inner tension arises, and there are two ways to resolve it — one is to change the behaviour so that it fits the belief; the other is to reinterpret things so that the conscience goes quiet. The second way is much cheaper, so most people take it. “I haven’t managed it, but at least I agree with it.” “That truth was meant for so-and-so.” “I’ll deal with it when things are a bit better.” Brothers and sisters, we’ve all said such things. This is exactly how “deluding your own selves” works at the psychological level.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight: Pride Is Leaving Our Originally Intended Position — Using Truth to Make Demands of Others Is Pride
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Using the truth to press down on others is the classic case of leaving our originally intended position. The truth belongs to God, and shining light on people is the Holy Spirit’s work; when I take the truth into my hand as a measuring rod to measure others, judge others and condemn others, I’ve sat down in a seat that isn’t mine. And God’s response is very clear: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

So the 321 vision says: selflessness means dealing with ourselves first, not using the truth to press down on others. The Lord Jesus asks: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3) Notice the Lord’s words — the other person’s is a “speck”, our own is a “beam”. Our eyes come fitted by nature with a magnifying glass for looking at others and a reducing glass for looking at ourselves. Doing the word means swapping those two lenses back.

A truly spiritual person isn’t the one who says the most, but the one who can live it out.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Doing Is Food for the Spiritual Life
sections.html:
“Jesus said to them, ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.’” (John 4:34)

So “doing” isn’t a burden; it is nourishment for life.

sections.heading: 1. What the Lord Jesus Said by the Well
sections.html:
The background to this saying is John chapter 4. The Lord Jesus had walked all day and sat down by Jacob’s well, tired and thirsty. The disciples came back from buying food in the town and urged him, “Rabbi, eat.” But the Lord answered, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.” The disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?” And the Lord spoke the words of verse 34.

See how wonderful this scene is: because the Lord Jesus had talked with the Samaritan woman and brought a broken life to God, his weariness was gone. Obeying the Father’s will didn’t drain him; on the contrary, it fed him.

Many people think: doing the word is hard work, and obedience is a strain. But the truth is exactly the opposite — it’s not doing that makes us wither; it’s not obeying that brings us pain.

sections.heading: 2. A Picture from the Body: Unused Muscles Waste Away
sections.html:
The human body God made bears witness to spiritual principles at every turn. Modern medical research on long-term bed rest and on weightlessness in space shows the same thing: muscles left unused for a long time waste away rapidly, strength drops markedly within a few weeks, and bone is lost too for lack of load. That’s why astronauts on the space station have to spend hours exercising every day; otherwise, when they return to earth, they can hardly stand. This is “use it or lose it”.

Our spiritual lives follow the same law. Hebrews 5:14 says: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.”

The Greek for “exercised” is gymnazō, the root of our word “gymnasium”; it refers to an athlete’s repeated training. Spiritual discernment isn’t something you hear; it’s something you train.

So, just as going without food leaves us hungry, a spirit that doesn’t do the word will die. Doing the word isn’t an extra burden; doing the word is the meal we need to eat every day.

sections.heading: 3. Only by Doing Do We Know: Obedience Is the Door to Knowing God
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus said something very important: “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” (John 7:17)

Notice the order: first the desire to do it, then the knowing. The world’s order is “understand it first, then do it”; God’s order is “do it, and then you’ll understand”.

It’s like learning to swim.
