sections.heading: Introduction: Understanding the Whole Book, Yet Never Getting into the Water
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today I’d like to begin with a picture.

There was a man who badly wanted to learn to swim. He was very earnest about it. He bought six books on swimming technique and read everything from the breathing angle for freestyle to the timing of the breaststroke kick. He watched hundreds of instructional videos online, until he could even tell you the angle of an Olympic swimmer’s palm as it enters the water. Three years went by, and he knew enough to teach a course. Then one day a friend invited him to the pool. He stood at the edge and kept putting off getting in. When his friend asked him why, he said, “I don’t fully understand it yet.”

Brothers and sisters, we laugh at him, but very often we are him. We’ve read a great many spiritual books, heard a great many sermons, taken a great many notes and saved a great many Bible-verse picture cards. Our “spiritual knowledge” is rich, but our “spiritual experience” is poor. We are like that man standing at the edge of the pool: we understand the whole book, yet we’ve never got into the water.

Let me tell you something that really happened. On 17 December 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, the Wright brothers achieved humanity’s first powered, controlled, manned flight. That flight lasted only twelve seconds and covered about thirty-six metres — less than the length of a modern airliner’s fuselage. At the time, plenty of people around the world were studying flight, many of them fully trained scholars, and there were many whose theories were more thorough than the Wrights’. The Wright brothers ran a bicycle shop; they had no university degrees. But they did something others wouldn’t: they pushed their glider up the sand dunes and flew, and crashed, and flew, and crashed, again and again, then went back and made adjustments. They didn’t understand first and then fly; they flew, and then they understood.

Here’s a fact even closer to every one of us. You and I all learned to walk, yet none of us learned by first understanding the mechanics. In a study published in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, the New York University developmental psychologist Karen Adolph and her colleagues recorded a day of activity for toddlers learning to walk. They found that the children took on average about 2,368 steps an hour — and fell on average seventeen times an hour. Work it out, and a toddler may take some fourteen thousand steps and fall about a hundred times in a single day. Not once did that child stand up because they had “figured it out”; they slowly figured it out because they “stood up again.”

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what today’s lesson wants to say to us. Our natural mindset is “understand first, then do,” but the kingdom of God works by “do, and then understand.” It isn’t that we know first and then obey; it’s that we obey first, and then truly know.

Today we’ll look at four things together: first, from “understand first, then do” to “do first, then understand”; second, two lies that stop us from acting; third, not spiritualising the “doing” but making it practical; and fourth, experiencing truth and freedom in the “doing.”

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Last Days of the Feast of Booths
sections.html:
Let’s first put our theme passage back where it belongs.

The Gospel of John was written by John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. Church tradition is unanimous that he wrote this book in his later years, around AD 85 to 95, in Ephesus in Asia Minor. By then most of the first-generation apostles had been martyred, and the church was made up of second- and third-generation believers facing all kinds of early heresies. John states the purpose of his writing very clearly himself:

“but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

Notice the order in that sentence: believe → have life. John’s whole book deals with one thing — true believing always leads through to life; believing that stops in the head is not what John means by believing.

As for time and place, John chapters 7 and 8 take place in Jerusalem at the Feast of Booths. “Now the feast of the Jews, the Feast of Booths, was at hand.” (John 7:2) The Feast of Booths was the most joyful festival of the Jewish year. It lasted seven days, and every household built a booth and lived in it, remembering God’s care for their ancestors as they wandered in the wilderness. The feast had two especially important ceremonies. One was the “water-drawing ceremony”: each morning at dawn the priests drew water from the Pool of Siloam, went up to the temple in procession and poured it out on the altar, remembering the water that came from the rock. The other was the “lamp-lighting ceremony”: four huge golden lampstands were lit in the Court of the Women, and their blaze lit up all Jerusalem, remembering the pillar of fire in the wilderness.

It was right in the midst of these two ceremonies that Jesus spoke. In answer to the water-drawing, he said, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” (John 7:37) In answer to the lamp-lighting, he said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” (John 8:12) He wasn’t teaching abstract doctrine; he stood in the scenes of daily life they could see and touch every day, and declared that he himself was the reality.

Then chapter 8, verse 30 says, “As he spoke these things, many believed in him.” (John 8:30) And so we come to verse 31: “Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him …”

Brothers and sisters, take special note: the Lord Jesus didn’t say these words to those who opposed him; he said them to “those who had believed him.” In other words, what the Lord is dealing with here is precisely the problem most common among those of us who already believe — we believe, and then we stop there.

Let’s look at a few key words.

First, “remain.” The original is μένω (menō), whose basic meaning is “to dwell, to stay, to continue in.” The same word appears again and again in John 15: “Remain in me, and I in you.” (John 15:4) So the literal sense of the Lord Jesus’ words is: “If you dwell in my word.” Not dropping by for an occasional visit, but moving in to live there for good. The truth isn’t a museum you tour; it’s a home you move into.

Second, “know.” The original is γινώσκω (ginōskō), which refers to knowledge that is experiential and relational, not merely the acquiring of information. The corresponding Hebrew word is יָדַע (yada), which the Old Testament uses to describe the deepest intimacy of knowing one another. This is the knowing of “you only know once you’ve tasted it,” not the knowing of “I’ve heard about it.”

Third, “make free.” The original is ἐλευθερόω (eleutheroō), meaning “to release a slave into a free person.” The Lord Jesus immediately explains what this freedom is in the verses that follow: “everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin” (John 8:34). “If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:36)

Put these three words together, and the structure of the verse becomes very clear. The original uses a conditional sentence — “if … then …” — forming a chain of four links:

Remain in my word → truly my disciples → you will know the truth → the truth will make you free.

Brothers and sisters, these four links come in order, and you cannot skip the first. You can’t start from the second link, much less jump straight to the fourth. Today many people want the freedom of the fourth link but won’t enter the obedience of the first; they want to know the truth but won’t first dwell in the word. The result: the more knowledge, the less freedom; the more familiar the doctrine, the drier the life.

This is the mindset today’s lesson sets out to correct. The 321 vision says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The mindset we want to change today is this one sentence — it isn’t understand first, then do; it’s do, and then understand.

sections.heading: 1. From “Understand First, Then Do” to “Do First, Then Understand”
sections.html:
Our natural mindset runs in a nice straight line: I figure it out first, then I do it. It sounds so reasonable, so responsible. But the kingdom of God is exactly the opposite: you go and do it first, and only then do you truly understand.

The Lord Jesus could not have said it more clearly:

“If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:31–32)

Remaining comes first; knowing comes after. This isn’t something only said in John 8. In the chapter just before, the Lord Jesus had already laid down this principle:

“If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” (John 7:17)

Look at how that sentence is built: desire to do → will know. The Lord Jesus didn’t say, “First research thoroughly whether I come from God, and once you’ve worked it out, then obey.” What he said was: set your heart on doing it first, and you will know who I am.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, the Bible is consistent on this from beginning to end.

“If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17) — Knowing doesn’t bring the blessing; doing does.

“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) — Notice the words “deluding your own selves.” The greatest danger of hearing without doing isn’t that we fail to grow; it’s that we develop an illusion that we have already grown. That is self-deception.

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24) — The Lord Jesus doesn’t tell the wise man from the foolish by “hearing”; both of them heard. He tells them apart by “does them.”

“Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.” (Psalm 34:8) — “Taste” comes before “see.” This is the most honest dietary advice in the whole Bible: you can’t fill your stomach by reading the menu.

The difference between “knowing about” and “knowing”

There’s a cultural difference here worth noticing. The ancient Greeks asked, “What is truth?” They pursued definitions and concepts — a system that could be clearly explained. That is exactly what Pilate asked as he stood before Jesus: “What is truth?” (John 18:38) And having asked it, he turned and went out — he asked a good question but didn’t wait for the answer.

The Hebrews asked a different question. They asked, “How shall I walk in the truth?” In the Old Testament, the root of the word for “truth” (אֱמֶת, emet) is related to “firm, reliable, something you can lean on.” Truth isn’t a proposition you can hang on the wall; it’s a rock you can stand on. If you never step onto it, you’ll never know whether it can hold you.

That is why the Lord Jesus used γινώσκω — the kind of knowing that has been tasted, walked through and proven. Brothers and sisters, you can “know about” God’s faithfulness; that is Information. But when you’ve reached the end of the road and you obey, and God truly holds you up — in that moment you “know” that God is faithful; that is Revelation. What stands between Information and Revelation is a single word: doing.

Two of the most vivid footnotes in the Bible

In John 9 the Lord Jesus heals a man born blind. He spreads saliva and mud on the man’s eyes and then says:

“Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (John 9:7)

Notice that Jesus didn’t let him see first and then tell him to go and wash. He told him to go and wash first. The blind man had no idea at the time what the point of it was — mud smeared on your eyes only makes you see less. But the text says, “So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.” (John 9:7) It was on the way there, in the act of washing, that he understood.

Luke 17 is even more striking. Ten men with leprosy stood at a distance and cried out for Jesus to have mercy on them.

“When he saw them, he said to them, ‘Go and show yourselves to the priests.’ As they went, they were cleansed.” (Luke 17:14)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the timing: “As they went, they were cleansed.” They weren’t cleansed and then went; they were cleansed as they went. Under the rules of Leviticus, you went to the priest for inspection after the leprosy had healed. But the Lord Jesus wanted them to set off while they were not yet healed. If they had looked down at their skin and said, “I’ll go once I’m better,” they would never have got better as long as they lived.

This is the order of God’s kingdom: action first, understanding after; obedience first, completion after.

Corroboration from psychology: ability grows out of action

In a 1977 paper in Psychological Review, the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his well-known theory of “self-efficacy.” Self-efficacy is a person’s belief about whether “I can do it.” Bandura identified several sources of self-efficacy, and the strongest and most stable of them he called “mastery experience” — that is, actually having done the thing successfully yourself, once. Encouragement from others helps, but it is far less powerful than succeeding once yourself; imagining and rehearsing help, but they too are far less powerful than succeeding once yourself.

In other words, the conclusion modern psychology reached after decades of research is that confidence is not the precondition of action; confidence is the product of action. And the Lord Jesus said it two thousand years ago: “If you remain in my word … You will know.”

Of course, the Bible is our highest standard; psychology is only corroboration. We don’t believe the Bible because Bandura was right. Because the Bible was right all along, human research, when it gets far enough, often ends up heading in the same direction.

The Chinese understood this long ago too. The very first line of Confucius’s Analects reads: “Is it not a delight to learn, and to practise what you have learned at due times?” In the oracle-bone script, the character for “practise” pictures a young bird flapping its wings over and over. Only when you keep exercising what you have learned does the joy come. Mere “learning” without “practising” brings no “delight.”

A 321 Insight: Working it out with the brain is slow; acting from the heart is fast

The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

People who rely on the brain need to calculate everything, think it all through and eliminate every variable before they dare to move. But the most important things in life usually can’t be calculated. You can’t calculate whether a person is worth your love; you can’t calculate whether this act of obedience will cost you. So you keep calculating, stuck in the same place, and the more you calculate, the more troubled you become.

People who rely on the heart are different. They know the Lord has already spoken, so they go and do it. It isn’t that they don’t use their brains; they just don’t put the brain in front of the heart. They obey first, and then, on the road of obedience, they let God give them light. The result is that the further they walk, the gladder they become, because with every step God shows them a little more.

The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. The first link of this chain is mindset. The mindset we want to replace today is: “Once I understand, I’ll do it.” Replace it with: “I’ll do it first, and the Lord will make me understand.”

Brothers and sisters, many people are stuck not because they don’t understand, but because they haven’t begun to act. You already have enough light in your hands to take today’s step.

sections.heading: 2. Two Lies That Stop Us from Acting
sections.html:
Satan is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44). His most effective strategy isn’t to stop you believing; it’s to get you to believe and then not act. And the two lies he uses most often are these.

The first lie: “I can’t”

We hear words like these all the time: I can’t share the gospel; I can’t serve; I can’t lead a Bible study; I’m not ready yet.

They sound very humble, but very often they aren’t humility at all. They’re just pretty wrapping paper around a refusal to begin.

Look at how the Bible deals with this lie.

When Moses was called at Horeb from the flame in the bush, his first reaction was:

“Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” (Exodus 3:11)

God’s answer is fascinating. God didn’t say, “You’re very capable.” God said:

“Certainly I will be with you.” (Exodus 3:12)

Moses still wouldn’t go. He said:

“O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10)

And God said:

“Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” (Exodus 4:12)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order of God’s words: “Now therefore go” comes first; “I will be with your mouth” comes after. God didn’t say, “First I’ll give you eloquence, then you go.” The words were given on the road.

It was the same with Jeremiah.

“Then I said, ‘Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.’ But Yahweh said to me, ‘Don’t say, “I am a child;” for you must go to whomever I send you, and you must say whatever I command you.’” (Jeremiah 1:6–7)

God wouldn’t even let him say “I can’t” out loud. Because once those words became his stock phrase, they would become the verdict on his life.

Then look at the servant who received one talent. He said to his master:

“I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.” (Matthew 25:25)

He was rebuked not because he lost money, but because he did nothing at all. His problem wasn’t ability; it was mindset. He thought “not moving” was the safest option, and it turned out that “not moving” was the only option that truly failed.

Here’s the truth: if you don’t do it, you will never be able to. Ability doesn’t come first and then the doing; ability is given by God in the course of doing. This is exactly what Bandura called “mastery experience,” and exactly what Paul said:

“I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:13)

Notice that Paul doesn’t say, “I am good at everything.” He says, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” The strength is given — and it’s given to you when you move.

The second lie: “I mustn’t fail”

The second lie is more hidden: if I do it, I must do it perfectly; I mustn’t fall; I mustn’t make mistakes; nobody must see my weakness.

And the result? The result is that we don’t dare to begin.

Brothers and sisters, we need to see through something: what lies inside perfectionism is often not holiness but pride. What it really cares about isn’t God’s glory but saving its own face. What it fears isn’t offending God but being embarrassed. The 321 vision puts it precisely: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. The subject of the sentence “I mustn’t fail” is, from start to finish, “I.”

But God’s law is this: fall, get up again, and you grow; fail, add correction, and you mature.

“for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16)

Notice that the Bible doesn’t say the righteous never fall. It says the righteous fall and “rise up again.” The difference between the righteous and the wicked isn’t whether they fall but whether they get back up.

Think of Peter. That night the wind and waves were high, and the disciples were all in the boat.

“He said, ‘Come!’ Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus.” (Matthew 14:29)

Then, seeing the strong wind, he was afraid and began to sink. We often laugh at Peter for sinking. But brothers and sisters, think it through: of the twelve men in that boat, only one knew what it felt like to walk on water. The other eleven didn’t get a drop on them — and didn’t get any experience either. What’s more, as Peter sank he cried out, “Lord, save me!” (Matthew 14:30) And the text says, “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him” (Matthew 14:31).

If you never get out of the boat, you’ll never sink. But you’ll also never know what it feels like when the Lord’s hand reaches out and takes hold of you.

Paul walked this way too:

“Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 3:13–14)

Even the apostle Paul said he had not yet taken hold. If even Paul was still running, what right do we have to demand that we get it perfect the first time?

Corroboration from psychology: those who fear failure don’t dare to learn

Decades of research by the Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck distinguish two mindsets: the fixed mindset and the growth mindset. People with a fixed mindset believe ability is fixed, so every challenge becomes a verdict on “Am I good enough?” — and so they avoid challenges and fear mistakes. People with a growth mindset believe ability can be developed, so every challenge is a chance to learn, and mistakes are simply data. Dweck summed up this research in her 2006 book Mindset.

Professor Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, in a 1999 study published in Administrative Science Quarterly, showed that in teams with high “psychological safety,” members are more willing to admit mistakes and raise questions — and so those teams actually learn faster.

Brothers and sisters, the church ought to be the place with the highest psychological safety in the world. Our worth isn’t built on performance; it’s built on the cross. Since God already knows us at our very worst and still loves us, why do we still put on a show of being perfect in front of our brothers and sisters?

A 321 Insight: Satan wants you to stop at perfection; God wants you to enter the process

The 321 vision says: change isn’t completed all at once; it grows through repetition. This is exactly the often-overlooked seventh of the eight stages of changing our mindset — Repetition.

Look at the common root of these two lies. The subject of “I can’t” is I; the subject of “I mustn’t fail” is also I. Both sentences put the focus on ourselves — this is the self-centred life of the old self. 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When the focus returns to Jesus, the first question changes — no longer “Can I?” but “Does the Lord want this?”

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Letting man be man means I allow myself to be limited, to get tired, to do things badly. Letting God be God means I believe that he is the one who accomplishes this, not I. And once you let go like that, you actually dare to move.

“For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13)

Brothers and sisters, even the “willing” is something he put there. So what are you still afraid of?

sections.heading: 3. Don’t Spiritualise the “Doing” — Make It Practical
sections.html:
There’s one more obstacle, a very common one, and it comes dressed in very spiritual clothing. It’s this: waiting to be moved before acting, waiting to be quite sure before moving.

Many people say, “I’m waiting for the Holy Spirit to move me.” That sounds beyond reproach. But brothers and sisters, we need to ask ourselves an honest question: could it be that God said it long ago, and I’ve been waiting for him to say it again?

In Deuteronomy Moses left us a vitally important sentence:

“The secret things belong to Yahweh our God; but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.” (Deuteronomy 29:29)

This sentence sorts the things of life into two piles. One pile is called “the secret things” — what tomorrow will bring, whether that person will change, what lies at the end of this road. These are God’s business, and he is under no obligation to tell you in advance. The other pile is called “the things that are revealed” — what God has already clearly commanded in his word. These are our business, and the text says it very directly: “that we may do” them.

And here’s where the trouble lies. We so often use the secret things as our excuse for not doing the revealed things. God says forgive, and I say I’m waiting to be moved; God says share the gospel, and I say I’m waiting for the right moment; God says love your neighbour as yourself, and I say I’m waiting for the other person to change first.

But the following things God has long since made perfectly clear; they don’t need us to wait for some “special prompting”:

“‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ … A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Matthew 22:37, 39)

“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” (Matthew 6:14)

“Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” (Matthew 28:19)

“To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.” (James 4:17)

Brothers and sisters, James puts it heavily. To know what you should do and not do it — the Bible calls that sin, not caution.

Those who watch the wind and the clouds reap nothing

Ecclesiastes has a sentence that might almost have been written for our generation:

“He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.” (Ecclesiastes 11:4)

If a farmer in Palestine insisted on waiting until the wind was exactly right and there wasn’t a single cloud in the sky before going out to his field, he could forget about a harvest that season. The weather always has its variables; those who wait for perfect conditions end up waiting in front of an empty barn.

Our spiritual life is the same. When I’m less busy, I’ll start my devotions; when I’m in a better mood, I’ll go and apologise; when my faith is bigger, I’ll share the gospel; when I’ve read the Bible through once, I’ll start serving. The result is endless preparation and no action at all. This is called spiritual stagnation.

The word the Lord Jesus used is μένω — “remain,” dwelling within. Not now and then, not only when you feel like it, but going on doing it. Someone who lives in the word doesn’t get up each morning and decide all over again whether to live in their own house today.

The Holy Spirit’s guidance gets you moving; it doesn’t make you stop

We need to straighten out a mindset: the Holy Spirit’s guidance never tells people to stand still where they are. Open the book of Acts, and every time the Spirit guides, it comes as a verb.

“But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, ‘Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.’ He arose and went;” (Acts 8:26–27)

Notice: God gave him only a direction, not a reason. Ahead lay desert, and Philip had no idea whom he would meet. But “he arose and went.” It was on the road that he met the Ethiopian eunuch, and only then did he understand why God had sent him.

“When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them.” (Acts 16:10)

That one word, “immediately,” was the key to the gospel entering Europe.

Paul also says:

“If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)

“But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16)

The words for “walk” used here in the original both mean walking, advancing step by step in order. The Spirit’s guidance is guidance on the move, not guidance standing still. A ship moored in harbour can’t be steered; the ship has to get moving before the rudder does anything. Brothers and sisters, if you never move, it’s hard for God even to adjust your direction.

Corroboration from psychology: replace “some day” with “when exactly”

In a 1999 study published in the journal American Psychologist, the New York University psychologist Peter Gollwitzer put forward the idea of “implementation intentions.” He found that general goals (such as “I’m going to exercise more”) have a low rate of follow-through; but if the goal is written as a concrete “if … then …” plan — specifying time, place and action (for instance, “On Tuesday at seven in the morning, I’ll run for twenty minutes from my front door”) — the rate of follow-through rises markedly. A number of follow-up studies have supported this effect.

This finding fits today’s lesson perfectly. “I’m going to forgive him” is a prompting; “At twelve noon today I’m going to make that phone call” is an action. What lies between prompting and action is simply a concrete point in time.

The father of American psychology, William James, proposed a theory of emotion in 1884 holding that behaviour and emotion run both ways: action can lead feeling, not only feeling lead action. He is commonly credited with saying: we don’t sing because we’re happy; we’re happy because we sing. Brothers and sisters, this holds just as true in the spiritual life: it isn’t that we love once we have love; we go and love, and love grows.

A 321 Insight: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit and act boldly; rely on the brain and ourselves and keep hesitating

All Three Foundations of 321 come into play here.

Jesus is my role model — how did the Lord himself live? “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” (John 4:34) He didn’t wait to be moved before obeying; obeying was his daily bread.

The Bible is my standard — God’s word has already put “the things that are revealed” into our hands. Once the standard is clear, we don’t need to go looking for a feeling to endorse it.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the Holy Spirit isn’t the brake that makes you stop; he is the engine that takes you onto the road.

The Old Testament reached this conclusion long ago:

“Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.’” (1 Samuel 15:22)

What God wants isn’t how thoroughly prepared we are, but whether we’re willing to obey.

Remember what Mary said to the servants at the wedding at Cana:

“Whatever he says to you, do it.” (John 2:5)

And what Peter said on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias:

“Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.” (Luke 5:5)

“But at your word” — these four words are the turning point of the whole spiritual life. Peter’s professional judgement said there’d be no fish; his experience said you can’t catch fish in the daytime. But he placed his own reasoning under the Lord’s word. And they enclosed so many fish that their nets were close to breaking.

sections.heading: 4. Experiencing Truth and Freedom in the “Doing”
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus’ promise is a clear chain: do, and you will know the truth; the truth brings freedom.

“You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:32)

Many people long for freedom yet are unwilling to take the step of obedience. This is one of the deepest contradictions of our age.

What is freedom?

People today think freedom means “doing whatever I like.” But in the very next verses the Lord Jesus gives a different definition:

“Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin.” (John 8:34)

Brothers and sisters, a heavy smoker smokes whenever he wants to, and he looks very free — but in fact he has to smoke even when he doesn’t want to. Someone who says whatever comes into their head the moment they get angry looks very spontaneous — but in fact they can’t control themselves. Real unfreedom isn’t “being unable to do what I want”; it’s “being unable to do what I should.”

Paul describes this struggle in words that cut to the bone:

“For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.” (Romans 7:18–19)

And then he found the way out:

“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)

“If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:36)

“Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.” (Galatians 5:1)

So freedom isn’t “doing whatever I like”; freedom is “having the power to live out God’s word.” This kind of freedom can only be received in the action of obedience, never in the speculations of the mind.

Three roads you can walk today

First, forgive others, and your heart is set free.

“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” (Matthew 6:14–15)

Joseph was sold into Egypt by his own brothers and thrown into prison for a crime he didn’t commit. Years later he said to his brothers:

“As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.” (Genesis 50:20)

Notice that Joseph didn’t first understand God’s purpose and then forgive; it was in the course of obeying all along the way that he gradually came to see God’s purpose. Bitterness is a pair of handcuffs we lock on ourselves, and the key lies in the act of forgiving.

Second, serve others, and your life is opened up.

“For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45)

Many brothers and sisters discover only after they start caring for others that God has been healing them all along. Once the channel of life begins to flow outward, living water comes rushing in from upstream.

Third, share the gospel, and your faith is built up.

“that the fellowship of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus.” (Philemon 1:6)

Your faith is built up as it “becomes effective.” Every time you open your mouth to bear witness for the Lord, what you yourself believe becomes a little more real.

Practice sharpens us: an analogy from the body

The writer of Hebrews uses an analogy from the gym:

“But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” (Hebrews 5:14)

The word for “exercised” is γυμνάζω (gymnazō), the root of the English word “gymnasium,” referring to an athlete’s repeated training. Look at the cause and effect in this sentence: first “exercised,” then able “to discern good and evil.” Spiritual discernment isn’t read into you; it’s trained into you.

Even our bodies bear witness to this. Modern neuroscience has confirmed the existence of “neuroplasticity”: the brain’s neural connections are strengthened by repeated behaviour, so that well-used pathways conduct faster and more efficiently, while connections left long unused gradually weaken. In other words, God made us the kind of creatures who are changed by what we do. Every time you obey, you carve a deeper path within yourself.

That is why the Lord Jesus said:

“One who has my commandments and keeps them, that person is one who loves me. One who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and will reveal myself to him.” (John 14:21)

Keeping comes first; revealing comes after. Brothers and sisters, if God seems very far away and unreal to you, it may not be that you haven’t read enough; quite possibly you haven’t done enough.

A 321 Insight: selflessness, obedience, experiencing God

The 321 vision says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

You see, true freedom is right here. When the “I” steps aside, Christ has room to live out his own life within me. This isn’t losing yourself; it’s losing the prison that shut the self in.

“I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice that “remains” here is the very same word as “remain” in our theme verse — μένω. Dwelling in him, dwelling in his word — the result is much fruit.

This is exactly what 321 calls the 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the nine (9) fruits of the Spirit.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, notice that not one of these nine fruits can be developed alone in your room. Patience needs someone to provoke you; kindness needs someone who needs you; gentleness needs someone who contradicts you. The fruit grows in relationships, and relationships grow in action. A life like this is true victory.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s place what we’ve seen today within the overall framework of 321.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. In today’s lesson each of the three foundations holds its own position. Jesus is my role model: he himself is the one who “did first and spoke after” — he washed the disciples’ feet first and then said, “For I have given you an example” (John 13:15). The Bible is my standard: the revealed things are already written there; there’s no need to wait for new instructions. The Holy Spirit is my guide: once you’re on the road, he will lead you step by step.

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The truest test of “let Jesus be King” isn’t in our meetings; it’s in our daily living. Only if the King’s word can turn straight into action is he truly King. If his word, on reaching me, must first pass through my analysis, my feelings and my timetable, then I am the king and he is merely a consultant.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 7:21)

The Goal — establish God’s system. A system isn’t established by holding meetings; it’s walked out step by step by a group of people who are willing to act.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The four obstacles in today’s lesson are really all the same disease: the self-centred life.

“I need to understand before I do it” — I want to keep control; this is the self-centred life.

“I can’t” — I’m afraid of losing face; this is the self-centred life.

“I mustn’t fail” — I want to keep up a perfect image; this is the self-centred life.

“I’m waiting to be moved” — I want God to fit in with my rhythm; this is the self-centred life.

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. So the key to breaking through in this lesson isn’t finding a better method; it’s laying down that “I.”

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5)

“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29)

Notice the Lord’s invitation: “Take my yoke upon you.” A yoke is for working, not for hanging on the wall to look at. When the Lord says “learn from me,” he is telling you to put on the yoke and go out into the field with him. You learn it in the field; you can’t learn it standing on the edge of the field.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When you’re willing to let go of your insistence that “I must understand it first,” you hand control back to God.

The fivefold change and the four shifts of perspective

The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

Notice that the starting point is mindset. Paul says:

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

“Be transformed by the renewing of your mind” comes first; “prove what is … the will of God” comes after. It’s the same principle as today’s theme: we aren’t changed after seeing God’s will clearly; we are renewed first, and then we see it clearly.

321 also stresses: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. The “doing” of today’s lesson isn’t a call to chase results or drive ministry harder; it’s a call to start doing in our nearest relationships. The person you need to forgive today, the person you need to care for — that is your “2.”

This is precisely the 235 relationships of 321: first become a “2” with a selfless person, supporting one another; then build the “3” relationship of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and go on to become the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, if you never start doing, you’ll always be on your own. For spiritual companions aren’t dreamt up; they grow out of working together, falling together and getting up together.

Last comes the shift of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

“Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2)

“while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

From man’s perspective, “understand first, then do” is prudence; from God’s perspective, “do, and then understand” is faith.

From an earthly perspective, failure is a loss; from a heavenly perspective, failure is tuition.

From a temporary perspective, waiting a little doesn’t matter; from an eternal perspective, every delay is a missed opportunity that can never come again.

The 321 Path of Serving is: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. On this path, you have to “move” at every station to reach the next. Stop, and there is no next station.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Crossing from “Knowing” to “Doing”
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five exercises. Let’s look at them one by one and drive them deep using the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Each day, choose one thing — do it first, talk later

Stop waiting until you fully understand. Today, choose one thing God has clearly commanded and go and do it: forgive one person; care for one person; share the gospel with one person. Break the stagnation with action.

Make it concrete. Don’t write, “I’m going to care for people more”; write, “At three o’clock this afternoon I’m going to phone so-and-so.” This is what Gollwitzer called an “implementation intention,” and it’s what the psalmist said:

“I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.” (Psalm 119:60)

The focus of the eight stages here is “Implementation.” You already have the Information — you’ve heard countless sermons. Revelation has come to you too — you’ve been moved by the Holy Spirit more than once. You may even have reached “Conviction” — you know in your heart that this is right. But the chain so often breaks at the fourth link: Implementation. Today, put that link in place.

Practice 2: Allow yourself to begin imperfectly

Tell yourself: I may fall, I may do it badly, but I will begin. Let growth take the place of perfection.

This practice corresponds to the stages of “Evaluation” and “Correction.” Notice that the eight stages already leave room for failure. The path of growth God designed assumes from the very start that you’ll do things badly; he doesn’t want you never to make mistakes — he wants you, after a mistake, to be willing to evaluate and to correct.

“Indeed, who despises the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10)

Today’s small step may look small to people, but it is great in God’s eyes.

“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things.’” (Matthew 25:21)

Notice that what the master praises is “faithful,” not “perfect.”

Practice 3: Stop waiting to be moved; start responding to the truth

When you know God’s word, stop asking, “Have I been moved?” and ask instead, “When do I start doing it?” Turn procrastination into immediate obedience.

This practice corresponds to the stage of “Conviction.” Conviction means: I don’t just agree; I hand myself over. Someone who is truly convinced no longer makes feelings a precondition.

“By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went.” (Hebrews 11:8)

Look at the last sentence: he went out, not knowing where he went. The starting point of the father of faith was a departure without knowing the destination.

Practice 4: Build a rhythm of “remaining in the doing”

Don’t be zealous only now and then; do a little every day: one act of obedience a day, one action a day, building up the foundation of your spiritual life.

This practice corresponds to the stage of “Repetition.” The theme verse says “remain,” and the emphasis falls on continuing. μένω means settling in to live, not passing through.

The toddler study we mentioned earlier gives us a lovely picture: they don’t practise walking once a month; every hour they take over two thousand steps and fall seventeen times. The growth of spiritual life is the same — it doesn’t come from the zeal of one special conference but from one small act of obedience every day.

“My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)

Practice 5: Depend on the Holy Spirit in the midst of action

Before every step of action, pray first: “Lord, I am willing, but I need you.” Let yourself experience God’s leading in the course of doing.

This practice brings us back to the first of the 321 foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide. We don’t act by willpower — that would crush us; we act by the Holy Spirit — and that sets us free.

“For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” (2 Timothy 1:7)

“being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 1:6)

Finally comes the eighth of the eight stages: Multiplication. Once you’ve truly walked through it, don’t hide it away. Go and tell someone: “This week I did something I’d never have dared to do, and this is how God led me.” Your experience will become someone else’s starting point. This is the “3” of the 235 relationships — spiritual parents passing life on to spiritual children.

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10)

sections.heading: 7. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Don’t wait until you understand before you do it; do it, and you will understand.

Don’t wait until you’re perfect before you begin; begin, and you will grow.

Don’t wait until you’re moved before you act; act, and you will grow more sensitive.

Brothers and sisters, the focus isn’t on “Can I?” The focus is on “Am I willing?” When you are willing, God will teach you.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the breakthrough in spiritual life usually doesn’t lie in “understanding more” but in “beginning to act.”

We often think what we lack is light; in fact what we lack is footsteps. The light God has given us has long exceeded the measure of our obedience. The writer Goethe is commonly credited with saying: knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do. Those words could hardly fit today’s message better.

When you take the first step, God leads you to the second; when you keep on doing, the truth becomes your life.

Remember the Lord Jesus’ chain: remain in my word → truly my disciples → you will know the truth → the truth will make you free. Four links joined together, and not one can be skipped. And the only one you are responsible for is the first.

From today, stop living only in your head. Let the truth get into your footsteps.

This is what letting Jesus be King looks like in practice — whatever he says, I do; not waiting until I understand before I do it, but doing it and then letting him make me understand. When we live like this, what receives the glory isn’t our cleverness or our ability, but the Lord who spoke. May all the glory go to him.

May you, before today is over, have done one thing you didn’t dare to do this morning.

keyVerses: “Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, ‘If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’”
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus, I declare:
I will no longer stay at knowing; I will step into action.
I won’t wait for perfection; I will begin to obey.
I won’t rely on myself; I will go forward relying on the Holy Spirit.
As I do, I will understand the truth.
As I obey, I will receive freedom.
My life will move from knowing, into doing, into receiving. Amen.
practices: Each day, choose one thing — do it first, talk later
Allow yourself to begin imperfectly
Stop waiting to be moved; start responding to the truth
Build a rhythm of “remaining in the doing”
Depend on the Holy Spirit in the midst of action
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You said, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” Lord, we confess that we so often stay at knowing and refuse to step into action. We use “I don’t understand yet” as an excuse, “I can’t” as a shield, and “I haven’t been moved yet” as a reason to put things off. Please forgive us.

Lord, we also confess that the root of all this is our self-centred life. We are afraid of losing face, afraid of failing, afraid of losing control. Take away our pride and give us humble hearts, so that we let man be man and let God be God.

Holy Spirit, give us a push today. Give us a clear name, a clear time, a clear thing to do. Let us no longer watch the wind and the clouds, but rise up and act. Reveal yourself to us on the road of obedience, so that we don’t merely know about you, but truly and really know you.
Lord, we are willing. We are willing, but we need you. Strengthen us, so that we take that step today.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:31–32) Share a time when you “obeyed first and only understood afterwards.” In that situation, what truth did God let you know that you hadn’t known before?

“He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.” (Ecclesiastes 11:4) Right now, what is one thing God has clearly commanded that you keep waiting on? Say specifically on what day, at what time and towards whom you plan to begin, so your small-group members can pray for you and hold you accountable.

l144.subtitle: The Right Mindset About Doing (Part 1) — Not Understand First, Then Do, but Do, Then Understand
l144.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

sections.heading: Introduction: No Child Learns to Walk Before Walking
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me ask you to play a short video in your mind. On the living-room floor, an eleven-month-old child pulls himself up by the coffee table. He lets go, wobbles, takes one step, then a second — and then, bump, he sits down hard on the floor. Mum and Dad, close by, are laughing, clapping, filming. The child pauses for a moment, crawls back on his own, pulls himself up by the coffee table again, and walks again.

Let me ask you a question, brothers and sisters: can that child walk?

No. Not at all. His balance is all over the place, his steps are crooked, and he falls several times a minute. If we graded him on whether he can or can’t, he would score zero.

So why does he keep walking? Because he wants to walk. Because his eyes are fixed on that pair of open arms in front of him. Because there is a longing in his heart far bigger than his ability.

A team led by Karen Adolph, a developmental psychologist at New York University, published a study in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, in which they actually filmed and tracked toddlers learning to walk. Here is what they found: a toddler takes on average more than 2,300 steps an hour, and falls about seventeen times. Seventeen falls an hour. Over a day, that is dozens, even a hundred or more, failures.

But brothers and sisters, have you ever seen a child who, after falling seventeen times, sat down in the middle of the living room, hugged his knees and said, “Forget it — I’m probably not cut out for walking. Crawling is safer”?

No. Not one.

So here is the question. Every one of us got up off the floor just like that — fell our way, walked our way, into walking. So when did we start to care more about whether we can than whether we will? When did we start preferring to sit still and know a great deal, rather than stand up and take a single step?

In the last lesson we said that true “doing” is lived out from within, not performed from without. Today we want to make this even more practical. Because many brothers and sisters have already nodded, already agreed — and still haven’t acted. Why? Because there are two large stones in the heart:

The first is “I can’t.” The second is “It’s too hard.”

This morning, God’s word is going to roll both stones away with its own hand. To the first stone, the Bible answers: the key is not whether you can, but whether you do it from the heart. To the second stone, the Bible answers: his commandments are not grievous.

Brothers and sisters, the title of this lesson is “Do It from the Heart — In Love It’s Not Hard.” May God this morning lift us up from the seat of “knowing,” and walk us out the door.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Books, Three Settings, One Answer
sections.html: We have three key passages today. They have not been thrown together at random. Each stands in a real-life setting of its own, and together they answer our two stones exactly.

sections.heading: 1. 1 Timothy 1:5: A Group of People Who Could Talk Well but Lacked One Thing
sections.html:
1 Timothy is a letter from the apostle Paul’s later years. It is generally thought to have been written between AD 62 and 64, after Paul’s release from his first imprisonment in Rome. It was addressed to Timothy, Paul’s spiritual son, whom Paul had left in Ephesus to shepherd the church there.

Paul states his reason for writing very plainly in verses 3 and 4: “As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine, and not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes, rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith” (1 Timothy 1:3–4).

Brothers and sisters, notice those words: “which cause disputes.” A group of people had arisen in the Ephesian church who could talk very well. They had words, they had genealogies, they had systems, they had research. Verse 7 says they were “desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm” (1 Timothy 1:7).

It was against that background that Paul wrote verse 5: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.”

The word “goal” is the Greek τέλος (telos), meaning end point, aim, destination. Paul is saying: you have talked so much and argued so long — do you know where all of it is meant to end? In love. Not in the heights of knowledge, but in the reality of love.

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely our first stone today. The people in Ephesus did not lack ability; they had too much of it. Their problem was not a shortage of skill but a heart that was wrong. Our problem is often the opposite: our hearts are actually good, but we are trapped by the words “I’m not good enough.” Paul recalibrates the scales: what God weighs has never been your talent. It is your heart.

sections.heading: 2. 1 John 5:3: People Who Claimed to Know God but Did Not Obey
sections.html:
1 John comes from the apostle John’s later years. It is generally thought to have been written around AD 90, very likely from Ephesus itself, to the churches of the province of Asia.

At that time, false teaching had begun to appear in the church in an early form of what would later be called Gnosticism. Its defining feature was to exalt “knowing” to the skies while making light of what the body actually does. They said: salvation comes through special knowledge, and the spiritual person need not care how he lives day to day.

So in chapter 2, verse 4, John names it directly: “One who says, ‘I know him,’ and doesn’t keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth isn’t in him” (1 John 2:4).

By chapter 5, John completes the thought: “For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous” (1 John 5:3).

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to the next verse here, because it is John’s own reason: “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4).

Look carefully: the reason the commandments are “not grievous” is not that God has lowered the standard. It is that the new life born of God overcomes the world. This is the most important step in letting Scripture interpret Scripture. Some people read “not grievous” and grumble to themselves: of course it isn’t hard for you apostles. No. What John means is this: whether it is hard does not depend on how heavy the commandment is, but on which life inside you is carrying it.

sections.heading: 3. Romans 8:6: An Honest Struggle and a Thorough Answer
sections.html:
Paul wrote Romans around AD 57, while staying in Corinth near the end of his third missionary journey, to the church in Rome, which he had not yet visited in person.

Romans 7 is the most honest struggle in the whole Bible: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good” (Romans 7:18). “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24).

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that us? We know we should act, yet we can’t carry it out. We resolve a hundred times and fail a hundred and one.

Chapter 8 is the answer. First Paul states the principle: “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit” (Romans 8:5). Then he states the outcome: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6).

The word “mind” here is the Greek φρόνημα (phronēma). It does not mean an occasional thought; it means the whole orientation of one’s thinking — the steering wheel of a person’s mind. Wherever your steering wheel points, that is where your life goes.

Brothers and sisters, there is one more detail worth noticing. Between Romans 7 and Romans 8 there is an obvious turn: in chapter 7 the word “I” appears with extraordinary density; in chapter 8 the word “Spirit” appears again and again. A person full of “I” knows only wretchedness; only a person full of the Spirit has life and peace.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless. Chapter 7 is the autobiography of the self-centred life; chapter 8 is the freedom of selflessness.

Three books, three settings — and together they make today’s answer: the goal of the command is love (1 Timothy 1:5); the commandment of love is not grievous (1 John 5:3); and the secret of its not being grievous is setting the mind on the Spirit (Romans 8:6).

Brothers and sisters, now let’s walk through this one key point at a time.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Key Is Not “Can I?” but “Am I Doing It from the Heart?”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when people don’t dare to act, their reasons usually come down to three sentences: I can’t. I’m not good enough yet. I don’t know how.

Those sentences sound very humble, but hidden inside them is a wrong mindset: I must have the ability first, and only then can God use me.

But the Bible, from beginning to end, never reads that way.

At the burning bush on Horeb, Moses said to God: “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10). And how did God answer? God did not debate his eloquence with him: “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak” (Exodus 4:11–12).

When Jeremiah was called, he said: “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” And God said: “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for you must go to whomever I send you, and you must say whatever I command you” (Jeremiah 1:6–7).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? God has never once answered, “You can.” God’s answer is “Go,” together with “I am with you.”

That is why our key verse says: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).

Paul lists three things here. None has anything to do with ability; all have to do with the heart:

A pure heart means motives that are unmixed. A good conscience means no accusation within. A sincere faith means a faith that is real.

The word “sincere” deserves a pause. In Greek it is ἀνυπόκριτος (anypokritos), which literally means “unmasked.” Its root, ὑποκριτής, originally meant an actor in the ancient Greek theatre who performed wearing a mask; it later became the source of the New Testament word for “hypocrite.”

Brothers and sisters, what a vivid picture. God does not want a beautifully acted play. God wants a real face. If your face has sweat on it, dust on it, hesitation on it — that’s fine, as long as it is your real face.

So please engrave this on your heart: what God values is not a perfect action but a genuine motive.

Elsewhere Paul states this principle in no uncertain terms: “For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what you have, not according to what you don’t have” (2 Corinthians 8:12). What God accepts is “according to what you have,” not “according to what you don’t have.” God never demands from you what you do not have.

When the prophet Samuel was in Bethlehem and saw how tall and handsome Eliab was, he thought, surely this is the anointed one. But Yahweh said: “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

Man looks at the outward appearance; God looks at the heart. This verse should hang in the heart of everyone who says “I can’t.”

Let’s go back to the picture of learning to walk. Why does the child learn? Not because he could already do it, but because he wanted to learn, and he kept on walking.

Psychology offers good supporting evidence here. Carol S. Dweck, a professor of psychology at Stanford University, drew on decades of research to distinguish a “fixed mindset” from a “growth mindset.” People with a fixed mindset see ability as fixed, so they fear failure, because failure proves “I’m no good.” People with a growth mindset see ability as something that can grow, so they see failure as part of the process, are willing to try again and again, and in the end really do grow.

Another psychologist, Albert Bandura, put forward his theory of “self-efficacy” in 1977. He pointed out that the strongest source of a person’s belief that they can do something is not other people’s encouragement but “mastery experience” — their own experience of succeeding.

Brothers and sisters, please notice the order here, because it matters enormously: you don’t first have confidence and then act; you act, and then confidence grows.

You have never dared to pray aloud because you have never opened your mouth to pray. You have never dared to share the gospel because you have never shared it. You have never dared to care for someone because you have never yet taken the first step towards anyone. Confidence is not something you sit your way into; it is something you walk your way into.

There is a saying commonly attributed to Mother Teresa that puts it beautifully: we cannot do great things, only small things with great love. Brothers and sisters, God has never asked you to do great things. God simply asks you to do the small thing in front of you with a sincere heart.

I think of a sister like the one found in so many small groups. Whenever it was her turn to pray aloud, she would always lower her head and pass the turn to the person beside her. Asked why, she said, “I don’t know how to pray. I’m afraid I’ll say it wrong.” Then one time a child in the group fell ill. She couldn’t hold back; the tears came, and she managed only one sentence: “Lord, please heal him.” And she couldn’t go on. That day, the whole group wept.

Brothers and sisters, “could” she pray? By human standards she never got out one complete prayer. But that was the most powerful prayer of the day, because it came from the heart.

This is a 321 insight: rely on the heart and your heart is glad; rely on the brain and you’re left with strain.

The person relying on the brain analyses everything: Is this appropriate? What will people think? What if I get it wrong? By the end of all that analysis, they are still sitting in the same place, and their heart is more and more weary. The person relying on the heart dares to act: Lord, I can’t, but I love you, so I’ll go. When it’s done, it isn’t perfect — but the heart is open and glad.

The Bible says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The wellspring of life flows not from the brain but from the heart.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision says the focus is not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances — Jesus is the focal point. “I can’t” has its focus on self. “Others do it better than me” has its focus on others. “The timing isn’t right” has its focus on circumstances. When you move your focus back to Jesus, you’ll find that whether you can or can’t isn’t the point at all — because the one doing the work was never you in the first place.

When you act from the heart, God is pleased even if it isn’t perfect. When you rely on the brain and stay where you are, you may know a great deal, but no life will grow.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: God’s Commands Are Really Not Hard
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the second stone is “It’s too hard.”

Deep down we often carry a secret complaint: being a Christian is exhausting. You have to love people, forgive, be patient, give, serve, deal with your temper. Who can do all that?

But the Bible says: “For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous” (1 John 5:3).

The word “grievous” is the Greek βαρύς (barys), meaning “heavy, weighty, crushing.” The Lord Jesus used the same word of the Pharisees: “For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them” (Matthew 23:4).

Brothers and sisters, put the two side by side and the truth comes out: the heavy burdens were put there by the religious system, not by God.

What did the Lord Jesus himself say? “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

The yoke is easy; the burden is light. Then why do we still find it so heavy?

Because we try to do it in the flesh.

Let me give you a picture. A car has a fine engine and a full tank, but the handbrake is still on. You press the accelerator and the car does move — but the engine roars, the body shudders, the tyres smoke, and it crawls along with great effort. You wouldn’t say the car is no good. You’d say: the handbrake is still on.

Brothers and sisters, that is many people’s spiritual life. The Holy Spirit is more than enough, grace is sufficient — but the handbrake of the flesh is still pulled up. So the harder you try, the more you smoke.

The lesson gives us the most practical example of all: loving our brothers and sisters.

Let me ask you: which is easier, to love or to hate?

From the standpoint of the flesh, hatred comes more naturally. When we are hurt, our first reaction is always to strike back, to defend ourselves, to remember. Love needs to be reminded; hatred doesn’t need to be taught.

But from the standpoint of life, love is the easy one. Why? Because love walks in the light, and hatred walks in darkness.

The Bible could not be clearer: “He who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no occasion for stumbling in him. But he who hates his brother is in the darkness, and walks in the darkness, and doesn’t know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:10–11).

What is it like to walk in the dark? You can’t see clearly, you trip easily, and walking is hard work. Every step you have to feel your way; every step your heart is in your mouth.

This is not just a metaphor; it is a physiological fact. When our eyes go from a bright place into darkness, the rod cells of the retina need about twenty to thirty minutes to adapt fully. And even once adapted, in that light we can hardly tell colours apart — we see only blurred outlines. Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what a person living in hatred looks like: the world loses its colour, people become blurred shadows, and every step must be guarded.

As for “weight,” medical research offers a reminder too. In a 2009 meta-analysis published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, Y. Chida and A. Steptoe of University College London reviewed a number of prospective follow-up studies and found that anger and hostility are associated with a raised risk of coronary heart disease.

Hatred really is heavier. It weighs not only on the heart but on the body.

On the other hand, what is it like to walk in the light? Clear, peaceful, steady. “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). With light, you dare to walk; with light, you walk steadily.

So the 321 insight is this: setting the mind on the Spirit brings life and peace; setting the mind on the flesh brings death and pain.

Living in God’s word is lightness and freedom; living in the enemy’s words is burden and confusion.

In Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis has a famous piece of advice. Don’t waste time bothering whether you “love” your neighbour, he says; act as if you did. As soon as you start doing that, you will find that the love really comes.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly the teaching of this lesson. Love doesn’t wait for the feeling before it acts; love acts, and then the feeling catches up.

So please remember this sentence: what is truly hard is not obeying God; what is truly hard is leaving God and still trying to live well.

God’s way is not hard — it simply requires you to switch systems. From the system of the flesh to the system of the Spirit; from man’s viewpoint to God’s viewpoint; from the earthly and temporary to the heavenly and eternal. The 321 vision says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry, and the first step is always mindset. Change the mindset, and the road changes.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Doing Has a Cost, but It Is Full of Worth
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, I need to say something honest here. It is true that God’s commands are not hard; and it is also true that doing them always has a cost.

Not hard doesn’t mean painless. Light doesn’t mean free.

The lesson uses a very beautiful picture: a woman who is pregnant.

Is pregnancy hard? In one sense, not at all, because the life grows by itself; no mother has to teach her unborn baby how to grow a heart. Medicine tells us that the baby’s heart begins to beat around the third week after conception, without the mother having to do a thing.

But in another sense, pregnancy comes at a great cost. It takes time — about forty weeks. It means enduring discomfort — morning sickness, an aching back, sleepless nights, moving about with difficulty. And at the end comes the pain of giving birth.

The Lord Jesus himself used this picture: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her time has come. But when she has delivered the child, she doesn’t remember the anguish any more, for the joy that a human being is born into the world” (John 16:21).

Brothers and sisters, look at the order: first sorrow, then joy; first anguish, then life. And the Lord says that once the child is born, “she doesn’t remember the anguish any more.” The cost has not vanished; it has simply been covered over by the joy of new life.

The lesson maps the spiritual process onto this very clearly:

Seeing and listening are like conception. The truth has come inside.

Thinking and speaking are like the pregnancy. The truth is digested inside, meditated on, spoken out.

Doing is like giving birth. The truth comes out from within and becomes visible life.

And if we don’t do it? Everything stays inside and can never become life.

Brothers and sisters, this is a serious matter. In obstetrics, a baby long overdue is a danger to both mother and child. It is the same spiritually: when we only take in for a long time and never live it out, we can suffer a kind of “spiritual obstructed labour.” You have heard many messages, taken many notes, attended many courses, yet your heart grows heavier and number. Why? Because too much truth has built up inside that has never been brought to birth.

So please remember this: if you don’t do it, truth stays as knowledge; if you do it, truth becomes life.

The Lord Jesus said: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

A grain of wheat left in the barn is very safe, very intact — and very alone. It remains a single grain for ever. Fallen into the earth, it must go into darkness, break open, disappear — and then a whole field grows up.

The cost has never been a loss. The cost is the ticket of admission.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). The old self is self-centred and clings to itself, and the result is only one grain; the new self is selfless and lets itself go, and the result is much fruit.

Psychology offers an interesting confirmation too. In a study published in 2008 in the journal Science, Elizabeth Dunn of the University of British Columbia in Canada, Michael Norton of Harvard University and their colleagues found that people who spent money on others were happier than those who spent the same money on themselves.

This is the very opposite of the world’s arithmetic, yet entirely in keeping with the Bible. Paul says: “In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’” (Acts 20:35).

Brothers and sisters, let’s make this “cost” a little more concrete. In real life, living out God’s word usually costs three things.

First, the cost of time. The phone call you need to make to show you care will take half an hour; the person you need to keep company will take an evening.

Second, the cost of face. If you want to apologise to someone, you have to lower your head first. If you want to share the gospel, you have to be ready to be turned down. If you want to admit your weakness, you have to take off your mask first.

Third, the cost of comfort. Going along with the flesh is most comfortable; going against it is least comfortable. Yet the Bible says: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). The Chinese Union Version, following many manuscripts, reads “take up his cross daily,” and that word “daily” tells us this is not a single heroic act but a little denying of self every day.

Not one of these three is paid in vain.

So the 321 insight is this: life does not stay inside; it is lived out.

Brothers and sisters, only those willing to pay the cost will see the fruit of life.

The Bible says: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9). Those words “in due season” are for everyone who is enduring right now.

Our Lord himself walked this way: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2). It isn’t that the Lord didn’t know the pain; it’s that he saw the joy beyond the pain.
